833ec5686b989f2b000d8fab284c359068d2a2b7:
docs(distro): audit found a second COW-bypassing raw frame write -- the futex PI path

While chasing the mpv crash, audited the kernel for the anti-pattern the cleartid
bug proved harmful: resolving a user address to a physical frame and writing it
directly instead of going through the checked path.  One more instance exists.

kernel/ipc/futex.c futex_user_word_map() (lines 541-564) does pt_translate ->
pfn_to_virt and returns a kernel-mapped volatile int *word, which its callers then
write atomically:

  volatile int *word = NULL;
  futex_user_word_map(t, uaddr, &word, &pkey);     // lines 581 / 654
  ...
  __atomic_store_n(word, zero, __ATOMIC_RELEASE);  // line 668, raw frame, writes 0

Same class as the cleartid defect, and it likewise writes 0, so on a page that is
still COW-shared with another task it would zero that task's copy as well.
Verified correct in the same file: exit_robust_list() (lines 680-713) uses
copy_from_user() / copy_to_user() -- so the kernel does have the right pattern and
both faulty sites are hand-rolled.

Also clarified the semantic boundary this makes explicit: raw frame writes are
CORRECT for MAP_SHARED pages, where every task legitimately maps the same frame
and all must observe the write; only COW-private pages make them wrong.
user_resolve_leaf() handles both cases properly.

Deliberately not fixed in this commit, for two reasons.

Trigger surface is narrow: this path only performs the write for PI
(priority-inheritance) and robust futexes, while mpv, LuaJIT, tumblerd and the JVM
use ordinary futexes (FUTEX_WAIT/WAKE), which go through the read-only
futex_user_load_locked().  So it almost certainly does not explain the intermittent
crashes, which is why the fix is not being rushed.

Fixing it has a deadlock hazard: futex_user_word_map()'s callers hold mm->lock --
the function documents "Caller must hold mm->lock" -- and the correct COW break
calls handle_cow_fault() (declared in kernel/include/mm/fault.h:11); if that takes
mm->lock, invoking it in place would self-deadlock.  The fix must therefore break
COW before acquiring mm->lock, or provide a lock-free path, and it cannot borrow
the cleartid approach of swapping in copy_to_user() because an atomic store is
required here and copy_to_user() is a memcpy.

Recorded as a located, unfixed instance of the class, with the fix requirements
above.
7174580e71ee3b30b16dd6d6a2b5dbb7d49c0c66:
docs(distro): record COW break is data-preserving (guest 20/20, host-matched) -- hypothesis

Tested a hypothesis that a real gap in earlier testing had left open: the 32 MiB
canary only ever READ its region, so it never triggered a COW break, meaning
COW-break correctness had not been exercised at all.  That mattered because mpv
forks (its ytdl/osc scripts), and after a fork the PARENT's writes to inherited
pages must COW-break; a break that copies or maps a zero page would zero the
parent's page and turn pointer fields into NULL, matching the observed signature.

Probe: the parent fills a page with the pattern (i ^ 0x5A), forks, and the child
sleeps 300 ms so it stays alive and the page remains COW-shared; the parent then
writes a single byte, forcing the break, and verifies the remaining 4095 bytes.
The control round does the same fill-and-write without forking, so nothing is
COW-shared and it must be clean under any implementation, which validates the
probe itself.

  host (Linux):  cow 00000000 clean   control 00000000 clean   # 5/5
  guest (A20OS): cow 00000000 clean   control 00000000 clean   # 20/20

bad = 0 in both rounds on both systems, so the COW break is data-preserving on
A20OS and the hypothesis is excluded.

Another normal closure of a hypothesis -- deterministic minimal reproducer, host
as reference, opposite binary outcome between host and guest would have proven it
-- only this one came back negative.

Reproducer: /tmp/opencode/cowtest.c, built with
gcc -static -nostdlib -ffreestanding -fno-builtin -fno-stack-protector -no-pie,
static and libc-free so it runs on both host and guest.
97963b6b6efab6576ef393e5e49bb4df08858c7c:
docs(mm): record PROVEN -- the futex PI path corrupts a COW-shared page across processes

Used the same deterministic minimal-reproducer-plus-host-reference method that
proved the cleartid bug, and this time proved the audit's second instance before
claiming it.

Probe: the parent fills a page with the pattern (i ^ 0x5A), sets the futex word at
page offset 64 to 0 (unlocked), then forks.  The child calls
futex(FUTEX_LOCK_PI), which stores the owner TID into the word, and exits while
still holding the lock.  The parent waits and checks its own copy: the word must
still be 0 and the pattern intact.  A correct kernel breaks COW for that store, so
it lands in the child's private copy and the parent is untouched; kernel/ipc/
futex.c futex_user_word_map() instead hands out a raw frame pointer and
__atomic_store_n() writes the shared frame.

  host (Linux):  pi 00000000 clean      pi-control 00000000 clean   # 5/5
  guest (A20OS): pi 00000001 POLLUTED   pi-control 00000000 clean   # 20/20

bad = 1 is precisely the word != 0 check failing while the pattern stays intact,
so the parent's futex word was rewritten across processes.  The pi-control round,
where the child dirties the page first and genuinely breaks COW, comes back clean
on A20OS as well, so the failure point is exactly "the kernel did not break COW
for this store" -- the same localisation as the cleartid bug.  Reproduction is
deterministic at 20/20 and the host is correct throughout, so this is a second
real cross-process memory corruption bug.

That confirms the earlier audit inference.  It is still unfixed: the fix must
complete the COW break BEFORE acquiring mm->lock (calling handle_cow_fault() in
place would self-deadlock, since futex_user_word_map() runs under mm->lock), and
the store must stay atomic, so copy_to_user() is not a substitute.

Reproducer: /tmp/opencode/pitest.c (static, libc-free, runs on host and guest).
f963b6f6c224aeb01f2bd1970c47ea9d23293687:
docs(distro): record fix plan for the futex PI COW bypass, with insertion points identified

Recorded how to fix the proven PI-futex COW-bypass bug, so the next step does not
have to rediscover the layout.

Call sites: kernel/abi/linux/sys_futex.c lines 49, 51 and 63 call
futex_pi_acquire() for FUTEX_LOCK_PI / FUTEX_TRYLOCK_PI and the adjacent branch.
All of them sit BEFORE the futex engine acquires mm->lock, which is exactly where a
COW break is safe to perform.

No exported helper exists for "break COW for a write": the relevant logic lives in
user_resolve_leaf() and is static.  So that logic -- handle_demand_fault() when the
leaf is absent, handle_cow_fault() when it is present but not writable -- needs to
be factored into an exported helper and called at those three sites before entering
the engine.  Only then is futex_user_word_map() handing out a raw frame pointer
safe, because the page is private by that point.  The store must stay atomic, so
copy_to_user() remains unsuitable as a substitute.

Verification: reuse the pitest reproducer.  After the fix the guest should report
pi 00000000 clean, matching the host, exactly as the cleartid fix moved 20/20
POLLUTED to 20/20 clean.
3ff243ef7fb3033f76e7135b6571cb0b7860490f:
fix(futex): break COW before storing through the futex PI path

Fixes the bug proven by the pitest reproducer, where the PI path corrupted a
COW-shared page belonging to another task.

Root cause: futex_user_word_map() returns a pointer into the kernel linear map for
the futex word, and futex_pi_acquire() / futex_pi_release() store through it
atomically.  When the page was still COW-shared, that store landed in the frame
both tasks mapped, overwriting the other task's word: the guest showed
pi 00000001 POLLUTED in 20 of 20 runs while the host was clean in 5 of 5, and the
control round (child dirties the page first, genuinely breaking COW) was clean on
A20OS too, which localised it precisely to the missing COW break.

Fix: new exported helper user_prepare_write(task_t *t, uint64_t va) in
kernel/mm/mm.c, factored out of user_resolve_leaf()'s write branch -- it calls
handle_demand_fault() when the leaf is absent, handle_cow_fault() when it is
present but not writable, then confirms the mapping is user-writable, returning
-EFAULT otherwise.  It is declared in kernel/include/sys/usercopy.h, which also
needed a `struct task_t;` forward declaration: without it the prototype is parsed
as declaring the struct inside the parameter list and -Werror rejects the build.

It is called at the top of futex_pi_acquire()'s loop and before the lock in
futex_pi_release(), i.e. BEFORE mm->lock is taken, because the COW break must not
run while holding that lock (calling handle_cow_fault() in place would
self-deadlock -- the reason this was not a one-line copy_to_user swap; the store
must also stay atomic, so copy_to_user is not a substitute either).  Putting it in
the ABI-agnostic engine rather than the Linux ABI's sys_futex.c covers both the
Linux and Native ABIs.

Verified with the same reproducer, same image, only the kernel changed:

  before: pi 00000001 POLLUTED   pi-control 00000000 clean   # 20/20 and 20/20
  after:  pi 00000000 clean      pi-control 00000000 clean   # 20/20 and 20/20, matching the host

Residual recorded honestly: the COW break happens before the lock, so a fork() in
the narrow window between the prepare and the in-lock store could re-COW the page.
Closing that completely needs an in-lock PTE writability re-check with
unlock-and-retry, which this commit does not do.

Reproducer: /tmp/opencode/pitest.c.
192040b2149723f44132e1c1de67abd633259a45:
fix(signal): break COW before remapping the signal trampoline

The signal delivery path carried the third instance of the raw-frame/COW-bypass
class.  signal_make_page_exec() translated the trampoline page to its physical
frame, unmapped it, and re-mapped the SAME frame writable+executable so the
sigreturn trampoline can run.  The signal frame itself is written with
copy_to_user() and was therefore already safe; the defect was the remap.  When the
page was still COW-shared with another task, that handed this task a writable
alias of a frame the other task also maps, so any later write through it corrupts
the co-owner.

Fix: call user_prepare_write(t, page) before the translate, so the page is private
(COW broken if needed) and the unmap/map operate on this task's own frame.  Also
adds the sys/usercopy.h include that declaration requires.

Verification, and a correction that has to be recorded:

  - Regression probes are all clean on the fixed kernel: ctidtest 5/5 (cleartid),
    cowtest 5/5 (COW-break correctness) and pitest 5/5 (PI futex).  So this change
    does not break the COW paths those exercise.
  - But the symptom load (60x java -version + 120x mpv --vo=null) still reproduces
    the mpv/LuaJIT crash with an identical signature:
        SIGSEGV: pid=925 code=13 sepc=0x638a6320 stval=0x8
        FATAL:   pid=925 signal=11 abi=0 pc=0x638a6320 sp=0x77dbbc40 comm=lua/console path=/extra/usr/bin/mpv
    So the signal instance is NOT the cause of those intermittent crashes, and the
    speculation in the docs entry that it was the more likely candidate is
    retracted.

Status after this commit: three instances of the raw-frame COW-bypass class have
been found and all three fixed (cleartid, futex PI, signal).  The mpv / LuaJIT /
tumblerd crashes remain unexplained.
30be75de9c7be2924bf1d527bd0876192221fc8e:

Following that:

  - The library that throws is LWJGL's bundled native:
    /usr/share/a20-media/1.21.11/natives/libopenal.so in the guest image, extracted
    at runtime to /tmp/lwjgl_root/3.3.3+5/x64/.  Its NEEDED list is
      libdl.so.2 libstdc++.so.6 libm.so.6 libgcc_s.so.1 libpthread.so.0 libc.so.6 ld-linux-x86-64.so.2

    libstdc++.so.6 being in NEEDED means the C++ that throws std::system_error
    lives inside this library.
  - It loads at all because the guest ships Alpine's gcompat
    (/lib/libgcompat.so.0, plus /lib/ld-linux-x86-64.so.2, libc.so.6,
    libpthread.so.0, libdl.so.2, libm.so.6); the library imports 283 symbols from
    the glibc ABI.

gcompat" chain, not to an A20OS kernel defect.  std::system_error is the classic
shape of C++ throwing after pthread / mutex / std::thread returns an error, and
those are exactly the calls a glibc-compat layer is most likely to get subtly
wrong.

Actionable direction: use musl-built OpenAL / LWJGL natives (or point LWJGL at musl
natives), or complete gcompat's semantics on this path -- rather than more kernel
hunting.

stripped, so naming the exact function would need its .eh_frame or a
symbol-bearing build; that is not required for the gcompat conclusion.

docs(mm): record clear VMA merge aliasing -- last structural lead closed

The merge logic is in kernel/mm/vma.c, not vm.c.  vma_can_merge (line 22) requires offset
continuity only where an offset exists: file_offset + (end - start) == b->file_offset for

offset, so merging two of them cannot alias anything; the off=0x2000 on the faulting VMA is a

685d83f0b693645d05b278673f3dabd343bbbc2c:
docs(distro): record new lead -- mremap frame refcount accounting

kernel/mm/mremap.c is the one page-moving path not yet checked, and musl malloc / LuaJIT's
allocator use it for growing large blocks.  The move maps the destination to the same physical
frame as the source and then drops the source mapping, so correctness depends on whether
pt_map/pt_map_huge take a frame reference of their own.  Both candidates do frame_get(pfn)
before pt_map, which only balances if pt_map also takes a ref:

  pt_map takes a ref: 1 -> get 2 -> map 3 -> unmap src 2 -> put 1   OK
  pt_map takes none:  1 -> get 2 -> map 2 -> unmap src 1 -> put 0   freed while dst maps it

The second case frees a frame a live PTE still points at -- exactly the shape of the symptom,
where a live object's fields read back as zeros.

mm_move_mapping_pages (line 128) is marked __attribute__((unused)), so the live path is the
earlier function (lines ~60-126), whose visible tail maps the destination but does not unmap
the source.  Next: establish whether pt_map/pt_map_huge increment the frame refcount, then
check the live move function's accounting end to end.
176338dc1e71ef33a4c79685e8e65c3f621c0e78:
docs(distro): resolve the mremap lead -- frame accounting is correct

pt_map (kernel/mm/mm.c:258) does not take a reference on the new frame; it only drops the
replaced one.  With those semantics the move path balances:

  rc=1 (src) -> frame_get 2 -> pt_map(dst) 2 -> pt_unmap_leaf(src, pa=NULL) 2 -> frame_put 1

so the frame is never freed while a PTE still points at it.  The frame_get/frame_put pair
keeps the count above zero while both mappings are live, and the source mapping's reference
is consumed by the trailing frame_put.  Lead closed.

Six hypotheses are now eliminated with evidence: COW break, clone/TLS, MADV_DONTNEED,
demand-fault install, VMA merge aliasing, and mremap frame accounting.  Further reading is no
longer the way to converge; the remaining work is behavioural -- reproduce LuaJIT's own
pattern instead of generic threaded churn, which already passed cleanly.

object -- the rbx+0x118..+0x148 pattern measured earlier.

fork/COW cycles, clone/TLS by 16 threads x 200 rounds, MADV_DONTNEED, demand-fault install,

66572843476fca9c24de577e1db08fbedef6d8c1:
docs(mm): record concrete suspect -- a short read is treated as EOF in the page-cache fill

page_cache_fill_vfile_page (kernel/fs/page_cache.c:624) is the first-time fill, and its
short-read handling is the one place that manufactures zeros in a file-backed page:

  int r = vf->ops->read(vf, (char *)data, PAGE_SIZE);
  if ((size_t)r < PAGE_SIZE)
      memset((char *)data + r, 0, PAGE_SIZE - (size_t)r);

Correct at EOF, wrong for a short read in the middle of a file: the page is then marked
uptodate with its tail zeroed, and since it is uptodate from then on every later reader gets
those zeros without re-reading.  That matches the breakthrough exactly -- a zero region inside
otherwise-live content, on first access only.

To confirm and fix: check whether vf->ops->read can return below PAGE_SIZE mid-file (and
whether the vnode->ops->readpage branch shares the assumption), then make the fill loop until
the page is full or the true EOF is reached instead of zero-filling on any short count.
10d2baf70396635322ed5a298bc2c8e9832dac2b:
docs(mm): record the failed short-read loop experiment and its rollback

Hypothesis: page_cache_fill_vfile_page zero-fills the rest of the page whenever vf->ops->read
returns below PAGE_SIZE, so a short read mid-file leaves a zero tail that later readers hit
without re-reading; the fill also does lseek/read/lseek on the shared vf->offset while holding
only the per-page fill_lock, so concurrent first-time fills of different pages of one file can
interleave on it.

Applied it -- loop until the page is full or a true EOF, zero-fill only what is past EOF --
rebuilt, and booted without any page-cache warming.  The first mpv run still crashed with the
same sepc=0x638a6320 and rc=139, so the change was reverted rather than left in the tree.

The trigger really is the first file-backed read (that is what the warming experiment proves),
but this is not how it corrupts memory.  Remaining candidates are what the fill does around the
read: the page-cache frame's identity/refcount when a file page is installed into a user PTE,
and whether that frame can simultaneously be in use as an anonymous frame.
f361ffeabde679c62031a6b5a18a731d90614fa7:
docs(mm): record that concurrent cold fills corrupt anonymous memory

Third freestanding probe (filefill): hold four patterned anonymous regions, then mmap mpv /
libluajit / libc / ffmpeg and touch one byte per page so every page takes a real first-time
page-cache fill, re-verifying all four anonymous regions after every touch.

  filefill files=0x3  pages_touched=0x386 (902 cold pages)  bad_anon=0x0

All three mpv commands also returned rc=0 in that boot -- not from any fix, but because the
probe incidentally warmed the page cache.  Third independent confirmation that warming removes
the crash.

So cold file fills by themselves do not disturb live anonymous memory.  What the probe does not
do that mpv does: fault those pages from several threads at once, and execute from them.  The
former is the stronger candidate and matches the code -- page_cache_fill_vfile_page does
lseek/read/lseek on the shared vf->offset holding only the per-page fill_lock, so two threads
filling different pages of the same file interleave on that offset and can fill a page from the
wrong file position.

Next probe: N threads faulting disjoint page ranges of one file concurrently while the main
thread verifies the anonymous patterns, and also verify the file contents read back against a
known-good copy, since a wrong-offset fill corrupts the file page rather than the anonymous one.
816e40504f0846898be861425796a6c8f2614e70:
docs(mm): identify missing offset locking in the page-cache fill path

grep offset_lock shows the lock is taken only in the syscall layer
(kernel/abi/linux/sys_fs.c -- read/pread/lseek) and never inside the vfile
ops->read / ops->lseek implementations.  page_cache_fill_vfile_page calls those ops directly,
so the shared vf->offset is manipulated with no lock at all:

  A: lseek(page1)  B: lseek(page2)  A: read -> gets page2's bytes  B: read -> page2 again

Two threads filling different pages of the same file concurrently therefore fill a page from the
wrong file position.  This fits every measured fact: first access only (an uptodate page is
never refilled, so warm runs never race); threaded programs only (a single-threaded fill cannot
interleave); and the corrupted thing is the file page rather than the anonymous one -- which is
why the filefill probe reported bad_anon=0 while mpv still crashed.

Fix direction: serialise the fill's offset manipulation per vfile, but not by taking
vf->offset_lock directly -- a page fault inside a read() syscall would re-enter and deadlock on
that same non-recursive mutex (sys_fs.c:164 warns about exactly this re-entry).  Either add a
dedicated per-vfile fill mutex or give the fill a positional read so it never touches the shared
offset.
5b01d3425bc772d90cdb25a35bd850bed956d85b:
docs(mm): record the fix recipe for the unserialised page-cache fill

The codebase already solves this one layer down: kernel/fs/block_cache.c serialises its own
fills with a striped lock array

  mutex_t *fill_lock = &bc->fill_locks[pcache_hash_key(page_no) & (PCACHE_FILL_LOCKS - 1)];
  mutex_init(&bc->fill_locks[i]);   /* at block-cache init */

with mutex_init/mutex_lock/mutex_unlock/mutex_trylock as the API (no static-initialiser macro
exists, so the array must be initialised at module init).

Apply the same shape to the vfile page cache so the fill's offset manipulation is serialised:
add a small striped mutex array in page_cache.c initialised at page-cache init, take it around
the whole lseek(page_base) -> read -> lseek(saved) sequence in page_cache_fill_vfile_page, and
do not use vf->offset_lock for this (a page fault inside a read() syscall re-enters and would
deadlock on that non-recursive mutex; sys_fs.c:164 documents the re-entry).  Keep
page->fill_lock as-is: it serialises the same page, the new lock serialises the shared offset
across different pages of one file.

Acceptance test with no page-cache warming anywhere in the harness: all three mpv commands
rc=0 and no lua-thread SIGSEGV, with tlstest/forktest/mmapchurn/filefill still running first so
any regression in their counters is caught.
1f32c959af06e497a0e20e11658db0506fc89d23:
fix(page_cache): serialize vfile fill offset access

page_cache_fill_vfile_page drives the filesystem through vf->ops->lseek and
vf->ops->read directly.  The syscall layer protects that shared vf->offset with
vf->offset_lock, but the fill path took no lock at all, so two threads filling
different pages of the same file interleaved:

  A: lseek(page1)  B: lseek(page2)  A: read -> gets page2's bytes  B: read -> page2 again

A page could therefore be filled from the wrong file position and then marked
uptodate, so the corruption was permanent and only ever appeared on the first
access to a file -- later runs found the pages cached and never raced.

Symptoms this fixes: mpv's LuaJIT threads (and tumblerd) dying on a NULL link
pointer, with a zero hole inside an otherwise-live object, on the first run after
boot.  Reproduced every boot; gone now.

Fills are striped by vfile pointer so every page of one file takes the same lock.
vf->offset_lock is deliberately not reused: a fault taken inside a read() syscall
re-enters this path and would deadlock on that non-recursive mutex (documented at
sys_fs.c:164).

Verified with no page-cache warming anywhere in the harness: the first mpv run
(which crashed on every boot before) now returns 0, all three reproducer commands
return 0, and the kernel log contains no SIGSEGV/FATAL at all.  The four stress
probes still report zero failure counters.

0f697ac6c54a92f1994f9762f3cb8965411908dd:
docs(network): record the pbuf double-free panic on first traffic

Recorded in docs/distro/network-pbuf-double-free.md.

Before any traffic the stack is fully configured: lwIP initialises with IPv4/IPv6/TCP/UDP/RAW/
ICMP/DHCP/DNS, virtio-net loads and binds (mac 52:54:00:12:34:56), the netif attaches as en2
with ip=10.0.2.15 gw=10.0.2.2 dns_count=1, and the guest's /etc/resolv.conf names 10.0.2.3.

But the first connection attempt (wget to a raw IP, no DNS) panics:

  lwIP assertion failed: pbuf_free: p->ref > 0
  [0] pbuf_free+0x194
  [1] etharp_input+0x415
  [2] ethernet_input+0x2f2
  [3] a20_lwip_process_netif_rx_tx_locked+0x154
  [5] driver_irq_dispatch+0x463

A pbuf whose refcount already reached 0 is freed again -- a double free of a received pbuf,
in the inbound ARP path.  It fires on the first packet, so every higher-level symptom
(including Minecraft's UnknownHostException) sits on top of it.

Next: read the RX hand-off in a20_lwip_process_netif_rx_tx_locked and the virtio-net receive
path, and check whether the pbuf is freed by both the driver side and lwIP's input chain (which
consumes and frees it).  Note the backtrace below etharp_input is unreliable
(ethernet_output+0x13f200867 is nonsense), so confirm the order rather than assuming it.

Also noted: ip addr show fails (AF_NETLINK not supported) and ifconfig fails
(ioctl 0x8912, No such device) -- not the cause, but they make in-guest network debugging hard.
6b20e12f6c95b4e78adc96b5f6d2eda4cc5ddc62:
docs(net): narrow the pbuf double free to the RX loop, and why not to guess the fix

The receive loop is a20_lwip_process_netif_rx_tx_locked (kernel/net/lwip_stack.c:325-342).
n->input is ethernet_input (registered line 234); line 339 frees the pbuf when input returns
non-OK.

That looks like a double free, but it follows lwIP's documented contract -- upstream's own
ethernetif_input() is written exactly this way.  The contract is only sound if ethernet_input
never consumes the pbuf before returning an error, and it propagates its inner error on some
paths (the IPv4 path returns what ip4_input returned), while ip4_input can free or queue the
pbuf before returning non-OK.  If so, line 339 frees an already-freed pbuf, the pool pbuf lands
with ref == 0, and a later pbuf_free -- etharp_input's own -- trips p->ref > 0.

Two candidate ownership models with different fixes, so do not guess: instrument the loop
(log p, p->ref, the return value) and the panic site (ref/next/tot_len), then re-run the raw-IP
wget.  That distinguishes "freed twice by this loop" from "freed once here and once in lwIP".
e7d2bb95232c824a4b759a8c4a6d7b91967de489:
docs(distro): resolve the ownership question -- line 339 is dead code, the double

Reading the vendored lwIP (kernel/external/lwip/src/netif/ethernet.c) settles the ownership
question: every one of ethernet_input's 12 exit paths returns ERR_OK, including
free_and_return (which pbuf_free()s first), and the normal exit carries lwIP's own note that
"the pbuf is freed or consumed, so the caller doesn't have to free it again".

So n->input(p, n) != ERR_OK is never true in the RX loop and line 339 is dead code, not a
double free.  The obvious "fix" of deleting that pbuf_free would have changed nothing.

The assertion therefore fires inside etharp_input's own final pbuf_free, meaning p->ref was
already 0 when the packet reached it -- the pbuf was freed while still in use, before that
point.  Nothing between pbuf_alloc (ref = 1) and ethernet_input decrements a reference, so the
damage is earlier than this packet: either the pbuf pool free list already holds a frame twice,
or the RX path runs from two contexts at once.  The panic ran in IRQ context on pid=0 idle, and
a20_lwip_process_netif_rx_tx_locked has two call sites (lines 369 and 387), so the locking
contract is the first thing to check.
5d6ff422531be97706460b9c0677d16119ffa477:
docs(distro): record the lead -- a single device's IRQ polls every device

a20_lwip_process_netif_irq_locked (kernel/net/lwip_stack.c:346-373) says in its comment that it
is the IRQ top-half entry "for a single virtio-net instance", but its body polls every device:

  for (int i = 0; i < A20_NET_MAX_DEVS; i++) {
      a20_lwip_netif_state_t *st = &g_netif_state[i];
      if (st->dev && st->ops && st->ops->poll)
          st->ops->poll(st->dev);
  }

and only then drains the target netif with a20_lwip_process_netif_rx_tx_locked() -- the same
drainer a20_lwip_poll_locked() runs over the whole netif list (line 387).  So there are two
independent ways to consume the same device's receive work.

g_lwip_lock is taken with spin_lock_irqsave, so on this single-CPU image the IRQ cannot interleave
inside the poll path; what matters is whether a device is polled and its frames delivered twice
for the same packet, in either order, so the pbuf reaches lwIP one time too many.

Next: read st->ops->poll() for virtio-net and confirm whether it also delivers received frames
into lwIP (the IRQ path calls it on every device).  If it does, the following drainer re-delivers
frames already consumed, and the fix is to make the IRQ path touch only its own device -- not to
change any pbuf handling.
73bec18bb39651b637363177dce72655ec9f4735:
fix(net): stop double-freeing pbufs after the UDP and raw send calls

lwIP's udp_sendto/udp_send (udp.c: pbuf_free at 371/407/425/428/440) and
raw_sendto/raw_send (raw.c: raw_sendto_if_src frees at 75/113) take ownership of the
pbuf and free it on every path, including error.  socket_inet.c freed it again after
those calls, so every UDP and raw send freed the same pbuf twice.  That corrupted the
pbuf pool, and the damage surfaced later as a lwIP assertion on an unrelated receive:

  lwIP assertion failed: pbuf_free: p->ref > 0
    [0] pbuf_free+0x194
    [1] etharp_input+0x415
    [2] ethernet_input+0x2f2
    [3] a20_lwip_process_netif_rx_tx_locked+0x154

which fired on the first connection attempt, so no networking worked at all.

Only the branch where lwIP was never called (no destination, not connected) still frees
the pbuf, which is why the surviving pbuf_free below is correct.

Verified: PANIC count 0 for the whole boot; wget to a raw IP now reaches TCP and reports
"Connection refused" from the QEMU gateway (i.e. ARP and the TCP handshake both work),
where it panicked at the ARP stage before.

Note this was reachable only because the earlier page-cache fix (36c14858) stopped the
first-run corruption that had been masking it.
732fa188d92fef95520c557cb338574b760e2927:

ffcfeefc3ee2d1fd3e31811a6355d321a44478a7:
fix(riscv64): resolve unused and undeclared symbol build errors

1. kernel/core/trap.c: dump_user_object was only *called* from the FAULT-BX block,
   which I had guarded with #if defined(__x86_64__), but the helper itself was left
   defined unconditionally.  On every other arch that is an unused static function,
   and -Werror=unused-function breaks the build:

     kernel/core/trap.c:70:13: error: 'dump_user_object' defined but not used
     make: *** [tools/targets-images.mk:181: .../core/trap.o] Error 1

   The helper is now guarded by the same #if defined(__x86_64__) as its call site.
   This is my regression, introduced with the SIGSEGV instrumentation.

2. kernel/drivers/bus/pci_bus.c: PHYS_MAP_LIMIT is defined only in
   kernel/arch/x86_64/include/platform.h, but the 64-bit-BAR relocation from
   568cf392 uses it under CONFIG_PCI_MMIO_ALLOC, which riscv64 also enables:

     kernel/drivers/bus/pci_bus.c:280:45: error: 'PHYS_MAP_LIMIT' undeclared

   Not my change (568cf392 is the "relocate a BAR placed above the 4 GiB direct map"
   commit) but it breaks every non-x86_64 arch.  The relocation exists only because
   x86_64's higher-half direct map covers just the first 4 GiB, so other arches get
   a "no address can reach this" fallback and relocate nothing, leaving x86_64
   behaviour untouched.

Verified: riscv64 and x86_64 both build clean.

aed34a7c7d7e41f2776c8d49c72ea79f608f88bc:
fix(chess): prevent crashes, correct search results, and reduce engine size

The AI and game state had memory-safety and correctness defects that made
the program unusable past a few dozen plies.

Memory safety / game loop (the reported SIGSEGV):
- MAX_UNDO was 64, but a game easily passes 64 plies.  record_move wrote
  move_notation[64], which is the notation_count field, so notation_count
  became ~14000 and the next write went through a wild pointer -- matching
  the fault (an sb of 'K' just above the stack).  make_move overflowed
  history[], corrupting history_len and the capture arrays, so unmake_move
  restored empty squares: the "pieces disappeared" symptom.  Raise MAX_UNDO
  to 1024 and bounds-check make_move/record_move.
- unmake_move never decremented the capture counters, so search inflated
  them without bound; undo now rolls back notation_count as well.

Search correctness:
- Zobrist was effectively unused: the child key was only key ^ zobrist_side,
  so every node shared a key and the TT returned unrelated scores.  Maintain
  g->hash incrementally in make_move (pieces, captures, castle, promotions,
  ep, side) and restore it from Move.prev_hash, then probe/store by g->hash.
- king_safety looked for the pawn shield one row behind the king.
- Drop the broken IID (re-probed a depth the search may not have written) and
  the non-verified LMR, keeping TT, PVS, null move and quiescence.

Performance:
- copy_position copies board+state only, not the 1024-entry history that the
  search duplicated at every node.
- mobility uses pseudo-legal counts instead of two full gen_legal passes.

Readability:
- add_move / castle_legal / rook_right / note_capture / piece_key factor the
  boilerplate out; gen_pseudo_legal shrinks from ~320 to ~85 lines and
  make/unmake from ~100 to ~60.  is_attacked uses direction tables.  A single
  compute_mobility_threats pass replaces the duplicated threat loop.  Net
  -330 lines, comments kept to the non-obvious spots.

Verified with perft (startpos 1-4, kiwipete 1-3, an ep/promotion position),
mate-in-N searches, ASAN/UBSAN random-game round-trips, and hash==compute_hash
assertions after every make/unmake.

c272ad909e7d5735bc7f9440938880a548043217:
feat(procfs): expose /proc/<pid>/exe and /cwd as magic symlinks

Linux serves both as magic symlinks, and musl's dynamic linker depends on
that: fixup_rpath() readlinks /proc/self/exe to expand $ORIGIN in DT_RPATH
and silently gives up when the readlink fails.  A20OS served them as regular
files, so Alpine's openjdk could not resolve its "$ORIGIN:$ORIGIN/../lib"
rpath and the launcher died with

  Error loading shared library libjli.so: No such file or directory

Mark the PF_PID_EXE and PF_PID_CWD vnodes as magic symlinks and answer

built-in scripts off does not stop it either.  Since a JVM is threaded too,
this is more fundamental for Minecraft than the GL work, so record the
evidence in known-issues.md.

0b2319a82866f2b73fc5ee7450b0fa7e109ddfc5:
fix(x86_64): size RAM from the multiboot memory map

that single range, so with -m 2G the kernel still managed only 262144 frames
(~1000 MB) -- which is what starved the JVM's heap ergonomics.

_start now saves the multiboot magic (EAX) and info pointer (EBX) into .data
before the BSS clear, and firmware.c parses the memory map: it takes the
available (type 1) regions, drops everything below the low 1 MiB (IVT/BDA and
the legacy hole), rounds to pages, and clips at the 2 GiB window that entry.S
directly maps with 1 GiB pages.  If the map is missing or empty it falls back
to the old 1 GiB range, so nothing regresses.

[PFA] total_frames=523993 (was 262144), Buddy+Slab 2020 MB free.  The desktop

f10da6ff48b44e56a6c177719380cee05804fdb3:
feat(fs): expose the DRM device's PCI identity for libdrm

Mesa's GBM backend calls libdrm's drmGetDevice2(), which refuses to
report a device it cannot classify.  This adds the sysfs nodes that
libdrm reads, so the DRM device is identified instead of being dropped.

Disassembling the guest's actual libdrm (2.4.131) showed it:

  - stats /sys/dev/char/<maj>:<min>/device/drm before anything else,
    and returns -EINVAL if that fails;
  - classifies by readlink()ing "<device>/subsystem" and matching the
    target against /pci, /usb, /platform, /spi, /host1x, /virtio,
    /faux (the two subsystem links must differ: the device-level one
    selects the virtio branch, the parent one confirms);
  - reads revision, vendor, device, subsystem_vendor, subsystem_device,
    plus uevent's PCI_SLOT_NAME and config, from the device directory.

What this adds, purely additively under the existing char-device nodes:

  - /sys/dev/char/<maj>:<min>/subsystem and .../device/subsystem as
    symlinks with the distinct targets above;
  - .../device/{revision,vendor,device,subsystem_vendor,subsystem_device},
    .../device/config (PCI config header) and .../device/uevent;
  - .../device/drm/{card0,renderD128}.

sysfs_devchar_name() also learns the DRM render node (226:128), which
was previously unresolvable; without it the render node had no sysfs
entry at all.

Verified in the guest: every node reads back correctly, the desktop
(labwc + xfwm4 + panel + thunar) brings up with no regression and no
panic/UBSAN, and a lookup trace confirms libdrm now walks the whole
identity instead of bailing out.

Still open: gbm_create_device() still fails ("DRI2: failed to create
gbm device") and Mesa still warns "failed to retrieve device
information".  The likely remaining gap is that the guest's device path
does not carry the virtio/PCI hierarchy that on Linux is
/sys/devices/pci0000:00/<bdf>/virtio0, so the parent lookup and the
PCI_SLOT_NAME derivation do not resolve as they do upstream; see
docs/graphics/3d-graphics.md section 9.

0508e58aa593bec3e380e00ac32e62fe9d56627a:
fix(sysfs): point DRM subsystem links to /sys/bus/PCI

Both links now read /sys/bus/pci.  Mesa's loader_get_pci_id_for_fd()
rejects any device whose libdrm bus type is not DRM_BUS_PCI, and libdrm
derives that type from this link's target string, so /sys/bus/pci is the
conservative choice; the comment records the constraint so it is not
"corrected" back to /sys/bus/virtio later.

Evidence, measured rather than assumed: switching the target between
/sys/bus/pci and /sys/bus/virtio leaves libdrm's read sequence byte-for-
byte identical, so this is a deliberate choice on Mesa's contract, not
an observed fix.

A finer trace (lookup + open + read on the attribute files) pinned the
real behaviour: during eglinfo -p gbm, libdrm operates on the render node
(226:128), reads uevent (86 bytes) and then opens and reads exactly four
attributes -- vendor, device, subsystem_vendor, subsystem_device -- all
of which return their values correctly.  It never opens revision (index
0) and never opens config.  So the flow stalls after those four reads,
not at any node this kernel fails to serve.

ClassNotFoundException for the main class, but the classpath is fine: the
class is in the jar.  Running with client.jar alone as the classpath

reading the jar.

  ADE/ALE: pid=165 sepc=0x418739a0 stval=0xc code=1
  [ERR] a3=0x8080808080808080

On x86_64 ordinary unaligned access does not trap (only alignment-
requiring instructions like movdqa do), and these repeat, so the kernel's
handling of the alignment exception is wrong.  The JVM therefore cannot
read the jar, which is why the class is "missing".  This is a kernel bug,
not a Minecraft or image-configuration problem.

Second and independent: booting with 3G instead of 2G panics during early

42ca1a8e82d5b82c35cfbf8a7313cd0d41ea0e18:
fix(pci): relocate BARs above the 4 GiB direct map

With 3 GiB RAM the QEMU q35 host bridge assigns the virtio-gpu's 64-bit
BAR to 0xc000000000 (above the 4 GiB that boot_pdpt_hh in entry.S maps).
pci_assign_bars trusted the firmware address and arch_pci_bar_to_resource
turned it into an unreachable address, so the first pci_virtio_write32
during early-boot driver probing page-faulted and the kernel panicked.

The fix relocates any non-I/O BAR whose address is at or above
PHYS_MAP_LIMIT (4 GiB, the direct-map top) into the covered 32-bit MMIO
window, exactly as an unassigned BAR is handled.  It only fires for
addresses the kernel cannot reach, so the existing 2 GiB behaviour is
unchanged.

Verified: a 3 GiB boot no longer panics and the desktop comes up; the
virtio-gpu is then used at a covered address.  RAM is still capped at 2
GiB by the memory-map clip, which is a separate, already-documented
limit.
4e0db56dc45a5efac38ebd3706ad3c505e710e05:
fix(signal): align signal-handler stacks to the SysV ABI

The delivery path built the rt signal frame on a 16-aligned boundary
(`sp &= ~15`) and jumped to the handler with rsp equal to that frame base,
so the handler was entered with rsp ≡ 0 (mod 16).  The x86_64 SysV ABI
requires a function to be entered with rsp ≡ 8 (mod 16) -- as if reached
through a call that pushed an 8-byte return address.  Compiler-generated
handler prologues assume this and align the frame for SSE accordingly, so
any SSE-using handler (musl/HotSpot code doing `movaps [rsp+X], xmmN`)
took a #GP on a misaligned stack.  Because the faulting instruction is in
the handler itself, the kernel redelivered SIGSEGV, pushed another frame,
and looped until the stack was exhausted.

This was the fault behind the JVM's `ADE/ALE ... stval=0xc code=1` storm
(code=1 is #GP, and stval there is stale CR2, a red herring): the JVM's
SIGSEGV handler could not even start.  It is also a plausible contributor
to the intermittent x86_64 userspace crashes.

The fix keeps the frame base 16-aligned (the embedded fxsave64 area must
stay 16-aligned), but enters the handler 8 bytes lower and places the
sigreturn-trampoline return address there for the handler's final `ret`.
The dedicated trampoline page drops its now-unneeded `pushq %rax` (the RET
already leaves rsp at the frame base).  The behaviour is x86_64-specific
via the new `arch_signal_handler_sp()` hook; other arches keep the frame
base as the entry sp.

Verified: the JVM jar-read no longer loops (0 ADE/ALE), its SIGSEGV
handler now runs and prints a clean fatal-error report, and the XFCE
desktop comes up with no component SIGSEGV and no kernel panic.
1c80df6d027cddc4b74b2f6ecf5ace362ae60dac:
docs(minecraft): correct the Minecraft/JVM fault diagnosis, record the two kernel fixes

minecraft.md claimed the JVM jar-read fault was an alignment exception (#AC)
handled wrongly by the kernel.  It is not: `code=1` is CAUSE_INSN_FAULT,
which on x86_64 is produced only by #GP, and the recorded `stval=0xc` is
stale CR2 (a #GP does not write CR2) -- a red herring.  The real cause was
that the kernel entered x86_64 signal handlers with rsp ≡ 0 (mod 16) while
the SysV ABI requires ≡ 8, so SSE-using handlers #GP'd in their own
prologues (`movaps [rsp+X], xmm0`) and the kernel redelivered forever.

Both bugs blocking the launch are now fixed and recorded:
  - 568cf392 (3G boot panic: a firmware BAR above the 4 GiB direct map)
  - 68abf68f (signal handler entry misalignment)

After the signal fix the JVM runs its SIGSEGV handler correctly and the
real remaining crash surfaces: it aborts at pc=0 while hashing (SHA-384)
the jar manifest, and hs_err reports a bad uc->uc_mcontext.fpregs -- the
A20OS ucontext embeds fpu[] where Linux carries an fpregs pointer, so the
layout does not match glibc/musl and programs that read the ucontext (the
JVM's implicit null checks, crash reporting) misread it.  Documented as
the next step; the "multi-threaded anonymous memory corruption" entry is
annotated with the new evidence.
4981b33c94f6606ddf01c189e7c9c346f0157764:
fix(signal): match the Linux and musl ucontext layout

A signal handler inspects its ucontext through its own libc headers, but
A20OS's rt_ucontext did not match the x86_64 ABI: uc_sigmask preceded
uc_mcontext, the mcontext used a private register order, and the FPU state
was embedded directly instead of being pointed at by `fpregs`.

Programs that read the ucontext (HotSpot's implicit null checks and its
crash reporter) therefore read every field at the wrong offset.  hs_err
logged `bad uc->uc_mcontext.fpregs: 0x0`, its "Problematic frame" printing
kept faulting, and the JVM reported `RIP=0` for a fault that was really in
JIT-compiled code.  At best that turns an implicit null check into a crash;
at worst it corrupts the context the handler acts on.

Match musl's <sys/ucontext.h> exactly:
  - mcontext_t becomes { gregs[23]; fpregs; __reserved1[8] } with gregs in
    REG_R8..REG_CR2 order (RIP at gregs[16], RSP at gregs[15]);
  - uc_mcontext moves before uc_sigmask, and __fpregs_mem[64] holds the
    fxsave64 image, referenced by uc_mcontext.fpregs;
  - build/restore_mcontext map registers in the ABI order and fxsave to /
    fxrstor from the fpstate at X86_SIGCTX_FPSTATE_OFF.

The frame base stays 16-aligned so the fpstate is 16-aligned for
fxsave64/fxrstor64 (fxsave requires 16, not 64).  fpregs must hold the
*user* address of the fpstate -- the frame is copied to user memory, so a
kernel-side address would be wrong; arch_signal_prepare_frame derives it
from the trampoline, which lives in that frame.  _Static_asserts pin the
offsets (uc_mcontext at 40, sizeof(ucontext_t) == 816, mcontext == 256).

Verified: hs_err no longer reports `bad uc->uc_mcontext.fpregs`, no
"error occurred during error reporting" self-faults, and it identifies the
faulting frame correctly (previously RIP=0).  Desktop boots with no
component SIGSEGV and no kernel panic.  The JVM's own crash now shows what
it always was: a genuine NULL deref in C2-compiled SHA5.implCompress0.
5ee93eef887712046c652802d395e75b59461b40:
fix(signal): report Linux si_code and si_addr for synchronous SIGSEGV and SIGBUS

A synchronous fault always reached the handler as si_code = SI_KERNEL with
si_addr left at 0.  Linux reports SEGV_MAPERR (or SEGV_ACCERR) in si_code
and the faulting address in si_addr; consumers key off both -- HotSpot
decides whether a SIGSEGV is an implicit null check (array/field accesses
rely on the fault rather than an explicit compare) from them.

Populate si_addr from the faulting address (TRAP_CTX_KScratch0, i.e. CR2 on
x86_64) and use SEGV_MAPERR for SIGSEGV/SIGBUS when no richer siginfo was
queued.  Other signals keep the existing SI_KERNEL path.

Verified no regression (desktop boots, no component SIGSEGV, no kernel
panic).  Note: this alone does not fix the remaining JVM crash -- its
implicit null check still fails on an array access -- so the cause is
elsewhere (see docs/distro/minecraft.md).
793b82101682270b55eeabfaa9d0533d799e3915:
fix(minecraft): set the launcher classpath and apply A20OS compatibility workarounds

classpath.txt is a single colon-separated line (no newlines), but the
launcher rewrote it with `sed 's|^.*/libraries/|...|'`: the greedy `^.*`
matched up to the last `/libraries/` in the whole line, collapsing the
classpath to one entry.  It then appended client.jar directly to the
(colon-less) result, so client.jar was never actually on the classpath --
producing `ClassNotFoundException: net.minecraft.client.main.Main`.  Rewrite
per entry (`[^:]*`) and normalise a trailing colon.

  - -Dos.name=Linux: LWJGL/Minecraft reject the platform name "A20OS".

53afaf959ca65b8618bdc02501b95fcd581fbbbe:
refactor(net): split stream writes larger than one queued message

A bound AF_UNIX socket (e.g. Xwayland's /tmp/.X11-unix/X0, which a client
connects to) is not channel-backed, so it takes the legacy queue path:
net_enqueue_msg_locked_fds -> net_enqueue_msg_locked_meta, which rejects
len > NET_MAX_PAYLOAD (65535) with EMSGSIZE because each net_msg_t carries
a fixed 64 KiB buffer.  Linux fragments a large stream write into several
skbs instead.

An X11 client that writes a request bigger than 64 KiB -- which Minecraft's
GLFW/Xlib does at window creation -- therefore died with
`XIO: fatal IO error 90 (Message too large) on X server ":0"`.

Split a stream write into NET_MAX_PAYLOAD-sized messages in the AF_UNIX
send path; the reader consumes them as the same byte stream, so no receive
change is needed.  SCM_RIGHTS fds ride on the final chunk (they were
already attached to the tail message).

Verified: with this, the Minecraft launcher gets past window creation (the
XIO/EMSGSIZE is gone) and on to the network/auth phase; desktop unchanged,
no component SIGSEGV, no kernel panic.

name plus a 16-byte union; the address ioctls fill a sockaddr (family +
packed bytes).  A20OS names its lwIP netif "en0" while users see "net0"/

e3d83934d370b331e64622748ceeff727b78f591:
feat(net): implement AF_PACKET raw L2 sockets so udhcpc can run DHCP

After the SIOCGIF* ioctls landed (8a66c9a4), udhcpc got as far as needing a
packet socket: socket(AF_PACKET, SOCK_DGRAM, htons(ETH_P_IP)) returned
EAFNOSUPPORT, so no standard DHCP client (or ifconfig/ip) could bring the
interface up.

Add AF_PACKET with the two types udhcpc uses:

* SOCK_DGRAM -- bind to sockaddr_ll gives the ifindex and ETH_P_* filter;
  send() builds the 14-byte Ethernet header from the bind/sendto address and
  the interface MAC; recv() strips it and reports the address in sockaddr_ll.
* SOCK_RAW -- carries the full frame both ways, gated on CAP_NET_RAW as on
  Linux.

TX is synchronous, straight to the netif's device send op.  RX cannot be:
lwip_stack.c captures frames holding g_lwip_lock, and that lock is never held
together with g_net_lock (LWIP_NO_THREAD_PROGRESS_CONTRACT), so captures go
into a small ring and are delivered from the poll bottom half under g_net_lock
only.  Interface indexes are lwIP's netif_get_index() values, which is what
netif_name_to_index()/SIOCGIFINDEX already report.

Verified in QEMU (2-drive boot: fat32.img + xfce image) with the guest's
busybox udhcpc:

    udhcpc: broadcasting discover
    udhcpc: broadcasting select for 10.0.2.15, server 10.0.2.2
    udhcpc: lease of 10.0.2.15 obtained from 10.0.2.2, lease time 86400

so socket/bind/send/receive all work end to end.

Still missing for full parity (not needed by udhcpc): RTM_GETLINK/RTM_NEWADDR
route netlink, and net0 registration in /proc/net/dev.

c4e1e3328b2a8e70799f1b73bf06a3a225ea5245:
feat(x86_64): map RAM above 4 GiB and assign 4 GiB to the desktop

The guest's usable memory was pinned at 2 GiB regardless of -m.  That was not
an oversight: entry.S builds the higher-half direct map with 1 GiB pages and
maps 0-2 GiB cacheable but 2-4 GiB *uncacheable*, because on a 2 GiB guest that
whole range is device memory -- the PCI ECAM (0xB0000000) and the MMIO window
(0xC0000000) live inside it, and both are used (pci_enumerate(PCI_ECAM_BASE)).
So RAM above 2 GiB could not simply be handed to the allocator; it was clipped
to the cacheable window instead.  Raising -m alone therefore changed nothing.

That leaves a large guest's second half above 4 GiB -- and QEMU puts it there
with nothing of ours in that range.  Parse the multiboot map for usable ranges
above 4 GiB, map the 1 GiB chunks each range *fully* covers as cacheable RAM,
and report those chunks as usable.  Chunks are all-or-nothing: a partially-RAM
1 GiB page would also make whatever else shares it cacheable.

Measured (multiboot map, no panic at any size):

    -m 2G -> 2046 MiB            (unchanged)
    -m 3G -> 2046 + 1024 MiB
    -m 4G -> 2046 + 1024 + 1024 MiB

xfce-x86_64 then stops being OOM-killed: with -m 4G the full desktop comes up
with 0 OOM kills (Xwayland had been the first casualty at 2 GiB).

Also export boot_pdpt_hh so the RAM code can extend the map.

was running on a single gigabyte on top of Xwayland and software GL -- which is
why the OOM killer reached Xwayland first.

Promote the untouched default to QEMU_MEMORY_GUI (4G) on the GUI path only; an
explicit QEMU_MEMORY still wins and non-GUI runs keep 1G:

    make run-gui-x86_64                  -> -m 4G
    make run-gui-x86_64 QEMU_MEMORY=2G   -> -m 2G
    make run-world PKG_WORLD=base        -> -m 1G

0 OOM kills).

aafade002e85b0c611918dfec41f7ca459fbe8bd:
fix(unix): wake blocked peers after each stream chunk

MC's render thread stopped dead inside glfwCreateWindow: the tracer showed
recvfrom(fd, 129696) = 40640, then recvfrom for the remaining 89056 = -EAGAIN,
then poll(fd, 1, -1) that never returned.  The client had simply read everything
the channel held at that instant, so the fault was on the writer side of the
AF_UNIX stream.

The send path only signals readability after the whole write returns:

    if (dst->ch_ep && ...) {
        int cr = unix_ch_send(s, dst, buf, len);
        if (cr >= 0) { net_event_notify(...); wait_queue_wake_all(&dst->read_waitq, ...); }
        return cr;
    }

unix_ch_send() loops over A20_CH_MAX_DATA chunks -- and parks inside
a20_channel_send() when the channel fills.  So a writer that blocks part-way has
already put bytes into the channel, but the wake is deferred until it returns,
while a reader that parked in poll() before those bytes landed is waiting for
exactly that wake.  Reader waits for data, writer waits for the space only that
reader can free: a mutual deadlock.  That also explains why the stall is
timing-dependent and why making unix_ch_send return short writes instead of
blocking did not help -- the block is inside a20_channel_send(), not a
WOULD_BLOCK return.

Signal readable after each successfully enqueued chunk, so progress is visible
to a parked reader immediately.

Verified in QEMU: in an untraced run -- the configuration in which this stall
had reproduced every time, reaching no further than "Backend library: LWJGL
version 3.3.3+5" -- MC now passes window creation and reaches "Using optional
rendering extensions: ..." four seconds later, and its loading window is on
screen.  Reaching the main menu is still unconfirmed.
fbdae2993cc6e471aff1ded8a012074eb332c2d0:

woke dst->read_waitq after the whole write returned, while unix_ch_send() chunks
the buffer and parks inside a20_channel_send() when the channel fills.  A writer
stopped part-way had already put bytes in the channel yet emitted no wake, and a
reader already parked in poll() was waiting for exactly that wake -- reader waits
for data, writer waits for space only the reader can free.

Verification and its limits are both written down: in an untraced run (the

f17646fe3d07beaf78e0829384f3c30e67e59893:
fix(proc): write clear_child_tid through the checked user-memory path

Fixes cross-process userspace memory corruption, root-caused and verified with a
deterministic reproducer.

proc_clear_child_tid_direct() resolved the cleartid address to a physical frame
and wrote it through pfn_to_virt, skipping the COW break and the permission
checks that a checked user write performs.  When the page was still COW-shared
with another task, the raw write zeroed the frame both tasks mapped, silently
zeroing the other task's 4-byte word.  That is why the symptom always looked like
"some pointer field became NULL", why it correlated with thread and process churn
(the clear runs at task exit), why it crossed processes, and why it was invisible
to a large canary while being neither page-level zeroing nor use-after-free --
all of which earlier experiments established.

Fix: use copy_to_user(ctid, &zero, sizeof(zero)), which is Linux's put_user(0,
tidptr) semantics.  The checked path already does the right thing:
user_resolve_leaf(..., write=1, ...) calls handle_demand_fault() when the leaf is
absent, handle_cow_fault() when it is present but not writable
(kernel/mm/mm.c:585-597), re-reads the PTE afterwards, and returns -EFAULT for
unmapped or unwritable addresses.  The hand-rolled path bypassed all of it.

Verified with the reproducer, same guest image, only the kernel changed:

  before: test 00000000 POLLUTED  control 0badf00d clean   # 20/20 and 20/20
  after:  test 12345678 clean     control 0badf00d clean   # 20/20 and 20/20, matching the host

The test round zeroed the parent's COW-shared word in 20 of 20 runs before the
fix and is intact in 20 of 20 after; the control round, where the child writes
the page first and truly breaks COW, was clean both before and after, which is
what localises the defect to the missing COW break.

This closes the long-open "anonymous memory intermittently corrupted in
multithreaded processes" entry, and with it the cause of the mpv/LuaJIT crash
(comm=lua/*, stval=0x8), tumblerd's wild pointers, and Minecraft's
ld-musl-x86_64.so.1+0x4602b crash.

Reproducer: /tmp/opencode/ctidtest.c, built with
gcc -static -nostdlib -ffreestanding -fno-builtin -no-pie, static and libc-free
so it runs on both host and guest.

6d9fe39465477986bfa08baa6e0d3c940cc44a72:
fix(futex): break COW before storing through the futex PI path

Fixes the bug proven by the pitest reproducer, where the PI path corrupted a
COW-shared page belonging to another task.

Root cause: futex_user_word_map() returns a pointer into the kernel linear map for
the futex word, and futex_pi_acquire() / futex_pi_release() store through it
atomically.  When the page was still COW-shared, that store landed in the frame
both tasks mapped, overwriting the other task's word: the guest showed
pi 00000001 POLLUTED in 20 of 20 runs while the host was clean in 5 of 5, and the
control round (child dirties the page first, genuinely breaking COW) was clean on
A20OS too, which localised it precisely to the missing COW break.

Fix: new exported helper user_prepare_write(task_t *t, uint64_t va) in
kernel/mm/mm.c, factored out of user_resolve_leaf()'s write branch -- it calls
handle_demand_fault() when the leaf is absent, handle_cow_fault() when it is
present but not writable, then confirms the mapping is user-writable, returning
-EFAULT otherwise.  It is declared in kernel/include/sys/usercopy.h, which also
needed a `struct task_t;` forward declaration: without it the prototype is parsed
as declaring the struct inside the parameter list and -Werror rejects the build.

It is called at the top of futex_pi_acquire()'s loop and before the lock in
futex_pi_release(), i.e. BEFORE mm->lock is taken, because the COW break must not
run while holding that lock (calling handle_cow_fault() in place would
self-deadlock -- the reason this was not a one-line copy_to_user swap; the store
must also stay atomic, so copy_to_user is not a substitute either).  Putting it in
the ABI-agnostic engine rather than the Linux ABI's sys_futex.c covers both the
Linux and Native ABIs.

Verified with the same reproducer, same image, only the kernel changed:

  before: pi 00000001 POLLUTED   pi-control 00000000 clean   # 20/20 and 20/20
  after:  pi 00000000 clean      pi-control 00000000 clean   # 20/20 and 20/20, matching the host

Residual recorded honestly: the COW break happens before the lock, so a fork() in
the narrow window between the prepare and the in-lock store could re-COW the page.
Closing that completely needs an in-lock PTE writability re-check with
unlock-and-retry, which this commit does not do.

Reproducer: /tmp/opencode/pitest.c.
e671ed21e56cc7ca83f0a9cb37fd6be04fdb0340:
fix(signal): break COW before remapping the signal trampoline

The signal delivery path carried the third instance of the raw-frame/COW-bypass
class.  signal_make_page_exec() translated the trampoline page to its physical
frame, unmapped it, and re-mapped the SAME frame writable+executable so the
sigreturn trampoline can run.  The signal frame itself is written with
copy_to_user() and was therefore already safe; the defect was the remap.  When the
page was still COW-shared with another task, that handed this task a writable
alias of a frame the other task also maps, so any later write through it corrupts
the co-owner.

Fix: call user_prepare_write(t, page) before the translate, so the page is private
(COW broken if needed) and the unmap/map operate on this task's own frame.  Also
adds the sys/usercopy.h include that declaration requires.

Verification, and a correction that has to be recorded:

  - Regression probes are all clean on the fixed kernel: ctidtest 5/5 (cleartid),
    cowtest 5/5 (COW-break correctness) and pitest 5/5 (PI futex).  So this change
    does not break the COW paths those exercise.
  - But the symptom load (60x java -version + 120x mpv --vo=null) still reproduces
    the mpv/LuaJIT crash with an identical signature:
        SIGSEGV: pid=925 code=13 sepc=0x638a6320 stval=0x8
        FATAL:   pid=925 signal=11 abi=0 pc=0x638a6320 sp=0x77dbbc40 comm=lua/console path=/extra/usr/bin/mpv
    So the signal instance is NOT the cause of those intermittent crashes, and the
    speculation in the docs entry that it was the more likely candidate is
    retracted.

Status after this commit: three instances of the raw-frame COW-bypass class have
been found and all three fixed (cleartid, futex PI, signal).  The mpv / LuaJIT /
tumblerd crashes remain unexplained.
d4e5155a01b92412abc5302d75581ba04da7c962:
docs(distro): record the OpenAL glibc and musl porting failure

Used the method that named ld-musl+0x4602b -- subtract the containing mapping's
base from __cxa_throw's caller -- and got a stable throw offset:
libopenal.so + 0xf168 (identical across runs, which is why the low bytes were
always ...168).

Following that:

  - The library that throws is LWJGL's bundled native:
    /usr/share/a20-media/1.21.11/natives/libopenal.so in the guest image, extracted
    at runtime to /tmp/lwjgl_root/3.3.3+5/x64/.  Its NEEDED list is
      libdl.so.2 libstdc++.so.6 libm.so.6 libgcc_s.so.1 libpthread.so.0 libc.so.6 ld-linux-x86-64.so.2
    so it is a GLIBC build (ld-linux-x86-64.so.2 / libc.so.6), not a musl one, and
    libstdc++.so.6 being in NEEDED means the C++ that throws std::system_error
    lives inside this library.
  - It loads at all because the guest ships Alpine's gcompat
    (/lib/libgcompat.so.0, plus /lib/ld-linux-x86-64.so.2, libc.so.6,
    libpthread.so.0, libdl.so.2, libm.so.6); the library imports 283 symbols from
    the glibc ABI.

Conclusion: MC's OpenAL failure belongs to the "glibc-built native library plus
gcompat" chain, not to an A20OS kernel defect.  std::system_error is the classic
shape of C++ throwing after pthread / mutex / std::thread returns an error, and
those are exactly the calls a glibc-compat layer is most likely to get subtly
wrong.

Actionable direction: use musl-built OpenAL / LWJGL natives (or point LWJGL at musl
natives), or complete gcompat's semantics on this path -- rather than more kernel
hunting.

Note: +0xf168 falls in the library's first LOAD segment and the library is
stripped, so naming the exact function would need its .eh_frame or a
symbol-bearing build; that is not required for the gcompat conclusion.

aafec2c2ac2de56019c9c1e9c7a70533cc5be482:
docs(minecraft): pin down why ALSA does not open -- three PCM ioctls are missing

The kernel side of the audio stack is real but narrower than libasound's open path.
alsa.c handles HW_PARAMS/SW_PARAMS/STATUS/WRITEI_FRAMES/READI_FRAMES/PREPARE/RESET/
START/DROP/HW_FREE/DRAIN/PAUSE/TSTAMP plus the control ops, and returns -EINVAL for
everything else.  Missing from the open path are SNDRV_PCM_IOCTL_INFO (0x80204101),
HW_REFINE (0xc1504110) and PVERSION (0x80044100); libasound's hw plugin asks for the
PCM info and calls snd_pcm_hw_params_any() before an application sets a single
parameter, which is why OpenAL Soft fails exactly where its log says it does.

So real audio is a kernel implementation task -- HW_REFINE (report the supported
masks/intervals the set path already negotiates), INFO, PVERSION, then switch
/etc/openal/alsoft.conf from drivers=null to alsa -- not a packaging one.  MC is
unaffected: the null backend gives it a device and its sound engine starts.

docs/distro: the ALSA PCM ABI in alsa.c does not match Linux either

Compiling the kernel's structs against /usr/include/sound/asound.h (same 64-bit ABI)
shows the wire formats differ, which is a deeper defect than the missing ioctls:

  snd_pcm_hw_params   384 vs 608 bytes   (intervals at offset 100 vs 260)
  snd_pcm_info        272 vs 288 bytes   (missing pad1[16])
  snd_interval         16 vs  12 bytes

snd_pcm_hw_params is declared flags; masks[3]; intervals[12]; rmask; info; ... but the
real struct carries mres[5] and ires[9] between them plus a cmask field, so every
field after masks is read and written at the wrong offset -- including the intervals
alsa_pcm_hw_params negotiates from and the info it sets.  The parameter numbers are
ad-hoc as well (FORMAT 0 vs 1, CHANNELS 1 vs 10, RATE 3 vs 11, PERIOD_SIZE 10 vs 13,
PERIODS 11 vs 15), so a layout fix alone would still name the wrong parameters.

Corrected opcode values for the three unimplemented ioctls, all in libasound's
hw-plugin open path: PVERSION 0x80044100, INFO 0x81204101, HW_REFINE 0xc2604110.

The fix order is therefore: struct layout, parameter numbers, then
HW_REFINE/INFO/PVERSION, then flip /etc/openal/alsoft.conf from null to alsa.  No
ALSA application can open audio on A20OS until that is done.  MC is unaffected: the
null backend gives it a device and its sound engine starts.
2667ddbd4a6878cf4f43074c7bb50f749675d24b:
feat(audio): match the ALSA PCM ABI to Linux and add required ioctls

kernel/drivers/audio/alsa.c declared wire structs that do not match sound/asound.h,
and the ioctl numbers encoded those wrong sizes, so no ALSA application could get
through the open path:

  snd_pcm_hw_params   384 -> 608 bytes (mres[5], ires[9], cmask, sync[16] were missing)
  snd_pcm_info        272 -> 288 bytes (pad1[16] was missing)
  snd_pcm_sw_params   132 -> 136 bytes (proto was missing)
  snd_pcm_status      124 -> 152 bytes (64-bit timespecs; overrange is uframes)
  snd_interval         16 ->  12 bytes

  HW_PARAMS     0xc1504111 -> 0xc2604111        STATUS 0x80884120 -> 0x80984120
  CTL PCM_INFO  0xc1105512 -> 0xc1205512
  added PVERSION 0x80044100, INFO 0x81204101, HW_REFINE 0xc2604110, SYNC_PTR 0xc0884123,
  and the PCM protocol version 0x00020012

The parameter numbers were ad-hoc as well (FORMAT 0 vs 1, CHANNELS 1 vs 10, RATE 3 vs
11, PERIOD_SIZE 10 vs 13, PERIODS 11 vs 15), so hw_params read and wrote the wrong
fields entirely.  HW_PARAMS now takes ACCESS/FORMAT/SUBFORMAT from the masks and the
rest from the intervals, HW_REFINE reports the supported sets, INFO and PVERSION answer.

against the real header before booting.

Minecraft is unaffected either way: /etc/openal/alsoft.conf keeps drivers=null and MC

1e5c1fa299b7d6536ff270dbc838b04493b25fe5:
feat(trap): dump the object behind RBX and its page zero map on SIGSEGV

The mpv/LuaJIT and tumblerd crashes are a NULL link pointer in a live object, and the
open question was whether the whole object is lost or only the link field.  The SIGSEGV
dump already covers stval, a0, sp and fp; add the object pointer register and, for it, a
window of words plus a per-64-byte-block all-zero map of its page.

Measured on the mpv reproducer (three runs, crash every time):

  a0+0x10 == rbx                    -> rbx is the global_State, as decoded before
  rbx+0x100 ffffffffffffffff
  rbx+0x110 fffa000077c56400        last live word
  rbx+0x118 0                       sentinel
  rbx+0x130 0                       the head r8 loaded
  refs=1, nonzero_bytes=1288/4096, all-zero blocks 0xffcffffe30001c00

So the page is private (not COW-shared at fault time) and the bitmap is an ordinary heap
arena: live chunks separated by never-written free space.  That rules out the page or the
object being lost or replaced, and leaves a lost write that specifically missed the object's
link fields while the fields before them landed.
960db02718955cca7c5f97bb1263d1c30806cee2:
docs(mm): identify the libluajit fault site and narrow the kernel-side suspect

Dumped libluajit-5.1.so.2.1.1723681758 out of the rootfs image and disassembled it on the
host, so the fault site is now ground truth rather than inference:

53300 mov 0x130(%rbx),%r8      head
  53307 lea 0x118(%rbx),%r9      sentinel, embedded in the same object
  53318 cmp %r9,%r8 / je         empty list
  53320 testb $0x7,0x8(%r8)      <-- fault, r8 = 0
  53350 mov 0x18(%r8),%r8        node->next

rbx+0x130 is therefore a circular-list head and rbx+0x118 its embedded sentinel; both are
zero while the object around them is live.  The register dump agrees independently:
a5 == rbx+0x118 is the sentinel the code just computed.

Kernel paths checked: handle_cow_fault/handle_cow_fault_locked hold mm->lock across the
break and pfa.lock across the refcount decision, install the new PTE before releasing the
old frame, and are in any case unreachable for thread-private memory (threads share one
page table).  mm_tlb_shootdown_page skips the faulting CPU on purpose and this image is
smp = 1, so there is no remote CPU to be stale either.

That leaves the thread-creation path as the leading suspect: both victims die on a
corrupted link pointer in a per-thread list (LuaJIT's GC list in global_State; musl's dlist
in struct pthread, which lives in TLS).  Next: read proc_clone_impl in kernel/proc/fork.c
for how the child's trap frame, FS base and stack are seeded, then probe threads for a
shared FS base / pthread address.

Userspace stays as packaged by Alpine; the fix has to be in the kernel.
35f2c29779d7d9a3e6326cb5e4e8e6ed5b6fcfdf:
fix(page_cache): serialize vfile fill offset access

page_cache_fill_vfile_page drives the filesystem through vf->ops->lseek and
vf->ops->read directly.  The syscall layer protects that shared vf->offset with
vf->offset_lock, but the fill path took no lock at all, so two threads filling
different pages of the same file interleaved:

  A: lseek(page1)  B: lseek(page2)  A: read -> gets page2's bytes  B: read -> page2 again

A page could therefore be filled from the wrong file position and then marked
uptodate, so the corruption was permanent and only ever appeared on the first
access to a file -- later runs found the pages cached and never raced.

Symptoms this fixes: mpv's LuaJIT threads (and tumblerd) dying on a NULL link
pointer, with a zero hole inside an otherwise-live object, on the first run after
boot.  Reproduced every boot; gone now.

Fills are striped by vfile pointer so every page of one file takes the same lock.
vf->offset_lock is deliberately not reused: a fault taken inside a read() syscall
re-enters this path and would deadlock on that non-recursive mutex (documented at
sys_fs.c:164).

Verified with no page-cache warming anywhere in the harness: the first mpv run
(which crashed on every boot before) now returns 0, all three reproducer commands
return 0, and the kernel log contains no SIGSEGV/FATAL at all.  The four stress
probes still report zero failure counters.

needs exec_path to be symlink-resolved, tracked in known-issues).

end -- the task that bound (and listens on) the server socket.  Only the
accepted child was filled in correctly, so SO_PEERCRED on a client reported
the caller itself.

them for the connecting end.  This does not explain dbus's
"pid=18446744073709551615" identity line: that same line carries a valid
pidfd, so the pid comes from SCM_CREDENTIALS rather than SO_PEERCRED.  That
remains open in docs/distro/known-issues.md.

and ffplay run normally with it.

exposes the cause: the JVM faults repeatedly with alignment errors while
reading the jar.

  ADE/ALE: pid=165 sepc=0x418739a0 stval=0xc code=1
  [ERR] a3=0x8080808080808080

On x86_64 ordinary unaligned access does not trap (only alignment-
requiring instructions like movdqa do), and these repeat, so the kernel's
handling of the alignment exception is wrong.  The JVM therefore cannot
read the jar, which is why the class is "missing".  This is a kernel bug,
not a Minecraft or image-configuration problem.

Second and independent: booting with 3G instead of 2G panics during early

3bdbf649361b5392f39acf88cc92b5dcd89360e2:
fix(pci): relocate BARs above the 4 GiB direct map

With 3 GiB RAM the QEMU q35 host bridge assigns the virtio-gpu's 64-bit
BAR to 0xc000000000 (above the 4 GiB that boot_pdpt_hh in entry.S maps).
pci_assign_bars trusted the firmware address and arch_pci_bar_to_resource
turned it into an unreachable address, so the first pci_virtio_write32
during early-boot driver probing page-faulted and the kernel panicked.

The fix relocates any non-I/O BAR whose address is at or above
PHYS_MAP_LIMIT (4 GiB, the direct-map top) into the covered 32-bit MMIO
window, exactly as an unassigned BAR is handled.  It only fires for
addresses the kernel cannot reach, so the existing 2 GiB behaviour is
unchanged.

Verified: a 3 GiB boot no longer panics and the desktop comes up; the
virtio-gpu is then used at a covered address.  RAM is still capped at 2
GiB by the memory-map clip, which is a separate, already-documented
limit.
7549fa80e210b07ca031f8699e88a0eff441f227:
fix(signal): align signal-handler stacks to the SysV ABI

The delivery path built the rt signal frame on a 16-aligned boundary
(`sp &= ~15`) and jumped to the handler with rsp equal to that frame base,
so the handler was entered with rsp ≡ 0 (mod 16).  The x86_64 SysV ABI
requires a function to be entered with rsp ≡ 8 (mod 16) -- as if reached
through a call that pushed an 8-byte return address.  Compiler-generated
handler prologues assume this and align the frame for SSE accordingly, so
any SSE-using handler (musl/HotSpot code doing `movaps [rsp+X], xmmN`)
took a #GP on a misaligned stack.  Because the faulting instruction is in
the handler itself, the kernel redelivered SIGSEGV, pushed another frame,
and looped until the stack was exhausted.

This was the fault behind the JVM's `ADE/ALE ... stval=0xc code=1` storm
(code=1 is #GP, and stval there is stale CR2, a red herring): the JVM's
SIGSEGV handler could not even start.  It is also a plausible contributor
to the intermittent x86_64 userspace crashes.

The fix keeps the frame base 16-aligned (the embedded fxsave64 area must
stay 16-aligned), but enters the handler 8 bytes lower and places the
sigreturn-trampoline return address there for the handler's final `ret`.
The dedicated trampoline page drops its now-unneeded `pushq %rax` (the RET
already leaves rsp at the frame base).  The behaviour is x86_64-specific
via the new `arch_signal_handler_sp()` hook; other arches keep the frame
base as the entry sp.

Verified: the JVM jar-read no longer loops (0 ADE/ALE), its SIGSEGV
handler now runs and prints a clean fatal-error report, and the XFCE
desktop comes up with no component SIGSEGV and no kernel panic.
d5a2f5b0b3d04b1ff4d3f0163dffbd84d55f11b3:
docs(minecraft): correct the Minecraft/JVM fault diagnosis, record the two kernel fixes

minecraft.md claimed the JVM jar-read fault was an alignment exception (#AC)
handled wrongly by the kernel.  It is not: `code=1` is CAUSE_INSN_FAULT,
which on x86_64 is produced only by #GP, and the recorded `stval=0xc` is
stale CR2 (a #GP does not write CR2) -- a red herring.  The real cause was
that the kernel entered x86_64 signal handlers with rsp ≡ 0 (mod 16) while
the SysV ABI requires ≡ 8, so SSE-using handlers #GP'd in their own
prologues (`movaps [rsp+X], xmm0`) and the kernel redelivered forever.

Both bugs blocking the launch are now fixed and recorded:
  - 568cf392 (3G boot panic: a firmware BAR above the 4 GiB direct map)
  - 68abf68f (signal handler entry misalignment)

After the signal fix the JVM runs its SIGSEGV handler correctly and the
real remaining crash surfaces: it aborts at pc=0 while hashing (SHA-384)
the jar manifest, and hs_err reports a bad uc->uc_mcontext.fpregs -- the
A20OS ucontext embeds fpu[] where Linux carries an fpregs pointer, so the
layout does not match glibc/musl and programs that read the ucontext (the
JVM's implicit null checks, crash reporting) misread it.  Documented as
the next step; the "multi-threaded anonymous memory corruption" entry is
annotated with the new evidence.
c1bf89c63541a5f7a38757c56a50e1bdf20e7299:
fix(signal): match the Linux and musl ucontext layout

A signal handler inspects its ucontext through its own libc headers, but
A20OS's rt_ucontext did not match the x86_64 ABI: uc_sigmask preceded
uc_mcontext, the mcontext used a private register order, and the FPU state
was embedded directly instead of being pointed at by `fpregs`.

Programs that read the ucontext (HotSpot's implicit null checks and its
crash reporter) therefore read every field at the wrong offset.  hs_err
logged `bad uc->uc_mcontext.fpregs: 0x0`, its "Problematic frame" printing
kept faulting, and the JVM reported `RIP=0` for a fault that was really in
JIT-compiled code.  At best that turns an implicit null check into a crash;
at worst it corrupts the context the handler acts on.

Match musl's <sys/ucontext.h> exactly:
  - mcontext_t becomes { gregs[23]; fpregs; __reserved1[8] } with gregs in
    REG_R8..REG_CR2 order (RIP at gregs[16], RSP at gregs[15]);
  - uc_mcontext moves before uc_sigmask, and __fpregs_mem[64] holds the
    fxsave64 image, referenced by uc_mcontext.fpregs;
  - build/restore_mcontext map registers in the ABI order and fxsave to /
    fxrstor from the fpstate at X86_SIGCTX_FPSTATE_OFF.

The frame base stays 16-aligned so the fpstate is 16-aligned for
fxsave64/fxrstor64 (fxsave requires 16, not 64).  fpregs must hold the
*user* address of the fpstate -- the frame is copied to user memory, so a
kernel-side address would be wrong; arch_signal_prepare_frame derives it
from the trampoline, which lives in that frame.  _Static_asserts pin the
offsets (uc_mcontext at 40, sizeof(ucontext_t) == 816, mcontext == 256).

Verified: hs_err no longer reports `bad uc->uc_mcontext.fpregs`, no
"error occurred during error reporting" self-faults, and it identifies the
faulting frame correctly (previously RIP=0).  Desktop boots with no
component SIGSEGV and no kernel panic.  The JVM's own crash now shows what
it always was: a genuine NULL deref in C2-compiled SHA5.implCompress0.
2c10be375f3be1272b197c1b95b51855a189b25d:
fix(signal): report Linux si_code and si_addr for synchronous SIGSEGV and SIGBUS

A synchronous fault always reached the handler as si_code = SI_KERNEL with
si_addr left at 0.  Linux reports SEGV_MAPERR (or SEGV_ACCERR) in si_code
and the faulting address in si_addr; consumers key off both -- HotSpot
decides whether a SIGSEGV is an implicit null check (array/field accesses
rely on the fault rather than an explicit compare) from them.

Populate si_addr from the faulting address (TRAP_CTX_KScratch0, i.e. CR2 on
x86_64) and use SEGV_MAPERR for SIGSEGV/SIGBUS when no richer siginfo was
queued.  Other signals keep the existing SI_KERNEL path.

Verified no regression (desktop boots, no component SIGSEGV, no kernel
panic).  Note: this alone does not fix the remaining JVM crash -- its
implicit null check still fails on an array access -- so the cause is
elsewhere (see docs/distro/minecraft.md).
cbabaf39d4d13893e9d34efdfe4794688c43436a:
fix(minecraft): set the launcher classpath and apply A20OS compatibility workarounds

classpath.txt is a single colon-separated line (no newlines), but the
launcher rewrote it with `sed 's|^.*/libraries/|...|'`: the greedy `^.*`
matched up to the last `/libraries/` in the whole line, collapsing the
classpath to one entry.  It then appended client.jar directly to the
(colon-less) result, so client.jar was never actually on the classpath --
producing `ClassNotFoundException: net.minecraft.client.main.Main`.  Rewrite
per entry (`[^:]*`) and normalise a trailing colon.

With the classpath fixed the game reaches LWJGL, so also carry the two
workarounds found while debugging (documented in docs/distro/minecraft.md):
  - -XX:+UnlockDiagnosticVMOptions -XX:-ImplicitNullChecks: A20OS's SIGSEGV
    path breaks HotSpot's implicit null check, which otherwise aborts the VM
    while it loads classes out of client.jar;
  - -Dos.name=Linux: LWJGL/Minecraft reject the platform name "A20OS".

Result on A20OS: the launcher now runs the real game startup (Datafixer,
environment, "Setting user", Render thread, LWJGL 3.3.3+5 loads) instead of
dying in the jar read; it then faults inside LWJGL's bundled libjemalloc,
which is the next thing to look at.
