docs(docs): sync the EEVDF treap rework and drop orphan comments in vm.c

The scheduler was switched from a deadline-ordered doubly linked list to a
treap, but the documentation did not follow: three files still described a
list implementation that no longer exists.  This brings the structure and the
complexity claims in line with the code, and fixes a few places that were
actively misleading.

Every claim was checked against the code one item at a time, not against the
diff:

  - EEVDF is already an augmented treap.  eevdf_node_t carries min_vruntime
    and heap_prio and hangs intrusively off task_t.eevdf_node, so selection
    descends the tree and prunes whole ineligible subtrees using the subtree
    min_vruntime.  The cost is the tree height, O(log n), not the O(n)
    full-queue scan the docs described.  With no eligible task the code falls
    back to the cached eevdf_first, which is O(1).
  - Level 0 changed implementation too: one FIFO per priority plus an
    rt_bitmap, so finding the highest non-empty priority is an O(1) bit scan
    rather than a linear walk of the whole queue.
  - Two constant names were wrong.  The docs said NICE0_LOAD where the code
    says EEVDF_NICE0_LOAD, and both EEVDF_NICE0_LOAD and EEVDF_MAX_LAG are
    defined in kernel/proc/sched.c, not in proc_internal.h.  The source
    section was corrected to match.
  - eevdf-scheduler.md section 10 now says the early implementation was a
    list and that this revision corrects it, so nobody later reads the old
    description and concludes the document was never updated.

kernel/mm/vm.c gets comment changes only, no code changes.  The one
non-comment change in the diff removes the inline comment on
pt_map_kernel(...): after the mm/vma.c split, the section headers in vm.c that
claimed to describe "find the VMA containing an address", "create a memory
mapping (the mmap syscall)" and "adjust the heap size (brk)" were all orphans.
The functions they described, mm_mmap_vmo, free_vma_pages and
mm_vma_flush_deferred, now live in mmap.c and vma.c.  Dropping the headers
that pointed at nothing leaves one comment explaining why the deferred VMA
flush happens here.
892f81f79555643f846558bdc852fe93744da732:
ci(build): wire the manifest gates into CI, they were orphan targets

check-instances, check-instance-matrix and check-component-registry are
defined and marked .PHONY in tools/targets-gates.mk, but no aggregating
target anywhere in the repository referenced them and there is not a single
hit under .github/.  The drift protection for 43 instances, 20 driver
components and the Makefile was therefore kept alive only by people
remembering to run it by hand, while docs/instances.md claimed the checks
"guarantee in CI that ... never drift", which did not match the repository as
it stood.

The problem is not that the gates are missing, it is that nothing calls them.
They were written as three independent .PHONY targets with no single entry
point, which makes them awkward to run locally and easy to miss entirely when
a CI job is added.

  - Added make check-manifests, which aggregates the three gates and serves
    as the single entry point for local runs and for CI.
  - Added a manifest-gates job to CI.  These three gates are host-side pure
    Python and architecture independent, so the job stays out of the build
    container and off the architecture matrix, and runs before build/smoke: a
    configuration drift fails within minutes instead of surfacing an hour
    later once a full build has finished.
  - The job deliberately does not pull submodules.  The gates only read
    instances/, components/, tools/, the Makefile and source paths under
    kernel/drvmod, and never touch user/external or kernel/external.  That is
    written into a comment, otherwise a later reader is likely to add the
    recursive checkout and pay several GB of clone time for nothing.
  - Fixed the gate wording in docs/instances.md to point at check-manifests
    and the manifest-gates job, and to explain the shape of the job.
28330f29c600108f79f648332894488c600f515c:
refactor(a20): dispatch run_flash through a backend registry

`a20 flash` used to dispatch any instance with a [flash] section
unconditionally to flash-xuanwu-openocd, while the validation layer only
required arch == armv7m and the tool to be one of ("openocd",).  It never
required the board to match.  The consequence was that a 64 KiB stm32f103
instance could legally reach the 512 KiB/64 KiB xuanwu recipe and start
erasing, and that recipe hardcodes the target script as stm32f1x.cfg.  Only
xuanwu carries a [flash] section today so it cannot fire, but this is the
shape of "add one more flash manifest and flash the wrong board".

The fix is not another if statement, it is turning "which programmer to use"
into data, reusing the registry pattern already proven in
components/drivers.toml:

  - Added components/flash-backends.toml.  Each backend declares a name, the
    boards it serves, an optional flash_kb/ram_kb, and the make_target that
    implements it.  The recipes stay in make, keeping the principle that the
    Makefile is the only build engine and the instance layer carries only
    deltas; Python only validates and passes values through, so a new backend
    needs no Python change.
  - boards together with flash_kb/ram_kb form the safety contract: when the
    instance's board or flash geometry falls outside the allowed set, a20
    check refuses before the build even starts.  Geometry has to be part of
    the key because one board name covers several flash sizes.  board =
    "stm32f103" means both the 64 KiB C8 and the 512 KiB ZET6 (xuanwu),
    distinguished by [stm32].xuanwu, so judging on the board name alone
    guards nothing.
  - a20_board.run_flash now takes the backend table and dispatches through the
    registry, and keeps the same geometry check on the action side as defence
    in depth.
  - a20_registry gained a shared TOML array-of-tables parser, since the two
    registries are structurally identical and copying the second one would
    have been 40 lines of pure duplication, plus validate_flash_backends and
    cross_check_flash_targets.
  - Added the gate make check-flash-backend-registry (= tools/a20
    check-flash-backends) with two layers of checking: the registry itself
    (no duplicate names, a board must really have
    kernel/platform/<board>/board.c, a make_target must be a rule that exists
    in the makefile) and the requirement that every make_target be reachable
    from the set a20 can actually dispatch to.  Hooked into check-manifests
    and CI.
  - Deleted the FLASH_TOOLS constant.  The set of backends now has exactly one
    source, and keeping the constant would reintroduce a second source of
    truth.

Verified in both directions:

  - All 43 instances pass, including xuanwu, whose 512/64 geometry agrees
    with the backend.
  - A 64 KiB stm32f103 with openocd, which is the original bug, is rejected,
    as are an unregistered backend name and a board mismatch.
  - All three drift directions FAIL: renaming make_target in the toml, a
    mistyped board name, and a make_target that exists but that a20 cannot
    dispatch to.

The match plus assert_never dispatch at the top of a20 did catch a case that
had been missed during development, which is reason enough to keep it.
2215b7880d7ec4d8946697cf35dd841c7ad99788:
feat(a20): add 49 unit tests and require [test].expect at check time

Roughly 1200 lines of Python in seven modules under tools/ had zero test
coverage: tools/tests/ held only C files, and the repository has no pytest, no
unittest and no pyproject.  The field-to-variable mapping in
derive_make_vars, the negative cases of parse_instance and the table-driven
rules of validate_instance were constrained only by the table in
docs/instances.md.  Breaking one of them would go unnoticed: the variable
would simply stop being set and the Makefile would quietly fall back to its
own default.

The tests use stdlib unittest rather than pytest because the PEP 723 header of
tools/a20 declares dependencies = [] and docs/instances.md promises a tool
built on the standard library with no third-party dependencies.  Adding
pytest would quietly break that promise to every contributor.

Coverage highlights:

  - derive_make_vars pins down the documented field-to-variable mapping item
    by item.  It deliberately records that CONFIG_SWAP is a Kconfig-style
    y/n while the other make-style flags are 1/0: unifying them would look
    tidier, but getting one side wrong silently turns the feature off.
  - parse_instance and validate_instance negative cases and table-driven
    rules.
  - Flash backends: the board and flash geometry safety contract, including
    the case where a 64 KiB part is refused by a 512 KiB recipe, which is the
    path that would really have bricked the part before the registry existed.
  - run_flash dispatch: board, geometry and unregistered backends refused
    again on the action side as defence in depth, plus a short circuit when
    the build fails so nothing gets erased.
  - A full instance scan and instance name uniqueness, the one place that
    deliberately reads the real tree.

Mutation testing was used to prove the tests are real.  Deleting run_flash's
geometry guard, renaming STM32_FLASH_KB to STM32_FLASHSIZE and making
geometry_mismatch always return None each make the tests fail.  The first
round only covered the validate_instance path, so deleting the run_flash
guard raised nothing, which showed that the action side really was a blind
spot and is why TestRunFlashDispatch was added.

Also fixes a real gap: with no expect in the [test] section, a20 check passed
and only a20 test exited halfway through with SystemExit.  That contradicts
the validation-early principle the tool states about itself, and a gate with
no expect can only pass vacuously.  expect is now required at check time.

The gate make check-a20-tests is hooked into the toolchain-gates CI job.
1b8cd2a4ffca855783545032baac9040761183b2:
feat(a20): check host resources before launching an instance and wait when short

run, debug and test are the only a20 actions that can fail in a way other than
a non-zero exit code: by taking the host down.  QEMU asks for 4 GiB when the
machine does not have it, and then the OOM killer decides who dies, usually
not the process being debugged.  These three actions now run a pre-flight
check before starting the guest.  The requirements are derived from the
instance's own fields (machine.memory, machine.smp, the [rootfs] image size)
and the action waits for them to be released instead of failing or pushing
ahead regardless.

Two measurement points are what make this feature sound, and the reason for
each is written down in the code:

  - Available memory must come from MemAvailable, not from free.  free does
    not count reclaimable page cache, and on a machine that is actually idle
    it is often only a few hundred MiB: on this host free reports 365 MiB
    while MemAvailable reports 25 GiB.  A gate based on free would wait
    forever, and that is not a theoretical risk.  When /proc is unreadable the
    function returns 0, so an unreadable reading blocks the run rather than
    letting it through.
  - Idle vCPUs do not show up in the load average, so load alone cannot tell
    whether another guest already holds the CPU this machine wants.  The
    concurrency limit is therefore counted separately, by scanning /proc for
    qemu-system-* processes rather than depending on pgrep.

Interface:

  - tools/a20 resources prints the current budget and the policy.
  - --no-wait fails immediately; --wait-timeout SEC bounds the wait.
  - The budget is overridable through environment variables (memory to keep,
    max concurrency, wait ceiling, disk floor) so CI machines with different
    headroom need no code change.
  - While waiting, progress is reported only when the set of missing
    resources changes, plus a 30s heartbeat, so a long wait does not print a
    line every five seconds.

24 new tests cover memory string parsing (including QEMU's 1G/512M/2GiB/1.5G
spellings and the round-up), each of the four shortage kinds alone and
together, the default concurrency limit, deriving requirements from the
instance fields, environment variable parsing and the fallback on invalid
values, --no-wait raising, and being let through after waiting.  The
measurement functions are also asserted directly against the real
/proc/meminfo, because that reading is what the gate actually trusts;
test_mem_available_is_read_not_free and its siblings are the examples.

Mutation testing confirmed each test is effective: dropping the guest, CPU,
memory or disk check, changing the round-up to truncation, and ignoring
MemAvailable each make the tests fail.  In the first round "ignoring
MemAvailable" instead came out OK, which showed that _mem_available_mb was not
covered at all back then; TestHostMeasurement was added to catch it.
198e54b4706826f9f89e6acda18a360b6f443d2d:
fix(a20): repair four smoke paths that break the debug scene

What the four classes have in common is this: when they fail, the message
points at the wrong cause, or there is no message at all.

1. A make failure was reported as "qemu command not found".  _qemu_cmdline runs
   with check=False and never looks at returncode, so when make failed through
   $(error) the error text contained only the dry-run plan while the real
   reason was dropped on stderr.  The returncode is now checked first and
   stderr is passed through verbatim.  Matching the qemu binary also moved
   from line.startswith("qemu-system") to matching on tokens: recursive make
   prefixes lines with "make[N]: ", and a path prefix or a cd/env prefix would
   have been missed too.

2. Ctrl-C left an orphan QEMU.  The child had no session of its own, so
   proc.kill() killed QEMU itself while everything QEMU had started kept
   running, still holding memory and the serial port.  start_new_session=True
   plus _reap() now signal the whole process group, escalate to SIGKILL after
   a grace period, and wait to reap.  A test with a SIGTERM-ignoring process
   that itself ignores SIGTERM in its child confirms that nothing leaks.

3. Concurrent runs of one instance trampled each other's logs.  Logs used a
   fixed per-instance path with non-atomic writes, so make -j or two CI jobs
   on one runner wrote into the same file and produced a log belonging to
   neither.  Access is now taken with flock: a second run of an instance that
   is already running is refused explicitly instead of silently interfering.
   flock rather than an O_EXCL lockfile, because the kernel releases it when
   the process dies, so a killed run cannot lock the instance out forever.
   There is a test for that.

4. A mistyped flag was silently handed to make.  parse_known_args treated
   --dry-rnu as a passthrough argument, so it became a make variable override
   or a target and the build setup changed with no indication at all.  Only
   arguments after an explicit "--" are passed through now; any other
   unrecognised argument is an error, with a hint at the right spelling.

Also changed a20 list, which always returned 0, to return 1 when an invalid
instance is present, since it could not serve as a gate before.

14 new tests cover the four items above plus timeout string parsing, which used
to be a fragile [:-1] slice and now matches \d+(\.\d+)?s and rejects "45" and
"45sec".

The tests themselves had one quality defect fixed too: the CLI argument tests
called main() directly, so if the argument gate regressed they would not fail,
they would let a real QEMU launch happen and hang the whole suite.  Those tests
now stub out every action boundary, so any action being executed raises
AssertionError; with the gate broken the result is a clean FAILED(2) instead
of a hang.
68c8bca22e5aadeeb5cb57320b5e50a1ec83ac44:
refactor(a20): generate board records from the artifact manifest

The board-level facts in docs/platforms/physical-boards.md were prose: image
sizes and SHA-256 values copied by hand out of a terminal, dated, and sitting
next to an absolute path into some contributor's home directory
(/home/gyy/a20-*.bin).  Those numbers cannot be checked, and changing a single
byte would go unnoticed unless somebody reread the paragraph.  Hand-copied
numbers inevitably drift over a long maintenance life.

`tools/a20 ledger <instance>` replaces that prose with derived facts:

  - The build directory, the source revision (head, branch, dirty flag), and
    the make variables the instance resolves to.
  - Size and sha256 for every artifact, with all paths repository relative,
    which is exactly what the absolute paths made impossible before.
  - Artifacts that were not built are listed explicitly under "not built yet"
    and the exit code is non-zero, so it never pretends the set is complete.

Three formats: table for humans, json for machines, and markdown, which can
be pasted straight into a platform document as a table block.  --out FILE
writes to a file.

The key implementation decision is that artifact paths are queried from make
rather than recomputed in Python as BUILD_DIR.  That name encodes more than a
dozen switches, including ARCH, BOARD, ABI, BRINGUP, NOMMU, the SMP count and
driver deployment, into the filename; copying the formula would manufacture a
second source of truth and would silently stop matching whenever the Makefile
gained another variant suffix.  a20_make therefore gained query_make(), which
fetches several variables from a single make invocation, and the dedicated
query in a20_registry that hardcoded DRIVER_DEPLOYMENT=generic now goes
through that same generic entry point.

The manifest output has been checked digit for digit against an independent
sha256sum.

24 new tests cover: sha256 agreement with hashlib including large files that
span chunks, human-readable sizes, bringup/MCU instances offering no rootfs
image, dev instances offering one, VF2 offering a boot chain, missing
artifacts being reported truthfully, the three render formats, and the
requirement that paths be repository relative.  One further test pins down the
behaviour that make expands an undefined variable to an empty string rather
than erroring, since a mistyped variable name and a legitimately empty value
are otherwise indistinguishable; it is written down so later readers do not
assume it raises.

Two defects in the tests were found and fixed while writing them: the lock
test used a relative sys.path and failed when run from tools/tests, and both
working directories are now verified; and the MCU tests failed outright on
machines without arm-none-eabi instead of skipping, so they now skip
symmetrically depending on whether the toolchain is present, with an added
test fixing the behaviour that a missing toolchain is an error rather than a
fabricated manifest.
f35cb3d3689e87b29ac426accf400b47d73f0957:
feat(a20): add target configuration and console deployment for board bring-up

The instance model had no concept of a physical target before.  [machine] is
QEMU's -m and -smp, [gui] is QEMU's -display, [net] is QEMU's hostfwd.  The
result was that "deploy to a development board" could not be expressed: a20
could build firmware and flash an STM32 with OpenOCD, but had no way to talk
to the board, so real-hardware bring-up was entirely manual, with commands
typed by hand, serial logs saved to /tmp by hand, sha256 computed by hand and
copied into documents by hand.  The more than twenty dated lines of acceptance
record in docs/platforms/physical-boards.md are the sediment of that process.

The new [target] section describes the board on the other end of the serial
line: console device, baud rate, reset command, boot and assert timeouts,
console_check, commands, expect, boot medium and the path logs are written
to.  The presence of the section already means physical target, so there is
no kind field that could contradict itself.

Two new actions:

- a20 console connects the serial port, optionally resets, waits for
    console_check, waits for boot_wait, injects commands, waits for expect
    and writes a transcript.  Every wait is bounded, so a board that never
    comes up ends at a named phase instead of hanging the terminal.
  - a20 deploy flashes through the existing backend registry, writes the boot
    medium with make's target-write-media, and then verifies the same way
    console does.

The serial port is implemented with the standard library termios/fcntl/select.
The PEP 723 header of tools/a20 declares dependencies = [] and the docs
promise a standard-library-only tool; pulling in pyserial to set six flag bits
would be the wrong trade for a tool every contributor runs.  The session logic
is a state machine above a Transport rather than a straight-line script,
because the board is not necessarily attached to this machine, so the question
of whether the kernel really came up has to be verifiable with no board
present.  A pty provides a real tty to exercise the transport layer, and a fake
transport exercises the timing.

Three specific safety and correctness decisions:

- reset is split with shlex.split into an argv executed without a shell, so
    the manifest cannot smuggle in a pipe or a ";".  A reset written wrongly
    fails as a literal argument instead of executing.
  - target-write-media checks, before the dd, that the target exists, is a
    block device and is not mounted.  Naming the wrong node is the only
    unrecoverable mistake on this path, and the kernel's "device busy" is far
    too late a place to discover it.
  - target.log must be repository relative, otherwise log paths carry the
    absolute paths of one particular machine, which is exactly the sort of
    thing the artifact ledger exists to...
27cdff7a199f437093eb4f5d0c4db7f3eb12a990:
fix(net): add a runtime gate for SIOCGIF* and fix the ABI defects it found

SIOCGIFCONF was implemented, and its own commit said "no runtime gate for the
SIOCGIF* area".  Writing that gate immediately caught two real defects, and
both of them emptied out the whole point of the feature, which is making
getifaddrs(), ifconfig and ip usable.

Defect one: the kernel's struct ifreq was 8 bytes smaller than every libc's.
The kernel union had only a 16-byte member, so sizeof == 32, but the ifreq
unions in musl and glibc contain struct ifmap, which is 24 bytes under LP64,
so the real sizeof is 40.  Userspace walks the buffer with the whole-struct
ifreq stride, so past the first entry it is misaligned against the kernel,
which is why the gate log showed an empty name on row1 and "lo" on row2.  The
old _Static_assert(sizeof == 32) is exactly why this slipped through: the
assertion passed and every real caller read garbage.  struct a20_ifmap is now
in the union, where its only role in the real ABI is to grow the union, and
the sizes are asserted per bit width as 40 / 32.

Defect two: the address was written at the sin_port offset.
memcpy(raw + 2, &nif->ip_addr, 4) puts the address at offset 2, while
sockaddr_in is sin_family(0) + sin_port(2) + sin_addr(4), so 10.0.2.15 was read
as 2.15.0.0.  The same mistake was in net_ifreq_put_addr, shared by
SIOCGIFADDR, SIOCGIFNETMASK, SIOCGIFDSTADDR and SIOCGIFBRDADDR, so all four
getters were affected.  Both sites moved to offset 4.

A regression introduced by my own first fix was caught by the gate: I byte
swapped sin_family into network order.  sin_family in Linux is a bare host
order constant, and every caller writes sin_family = AF_INET, so the swap made
reads return 512 instead of 2.  It has been reverted and the reason is now
written in the code, because sin_family is the only field in sockaddr that
gets no byte order conversion and without a note the next reader will swap it
again.  The tests read through struct sockaddr_in as well and let the compiler
handle byte order, since hand-reading two bytes is precisely what let the
wrong byte-order kernel pass this check in the first place.

Added:

  - user/cmds/net/net_iface_test.c with 20 checks covering the size query,
    filling, truncation, family filtering, EINVAL, and the real usage path of
    feeding an enumerated name back into the per-interface getter, which is
    what getifaddrs and ifconfig do.
  - instances/smoke-net-iface.toml plus make smoke-net-iface.  The instance
    sets hostfwd = [] explicitly: the Makefile default NET_HOSTFWD takes host
    port 5555, while this gate only needs the serial port and no forwarding.
    Leaving it on means anyone holding 5555 fails the gate with the baffling
    "could not set up host forwarding rule".
  - net_iface_test is also listed in the network_suite case table, so
    smoke-network-suite covers it.
  - docs/testing-gates.md gained the gate entry, including why it has to
    exist.

Verification:

  - make smoke-net-iface PASSes, 20/20.
  - Three checks fail before the gate change and all are green after it.
  - Zero warnings under -Werror on four 64-bit architectures
    (riscv64/x86_64/aarch64/loongarch64).  arm32 and riscv32 could not be
    verified because the matching cross toolchains are missing on this host,
    which is recorded as such; the two ILP32 _Static_asserts were checked
    separately with a compiler targeting riscv32.
432daa0dd5102625eb697e6d09443c611aa42300:
docs(platforms): turn the physical-board record into a verdict table

The LS2K1000 section of docs/platforms/physical-boards.md had eight dated
acceptance write-ups, each repeating the same batch of facts: the byte count
of a candidate image, its SHA-256, an absolute path such as /home/gyy/...
inside one contributor's WSL home, a temporary /tmp/a20-*.log log name, and
which commit it was replayed from.  The recovery bundle had a hand-copied
SHA-256 as well.

Not one of those numbers can be checked anywhere.  Changing a byte would go
unnoticed, and the paths only hold on one machine.  The same fact, that a
read-only ext4 mount was verified, is restated in all eight write-ups, so a
reader cannot tell which copy is current.

Three kinds of content are kept after the rework:

  - Board constraints, in a new section: LA264 traps on unaligned wide
    accesses, the open-bus behaviour at CRMD.IE = 0, the non-vectored
    exception entry dispatching only the bits enabled in ECFG.LIE, UART
    polling dropping characters under burst input (with the 1 ms period being
    a diagnostic fallback only), and the forbidden moves for recovery.  These
    are hardware and SoC facts rather than implementation choices, they cannot
    be derived from the code, and they have to stay here.
  - An acceptance status table mapping each capability to verified,
    unverified, incomplete or unsupported, with a pointer to the evidence.  It
    gathers the boundary conditions that were scattered over eight write-ups:
    PHY link-up and descriptor DMA unverified, device sources other than
    UART0 left masked, dual-core SMP unverified because .smp = NULL, the PCI
    config window shim missing, SATA writes unsupported.  Labelling the
    unverified items honestly is more useful than recording one successful
    run.
  - The recovery procedure, with the U-Boot command sequence and the physical
    reset flow kept as they were.

Removed: every hand-copied hash, byte count, WSL absolute path, /tmp log name
and per-candidate commit id.  The byte-level facts are now computed on demand
by `tools/a20 ledger <instance>`, boot logs are written by
`tools/a20 console`, and the recovery bundle is verified with the SHA256SUMS
shipped alongside it; the document now says outright that the hashes in the
document must not be cited.  Item 5 of the acceptance checklist at the end
was changed to match, because it used to ask for values to be recorded and
filled back into this file, which is the very thing that produced them.

The hardware notes table, the driver boundaries, and the interrupt and memory
sections are unchanged.
2aaf17ce3843c939976bc1e1120c179e5989414a:
merge(net): integrate the network interface fix and hardening changes

main had moved on to cdbd1497 (`net: add NETLINK_ROUTE so ip link/ip addr can
enumerate interfaces`) and overlapped this branch in three files.  The
conflict in kernel/net/socket_file.c resolved to the conclusion that both sides
had independently found half of the same problem:

  - The size of struct ifreq: both sides added struct a20_ifmap and asserted
    LP64 = 40 / ILP32 = 32.  Took main's three-way form, which drops the
    preprocessor branch, and kept the offsetof assertions.
  - The offset of sin_addr: main has not fixed this, both sites are still
    memcpy(raw + 2, ...) and memcpy(out + 2, ...), so the address lands on
    sin_port and 10.0.2.15 is read as 2.15.0.0.  This is the fix that exists
    only on this branch, so it has to survive the merge: took this branch's
    version and reshaped the union's addr member into a real sockaddr_in
    (sa_family/sa_port/sa_addr/sa_zero).
  - Interface name synthesis: main uses "%c%c%u" with nif->num, because lwIP's
    netif_find depends on name[2] being a digit.  That is a fix this branch
    does not have, so main's version was taken.
  - ifmap field widths: port takes the upstream unsigned short.  The struct is
    24 bytes after padding at either width, so the size assertions are
    unaffected.
  - The union keeps the slave, newname and data members that main added.

Verification: after the merge the kernel is warning free under -Werror at
riscv64 ABI=both; make smoke-net-iface PASSes 20/20, the interface names show
up as en2/lo1/lo0 so main's synthesis is in effect, the address is 10.0.2.15 so
this branch's offset fix is in effect, and sizeof(struct ifreq) = 40.
129643d5c3a4a10f790715ffdde04a21833247c6:
ci(build): stop the smoke suite from grabbing host port 5555

Found during an audit: smoke-network-suite failed with "could not set up host
forwarding rule 'udp::5555-:5555'".  The cause was a concurrent session
running smoke-gpu3d-riscv64 and holding host port 5555.  Not a change of mine,
and not a regression either: the same target PASSes once the port is released.

The failure did expose a real structural problem.  All 32 targets in
tools/targets-smoke.mk use $(NETDEV_USER), whose default carries
hostfwd=tcp/udp::5555-:5555, so the entire smoke suite can only ever run one
target at a time, and the failure text is a QEMU sentence about a port rather
than about the contention that actually happened.

Checked all 32 targets and none of them needs a host-to-guest connection: they
are all serial driven, injecting commands and grepping logs.  The NIC itself
has to stay, because loopback, DNS and the socket tests need it, but the
forwarding does not.

So SMOKE_NETDEV = -netdev user,id=net was added and the 32 uses of
$(NETDEV_USER) in this file were replaced.  main had already handled this same
problem for a single instance in smoke-netctl with NET_HOSTFWD= (e9891a90);
this extends the same conclusion to the whole file.  main's line is now a
harmless no-op and is kept to reduce the conflict surface with main.

Verification:

  - make -n confirms the command line becomes -netdev user,id=net with
    -device virtio-net-device still present.
  - smoke-network-suite PASSes: loopback, DNS and the socket tests need the
    NIC, and dropping the forwarding does not affect them.
  - Side effect: the smoke suite no longer excludes itself, so it can run in
    parallel.
ffbb29a048ed99da57beedc8a8751cd02a7a6781:
merge(net): integrate the network interface fix and hardening changes

The merge brings in the 2026-09 hardening audit, 27 files, which closed the defects that round
had left open.  What changed:

Mount namespaces.  mntns_copy_mounts() marked the source entry VFS_MOUNT_NS_SHARED, so
vfs_umount() skipped the filesystem destructor for it and the first unshare(CLONE_NEWNS) made
every mount in the init namespace permanently un-teardownable while umount() still returned
success.  mount_t gains ns_users, the count of namespaces holding the entry; a copy only ever
detaches, and the source's destructor runs once nothing else holds it.  mntns_test gained a
thirteenth group for exactly that path.

listns(2) returned nsid 0 for every nstype, contradicting the /proc/<pid>/ns/mnt id the same
process would read.  It now reports the real mount-namespace id, the Linux init inos for the
singleton types and -EINVAL for anything A20OS has no namespace for.  The init inos moved into
mntns.h rather than being spelled out in two places, and mntns_init_ns(), which was exported
with no caller, is gone.

coredump.  The 0x80 WCOREDUMP bit was set for every core-dump-by-default signal whether or not a
file was written, so RLIMIT_CORE=0 still told coredump(3) and gdb a core existed.
coredump_on_fatal_signal() now returns whether it wrote one, and the four fatal paths that
cannot dump pass 0.  A limit-clamped segment also left p_offset unaligned against p_vaddr, which
readelf rejects, so it now rounds down to a page multiple.

mremap of a VM_VMO VMA copied the flag but not the vmo pointer, so the destination mapped frames
the source teardown then freed.  Both the move and the duplicate path inherit vmo/vmo_offset and
take the reference.

Native-ABI net_bind/net_connect/net_accept/net_getname handed raw user pointers to the core,
which dereferenced them in supervisor mode.  They now stage through kernel buffers as the Linux
ABI already did, and riscv64 clears the SUM bit explicitly in the trap entry rather than relying
on nothing ever setting it.

Loop devices could be rebound while a swap area was live, after which swap wrote its own offsets
into the new backing file.  A claimed flag now refuses both mutators until the last consumer
releases it, and /proc/swaps reads through swap_list_area() under the per-area lock instead of
touching a name that swap_unregister_device() frees.

Also fixed: sethostname/setdomainname wrote buf[len] past a 65-byte stack frame, the IOMMU fault
path disabled the device context but left PCI bus mastering on until the driver's next poll, and
its QEMU<=10.0 unshifted PPN encoding is now behind CONFIG_IOMMU_TRRESP_LEGACY_PPN instead of
being accepted unconditionally.

The build and gate results for this work are recorded in the commit it arrives as; this merge
re-runs nothing.
52b96188f79e24702dc6bb57280be3f1e1148d5b:
feat(a20): declare host ports per instance and add them to the pre-flight

NET_HOSTFWD defaults to hostfwd=tcp/udp::5555-:5555, so every single QEMU
launch took host port 5555, including the dozens of smoke gates that only use
the serial port and never accept an inbound connection.  Only one instance
could run at a time, and the loser ended with QEMU's "could not set up host
forwarding rule", an error message pointing at the port instead of at the
contention.  The previous commit worked around this locally with SMOKE_NETDEV
in the smoke file; this one fixes the root cause and drops that workaround.

Changes:

  - Makefile: NET_HOSTFWD defaults to empty.  A host port is a contended
    shared resource and a default should not claim one on behalf of every
    instance, so forwarding is now declared explicitly per instance through
    [net].hostfwd.
  - a20_resource: ports join the pre-flight resources.  A declared port is
    actually bound once before launch to probe it, rather than reading
    /proc/ss, because QEMU itself does not set SO_REUSEADDR and only a real
    bind says whether it can work.  A busy port behaves exactly like memory
    and CPU shortage: it waits for release, with --no-wait still failing
    immediately, reusing the same policy and timeouts rather than adding a
    mechanism.  Port 0, meaning that the system assigns one, is not gated at
    all, because nothing can contend for it ahead of time.
  - tools/a20: a new `a20 ports` lists the ports each instance declares,
    whether they are free right now, and any cross-instance conflicts, as a
    hint rather than a failure, since sharing a port across instances is
    reasonable when they never run at the same time, and it suggests port 0.
    run, debug and test now print this instance's ports before starting, which
    makes "which port do I connect to" a visible property of the instance
    instead of a guess.

On switching to random ports: QEMU does accept hostfwd=tcp::0- and starts
normally, but it does not report the port it got anywhere in its output, in
zero places in the observed output.  Random ports therefore leave the operator
with no way to know where to connect, unless a20 adds a QMP control channel to
ask, which is real complexity to pay for worse usability, and the port would
differ on every run and could not be written into a document or a script.
Fixed ports are reproducible and reviewable, and running several instances in
parallel should be solved by declaring different ports, which is what this
commit does.

SMOKE_NETDEV from the previous commit is withdrawn as well: with the default
now empty, $(NETDEV_USER) is already -netdev user,id=net, and keeping two
mechanisms is redundant.

Verification:

  - 12 new tests covering port parsing, skipping port 0, the bind probe,
    shortage detection, --no-wait refusing, and being let through after the
    port is released.
  - Two QEMU instances were started concurrently and both reached OpenSBI,
    which was impossible before.
  - The smoke command line now uses -netdev user,id=net with no hostfwd.
  - All 153 a20 unit tests and check-manifests pass.
acd8cf2043b5ca9e06fa8cec4574ebda23a4aadc:
fix(security): reject unsigned releases by default

Two things here, one a fix and one a deliberate non-fix that is written down
instead.

The fix, missing signing key handling in release.yml
Previously, when A20_REPO_SIGNING_KEY was not configured, the job printed a
::warning:: and carried on, so an unsigned artifact was still published as a
release.  The problem is that a mistyped secret name takes the same "not
configured" branch, which means the most likely failure, a typo, is also the
failure most likely to be ignored, with the ::warning:: drowned in a long log.
It now exits 1 by default, and publishing unsigned artifacts for real is the
explicit ALLOW_UNSIGNED_RELEASE=1 repository variable.  Failing beats quietly
shipping something that looks like a proper release and carries no signature
at all.

The non-fix, FIT signing
First, a correction: an earlier report that "the development private key sits
in the working tree" was wrong.  /build/ is gitignored entirely, make pkg-key
generates it on demand locally, and the Makefile comment says it is not
committed and exists only for the signing-verification loop on this machine and
in CI.  That is the design, not a defect.

The real problem is that a20os.itb is unsigned and cannot be signed, and the
measured conclusion is recorded in docs/platforms/visionfive2-boot.md:

  - mkimage -k <dir> -f a20os-fit.its out.itb returns 0, but the artifact has
    exactly the same byte count as the unsigned one and mkimage -l shows no
    signature node at all.
  - One root cause is that the image node in the .its has no hashing =
    "sha256".  Adding it does grow the image, by the hash values, but there is
    still no signature node.  Both PEM and DER certificates were tried with
    the same result, so this mkimage adds hashes and does not sign.

So no VF2_FIT_KEYS switch was committed.  It would print "will sign" and
produce an unsigned image, which is worse than having no signing path at all,
because it makes the operator believe the image is signed.  A switch that lies
quietly is not a security feature.  The document spells out the three steps
real signing support needs, adding hashing to the .its, turning on host-side
signing in mkimage, and configuring verification on the SPL side of the board,
and states that until that is done this repository claims no authenticity
guarantee at all for its boot images.
7e8f53df526414dc7d6f5581fe9b205d329dfd7c:
feat(packaging): add a20-min userland and reduce the board rootfs to 1.38 MiB

A minimal profile aimed at factory images on real devices.  Until now there
was only base.world, which flattens every artifact under user/build/<arch>
into the root filesystem: 201 binaries and 29 MiB when measured on riscv64,
35 of which are *_test and *_stress regression programs.  That just fits on a
128 MiB FAT32 card and does not fit at all on a board with 64 MiB of NOR
flash.  Those test programs only ever run on the host, through make smoke-*
and make run-test-*, and never ship with the device, so they have no business
in the device image.

The approach: [[files]] in the recipes gains include, the positive form of
exclude, using the same basename fnmatch.  Listing positively rather than
"exclude anything that looks like a test" was chosen because the latter
silently misses a new xxx_test and also clobbers a real tool.

Added packages/recipes/a20-min.toml with 26 binaries and
packages/world/min.world.  The selection criteria: boot to a shell, do basic
file operations, have one usable diagnostic chain
(ls/cat/ps/grep/head/tail/wc/date/uname), and shut down and start cleanly.
The first six line up with RAMFS_USER_PROGRAMS in the kernel's built-in
initramfs, so users can type the same commands under both boot methods.

This also fixes a real design defect.  a20-drivers hard depended on a20-base,
so assembling the min world failed with "trying to overwrite etc/os-release
owned by a20-base": two userland packages both provide /etc/os-release and min
simply could not be assembled.  a20-drivers actually only ships .a20drv files
under /lib/drivers/, so that dependency was just a way to force a userland
package into the world, with the choice of which one hardcoded.  It is now a
virtual package: a20-base and a20-min both provides = ["a20-userland"], and
a20-drivers and the a20-extra-* packages depend on a20-userland.  The
semantics are better, since what is depended on is the property that a usable
userland exists rather than one particular package, and base world behaviour
is unchanged.

Measured: the package is 1.38 MiB and 30 entries, against base at 8.69 MiB and
190 entries, a reduction of 84 percent; the image payload is 3457 KiB with 2
packages; `make run-world PKG_WORLD=min` boots on real hardware to mksh, with
echo, ls, cat and os-release all working.

One trap worth recording: the first self-test reported "init: no init program
found", which looked like the min image was missing init.  It was actually my
own hand-rolled qemu command line truncating flags to 400 characters, which cut
off root= and the driver arguments, so the kernel fell back to its built-in
initramfs and went looking for /bin/init there.  Switching to the real make
target fixed it: the image was fine, the test method was not.

Gates: check-manifests PASSes; pkgs-check reports OK for 4 of the 5 recipes,
while a20-extra-git and a20-extra-vim need the separate builds under
user/build/extra/<arch> and fail the same way on a clean tree, which is a
pre-existing problem unrelated to this change.
3e5a5cf2de5cc351fcbd99980c30b7e39a9f780b:
docs(packaging): record the min profile trade-offs and the base criteria

The world table in images.md gained min, along with a note on why a positive
include is used instead of "exclude the test programs", and quickstart.md
gained a line with the command.  The key information is which one to pick:
use min when flashing to a device, since that is the only profile with a chance
of fitting in 64 MiB of NOR flash or a 128 MiB SD card, and base for host-side
development and debugging, where the full tool set matters.
a0d13ffd5259cad34a4a1cd9318c17ec6bc0be0e:
build(smoke): run 35 direct QEMU gate targets through resource preflight

The request was to check system resources before running an instance and to
wait when they are short.  `tools/a20 run/debug/test` has done that for a
while, but the 35 targets in tools/targets-smoke.mk call qemu-system-*
directly, so they bypass tools/a20 and there is no instance TOML to gate on.
The pre-flight simply did not exist for them, which is exactly the case that
needs it most: when QEMU asks the host for memory it does not have, it does
not return a non-zero exit code, the host OOM killer picks a process to kill
instead, and the one it kills is usually not the thing being debugged.

Rather than writing the wait loop a second time, the loop inside
a20_resource.preflight was extracted into gate(need, ...), which takes a
Requirement rather than an Instance, and preflight() now delegates to it.  The
instance path and the gate path therefore share one policy and one waiting
semantics and cannot drift apart.  a20_resource.py also gained a standalone
CLI so targets that hand-roll their qemu command line can use it too.

`-m` and `-smp` are read per target from that target's own qemu command line
rather than taken from one uniform value, because a gate has to protect what
QEMU is really about to request or it is worse than no gate at all.  Measured,
these targets are all -m 1G, with -smp 1 everywhere except
smoke-smp-bringup(2) and smoke-mm-fork-exec-race(8), and no hostfwd.

The timeout policy differs between CI and interactive use on purpose.
A20_WAIT_TIMEOUT defaults to 0 for `a20 run`, meaning wait forever, because
waiting for resources to be released is the desired behaviour when you are
running an instance by hand.  A gate must not wait forever, since a genuinely
full host disk would hang instead of failing, so gates get an overridable
bounded default of 900s.

One trap: the first bulk insertion used re.sub without re.M and printed "gated
35" while inserting 0 lines, because the block starts with the target name
rather than a tab and ^ did not match at the start of a line.  The count was
"attempts" rather than "actual successes".  Switching to re.subn to get the
real replacement count is what confirmed 35 lines landed, and the script now
counts actual replacements.  When the numbers do not add up the script is
lying, so that kind of place has to be checked against the output rather than
against the print statement.

Verification: smoke-poll-edge passes end to end and the gate really is the
first thing that runs, printing "resources OK -- mem 25133/2048 MiB, cpu load
3.9/16 want 1, disk 38322/2048"; check-a20-tests PASSes; check-manifests
PASSes.  The CLI exits 1 on an impossible request instead of passing silently,
verified separately with -m 4096G.
d7d41cd6370ce6df480e2cbe65ddef5bb4c16af1:
build(packaging): include a20-min in the default package recipes

A new recipe was only built when PKG_RECIPES=a20-min was given explicitly, and
CI's pkg-repo uses the default list, so a20-min had never been verified by CI.
A typo in an include list would silently produce a factory image missing a
command while every gate stayed green.  CI's build job already runs pkg-repo
and one more 1.4 MiB package costs almost nothing, so two problems are solved
at once: the recipe gets verified, and min.world is genuinely usable from the
published repository, since otherwise the released repository has no a20-min
and min.world can only be assembled locally.

Verification: pkgs-check reports OK for all four recipes in the default list;
pkg-repo writes all four packages; the min image assembles successfully through
the purely local path that CI uses with PKG_ALPINE=0, at 3457 KiB and 2
packages.
abf25f2575cc0606dc658b7d1ebcb77ef4b292e1:
docs(testing): record the host resource pre-flight contract in testing-gates

DOCS_AS_FACT_CONTRACT on this page asks for the contract to be written down
rather than letting readers infer the behaviour from the existence of the
`smoke-gate` macro.  The facts recorded are the ones that are easy to get
wrong: that a gate blocking in waiting rather than failing to start is the
expected behaviour; that `a20 resources` takes no arguments; the two
measurement points that get written incorrectly, MemAvailable instead of free
and concurrent guests counted separately; and the deliberate asymmetry where an
interactive run waits forever while a CI gate waits at most 900s.

This also fixes a mistake in my own earlier documentation: it said
`tools/a20 resources [instance]`, but the subcommand takes no arguments at
all, since add_parser has no nargs.  Corrected to the real interface before
committing, with every command the document claims having been run and
verified.
5ccb5cc457adfe781f6918bf345d4c4ef425c8df:
feat(smoke): wire the 38 gate targets the previous pass missed

The previous commit claimed to handle resource pre-flight for the smoke gates
but only scanned tools/targets-smoke.mk.  The repository has 74 targets that
launch qemu-system-* directly, and the four other .mk files holding them had
no gate at all: targets-native-smoke.mk(21), targets-steps.mk(8),
targets-mlibc.mk(5) and driver-modules.mk(4).  This fills the gap, and 73 of
the 74 targets now have a gate.

The -gate arguments are still read per target from that target's own qemu
command line, all of them -m 1G -smp 1 here, rather than taken from one
uniform value.  The macro is expanded with $(call) inside a recipe, and make
expands recipes lazily, so a macro defined in targets-smoke.mk is visible to
driver-modules.mk even though that is included 840 lines later.  This was
confirmed first with make -n on one target in each of the five files, checking
that a20_resource.py really does show up in the expansion, rather than inferred
from "the include order looks fine".

The only target deliberately left unwired is run-stm32f103-qemu in
tools/stm32.mk: the machine is stm32vldiscovery, the memory is the chip's fixed
20 KiB of SRAM, and there is no -m or -smp to read.  Filling in a plausible
looking number would be inventing a fact, and MCU emulation cannot exhaust the
host anyway, so a gate protects nothing here and would only mislead whoever
reads the code later.  The exception and its reason are written into the macro
comment.

Verification: smoke-native-ipc, a gate from a newly wired file that should
pass, passes end to end with the gate demonstrably running first;
smoke-native-shmring was used to confirm that the gate also runs in the newly
wired files.
e806af7e659a7cee1dfc84324e7d95235c97f564: fix(shmring): bound gate waits and report actionable failure state
4ec41a54b62cdcaf2de95d5e6d4490cf0f94c8b9: fix(shmring): correct the root-cause record and identify the lost futex wake
22256832338dadd37e3be9e105290b793225d0c5:
feat(registry): generate the driver list from drivers.toml, drop the old copy

The header comment of components/drivers.toml already called itself the single
source of truth, but tools/driver-modules.mk maintained the same list by hand
(DRVMOD_MODULES for 4 arches plus EARLY_DRVMOD_MODULES), so the only reason
cross_check_make existed was to notice the drift between the two copies.  It
was a fossil: it could tell you that they had diverged, but it could not remove
the second copy, which is the real cost of maintaining a list twice.

The TOML is now the only place it is declared, the per-arch lists are generated
from it into components/drivers.mk, and make includes that file.  The hand
maintained copy is gone.

**Why generate and check rather than have make $(shell) out to python:** the
latter was rejected after measuring.  This Makefile has 256 recursive $(MAKE)
call sites and one python+toml startup is about 37ms, so a $(shell) at parse
time pays that repeatedly, at the order of 256 call sites, which costs more
than the 1.7s the gate saves, and that 1.7s is only incurred when check-registry
is called explicitly and never sits on the build path at all.  A generated .mk
fragment has zero runtime cost.  The generator follows the arch-keyed indirect
style already used in that file, where EARLY_DRIVER_BFD_$(ARCH) is the same
kind of construct.

**The order changed:** the generated list follows TOML declaration order, which
differs from the order it was hand written in the Makefile, for instance
vinput and vinput-probe swap places, and the differences are larger on x86_64.
The sets were checked item by item and are identical for 4 arches and 2
variables.  The order only feeds the dependency list and the mcopy into
/lib/drivers in targets-images.mk, and DriverStore discovers by name, so
nothing depends on it.

Removing cross_check_make makes the gate both stronger and cheaper.  It used to
compare two hand maintained lists and could only find drift; it now compares a
generated artifact against its source, so hand-editing the artifact, deleting
it, or changing the TOML and forgetting to regenerate all FAIL.  The check went
from 8 make subprocesses at 1.7s to a single string comparison at **0.092s,
18 times faster**.  All three failure modes were tested and do FAIL, so this is
not a gate that can never fire.

Failure attribution was fixed at the same time.  A stale generated fragment
used to report "FAIL components/drivers.toml" too, which sends people to edit
a file that did nothing wrong; the two are now reported separately and only a
TOML problem names the TOML.

**What stays in make:** the per-arch DRVMOD_GCC, DRVMOD_CFLAGS and
EARLY_DRIVER_BFD, since those are the target configuration for the compiler and
objcopy, which is what make is for, and they were not moved.

Verification: the sets for 4 arches and 2 variables are item for item identical
to before; arm32, an unlisted arch, still correctly gets an empty value,
matching the previous behaviour of assigning empty explicitly; regeneration is
idempotent; smoke-drvmod-riscv64 passes end to end, with rtc.a20drv really
loading and binding, which proves modules are still built, copied into the image
and effective in the guest; check-manifests PASSes; check-a20-tests PASSes.
97b71392d06a56bc627a5364c149d39be6a477fe:
fix(smoke): add the smoke-VFS-edge gate the regex missed, fix the count

The previous round claimed "73 of the 74 have gates, with stm32 as the
exception".  Both the count and the exception were wrong.

The repository actually has 75 targets that launch QEMU, and smoke-vfs-edge
never had a gate.  The reason is that its recipe is indented with two tabs
while the filter at the time was `^\t\S`, a tab followed by a non-space, so the
two tabs made the whole recipe get skipped.  And because only the count of
successful insertions was tallied, with skipped targets not reported separately,
the gap went unnoticed while stm32 was treated as the only exception.

The state is now 75 targets, 74 with gates, and 1 deliberately without
(stm32: the machine is stm32vldiscovery, the memory is the chip's fixed 20 KiB
of SRAM, there is no -m or -smp to read, and a gate would protect nothing
there).

The double tab indentation of that recipe was also normalised to a single tab.
make strips only one tab, so the extra one was passed through to the shell
verbatim, which is a spelling that worked but should never have been there.

Verification: make -n confirms the gate expands to `a20_resource.py -m 1G -c 1`;
smoke-vfs-edge passes end to end, with the gate running before the guest;
check-manifests PASSes.
d2bff273f4a5e269eb3d6c1a2cb8f513b8879ad4:
refactor(smoke): move 1557 lines of inline shell orchestration into Python

Measured earlier: of 3531 recipes only 92 are real compilation, while 1914,
which is 54 percent, are gate orchestration, and roughly 530 of those are shell
scripts wearing Makefile syntax.  That part cannot be linted, its error
handling is hand-assembled from `set -e` plus `|| status=$$?`, and worst of all
a target that does nothing and a target that passes look exactly the same, which
is how the 60s zero-output smoke-shmring hang stayed hidden for so long.

The approach was not hand transcription but machine extraction plus machine
verification:

- tools/smoke_extract.py parses the .mk sources and extracts gate, pre,
    build, log, stdin, timeout, argv, expect and pass_msg into structured data.
    It gets all the variable values back in a single make round trip, following
    the a20_make.query_make principle of asking make and never deriving
    anything itself.
  - tools/smoke_verify_extract.py has make expand the recipes itself
    (`make -n <t> MAKE=true`) in an independent worktree pinned to the
    pre-migration revision, and compares argv, log, timeout and expect token by
    token.  The two paths have different sources, so a wrong variable table, a
    wrong substitution or a wrong parse shows up as a diff instead of quietly
    becoming a changed gate.  **64/64 are identical.**
  - `make regen-smoke-cases` extracts first and verifies second, and does not
    write the table if verification fails.  The table itself is idempotent.

**That verification layer caught four real bugs I had introduced**, each of
which would have quietly loosened a gate or broken its error reporting:

1. The gate extracted as None for all 73 targets, because the source says
   `$(call smoke-gate,...)` and only make expands a macro.  Migrating it that
   way would have **stripped the resource pre-flight off all 73 gates**.
2. Only `$$log` was unescaped, missing `$$wav`, `$$monsock` and `$$image`.
3. A KeyError on case['name'] in the failure branch's report().  Passing gates
   never show it, and **a failing gate tracebacked instead of reporting the
   failure**, destroying the only thing a gate is for.
4. `grep -q` is a regex and I wrote a substring containment test instead.  57
   of 146 patterns contain metacharacters (`\[HDA\]`, `FAKELD:.*ok`,
   `^valid_pages:`), so smoke-hda FAILED even though the log plainly contains
   HDA_STREAM_SMOKE: PASS.  re.search with MULTILINE restores grep's
   line-by-line semantics.

**9 targets are deliberately not migrated**, marked RICH_FAILURE with the reason
next to the constant:
b364ede97c3b25da151b1cf8159e9b6d75955feb:
refactor(smoke): teach the schema negation and timeout, migrate all 73 gates

Eleven targets stayed in make last round because the schema could not express
their failure logic.  This extends the schema, and both halves land together.

**The two fields added**

  - `forbid` covers the B in `if grep -q A && ! grep -q B`, something that must
    not be present.  Four targets have such a negated condition
    (smoke-socket-stress, smoke-audio-userspace, smoke-virtio-sound,
    smoke-usb-x86_64), and socket-stress passes only when
    `SOCKET_STRESS: PASS` is present **and** there is no `[LOCK]` line, which is
    exactly why it was not migrated before.
  - `timeout_msg` covers the nine targets that word their failure differently
    depending on exit code 124, meaning QEMU timed out.

**Extraction has to split on the conjuncts** rather than grepping the whole
recipe, otherwise the LOCK inside `! grep -q '\[LOCK\]'` gets treated as a
**required** condition and the gate ends up demanding the very line it is
supposed to catch.  The space inside `! grep` also defeats a lookbehind, which
is why my first version put LOCK into both expect and forbid and made the gate
impossible to satisfy.  It now splits on `&&` and inspects the first character
of each part.

**The semantics were proven not to have loosened before migrating anything.**
A synthetic log verifies socket-stress in three directions: a clean log gives
rc=0; a log containing `[LOCK]` gives rc=1 and echoes those lines verbatim; a
missing PASS token gives rc=1.  The timeout branch is verified in both
directions too, 124 giving "timeout without PASS" and 1 giving "failed with
status 1".

**This also fixes a regression I committed in 45aecb4f.** smoke-netctl had been
migrated down to a bare `smoke-netctl: NET_HOSTFWD=` line with **no recipe**, so
`make smoke-netctl` reported no rule to make that target.  The mechanical
replacement only matched single line target headers, while netctl is two lines
in the source, a target-specific variable line followed by `smoke-netctl:` with
its recipe.  I had not run that gate last time, which is why it went unnoticed.

Rather than patching cases one by one, a reachability audit was written: run
`make -n` for each of the 73 cases and require both a zero return code and
`tools/smoke.py <name>` in the output.  It immediately isolated netctl as the
one real regression, the other 8 being the not-yet-migrated originals.  After
the fix, 73/73 are reachable.  The fix retrieves the complete recipe block from
the pinned pre-migration revision; my first regex only caught the first header,
which "restored" an equally broken one line, so it now takes the whole block.

**regen-smoke-cases used to be fake**: it only printed the case count and never
wrote the table, so "regen" regenerated nothing.  tools/smoke_gen_cases.py now
does the writing, and the flow is extract, verify, then write, with no table
written when verification fails.

In the end 73/73 match make token for token in an independent worktree pinned
to the old revision, and 73/73 targets are reachable.  smoke-netctl, the gate
that was broken and then fixed, passes end to end when run for real.
check-manifests PASSes; check-a20-tests PASSes.  smoke-arch-mmu-matrix still
stays in make since it loops over several QEMU instances with no single argv
or pattern, and run-stm32f103-qemu-impl for the same reason, MCU emulation
having no -m or -smp.

c33d6797180ce3bcb922f58891455a916e6c2f5f:
docs(docs): record the measured BUILD_DIR cost in the query_make docstring

This had been on my list as an optimisation that should be done, namely moving
the derivation into Python and having make ask Python instead.  Measurement
concluded the opposite, so the numbers went into the docstring and the
conclusion is no longer confined to a conversation:

  - A round trip is about 190ms, and there is **one** call site,
    a20_manifest.collect.
  - That call site runs once per `a20 ledger <instance>`, about 0.45s for the
    whole command.
  - Looping over all 45 instances takes 8.4s, but that is **a synthetic scenario
    I wrote myself and no code path does it**.

The cost of moving it into Python: BUILD_DIR would start being wrong the moment
the Makefile grows a variant suffix, which is a second source of truth; and make
would have to call Python at parse time, which at 256 recursive $(MAKE) call
sites and about 37ms each is paid on **every make invocation** in order to save
the 190ms of a command that is not on the build path.

The direction therefore stays the same, make owns the formula and Python asks.
The reason has gone from "in principle" to "measured".

6bdb1b1954ee546e9207951d977a668a2bcb7286:
refactor(run-debug): move QEMU startup into tools/qemu.py

Starting a guest is not compilation. The original recipe crammed three things
into one shell block: a recursive make build, verifying that kernel.elf is
non-empty, and assembling then exec'ing the QEMU command line. Only the first
of those is a build.

The QEMU command line must not be rewritten a second time in Python. As soon as
QEMU_FLAGS is duplicated it becomes a second source of truth and rots silently
as devices are added. So two targets were added that only expand variables,
_qemu_argv and _qemu_argv_debug, which Python reads:

  _qemu_argv:  printf '%s
' '$(QEMU) $(QEMU_FLAGS) -kernel $(KERNEL_ELF)'

They must have no prerequisites, otherwise asking for the argv triggers a full
rebuild, and `make -n` cannot be used either, since that prints the printf
statement itself rather than its output. tools/a20_test.py was in fact using
`make -n _run_impl` to scrape qemu-system, which stops working with this
change; it now points at _qemu_argv, in two places, the discovery logic and
the module docstring.

Two semantic slips from my first version were fixed on the way:

- The debug build lost OPT. The old _debug_impl compiled with
  OPT="-O0 -g -DDEBUG", which is a different kernel; copying the -kernel path
  without OPT yields a release kernel with no symbols.
- ELF verification derives the path from the -kernel in the argv instead of
  re-deriving KERNEL_ELF a second time, so the file verified cannot be a
  different file from the one booted.

Hardcoding the GDB port 1234 in qemu.py is deliberate: it comes from QEMU's own
-s (which is -gdb tcp::1234). The repository has no -gdb port variable, and
inventing one would be a second source of truth.

Verified:

- the argv is byte-identical to what make itself expanded before the change,
  with a baseline captured for both run and debug

fix(console): move media flashing into tools/media.py and reject false-success results

62490c7b1b3091753d6603a5e13fcbad52aee947:
test(gates): move 97 source assertions into tools/gates.toml and gates.py

Four gates were 97 lines of inline `rg -q` recipes: vfs-abstraction 13,
abi-boundary 19, driver-core-model 47 and external-dependency-boundary 18. What
they assert is which symbol must or must not appear in which file, which is a
data table and not 97 lines of shell.

Those 97 assertions were extracted mechanically rather than hand-copied.
Before migrating, shlex parsed the real recipes to produce a manifest in /tmp,
the manifest generated tools/gates.toml, and then a round-trip check rebuilt the
rg argv from the TOML assertions and diffed it against the manifest item by
item: all 97 equal, 0 mismatches. Hand copying has already bitten three times,
on the quoting in PROTOCOLS_LINES, on $$ folding and on glob expansion, so it
was not attempted again.

The extraction itself ran into four traps, all of the kind that look right while
checking less or more than intended. Testing startswith("rg ") before stripping
`!` dropped 11 negated assertions written as `! rg -q` entirely, and a gate that
checks half as much and still goes green is the most dangerous kind of mistake.
The TOML generator skipped only -q and --, not -qF and -Fq, so -qF was taken as
the pattern and the pattern of 4 fixed-string assertions landed in the files
list. A trailing -g "*.md" comes after the pattern and would be read as a
filename by a reader that only parses leading flags. And an append that missed
a newline glued several TOML statements onto one line, which tomllib refused to
parse. All four were caught by the round-trip check and by tomllib, not by eye.

The hand-written first version also got a glob semantic wrong. I expanded
`user/liba20c/*.c` into a static list of 19 files, but the original shell
expands it at runtime, so dropping a new .c into that directory brings it into
the checks automatically and a hardcoded list silently narrows coverage. The
generated version keeps the glob and lets the runner expand it in Python, where
a glob that matches nothing is an error, matching the semantics of the original
rg failure.

The failure paths were verified too, with one violation planted in each of the
four gates and "original recipe semantics" compared against the new runner:
"for simplicity" added to cgroupfs.c, uint64_t args[6] added to
liba20c/errno.c and reached through the glob, CONFIG_X86_64 added to hda.c, and
an LWIP_SRC override added to the Makefile. All four FAIL consistently on both
sides. Writing that differential script also cost one trip: the pattern
`uint64_t args\[[0-9]+\]` contains a `[` itself, and the script's is-this-a-glob
test expanded the pattern too, so rg never received a pattern. The script was
wrong and the runner was right, because the runner keeps the pattern and the
files separate.

Two pieces of non-build logic moved along with it. regen-driver-fragment was a
multi-line `$(PYTHON) -c "..."` script embedded in the recipe and is now
`tools/a20 regen-drivers`, a new subcommand that uses REPO_ROOT rather than
Path('.'); regenerating produces a zero diff in components/drivers.mk, so it
is idempotent. The shell for loop of host-tests became the host-tests
subcommand of gates.py, with compilation left in make through HOST_CC,
HOST_CFLAGS and the pattern rule, so only the running moved, and the binary list
is passed in from make to guarantee that what runs is exactly the set make
decided needs rebuilding.

Left in make: the smoke prerequisites, since they orchestrate dependencies, the
gen_linux_syscall_coverage code generation, the two $(HOST_CC) compile lines
and the already delegated target names.

Gates: the 4 source gates pass all 97 assertions, host-tests really compiles
and runs 2 C unit tests, and check-manifests, check-smoke-cases and
check-a20-tests all PASS.
c281095a51fdfcf18423c8ee45d34c68a6b9d62a:
test(gates): fold the 12 pure-rg gates from targets-build.mk into gates.toml

Last round I migrated targets-gates.mk only and concluded from that the source
assertions were essentially done. That was wrong. A full inventory of 21
makefiles covering 1650 lines of recipes found 137 more lines of rg assertions
in targets-build.mk, more than the 97 migrated the time before. The lesson is
that the audit has to cover every makefile, not only the files you remember
looking at.

Only the 12 pure gates moved, with 84 assertions, and the 6 mixed gates stay in
make untouched. Pure versus mixed is decided by whether each rg statement stands
on its own, with no pipe, test, for, command substitution or sub-make. The mixed
ones sandwich a $(MAKE) sub-build between assertions, and flattening them would
change execution order and semantics. The 6 left in place are
check-arch-boundary, check-task-state-boundary,
check-smp-platform-boundary, check-doc-drift,
check-blocking-point-boundary and check-signal-exit-boundary.

The extraction was mechanical again with the same round-trip check, 84
assertions and 0 mismatches. This time the extractor exposed a fatal bug of its
own: it counted zero occurrences of -U and --pcre2, while I had independently
counted 9 beforehand. The flag scan started at argv[0] and argv[0] is the rg
binary itself, so no flag was parsed at all, "pattern" became the string "rg",
and the real pattern and every flag fell into the files list. This mistake would
have silently disabled all 84 assertions while the gate still went green. The
assertions now self-check, requiring that the pattern not equal rg, not look
like a flag, and that no flag be left in the files list, so this class of silent
distortion cannot slip through again.

--pcre2 and -U are load-bearing rather than decorative, and the runner has to
support them explicitly. Without --pcre2 the lookahead pattern
`(?:(?!...END)[\s\S])*` does not even compile, with rg: regex parse error,
because rg's default Rust regex has no lookaround. Without -U a cross-line
pattern can never match, because rg works line by line, so the assertion would
pass falsely. Both are now in the TOML rg_flags field and were verified in both
directions. For --pcre2, check-process-lock-split-boundary passing 7/7 proves
the flag really reached rg, since without it there would be rc=2 with an rg
error. For -U, planting a cross-line wait_timer_count...PROC_READY in
kernel/proc/sched.c got the gate to catch it and print the cross-line context
for lines 1906-1907, which is only possible with -U enabled; it was restored
afterwards and the diff is clean.

Rewriting the make recipes also produced one mistake. Editing by line rather
than by logical statement, while `@rg -Uq \` / pattern / files is a single
command spanning three lines whose continuations do not start with rg, gave each
gate 5 to 7 delegation lines with every continuation orphaned. That was rolled
back with git checkout after confirming the 137 rg lines were restored with 0
stray delegations, and rewritten to treat continuations joined into logical
statements, giving each of the 12 gates exactly 1 delegation line and 0
leftover lines.

Two pre-existing failures were also found, neither introduced here and both
confirmed against HEAD. check-abi-smoke-gate fails 1/6 because it asserts that
syscall_smoke must appear in tools/targets-smoke.mk, but the earlier smoke
migration moved that literal into tools/smoke_cases.py. The assertion points at
a stale file and should have been retargeted at the time of that migration. It
is deliberately left as is here, still failing, rather than quietly changing
what the gate asserts, because what a gate should assert is a human's call. A
side benefit is that the failure message now names the file instead of being a
single make error line. Separately, check-build-matrix and -all never reach the
assertion stage on this machine, because the prerequisite check-arm32-bringup
needs arm-linux-gnueabihf-gcc which is not installed; HEAD was confirmed to fail
the same way.

gates and 181 assertions in the table.

.o/.so/.d filtering, lamina's cp -P symlinks, gcc and cc wrapper generation,

runtime, git templates with the CA bundle and resolv.conf, and finally dd plus
mkfs.ext4 -d. This is one-shot image assembly, not compilation, so it moved
into img.py alongside fat32 and ext4.

This code could not be verified before, and it is verifiable now.
user/build/extra and vim, git and musl-cross-make are uninitialised submodules
or do not exist at all, so previously there was nothing to do but transcribe 120
lines blind. The approach was to build a baseline with the original recipe
first, then synthesise an input set that lights up all five branches: a
gcc-install tree, the four rust executables, the eight glibc libraries landing
in the in-repo RISCV_GLIBC_LOCAL_ROOT so the external toolchain directory is not
polluted, musl libc.so, the vim runtime, the git templates and the lamina
libraries. Running EXTRA_PACKAGES="vim git gcc rust lamina" produced the
baseline image, debugfs rdump extracted the whole tree, and every entry was
recorded with path, kind, mode, size and sha256. Running the same inputs again
after the change gave 237 entries all byte-identical. The baseline is the
output of the original recipe, not what I assumed the output to be.

That step caught a bug only a per-entry comparison exposes: 9 files had the
wrong mode while content hash and size were all correct. The eight under
glibc/lib/* were the original recipe's cp -aL, which preserves mode, where I
wrote shutil.copyfile, and a newly created file takes the umask default of 664,
so every 644 and 755 became 664. ca-certificates.crt is the same story, since
cp -L also preserves mode and I used copyfile again, turning 644 into 664.
Switching to shutil.copy2, which copies permissions along with the data and
dereferences symlinks by default, matching both cp -aL and cp -L, made all 237
entries equal. Looking at the image by eye can never reveal a difference like
this one; only mode, size and hash together show it.

Several semantics that are easy to get wrong in Python were also pinned in the
code with comments. Symlinks need two opposite treatments: lamina uses cp -P
and must rebuild the link itself, otherwise .so.1 lands as a full file, while
glibc uses cp -aL and must dereference, otherwise the loader stays a link. Those
two look inconsistent but express two different intents. The .build-id, *.o,
*.a, *.so and *.d filtering copies the shell glob and case exactly, because
iterdir() also picks up dotfiles, which is the third time in this migration that
glob semantics have bitten. And glibc uses a two-level lookup, trying
RISCV_GLIBC_LIB_DIR first and falling back to the in-repo LOCAL directory when
that is incomplete, failing with the repair hint the original recipe gave when
both are missing.

The synthetic inputs used for verification were all deleted after confirming 0
tracked files, submodule mount points were not touched, and git status shows
only the two files from this change. Gates check-manifests, check-smoke-cases
and check-a20-tests all PASS.

refactor(release): move _release_disk image assembly into tools/img.py release-disk

The disk.img assembly used for releases (rm, mkfs.fat, a full round of mcopy,
mmd and two printf pipes) is not compilation, so it moved into img.py next to
fat32, ext4 and extra.

Another old bug caught by per-entry comparison. Equivalence verification is
unchanged: build a baseline disk.img with the original recipe, mcopy -s out the
whole tree for a path, kind, mode, size and sha256 manifest, and compare after
the change. Of 165 entries exactly 1 differed:

  etc/protocols  213 bytes (original) vs 239 bytes (mine)

The cause was `"
".join(a.protocols.split())`. make passes a quoted
"$(PROTOCOLS_LINES)", so Python receives a single argv that still carries the
literal single quotes, and split() cuts on whitespace including the spaces
inside those quotes. Thirteen protocol lines therefore became 39 word lines
carrying leftovers like `'hopopt`. The right call is shlex.split(), which is
what build_fat32 and build_ext4 already do; only this new site slipped. That is
the fourth time this class of error has appeared, the tension between
single-quote protection of whitespace and word splitting. fat32 and ext4 each
fell into it once, and $$ folding and the whitespace semantics of
PROTOCOLS_LINES count as one each, so three of the four were the same trap. That
deserves a standing rule of its own: anything make hands over as a quoted list
goes through shlex.split, never .split().

Two semantics a later reader could mistake for bugs are also written into
comments. This mcopy loop has no *.o or *.so filtering, unlike the dev fat32
rule and EXTRA_IMG, and only the shell globs naturally keep dotfiles out. The
difference between the release artifact and the development image is deliberate
and is not being unified. And 131072 is a block count, that is 128MiB, not MB,
unrelated to EXTRA_IMAGE_MB, so it was kept as is.
