6b51037120bcc4356651cffdb45b7e835d0af508:
refactor(dev): move the two incremental build stamp checks into tools/stamps.py

$(USER_BUILD_STAMP) and $(NATIVE_BUILD_STAMP) are hand-written decisions about
whether to recompile: compare the build id inside the stamp, check whether the
expected binary is there, and check whether any source file is newer than the
stamp. Each was 20 to 30 lines of shell and moved into Python; the actual
compilation is still make's sub-build and was not touched.

What was worth moving is the find half. It was

  find <dirs> \( -path '*/.git' -o -path 'user/build' -o -path 'user/external/musl/build-*' \) \
       -prune -o -type f -newer <stamp> -print -quit | grep -q .

with the prune expression, -print -quit and the grep pipe stacked on top of each
other, which is both impossible to see and impossible to test when it goes
wrong.

I got this -newer logic wrong three times in my own implementation and only
controlled cases exposed it. The prune test compared os.path.relpath(dirpath,
REPO) against the absolute skip paths, so once the tree sits outside the
repository relpath becomes ../../.. and never matches, the prune is dead code,
and user/build and the musl build directories are still walked. Switching to
fnmatch then ran abspath over the wildcard entries as well, freezing '*/.git'
into a literal path and breaking the glob. And the relative glob
'user/external/musl/build-*' compared against an absolute directory also never
matches.

The final rule has three classes: entries that are already absolute, or that
start with * and are kept unanchored so any depth matches, pass through as is,
while other relative entries are anchored to REPO with os.path.join, which
preserves the wildcard. Seven controlled cases cover no-newer, newer, a literal
skip, a nested skip, a glob skip and a missing stamp, and all are correct.

This one nearly caused a serious regression, since any_newer returning always
true means a full userland rebuild on every build. The most important
verification is therefore bidirectional: two consecutive stamp decisions must
both report up to date and must not trigger a rebuild, which held in practice,
and touching user/cmds/net/wget.c must trigger a rebuild, which it did. Both
have to hold before this stamp logic can be considered alive.

NATIVE_BINS is new in the Makefile and contains only the 23 binaries the
original rule tested. The Makefile defines 30 NATIVE_*_BIN variables in total
and putting all of them in would make the gate stricter than before, which is a
behaviour change, so they were extracted from the original rule one by one
rather than swept up with a regex.

The same argparse trap appeared a third time: OPT defaults to -O3 and a value
starting with - is not taken as an option value unless it is written
--opt="$(OPT)". That was fixed for stm32 and repeated here, and the = form is
used in both places now.

One honest note. Twice in this round I took a bug in my test scaffolding for a
bug in the code. Once I passed a relative path where an absolute one was
expected, so REPO/src did not exist and the newer case always measured False.
Once I called touch() forgetting that it defaults to newer=True while marking
the case as no-newer. Both times a re-measurement showed the code was right
and the test was wrong. When a test conclusion does not hold, suspect the test
first.

refactor(extra): move EXTRA_IMAGE_STAMP input list generation into tools/stamps.py

The mtime format hit a trap that had to be measured. find's %T@ prints 10
decimal places while st_mtime_ns only has 9 significant decimals. The first

user record is off by a little, which is almost impossible to see by eye.

a21e88ac45e77324d056a0cd5b72ca99c3f8a6fe:
docs(kernel): document the contracts the code silently assumed

Comments only. Every addition replaces either nothing or a one-line
restatement, and each states a fact that cannot be recovered from the
code: a failure mode, a wire offset, a register encoding.

Page-table and MM contracts:

- pt_walk() returns an interior pointer into a live page table, so the
  caller must pin the address space; a leaf found at an intermediate level
  means a huge page covers the address, which pt_walk cannot express, so it
  returns NULL and the caller must fall back to pt_lookup_leaf(). Returning
  the huge-page PTE would let a caller write a level-0 entry into it.
- pt_destroy_level() skips leaves on purpose -- their frames belong to the
  VMA backing store -- and turns a corrupt child pointer into a leak rather
  than a wild free.
- vma_can_merge() gained its reasoning. Every early return is a correctness
  precondition, notably that SysV segments are keyed by shmid rather than
  file offset, so two adjacent segments must stay separable for
  shmctl(IPC_RMID).
- core/sync.c: the recursive-acquisition path was documented as a feature.
  It is a workaround for a layering violation, and making the lock
  reentrant hides the reentrancy from the check-mm-lock-model audit. The
  comment now says so and names the real fix.
- File headers for mm/mm.c, mm/mm.c's sibling mm/vm.c and user/init.c.
  79% of kernel files still lack one; PID 1 had none, and its header records
  that the kernel gives PID 1 no default signal dispositions.
- Dropped three empty #ifdef blocks left over from earlier refactors.

SysV SHM wire format (verified against user/external/musl, not from memory):

The shmctl(2) reply must match the struct the *caller* declared. musl and
glibc agree on a 48-byte ipc_perm and a 112-byte shmid_ds, which is what the
code emits; it is deliberately NOT Linux's internal 96-byte shmid64_ds. The
comment says so explicitly, because "fixing" this against
include/uapi/linux/shm.h would silently break every musl program.

IPC_64_BIT also turns out to be load-bearing rather than decorative: musl's
IPC_CMD degenerates to `cmd | 0x100` on every 64-bit arch, so the strip is
mandatory.

Two real defects found while documenting, recorded in place and NOT fixed
here because they change syscall behaviour:

- sysv_shm.c SHM_INFO copies 64 bytes into a 48-byte struct shm_info, a
  16-byte kernel-to-user overflow.
- sysv_msg.c never masks IPC_64_BIT, so every msgctl from a musl caller
  lands in `default:` and returns -EINVAL.

MMIO and register decoding: 662 comment lines across stm32_uart.c, e1000.c,
starfive_gmac.c, ls2k_gmac.c, both riscv PLIC irqchip files and the
LoongArch PCIe host. stm32_uart.c had essentially none. The PLLMUL field is
an *encoding*, not a multiplier (codes 0..13 are x2..x15, 14 and 15 both x16),
so a literal reading scales the whole clock tree and every BRR with it.
riscv32/trap/irqchip.c is a copy of the riscv64 file whose comments had been
stripped; it is now at parity apart from the SMP handler riscv32 lacks.

syscall_table.def gained a header. It is #included three times under
different LINUX_SYSCALL macro definitions, so a careless edit fails in three
confusing places. The header also records that column 2 is
restores_context and not the syscall number -- the single most likely
misreading -- and that exactly execve, execveat and sigreturn must be 1,
with the distinct consequence of each mis-setting.

Verified: riscv64 and x86_64 kernel-only build under -Werror; tools/gates.py
reports the same 16 pass / 4 fail as before, and those 4 fail identically
with all of this work stashed.

Chinese, code comments in English, matching the ~98% of existing comments --
and then states the part that was actually missing judgement: what earns a
comment (why, invariants, hidden values, real bugs, contract blocks) versus
what should be deleted (identifier restatement, line-by-line narration,

8aafc681da5446596b0171a300701dec7108a8ba:
docs(kernel): finish the comment-language unification in kernel

docs/CONTRIBUTING.md §4.1 says code comments are English. This finishes the
job: kernel/ is now free of Chinese comments, matching docs/ staying Chinese.

Accuracy was the priority, not fluency. The comments that mattered most:

- The per-arch W^X finalizers (kwx.c x4) explain the one ordering that
  silently bricks a boot: build the new mapping off to the side and install
  it with a single write, because installing NX huge pages before the split
  leaves the CPU dependent on leftover TLB entries, and the first miss
  faults fetching from an NX .text whose trap vector is NX too. The riscv64
  and x86_64 notes record that this was hit for real on an SMP=2 build.
- fault.c's two COW comments keep the 0x63636363 corruption signature and the
  reasoning that the PTE must be updated before frame_put, since a stale PTE
  pointing at a recycled frame is what user memory ends up reading.
- aslr.c keeps every numeric bound, because the entropy bit counts are
  derived from the fixed vDSO/vvar and TLS addresses and cannot be recovered
  by inspection.
- uxfs.c keeps its concurrency contract: one request mutex per mount, stale
  replies dropped by req_id, -EIO after a link drop.
- virtio_net's deadlock cycle (g_lwip_lock -> blocking send -> IRQ -> lwIP
  callback -> g_lwip_lock) stays intact; it is the reason nonblock exists.
- sys_fs.c keeps the foreground-group fallback, which is what stops busybox
  ash from raising SIGTTIN against its own group and freezing init with it.

Also corrected three board/vendor names that carried Chinese glosses inline
(Loongson 2K1000, StarFive VisionFive 2, a docs/pz/28 path reference).

Verified by building the tree before and after and comparing disassembly:
riscv64 and x86_64 are byte-identical, which proves no code changed. All 19

9c03a2795df127d7f22fd6cb6d6889a5104e3ba8:
feat(a20): make the exit code the error contract

Every failure used to surface as whichever Python exception happened to escape,
so neither the exit code nor the message was designed. Two confirmed by hand:

    $ tools/a20 ledger stm32f103-xuanwu
    a20_make.MakeQueryError: Makefile:552: *** ARCH=armv7m requires ...
    $ env PATH=/nonexistent tools/a20 ledger qemu-riscv64
    FileNotFoundError: [Errno 2] No such file or directory: 'make'

Both are common operator-fixable errors, yet reading a traceback was the only
way to understand them.

The exit code contract is now:

    0    success
    1    a20 refused to run, or the instance failed its own declared checks
    2    command line usage error (argparse's own exit(2))
    3    a delegated tool failed (make / QEMU / OpenOCD / script)
    124  timeout

make's exit code is no longer passed through. make returns 2 for "no such
target", and that 2 used to become a20's own exit code, making it impossible
to tell apart from an a20 argument mistake. exec_make now raises ToolError on
failure and a20 picks the exit code itself.

Stream convention: per-item failure messages move to stderr while the report
itself stays on stdout. So `a20 check > report.txt` now captures the pass list,
failures land in `2>err.txt`, and CI can handle the two separately. check,
list, ledger and ports previously wrote FAIL to stdout, which `2>/dev/null`
could not filter.

Fixed along the way:

- `a20 ports` returned 0 whether or not it could read the inventory; it now
  fails when it cannot.
- The port conflict hint moved from stdout to stderr, since it is a diagnostic
  and not a result.
- `regen-drivers` is the only command that writes into the repository and had
  neither --dry-run nor error handling. Both are there now.
- `InstanceBusy` was declared but never raised or caught; the lock actually
  threw a bare SystemExit, so "this instance is taken by someone else" could
  not be told apart from any other failure. The dead class is removed in favour
  of the one that is really raised.
- The two SystemExit calls in `_qemu_cmdline` become ToolError as well.
- Two places that silently dropped arguments are fixed too: the armv7m run
  path and the flash step both hardcoded `[]`, so `a20 run <mcu> -- -j8` quietly
  lost its -j8.

One uncertainty worth recording: FileNotFoundError can mean either that make is
not installed or that the user pointed --out at a nonexistent directory.
Reporting "make is not in PATH" for both points the operator in a completely
wrong direction, so the missing filename is now distinguished, and a missing
path reports the OS error verbatim.

Verified with 10 new TestOperatorErrorContract cases that pin the contract:
distinct exit codes, a did-you-mean for a mistyped instance name, the exact
format of errors and hints, make's 2 no longer impersonating a usage error,
124 preserved, exec_make raising instead of returning a status, schema
violations producing a clean error instead of a traceback, and semantic errors
not landing on stdout.

The tool's own suite is at 171 tests OK, up from 161. check-manifests,
check-smoke-cases and check-a20-tests all PASS.
d8c2fa2e9a72bdfaf925bbf70ba3422717bc86c1:
test(a20): gate every command on host resources and recheck before launch

Before starting an instance, look at the host resources first. If they are
short, wait until they are released rather than starting anyway, and rather
than printing "not enough resources" and giving up. The reason is that when
QEMU over-requests memory, the process the OOM killer picks as a sacrifice is
often not QEMU at all but the kernel compiling right next to it.

The wait used to print a single line:

    a20: waiting for host resources (mem 1001023 MiB, 1 vCPU, ...) -- memory: need ...

What is blocking and how to proceed are now stated separately:

    a20: waiting to qemu-riscv64 -- host resources are short
          have/want: mem 1001023 MiB, 1 vCPU, disk 2048 MiB
          blocked:   memory: need 1001023 MiB, available 12715 MiB
          to proceed: free memory (stop a guest or a build) and retry
          press Ctrl-C to give up

Every shortfall carries its own remedy; the guest slot one even names the
default cap of one guest per 4 CPUs and points at A20_MAX_CONCURRENT. The
timeout error carries the remedy too.

Bad environment variables are no longer swallowed silently. A20_MAX_CONCURRENT=many
used to fall back to the default quietly, looking like it had taken effect when
it had not, with "hangs for no apparent reason" as the only symptom. It now
warns.

Gating now covers every path and distinguishes guest work from build work. Only
run, debug and test were gated before; build, flash and package ignored
resources entirely even though they consume disk too. Gating cannot be
one-size-fits-all though: `a20 package` never starts a guest, so charging it
guest memory would just make the two commands interfere. evaluate() gained a
guest switch, guest=True checking memory, CPU, guest slots and host ports to
avoid the OOM killer and port conflicts, guest=False checking only disk.

--dry-run is finally side-effect free. This was measured, not guessed:

    # before: had to be killed, exit 124
    $ A20_RESERVE_MEM_MB=999999 tools/a20 debug qemu-riscv64 --dry-run
    # after: 0.1s
    $ same
    qemu-riscv64: no host port forwarding (nothing to connect to)
    make -C ... ARCH=riscv64 BOARD=qemu-virt-riscv64 _debug_impl

Worse was console: it ignored --dry-run entirely, opened the real serial port
and injected target.commands into a board that was already online, which is the
exact opposite of what the flag promises. It now prints every step it would
take, which serial port, which baud rate, which reset command, which prompt it
would wait for, what it would inject, what it requires and where the transcript
would go, and sends not a single byte. deploy reuses console and is fixed with
it.

The TOCTOU window is closed. The gate used to run before the build. A full
kernel build takes minutes, and by the time QEMU really starts, the memory and
ports that were granted earlier may already be gone, especially host ports,
which the first runner to ask takes. The check now runs again immediately
before launch and that second check is authoritative; the first one stays only
to fail fast, not to grant passage.

171 tests OK. check-manifests / check-a20-tests PASS.
114b61555c0bb6c87cfa0980094a7ee437eb366c:
feat(a20): report smoke progress live lock before build reap every guest

Silence is the worst kind of feedback. QEMU's output always went only to a log
file, so a boot that takes minutes to reach the first marker looked like four
minutes of nothing on the terminal followed by one line saying PASS or FAIL.
That is indistinguishable from a hang, which is the most unpleasant part of
running smoke.

Each expected marker is now reported as it appears, with a heartbeat in
between:

    [  0.3s] seen: part ok
    [  0.3s] seen: System is going down for power-off NOW
    [ 15.0s] waiting: 1/3 markers, 20481 bytes of guest output so far

The implementation just reads the log the guest was already writing once more,
so the cost is negligible.

The failure message was rewritten too. The old

    FAIL (exited with status 0); missing patterns: ['A', 'B']

was ugly in two ways: `exited with status 0` next to FAIL looks
self-contradictory, since a clean guest shutdown is supposed to return 0, and
it leaked a Python list repr into human and CI logs. Now:

    f: FAIL -- 2 of 2 expected marker(s) never appeared (the guest exited with status 0)
      missing: NEVER_ONE
      missing: ALSO_NEVER
      transcript: .../f.log (last 80 lines below)

The guest exit code is secondary information. Whether the markers appeared is
the criterion.

The lock did not lock the thing it exists to prevent. `_exclusive` was taken
after `build_instance`. So running the same instance twice, whether via
`make -j` or two CI jobs on one runner, had both sides compile a full kernel
and write into the same BUILD_DIR, with the loser finding out only at the end.
Taking the lock first is the whole point of the lock.

Guests could become orphans. `_reap` only ran on the timeout and Ctrl-C paths.
Any other exception left QEMU alive holding hostfwd ports and 1-4 GiB of
memory, and it was started in a new session so a SIGKILL to a20 could not
reach it, while the kernel released the flock immediately. The instance
therefore looked idle to the next run, which then lost the port race to a guest
nobody tracks any more. Reaping now happens in a finally block, so every exit
path is covered.

Along the way:

- `console --dry-run` and `deploy --dry-run` ignored the flag entirely and
  opened the real serial port to inject commands into an online board. They now
  print every step they would take and send not a single byte.
- The gate gained a guest scope: build, flash and package only check disk and
  are no longer blocked by a guest happening to be running, while run, debug
  and test check memory, CPU, guest slots and ports.
- A mistyped instance name now gets a did-you-mean. The cutoff is 0.75: at 0.6,
  `smoke-poll-edge`, which is a make target and not an instance name at all,
  would have been confidently matched to `smoke-ppc64le`, which is worse than
  offering no suggestion at all.

Verified with 7 new tests covering per-marker reporting, timeouts being
reported rather than hanging, the lock preceding the build, the guest still
being reaped when _wait raises, console --dry-run not touching the serial port,
the build scope not looking at guest memory, and every shortfall carrying a
remedy. 178 tests OK. check-manifests / check-a20-tests PASS. Real hardware
smoke-riscv64: PASS, with markers reported live as expected.

d1ff8bf9f203df81b03307ebd6c4a4b5702d2362:
fix(a20): bound serial writes and the reset command fix the TIOCEXCL comment

docs/instances.md claims every console wait is bounded. Checking the code
found two that were not:

1. The `while data:` loop in SerialTransport.write had no deadline. When the
   board stops accepting bytes, whether the UART wedged or a second process
   holds the port, os.write keeps raising BlockingIOError, so the loop turns
   forever. That is precisely the case where hanging is worst, because the
   operator is holding a board that may need a power cycle while the screen
   shows nothing. After 10 seconds it now names the device and the reason.
2. The subprocess.run in `_run_reset` had no timeout. With no probe attached,
   openocd waits forever and the console session inherits that wait. A reset is
   a pulse, so 60 seconds means it is waiting for something else, which is now
   what it says.

The comment above TIOCEXCL was corrected in passing. It used to read "Refuse
to let a second process fight over the same adapter", but the
contextlib.suppress(OSError) right below means the port is still taken as
usual when TIOCEXCL is refused, so the code was making a promise it does not
keep, which is exactly the class of problem this pass is cleaning up. It now
states what it actually does: a best-effort courtesy, not a guarantee.

f83bbd7be3b51ef34be498a53f80603669a67bd0:
fix(a20): add a20 show and fix _watch missing the last log read

`show-vars` answers "what will make see", but when choosing an instance the
questions are "can I run it, what will it cost, what will it touch". `a20 show`
answers all of it on one screen: available actions, board, resource
requirements, host ports, serial devices, media to be written, expected serial
line. `needs` uses the same requirement_for as the launch gate, so the numbers
shown are the numbers checked at run time and cannot drift from the gate.

_watch reported FAIL when the guest exited normally. This was found while
chasing a gate failure that appeared exactly once and did not reproduce in 9
reruns, 3 of them under full load. It is a real bug, in code this series
introduced itself:

    rc = proc.poll()
    if rc is not None:
        return False          # <-- returns without one more read of the log

A guest can write its last marker and exit between two polls. The log is
flushed by the process or thread that wrote it, which lands slightly after the
process exits, so this round returns without the final read, the marker is
never seen, and a completely healthy boot is judged missing a marker, that is,
a false FAIL.

There is now one more read before returning. It looks redundant, so a comment
explains why; otherwise someone will eventually "simplify" it away and bring
the bug back. The regression test reproduces it exactly with a fake proc: the
first poll reports running, the sleep writes the final marker, the second poll
reports exited, and without that extra read the marker is always missed.

`a20 show` reuses `applicable_actions` and `default_board` instead of
duplicating the decisions in cmd_show, and falls back to `default_board(arch)`
when `board` is empty, the same as make.

0533108bc9f072c63f03fe63cddff957d422e2bd:
fix(net): make AF_ALG fail closed instead of fabricating crypto output

AF_ALG is a trust interface: a caller asking the kernel for "sha256" or
"cbc(aes)" has no way to detect a stub returning predictable bytes.  The
previous implementation accepted a dozen well-known algorithm names and
then produced:

  * "digest" = 0xa5 ^ i XOR-folded over the input, for md5/sha1/sha224/
    sha256/sha384/sha512 alike;
  * "ciphertext" = the plaintext buffer, byte for byte, for
    salsa20/cbc(aes)/ecb(aes)/ctr(aes) and both aead names.

Every call returned success.  Userspace crypto libraries probe for AF_ALG
and, on a positive answer, feed the result into a TLS handshake, a
signature check, or a password KDF.  A stub that returns success is thus
strictly worse than no AF_ALG at all: the caller is confidently wrong.

A20OS has no kernel crypto provider, so the registry now advertises no
algorithm at all.  bind() returns -ENOENT for every name, which is what
Linux returns for an unregistered algorithm and which correctly steers
userspace to its own implementation.  socket(2) still succeeds so callers
can probe cheaply; send()/recv() refuse with -EOPNOTSUPP as defence in
depth.  setsockopt(ALG_SET_KEY) likewise refuses instead of accepting a
key it cannot install.

The registry is kept as a table with an explicit `accepted` column so the
surface is documented and adding a real provider is a one-line change
rather than a rediscovery.  Two rules are recorded in the file: never
enable an entry before the primitive is real, and prefer userspace
cryptography over hand-rolled kernel primitives.

While here, drop the per-socket `alg_last` staging buffer.  It existed
only to feed the fake digest, and cost 2 KiB on *every* socket in the
system including TCP and UNIX ones.  Also drop the AF_ALG clause in the
poll revents path, which was the only other reader of that buffer.

Fixes the loadavg-class of defect: an unimplemented facility must report
absence, not invent output.  alg_test.c already treats -ENOENT on bind as
ALG_TEST: SKIP, so the existing gate needs no change.

riscv64 -Werror build clean.
fe888258c3cc13d92c0b3603a063b4c815e46aa3:
test(proc): gate reboot/poweroff on CAP_SYS_BOOT and pagemap on task ownership

Two holes in proc access control, in different files and for different reasons.

`sys_reboot()` in `kernel/abi/linux/sys_proc.c` had no privilege check at all.
Every arm terminates the machine: `LINUX_REBOOT_CMD_RESTART` calls
`firmware_reboot()`, and `LINUX_REBOOT_CMD_POWER_OFF` (magic1 == 0, the busybox
convention) calls `firmware_shutdown()`. The only thing standing between an
unprivileged process and a denial of service was a pair of constants published in
the Linux uapi header. The magic check is argument validation, not authorisation.
The whole entry point is now gated on `CAP_SYS_BOOT || euid == 0`, matching what
the kexec entry points in `sys_missing.c` already do, and the check runs before
the magic dispatch so no arm can bypass it. A null `proc_current()` returns
`-ESRCH` and a failing capability check returns `-EPERM`.
`user/cmds/core/{poweroff,reboot}.c` call this from the root init shell, so the
normal poweroff path is unaffected.

In `kernel/fs/procfs/procfs.c`, `procfs_fread()`'s `PF_PID_PAGEMAP` branch was
the only per-pid content reader without a `proc_task_may_access()` check. Every
8-byte entry is a page frame number, and the file's length is the whole 256 GiB
user VA range, so any process could read the complete physical page map of any
other process. That defeats userspace ASLR outright and exposes the kernel
direct-map layout, which matters more here than on Linux because A20OS has no
KASLR to fall back on. `fd`, `fdinfo`, `exe`, `cwd`, `maps` and `smaps` were all
gated; pagemap was simply missed. It now applies the same check, with the same
`-EACCES`, at the point of read, and releases the looked-up task before
returning. Gating the read rather than the open is sufficient because
`procfs_priv_create()` only sizes pagemap and computes no content.

Verification scope: the riscv64 `-Werror` build is clean. No runtime behaviour
test is recorded for either change.
48904a9b641c4b42596412b6caa697299568f4fb:
fix(proc): report measured I/O counters and load averages

Three /proc surfaces reported invented numbers.  Monitoring reads them as
measurements, so a wrong value is worse than a missing file.

/proc/<pid>/io reported CPU ticks as byte counts -- rchar was
t->total_time and wchar was t->child_stime, with syscr/syscw/read_bytes/
write_bytes hardcoded to 0.  Implement the counters instead of blanking
them, since per-process I/O accounting is what capacity planning needs:

  * rchar/wchar/syscr/syscw are charged in vfs_read_file/vfs_write_file,
    the choke point every read(2)/write(2) passes through, so they cover
    page-cache, direct and non-file vnodes uniformly;
  * read_bytes/write_bytes are charged in block_cache at the three sites
    that actually reach the device, so cached I/O correctly leaves them
    near zero;
  * all six use relaxed atomics, matching the existing perf_page_faults
    convention: these are statistics and must not order the I/O they
    describe.

  Attributing device I/O to proc_current() is deliberate and differs from
  Linux, which charges writeback to kswapd/flusher threads.  A20OS has no
  flusher threads -- writeback runs in whoever triggered it -- so the
  current task is the right owner.  That reasoning is recorded at the
  helper so it is not "corrected" toward Linux later.

/proc/loadavg was the constant string "0.00 0.00 0.00 1/64 1".  Add
kernel/proc/loadavg.c maintaining the 1/5/15-minute EMAs in Q16 fixed
point, sampled from the scheduler tick alongside the existing PSI sample.
Sampled as RUNNABLE + RUNNING, matching Linux's nr_running; D-state tasks
are excluded because A20OS has no D state (see below).

/proc/pressure printed avg10 correctly but hardcoded avg60/avg300 to
"0.00" even though psi_tick() computes both.  Pass all three averages to
the formatter.

The mem and io pressure lines are structurally zero rather than
unimplemented, and now say why: PSI "io" counts tasks stalled on I/O, but
every A20OS device transfer is synchronous (block_cache calls
read_sector inline, virtio-blk completes by polling), so a task doing I/O
runs rather than waits.  The old "not instrumented" wording read as an
open to-do and invited someone to invent a number.

Also drop the AF_ALG POLLIN special case in net_poll, which was the last
reader of the staging buffer removed in the previous commit.

Builds clean with -Werror on riscv64, aarch64, x86_64 and loongarch64.
63360cbf81c06d0e2152df12a7fb3fb11a296508:
fix(net): stop setsockopt/getsockopt reporting options it did not honour

Three places in the socket option layer returned success for settings that
were discarded, which is the most dangerous shape of missing feature: the
caller has no way to notice, so it proceeds on a false belief.

Unimplemented SOL_SOCKET options returned 0 from a bare catch-all.  This
swept up SO_BINDTODEVICE, SO_DOMAIN, SO_PROTOCOL, SO_RXQ_OVFL and
anything else added later.  A server that sets SO_BINDTODEVICE to pin a
tenant's traffic to one interface would believe it had isolated that
tenant, and would not have.

Unimplemented IPPROTO_IP options likewise returned 0, silently discarding
IP_TTL, IP_TOS, IP_OPTIONS and IP_TRANSPARENT.

TCP_CONGESTION reported the literal string "cubic" while the stack has
only lwIP's Reno -- verified by grepping the vendored tree, which has no
cubic or bbr anywhere.  Tuning and monitoring tools read that name and
reason about a CUBIC implementation that does not exist.  Report "reno",
which is what setsockopt already accepted (every name, since it discards
them); this keeps get and set consistent.

TCP_INFO wrote a state byte at offset 0 and zeroed the remainder.  No
struct tcp_info is modelled anywhere in the tree, so callers decoded
tcpi_rtt, tcpi_total_retrans and the rest as measured-and-zero -- which
is indistinguishable from a genuinely idle connection.  Refuse it.

The policy, now stated in the code: a setsockopt the kernel cannot honour
must fail with -EOPNOTSUPP, never silently succeed.  Enumerated options
keep their own -EOPNOTSUPP rather than falling into a catch-all, so
adding one cannot accidentally be absorbed by the default.

riscv64 -Werror build clean; no in-tree userland sets any rejected option.
23175f9a0194d170318a7822a65a7b5861fa2e4f:
fix(proc): populate getrusage counters and separate user from system time

sys_getrusage built its 144-byte reply from total_time alone, writing it
into ru_utime and leaving ru_stime permanently zero.  total_time is
utime_ticks + stime_ticks, so every consumer saw all of a process's CPU
time attributed to user mode -- `top` and friends split the two columns,
and half the time was simply missing from the system column.

The other sixteen slots were memset to zero, so ru_minflt, ru_majflt,
ru_inblock, ru_oublock, ru_nvcsw and ru_nivcsw all read as "measured, and
the value happens to be zero".

Fill them from the counters the kernel already keeps:

  * ru_utime/ru_stime from utime_ticks/stime_ticks, separately.  The
    ticks/100 -> seconds conversion is unchanged and still correct:
    accounting runs once per 100 Hz scheduler pass, even though
    TICKS_PER_SEC itself is the hardware timebase frequency.
  * ru_minflt/ru_majflt from perf_page_faults{,_maj}.
  * ru_inblock/ru_oublock from the io_read_bytes/io_write_bytes added in
    the previous commit.
  * ru_nvcsw/ru_nivcsw from a new voluntary/involuntary split.

The split is classified at the switch site rather than guessed: park.c
moves a task to PROC_BLOCKED before it goes off-CPU, so an outgoing task
already in PROC_BLOCKED gave up the CPU voluntarily and anything else was
preempted.  perf_switches remains the sum of the two, so
PERF_COUNT_SW_CONTEXT_SWITCHES is unaffected.

ru_maxrss is left zero.  It needs a peak-RSS watermark that A20OS does not
track, and the existing /proc/<pid>/statm RSS walk is a page-table scan
that does not belong on the getrusage path.  ru_ixrss/ru_idrss/ru_isrss/
ru_nswap/ru_msgsnd/ru_msgrcv stay zero, which is the truthful answer: no
such accounting exists.

Builds clean with -Werror on riscv64, aarch64, x86_64 and loongarch64.
75ec21f0b7950b846e23b5dcbc27c89db9c55053:
fix(block): flush the device before fsync returns

block_dev_t had no cache-flush primitive at all: read_sector, write_sector,
capacity, sector_size, release.  Every fsync() therefore returned once the
data had reached the device's volatile write cache, so a power cut could
still lose committed data.  A database on this would lose transactions it
had been told were durable.

Add an optional block_dev_t.flush and call it at the end of
bcache_sync_common(), after the data and outside the cache lock.  Devices
that cannot honour it leave the pointer NULL, which is documented at the
interface as "no durability guarantee" rather than "not implemented yet".

Implementations:

  * virtio-blk issues VIRTIO_BLK_T_FLUSH.  Per virtio-blk 1.1 s5.2.6 a
    flush request is header + status with no data descriptor, so
    submit_req grew an explicit flush mode rather than reusing the
    three-descriptor read/write chain.  The completion copy-back is now
    guarded on a non-zero length, since a flush has no buffer and this
    build runs UBSan.
  * loop forwards to an fsync of its backing file, which is exactly what
    its durability reduces to.  This needed a vfile-level vfs_fsync_vfile,
    factored out of the existing fd-based vfs_fsync.
  * block_dev_ops_t already declared a flush op that nothing ever set; it
    is now wired for virtio-blk.

The real bug this surfaced: both block_dev_t wrappers in fs/mount_setup.c
-- partition_block_dev and class_block_dev -- forwarded read_sector and
write_sector but not flush.  Since every filesystem mount sits on a
partition, that silently stripped the new capability from the entire tree,
and fsync() on ext4 returned -EOPNOTSUPP once the plumbing was in place.
Both now forward, returning -EOPNOTSUPP when the underlying device cannot.

Add A20_PERF_BLOCK_FLUSHES so the path is observable, and a new
smoke-fsync-durability gate with user/cmds/core/fsync_durability_test.c.
The test asserts the flush counter advances, not merely that fsync()
returns 0 -- it returned 0 before this change too, which is the whole
point.  It writes to /extra rather than /tmp because the bootstrap root is
ramfs and has no device to flush, and it arms /proc/a20/perf before
measuring because collection is dormant until the first read.

Verified: smoke-fsync-durability PASS with block_flushes advancing and no
virtio I/O errors, confirming the T_FLUSH request completes.  Also PASS:
smoke-vfs-stress, smoke-swap, smoke-syscall-ext, smoke-abi-linux,
smoke-network-suite, smoke-sched-stress.  Clean -Werror on riscv64,
aarch64, x86_64, loongarch64.
47b935b33a38be76e86d4d3d77aeed85b7455f8b:
fix(ahci): issue FLUSH CACHE EXT for durable fsync

The previous commit gave the block layer a flush primitive and implemented
it for virtio-blk and loop.  AHCI kept none, so on a SATA disk fsync()
would still return once the data reached the drive's volatile write cache
-- exactly the failure the flush primitive exists to prevent.

Issue ATA FLUSH CACHE EXT (0xE7) through a new no-data command path:

  * LBA = 0xFFFFFFFF with count 0, which ACS-4 defines as "flush the entire
    cache".  There is no narrower form to expose: a port flush is inherently
    device-wide, and the block interface has no range parameter.
  * PRDTL = 0, because the command moves no data, and CFLAGS bit 6 (Write)
    stays clear.
  * Serialised against ahci_rw on the port mutex so a FLUSH cannot interleave
    with a multi-sector write on the same port.

To avoid duplicating the completion path, the wait loop shared by the data
commands is factored out into ahci_wait_complete() and now serves both.  It
skips the completion copy-back when the transfer length is zero, since a
no-data command has no buffer to sync.

FUA is deliberately not implemented.  It would need a per-request durability
flag on block_dev_t, which the interface does not have; adding one for a
single caller is not justified, and flush-after-write is the portable
equivalent.  Recorded here so the omission reads as a decision rather than
an oversight.

Verified by compilation only: ahci.c is behind CONFIG_AHCI and no instance
or smoke gate instantiates an AHCI controller, so there is no runtime path
to exercise this.  Recompiled clean for x86_64 via the ahci.a20drv drvmod
target.  A gate attaching an ich9-ahci device is the missing piece and is
noted in docs/roadmap.
5cc031cd54d62ffb5d73edfd5b150ea1eaba2e2e:
feat(net): add an IPv4 packet filter so the host can be exposed safely

A20OS had no netfilter, conntrack or NAT anywhere -- verified by grep across
both kernel/ and the vendored lwIP.  That is not a missing feature but a
deployment blocker: the box cannot be put on a network it does not trust,
because nothing can drop a packet.

This is the first slice, matching the cost estimate in
docs/roadmap/next-horizon.md: an ordered rule table with accept/drop
verdicts, per-rule and aggregate counters, and a procfs control surface.
Conntrack and NAT are deliberately absent -- they need state that outlives a
single packet and are separate work.

Hooks sit at the two device-facing points, per the same doc:

  * a20_lwip_process_netif_rx_tx_locked, before n->input(), so a filtered
    packet never reaches the IP layer, wakes no socket and builds no state;
  * a20_lwip_linkoutput, after the frame is assembled and before transmit.

Both run with g_lwip_lock held, so the evaluation path only reads the
caller's frame buffer and bumps relaxed counters.  It never allocates,
blocks, or calls into lwIP, which is what docs/net/network-lock-contract.md
requires of a hook.  That constraint is recorded in the header.

Rule matching covers direction, protocol (named or numeric), source and
destination address, and source and destination port, each independently
wildcardable.  Addresses and ports render back in dotted-quad/decimal form
so a rule can be verified by reading /proc/a20/netfilter.

Default policy is accept and no rules are installed at boot, so an
unconfigured system behaves exactly as before.  Adding the filter therefore
cannot regress an existing deployment.

Control surface is /proc/a20/netfilter: read for policy, counters and the
rule table; write "add <rule>", "del <n>", "reset".  Malformed rules are
rejected with an error rather than installed, so a typo cannot silently
widen or narrow the policy.

smoke-netfilter (new gate) with user/cmds/net/netfilter_test.c verifies the
control surface, that malformed rules are rejected, and -- the part that
matters -- that a UDP send matching a drop rule actually increments
out_dropped in the live data plane.  Observed NETFILTER_TEST: PASS
dropped=3 out_packets=3, so the transmit hook fires for real rather than the
test passing vacuously.  It also checks the same traffic with no matching
rule is not dropped, so the drop is attributable to the rule.

Clean -Werror on riscv64, aarch64, x86_64, loongarch64.
27e90ca1d8dddb9c0323d04c9d0657a37c11c520:
build(tools): enforce fail-closed behavior with a regression gate

The fixes in this series all share one shape: a facility that could not do
what it claimed started reporting success instead of admitting absence.
That is the most dangerous class of missing feature, because the caller
cannot detect it and proceeds on a false belief -- an AF_ALG "sha256" that
is really 0xa5^i, a fsync() that never reaches the disk, a setsockopt that
accepts SO_BINDTODEVICE and discards it.

Nothing locked that in.  The existing gates are marker checks, which prove a
string exists but not that a bug stayed fixed, so this gate is deliberately
mostly *negative*: it asserts each specific anti-pattern stays absent.

Negative (the bug must not come back):
  * AF_ALG advertises no algorithm -- no table entry may be marked accepted
  * no success catch-all for unhandled SOL_SOCKET options
  * TCP_CONGESTION does not hardcode an algorithm the stack lacks
  * /proc/loadavg is not the constant string
  * /proc/<pid>/io does not report CPU ticks as byte counts
  * PSI does not discard its computed avg60/avg300
  * getrusage does not conflate utime and stime

Positive (the fix must stay wired, not merely present):
  * /proc/<pid>/pagemap is gated on task ownership
  * sys_reboot is gated on CAP_SYS_BOOT
  * block_dev_t declares flush, both mount_setup wrappers forward it, and
    block cache sync calls it
  * virtio-blk and AHCI still issue a flush command
  * both netfilter hooks, the load-average tick sample and read/write I/O
    accounting remain wired

Verified the gate actually fails: reintroducing the SOL_SOCKET catch-all and
the constant loadavg string made it report
"FAIL setsockopt still reports success for discarded SOL_SOCKET options"
and exit non-zero.  A gate that cannot fail is the same defect this series
exists to remove, so it was tested against a deliberate regression before
being committed.  Restored and re-confirmed PASS.
4ca5c34e2b79a95fad441e5376da01ad1432d589:
feat(proc): honour prlimit64s pid and enforce RLIMIT_AS and RLIMIT_NPROC

Three defects in the rlimit surface, all of the "reports success without
doing anything" kind this series has been removing.

prlimit64 discarded its pid argument outright -- `(void)pid;` -- so it could
only ever inspect or change the calling task's own limits.  A supervisor had
no way to inspect or adjust a child, and the kernel's own tools could not use
it.  It now resolves the target, allows reading any task's limits, and
requires CAP_SYS_RESOURCE or a matching uid to change another task's.

sys_setrlimit and the set half of prlimit64 returned 0 for every resource
outside STACK/CORE/NOFILE.  Setting RLIMIT_AS and being told "ok" means the
caller believes the address space is capped when nothing caps it, so an
unenforced resource is now -EINVAL on set.

RLIMIT_AS and RLIMIT_NPROC were undefined and unenforceable, so a single
process could exhaust host memory.  Both are now real:

  * RLIMIT_AS caps the address space, checked in proc_mmap before mm->lock is
    taken.  total_vm only grows, so the unlocked read can under-count and let
    a later mapping slip through but can never falsely reject one that fits.
  * RLIMIT_NPROC caps processes per real uid, matching Linux's uid-scoped
    semantics so a fork bomb is bounded no matter how many processes the
    account already has.  Checked before the task slot is taken so a
    rejected fork leaves no trace.  CAP_SYS_RESOURCE is exempt.

getrlimit on an unenforced resource still reports RLIM_INFINITY.  That is the
truthful answer -- no limit applies -- whereas ENOSYS would misreport which
resources exist.

The three entry points duplicated the same switch three times, which is how
they drifted apart; they now share rlimit_get/rlimit_set.

Limits inherit across fork and default to 0 (unlimited) so an unconfigured
system behaves as before.

Verified: smoke-abi-linux, smoke-proc-stress and smoke-futex-stress PASS
(poweroff reports buddy audit errors=0), clean -Werror on riscv64, aarch64,
x86_64, loongarch64, and check-honesty-policy still green.
4924f9d4e716c4b7e9b39d5f9b792ff8914bb054:
fix(sched): implement round-robin selection for SCHED_RR

sched_task_rt() folds SCHED_FIFO and SCHED_RR into one test, and the RT
queue is a plain per-priority FIFO, so the two policies were
indistinguishable: an SCHED_RR task ran to completion and starved every
same-priority peer.  A program that set SCHED_RR to share a core got
unbounded starvation instead of round-robin.

rt_pick_best_locked() now rotates the head of a busy queue when it belongs
to an RR task, so each pick advances to the next peer.  Two properties are
deliberate:

  * SCHED_FIFO heads are never rotated.  That is what makes FIFO
    run-to-completion and keeps it ahead of an RR peer at equal priority,
    matching Linux.
  * A lone RR task is not rotated, so it keeps the CPU rather than being
    penalised for having no competition.

The rotation reuses rt_unlink_locked/rt_enqueue_locked under the existing
runqueue lock, so it adds no new locking and stays O(words) as before.

Scope, stated plainly: this yields RR among peers when the scheduler next
runs, not on a timer slice.  Forcing a switch mid-slice requires kernel
preemption, which A20OS does not have -- there is no CONFIG_PREEMPT and only
a need_resched flag consumed at safe points.  So an RR task that never blocks
still runs until it blocks.  That is a preemption gap, not something this
change introduces or can fix, and the comment at the pick site says so to
stop the rotation being mistaken for a full timeslice.

Verified: smoke-sched-stress and smoke-proc-stress PASS, clean -Werror on
riscv64.
4969adda567d0d9431634132aed95cfc20cea4c5:
docs(roadmap): state the fail-closed principle and what a server still needs

The code changes in this series fixed real defects, but a fix that is not
written down gets reverted by the next person who does not know why the
code is shaped oddly.  Three documentation changes.

docs/security/hardening.md gains the principle the whole series enforces:
an unimplemented facility must report absence, never fabricate output.  The
justification is the asymmetry of failure modes -- a missing feature makes the
caller take a fallback path, a stub that returns success leaves it certain it
is safe, and usually it is trusting the kernel precisely where it should not.
The section tabulates each interface fixed (AF_ALG, the setsockopt
catch-alls, fsync, three procfs files, reboot, prlimit64) with its old and
new behaviour, and states the corollary that enumerated interfaces must not
fall through into a shared `return 0` -- which is exactly how SOL_SOCKET
swallowed SO_BINDTODEVICE.

Also corrects two stale facts: capabilities are 16, not 15, and seccomp is
implemented but no service in the tree installs a filter.  A document that
overstates a control is the same defect class this series removes.

Adds a storage-durability section recording that fsync() now reaches the
device, and naming the packaging wrappers in fs/mount_setup.c as the place
this is most likely to regress: they forward read/write but originally not
flush, and because every mount sits on a partition that silently stripped
durability from the whole tree.

docs/roadmap/next-horizon.md: netfilter was estimated here at 3-5 days and
is now implemented, so the section states the delivered behaviour, its
control surface, its gate, and what remains (conntrack and NAT, which need
cross-packet state).  Its header claimed nothing in the cycle was
implemented, which is no longer true.

docs/server-readiness.md is new.  It records the current server-deployment
boundary in one place: the storage durability model and the ext4 journal
gap, the network limits ranked by severity (the global lwIP lock first,
because it decides whether multi-core networking is possible at all), the
isolation model and why containers cannot be built, scheduling and the
preemption gap, what observability is still missing, reliability, real
hardware and virtualisation, then a ranked blocker table and a short list of
first actions that need no design decisions.

It is blunt about the conclusion: A20OS is currently a desktop/research
kernel under QEMU, and putting a database on it is not safe until the P0
items close.  Every claim is file-located so a reader can check it rather
than take it on trust.

Linked from docs/README.md in both the quick-start and research sections, and
from the improvement TODO.
a6d44e03cd01e93a4e6c2819be18602b8b9d8084:
feat(procfs): expose /proc/pressure as CPU memory io matching Linux

A20OS published /proc/pressure as one flat file.  Linux exposes a
directory with cpu, memory and io, and that is the path systemd and
pressure-stall tooling open -- a flat file is not substitutable, so a
server's monitoring stack would simply find nothing.

Add PF_PRESSURE_CPU/MEM/IO, mark the parent as a directory, and wire the
child lookups plus the readdir table.  The parent keeps rendering the cpu
line so `cat /proc/pressure` still shows something useful.

Splitting the renderer also fixed a real bug: the flat file called
psi_render_memio() twice, so memory and io were emitted as two byte-identical
lines rather than one line each.  psi_render_memio is replaced by separate
psi_render_mem() and psi_render_io().

The mem and io values are still structurally zero, and for the same reason
as before: all A20OS device I/O is synchronous, so no task ever stalls on
it.  That is stated in the renderer rather than implied.

Extended smoke-fsync-durability to read all three resource files and check
each carries a `some` line with avg10/avg60/avg300/total.  Observed
psi_cpu="some avg10=0.00 avg60=0.00 avg300=0.00 total=0", confirming the new
paths resolve.

While verifying I hit a self-inflicted false alarm worth recording: the PASS
line kept coming out truncated, and my first two theories (stale binary,
then a dropped newline) were both wrong.  Checking the built binary's
strings proved the new assertions were present and had run; the real cause
was that procfs content keeps its trailing newline, which landed inside the
printf and split the line.  Added a chomp() before printing.  The lesson is
the one this series keeps teaching -- a passing test is only evidence once
you have confirmed which assertions actually executed.

Clean -Werror on riscv64, aarch64, x86_64, loongarch64; check-honesty-policy
still green.
891bbede499103ae9189bbf9014604cf20207bc8:
fix(proc): drop the dead MAX_PROCS constant and correct a doc claim about pid_max

MAX_PROCS (consts.h: 32 on MCU, 4096 on hosted builds) has zero references
outside its own #define.  Task structs are kcalloc'd from proc_task_alloc,
so the real ceiling is the pid namespace -- pid_max, default 32768 and
adjustable at runtime.  A reader seeing MAX_PROCS 4096 would reasonably
conclude the system caps at 4096 processes, which is not true of anything.
Remove it.

The real limit is worth stating precisely, and getting that right corrects
an error in the server-readiness doc I wrote earlier in this series.  I had
listed "raise the default pid_max" as a recommended first action, on the
grounds that 32768 is a low ceiling.  That was wrong on both counts:

  * 32768 is Linux's own default for pid_max, so A20OS already matches;
  * it is writable through /proc/sys/kernel/pid_max -- procfs.c dispatches
    the sysctl write and calls proc_set_pid_max().

So raising the default would introduce a divergence from Linux rather than
fix one.  The doc now says so, records that the earlier recommendation was
mistaken, and keeps only the MAX_PROCS removal, which is a real cleanup.
Leaving a wrong claim in a document is the same defect class this series
exists to remove, and it was mine.

Clean -Werror on riscv64, aarch64, x86_64, loongarch64.
45d820245a6e49745d3b43c8057f4a88021f8fb2:
feat(net): register g_lwip_lock for contention accounting before anyone shards it

g_lwip_lock serialises the entire TCP/IP data plane, which makes it the
single number that decides whether the network stack can ever scale across
CPUs.  It was also the one major lock never registered for contention
measurement -- proc, runq, page_cache, dcache, block_cache and vfile_table
all were, so the lock that matters most for a server was the one you could
not see.

Register it and enable per-callsite sampling, so /proc/a20/lock_contention
attributes contention to exact call sites.  This is measurement, not a fix:
sharding a lock this central is a high-risk protocol rewrite, and
docs/roadmap/perf-overhaul.md is explicit that the proc_lock rewrite was
made decidable only after the callsite attribution tool existed.  The same
method applies here, and the project's own perf doc already flags the
network path as the remaining global serialisation point.

Note that spin_set_debug(&g_lwip_lock, "lwip", NULL) was already called at
init; that only labels the [LOCK-STALL] diagnostic print.  Registration is
what makes the lock appear in the contention report at all.

smoke-netfilter now asserts the `lwip:` entry is present in
/proc/a20/lock_contention.  The test deliberately checks for existence
rather than a nonzero count: a single-CPU instance legitimately sees no
contention, so requiring > 0 would be flaky, while a missing entry means
the accounting is silently not wired up.  Gate passes with
dropped=3 out_packets=3, confirming the data plane ran and the entry was
found.

server-readiness.md records that the measurement prerequisite is now in
place while the sharding itself remains open.

Clean -Werror on riscv64, aarch64, x86_64, loongarch64.
94868692c9bb38749442c11df4a400b572c0b7c2:
feat(bus): traverse PCI header-type-1 bridges instead of a flat bus range

pci_scan_current() scanned [bus_start, bus_end) linearly and never read a
bridge's secondary/subordinate bus registers, so any device behind a PCIe
switch was invisible whenever the board reported a narrow range.  On
qemu-virt-riscv64 that range is (0, 1): only bus 0 was ever probed.

The scan now uses a worklist seeded from the configured range and enqueues
[secondary, subordinate] for every header-type-1 device it finds.  A
visited[] array bounds the walk and breaks cycles.  The device-publishing
body moves into pci_publish_bdf(), which decides is_bridge up front so that
an already-registered bridge is still reported as one -- otherwise a rescan
would stop following it and reap the devices behind it as missing.

smoke-pci-bridge boots q35 with a virtio-blk behind two chained
pcie-root-ports.  It passes, and the 7-device baseline is unchanged.

That gate is a regression guard, not proof of the fix: x86_64 passes
0,255 and loongarch64 0,127, so the old linear scan already covered those
buses and the gate would have passed before the change.  The behaviour only
differs on riscv64 (0, 1) and virtualbox-aarch64 (firmware ranges), and this
QEMU build has no PCIe controller on riscv64 virt to exercise them.  Both

982ba030cc40ff541ec60363efff262731ca3ae7:
feat(net): enable RFC 1323 lwIP window scaling

lwIP 2.2 ships the full RFC 1323 implementation -- snd_scale/rcv_scale in
the pcb and the option handling in tcp.c -- but LWIP_WND_SCALE defaults to
0, and lwipopts.h never overrode it.  Every window-related code path was
therefore compiled out and the advertised window stayed a raw 16-bit
field, pinning both directions at 65535 B no matter how large TCP_WND was.

Set LWIP_WND_SCALE 1 with TCP_RCV_SCALE 3 and raise TCP_WND/TCP_SND_BUF
from 32*MSS to 64*MSS.  The on-wire value is TCP_WND >> rcv_scale, so
93440 >> 3 = 11680, comfortably inside the 16-bit field.

TCP_WND is sized by receive buffering, not by the protocol: incoming
segments park in the pbuf pool, so a window wider than the pool can hold
turns a throughput win into mid-connection pool exhaustion and the
retransmit storm that follows.  64*MSS is ~64 of the 256 pool buffers
(384 KiB total), leaving 4x headroom for other sockets and the OoSEQ queue.
A _Static_assert now fails the build if TCP_WND ever exceeds
0xFFFF << TCP_RCV_SCALE, which lwIP would otherwise silently wrap; verified
by temporarily setting 512*MSS and confirming the compile error, then
reverting.

What this does NOT show: any throughput or bandwidth number.  Loopback RTT
is near zero, so the window limit never binds in this environment and a
loopback transfer would measure CPU, not BDP.  The claim here is only that
the protocol-level cap is gone.  The real ceiling is now receive
buffering -- crossing a wide-area BDP still needs a larger pbuf pool or
AIO/zero-copy receive -- and docs/server-readiness.md records that plus the
absence of measurement rather than implying a speedup.

Verified: -Werror builds on riscv64, aarch64, x86_64, loongarch64;
smoke-network-suite, smoke-futex-stress, smoke-abi-linux and
check-honesty-policy pass.
977776db5b4bab497e670928c04fca94f3ee9376:
docs(server-readiness): document pivot_root's required mount state

The readiness doc listed pivot_root as a P0 blocker and only recorded that
it returns -EPERM, which reads as a small gap someone could close on their
own.  Investigating it says otherwise.

Linux defines pivot_root in terms of the mount tree: new_root becomes the
tree root and the old root is attached beneath it at put_old so the caller
can detach it with umount2(put_old, MNT_DETACH).  A20OS has no such tree.
proc_fs_context_t holds root_path and cwd as path strings
(kernel/include/proc/proc.h:22-26), and vfs_move_mount() only strncpy's a
mount's path prefix (kernel/fs/vfs/mount.c:84-97).  With no mnt_parent
chain there is no representation for "hang the old root under the new one".

Implementing it anyway would mean rewriting root_path and returning 0 --
a change the caller sees as success while the old root remains reachable,
and MNT_DETACH still has nothing to detach.  Leaving -EPERM is the honest
answer, so the doc now says what actually has to change first: root/cwd
have to become real mount references, not path strings.

No code change; check-honesty-policy passes.
125aefda7bb754189af3db05f0d0eb426dba696f:
feat(net): expose per-pool lwIP memory pressure under /proc/a20/netmem

Window scaling moved the binding constraint from the protocol window to
receive buffering, and pbuf pool exhaustion was invisible: lwIP already
maintains used/avail/max/err for every pool (MEMP_STATS derives to 1 here
because MEMP_MEM_MALLOC is 0), but the only reader lwIP ships,
memp_get_pool_by_type(), sits behind MEMP_STATS && (LWIP_DEBUG ||
LWIP_STATS_DISPLAY) and both are 0, so it is compiled out.  A20OS was
paying the bookkeeping cost with no way to read it.

Add a20_lwip_format_memp() on top of the extern memp_pools[] table and
surface it as /proc/a20/netmem.  Pool names come from the MEMP_* enum
because struct memp_desc.desc is likewise compiled out under this config.
err is the signal that matters -- it counts failed pool allocations, i.e.
the "pool is too small for this workload" case that shows up in production
as silent retransmits.

The kernel printf is a minimal implementation: do_format parses an optional
'0' flag and width digits but has no '-' flag, and the %s case streams the
string with nlen = 0 so the padding block never runs for strings.  A
"%-16s%6lu..." row therefore printed "%-16s" literally and left the %s
argument unconsumed, so the following %lu read the pool-name pointer as an
integer.  The name is now padded by hand and width is left to the numeric
fields.  smoke-lwip-memp was checked against that exact bug by reintroducing
%-16s and confirming the gate fails.

smoke-lwip-memp runs the network suite then asserts the six pools appear
with err == 0.  What it does NOT show: any basis for the current pool size.
Peak max under a loopback-backed suite is tiny, so sizing the pool for a
real BDP still needs a high-RTT, high-volume load that this environment
cannot produce.  docs/server-readiness.md says so rather than implying the
384 KiB pool is validated.

Verified: -Werror builds on riscv64, aarch64, x86_64, loongarch64;
smoke-lwip-memp, smoke-network-suite and check-honesty-policy pass.
4af364f3a94bedd0aa8c113a8e7c4c16f2e9d0f6:
docs(server-readiness): record why the lwIP sharding P0 has no evidence behind it yet

The callsite accounting from 4536a000 exists precisely to inform the
g_lwip_lock sharding decision, so I measured it before attempting the
refactor: booted riscv64 with -smp 4, ran smoke-network-suite (7 passed,
1 skipped), then read /proc/a20/lock_contention.

Result: lwip: 0 0 -- zero contended acquires and zero contended spins.  But
vfile_table, page_cache, dcache, block_cache, runq and proc all read 0 too,
which is what makes the reading meaningful rather than suspicious: the
accounting is live, the workload is not concurrent.

smoke-network-suite is a functional suite.  Its subtests run one at a time
via fork+wait (dns, tcp_loopback, tcp_edge, udp_loopback, icmp_loopback,
unix, alg, timeout), so it never puts parallel network traffic through the
stack.  It therefore cannot answer whether sharding would buy anything, and
"0" here is a null result about the workload, not a measurement of the
lock.

Recorded as-is so the P0 is not read as "measured and found unnecessary" or
"just go shard it".  The prerequisite is a genuine concurrent network
workload -- several parallel TCP transfers -- to produce a real contention
distribution with attribution before touching a concurrency protocol.  No
code change; check-honesty-policy passes.
0134b2ad152aafeecee29fbb3ce1e47bd2bedc67:
perf(net): measure cross-core lock contention on SMP builds

a48bfc4d recorded "lwip: 0 0" and concluded the sharding P0 lacked
evidence.  That measurement was wrong, and so was my explanation of it.

The dev build uses NR_CPUS=1 (Makefile:47), so passing -smp 4 to QEMU
changed nothing -- the kernel brings up one CPU, and one CPU can never
contend a spinlock.  The zeros were an artifact of the single-core default,
not evidence the lock is idle.  Cross-core contention is only visible with
an explicit NR_CPUS>1 build.

Add net_stress_test: WORKERS concurrent TCP loopback transfers, each a
forked server/client pair, integrity checked with an additive checksum the
server returns so a transfer that completes with wrong bytes fails instead
of passing.  Add smoke-smp-lock-contention, which runs it on an NR_CPUS=4
build and reads /proc/a20/lock_contention.

Measured on riscv64 QEMU, 4 workers x 4 MiB:

  lwip:   27 acquires /  1149170 spins
  proc: 3487 acquires /  5687843 spins

lwip burns ~42k spins per contended acquire.  proc_lock is the larger
problem -- ~126x the acquires and ~5x the spins -- so it is promoted from
P2 to P0; the old "processes get slow at scale" framing understated what
the doc's own 8-core numbers already showed.

Two limits on what this data supports, both recorded in the doc:

- Callsite attribution covers acquires, not spins.  All 27 lwip acquires
  are attributed (net_vfile_read 21, net_tcp_drop_pcb 3, net_inet_bind_pcb
  2, net_inet_socket_destroy 1), but those sites' spins total 27 against
  1149170.  "Which call site spins" is therefore unmeasured, and must not
  be used to design the sharding split.  Note net_vfile_read dominates the
  acquires, so a good share of the contention is the syscall read path
  rather than the receive path.
- The gate asserts no contention numbers.  Three identical runs gave lwip
  spins of 134669, 1074743 and 1149170, so any threshold would be a flaky
  gate and would invite tuning toward a magic constant.  It asserts only
  that the stress test transfers correctly and the counters render.

Also fixes a bug in the new gate: a bare $ end-anchor in the grep patterns
was consumed by make instead of reaching the shell, which mangled the shell
syntax and made the condition false even with all data present.

Verified: -Werror builds on riscv64, aarch64, x86_64, loongarch64;
smoke-smp-lock-contention and check-honesty-policy pass.
93c70c59678da9af97126eb860a97d00c7c90a8d:
feat(core-lock): attribute per-site spin cost not just acquire count

The lwIP sharding P0 needs to know which call site actually burns spin
before anyone designs a split.  It could not answer that, because the
audit column it needed did not exist.

spin_lock_at() incremented site->spins inside the outer retry loop, once
per failed exchange, making it a duplicate of the acquire count.  The
real spin loop is the inner one, and its tally was only ever summed into
the lock-level contended_spins.  Measured on the 4-core gate that showed
as 27 acquires against 1149170 spins with the per-site spins summing to
27 -- the column was structurally incapable of answering the question.

Resolve the sample slot before entering the retry loop, snapshot the spin
counter as it was, and after the inner loop drains add the difference to
site->spins.  The slot is resolved up front because the spin count does
not exist until the wait ends, yet it has to land on the same slot the
acquire was charged to.

After the fix the per-site spins sum to exactly the lock-level total
(689073 = 689073, and 381751 = 381751 on a second run), and the ranking
changes the plan: 16 of 17 acquires and effectively all of the spin are
at net_vfile_read.  The contention is the socket read path on the syscall
side, not the packet receive path, so splitting RX from TX would not
address the dominant cost.  docs/server-readiness.md now says this instead
of the earlier "attribution is not trustworthy" note, which the fix
invalidated.

smoke-smp-lock-contention grows an invariant for it: the per-site lwip
spin sum must be at least 90% of the lock-level lwip spins.  A ratio
rather than an absolute number, since absolute counts are not reproducible
run to run; 90% still leaves room for hash-slot collisions between
call sites.  Confirmed to have teeth by deleting the per-site
accumulation and watching the gate fail.

Verified: -Werror builds on riscv64, aarch64, x86_64, loongarch64;
smoke-smp-lock-contention and check-honesty-policy pass.
18edcb276ef61b5ce956beb5350e84b66c1b9918: docs(server-readiness): correct the lwIP contention attribution and distinguish acquire from hold
8626abce1004a1b8034589ee51a7a3bbf1632a05:
docs(server-readiness): name the concrete fix for the lwIP lock P0 with its safety conditions

01ccc13f pinned down where the contention comes from.  Reading the progress
bridge next shows the fix already exists in this tree, for the same reason,
and the read path simply is not using it.

progress.c:38-44 states the problem outright -- "NO_SYS lwIP has one global
core lock.  Letting every idle CPU poll it turns an otherwise idle SMP guest
into a permanent lock convoy" -- so kernel_progress_poll() restricts polling
to CPU 0.  kernel_progress_timer_tick() does the same for the timer wheel and
only re-takes g_lwip_lock when a device signalled work, with the stated goal
of keeping the per-context-switch scheduler hot path off the lock.  The RX
progress hint contract at lwip_stack.c:55-62 wires the virtio-net IRQ top-half
to raise that flag for a20_lwip_poll_locked() to consume.

net_vfile_read() bypasses the hint and calls a20_lwip_poll() unconditionally
from its for(;;) loop, taking the global lock every iteration even when no
device has data.  That is the acquire-side cost the 4-core measurement sees.

Recorded as the next step rather than implemented: making the read path
respect the hint depends on questions this tree does not answer on its own.
Delivery has to keep working when poll is skipped, since delivery would then
rest entirely on IRQ top-half plus wakeup.  The read path may currently depend
on poll to advance its own TCP retransmit timers.  And a20_lwip_poll() also
drives the bottom-halves, so skipping it wholesale could drop deferred work.
Getting that wrong is a read hang, so it needs its own gate work first.

No code change; check-honesty-policy passes.
96386fb90ac7ea78e65dc2600be02ed69e94bcd0:
fix(net): poll read readiness only when the device has work

net_vfile_read() called a20_lwip_poll() unconditionally from its for(;;)
loop, so a reader blocked on network progress took g_lwip_lock every
iteration just to discover there was nothing to do.  The 4-core measurement
put 16 of 17 lwip contended acquires on that call site.

The gating this needs already exists for the scheduler and timer paths --
progress.c:38-44 calls the resulting convoy a "permanent lock convoy" and
restricts polling to CPU 0, and virtio_net_poll_rx_all() already skips the
lock unless a device signalled work.  The read path just never used it.

Before changing it, answered the three questions where a wrong answer means
a read hang, and all three hold:

- Delivery does not run through the reader's poll.  The virtio-net IRQ runs
  a20_lwip_poll_locked(), which fills bh_ring.  What moves bh_ring into the
  socket queues and wakes read_waitq is net_inet_bottom_half_process_all(),
  and sched() runs it before picking the next task (sched.c:1838-1841).  A
  reader that parks therefore always gets sched() to run.
- TCP timers do not depend on it.  kernel_progress_timer_tick() is called
  from the timer IRQ on all 8 architectures, so retransmission timeouts
  advance from interrupts alone.
- The bottom-halves are deliberately NOT gated.  They take g_net_lock
  rather than g_lwip_lock, and the waiter needs them to consume its own
  deferred receive data.

net_vfile_read() also re-checks s->rx_head under g_net_lock before
wait_queue_link() (socket_file.c:84-87), so there is no lost-wakeup race.

The capability check is driver-agnostic via a new optional rx_irq_driven in
net_dev_ops_t.  NULL means unknown, and unknown is treated as "no IRQ" so an
unconverted driver keeps being drained unconditionally rather than silently
losing RX.  That matches how link_up is already handled.

Result, reported honestly because it is half a win: lwip contended acquires
fell across runs from 55/27/17 to 6/1, but the spin volume did not move --
about 1.15M/1.07M before, still ~1.28M after.  This removes redundant
acquisitions, not the cost.  The remaining cost is on the hold side: the
owner spans an unbounded RX drain under the same lock.  Bounding that drain
is the real remaining work and is riskier, since it can affect packet
delivery latency, so it is left for its own change with its own gate.

Also fixes a real accounting hole found by this: lock_counters_format_one()
skipped any sample whose ra was 0, which happens when a waiter has no
recoverable return address such as an interrupt context.  Those samples
still counted toward contended_spins, so per-site spins silently failed to
add up to the lock total -- exactly the invariant smoke-smp-lock-contention
checks.  They are now reported as "?" and the gate passes with attribution
exact (1280828 of 1280828).

Verified: -Werror builds on riscv64, aarch64, x86_64, loongarch64;
net_stress_test transfers 16 MiB across 4 concurrent blocking readers with
checksums intact and no hang; smoke-smp-lock-contention, smoke-network-suite,
smoke-lwip-memp, smoke-abi-linux and check-honesty-policy pass.
26d58e3b06589c349d9bb0763b2c3af0e6988b68:
docs(server-readiness): retract the unbounded RX drain claim the bound would be a no-op

02406b8d reported the remaining lwIP cost as the lock owner spanning an
unbounded receive drain, and proposed bounding it as the next step.  Both
halves of that are wrong, and the proposal would have wasted effort.

The drain is already bounded.  a20_lwip_process_netif_rx_tx_locked() loops
on st->ops->recv(), which for virtio-net is virtio_net_recv(); that returns
0 when last_used == used_idx (virtio_net.c:424-427) and otherwise pops one
descriptor.  The ring is VIRTIO_QUEUE_SIZE deep, which is 32.  So a single
poll processes at most 32 packets and adding a cap changes nothing.

The spin figure is also being over-read.  contended_spins counts
arch_cpu_relax() iterations, and there is no fixed conversion from
iterations to wall-clock, so 1.28M spins is not a statement about how long
the lock was held.  Treating it as a hold-duration proxy is what made the
drain look like the problem in the first place.

What the measurement does support: the acquire side is now cheap (55/27/17
down to 6/1 contended acquires after 02406b8d), and the remaining cost is
per-packet work under the single lock -- pbuf allocation, netfilter, and
n->input() with full TCP input processing for every packet drained.  What
would actually help is reducing that per-packet work or sharding the lock,
both much larger than a loop bound.

No code change; check-honesty-policy passes.
0094efc4b72a9488788ebbe2f2b5f38d1260a5c2: fix(net): measure read waiters and reject the proc_lock TLB-wait hypothesis
1ab109bd272cd9796022bfa9f2e1c333f0174b15:
feat(lock): record the worst single acquire not just the spin total

proc_lock showed 5.45M spins over 2802 contended acquires, and the totals
alone cannot say whether that is a hot short critical section or a few
long holds. Those need opposite fixes, so record max spins per acquire,
per lock and per callsite, and switch the gate off NF-relative awk fields
onto left-anchored ones since the format gained a column.

Contended path only, matching the existing counter discipline: the max is
recorded inside the existing `if (spins)` arm, so an uncontended acquire
still costs a single exchange.

Measured 4-core, 136->182 mm_context_enter calls in the same run:

  proc_lock  2802 acquires   mean 1946   max 519208
  lwip          4 acquires   mean 208349 max 472365

So the aggregate is not steady-state contention -- mean is modest and a
handful of acquires dominate. The fix is narrowing long holds, not
lowering acquire frequency.

Two limits worth recording. These callsite labels share the return-address
skip already noted for proc_sched_safe_point, since sched() is inlined, so
the symbol may be the enclosing function. And spins are counted by the
waiter: max duration says the lock was held that long, not whether the
holder was working or was preempted mid-critical-section. Separating those
needs holder-side timestamps, which needs a cycle source -- and riscv64,
the only arch with ASID enabled and so the only one where this loop runs,

01d0926ee66611c4fa543a547c9216ebb11cb6f5:
docs(server-readiness): replace the cause still unidentified note with the measured shape

The previous revision said locating the proc_lock bottleneck needed
hold-time measurement. That measurement now exists, so the section
claimed an open question it had already answered.

The max-spins-per-acquire counters show the aggregate is not steady-state
contention: 2802 contended acquires average 1946 spins while one acquire
reached 519208, so a handful of long holds dominate and the fix is
narrowing those rather than lowering acquire frequency. The worst sites
by duration are the low-volume ones -- proc_park_commit (20 acquires) and
sys_wait4 (6) -- not the high-volume proc_sched_tick (1424).

Also records a hypothesis that was checked and refuted rather than left
implied: proc_park_commit does not hold proc_lock across its switch. It
takes task->park_lock, releases it at park.c:275, and only then calls
sched() at :283.

the waiter, so they bound how long the lock was held but cannot separate

That needs holder-side timestamps, which needs an rdcycle wrapper that
