31c6d06ff0ce647317cd4a7ba6425047e2ec3f13:
docs(server-readiness): record why the proc_lock holder cannot be timed under QEMU

An earlier revision of the readiness doc left the remaining gap in proc_lock attribution as "an
rdcycle wrapper for riscv64". That was wrong in a way worth writing down: the wrapper is not
the blocker, the measurement environment is.

Adding arch_read_cycle() for riscv64, aarch64 and x86_64 (riscv32 already had one; other arches
return 0 as a no-counter sentinel) and stamping it at acquire produced two failures in a row.
Subtracting gave hold=18446744009993433250, a 64-bit underflow, because QEMU TCG derives
rdcycle from host time and it is not monotonic across vCPU threads. Rejecting backwards samples
removed the underflow but still reported holdmax=31958042598, about 32 seconds, for critical
sections that last microseconds. Neither number is a hold time, so the accounting is not
committed. A column that prints 1.8e19, or 32s for a microsecond hold, is worse than an absent
column: it reads like a measurement. Whether a holder was working or was preempted remains
open, and the way forward is real hardware (VisionFive 2 / LS2K1000) or a time-independent
proxy such as counting scheduler switches inside the hold.

What the data does support was then established without a clock. All 69 proc_lock acquisitions
in the tree use spin_lock_irqsave, with no IRQ-enabled spin_lock anywhere, so a holder cannot
be preempted by a timer interrupt mid-hold. No sched() or proc_yield() appears inside a
proc_lock critical section either, so it cannot voluntarily yield. That leaves the holder
genuinely executing for the duration, which is what the max= measurement points at: a handful
of very long holds rather than steady contention. Preemption is ruled out structurally.

The first candidate named for that shape was mm_sync_shared_dirty_for_vnode() at mmap.c:37,
which takes proc_lock with interrupts disabled and then walks every task, takes each mm->lock,
every VMA and every page-table leaf, calling page_cache_get, page_cache_mark_dirty and
page_cache_put underneath. It is reached from read() at file.c:94, from fsync at file.c:299 and
from msync at sys_mm.c:183, and the shared_file_maps fast path is genuinely live because
vnode_shared_map_inc runs on the mmap and vma paths. That accounted for all three measured
traits at once: millions of spins, a handful of very long holds, and no preemption involvement.
The proposed fix was to stop doing a whole-system scan under a global lock, by reversing the
index by vnode or sharding per mm, rather than splitting proc_lock per wait object as the P0
row had proposed.

That single-site claim is retracted here. A wider scan of every proc_lock critical section
found at least four hot paths that walk the whole task list with interrupts disabled:
mm_sync_shared_dirty_for_vnode() at mmap.c:37, proc_get_vm_stats() at proc.c:200 on a procfs
read, loadavg_sample_counts() at loadavg.c:54, and cgroup memory accounting at cg_mem.c:116.
proc.c:322 walks the list too, but it sits inside CONFIG_DEBUG_SCHED_STATE and only fires from
the hang diagnostic, so it is excluded as a hot path. Nothing in the measurements distinguishes
these. Naming one was the same mistake as the earlier TLB claim: picking the most plausible
candidate without evidence that separates it from the others, and the evidence that would
separate them, hold duration per site, is exactly the quantity QEMU cannot supply. So what
stands is only the preemption refutation, the handful-of-very-long-holds shape, and the cause
class, an unbounded whole-system traversal under a global lock. The specific hotspot still
needs real hardware or a time-independent proxy.

The cause class is retracted too, and the deeper defect turns out to be in the measurement.
Checking the candidates against the workload that produced the numbers: net_stress_test's
read() and write() are socket calls, so mm_sync_shared_dirty_for_vnode() is never reached, and
proc_get_vm_stats() has exactly one caller, the PF_MEMINFO case in procfs_render.c, while the
gate cats /proc/a20/perf and lock_contention rather than meminfo. The candidates are cold for
this measurement and cannot be its cause. More important, the lock counters have no reset entry
point, so they accumulate from boot, and the 905K-1.37M spin maximum attributed to the stress
phase may have happened during boot instead. Every reading of "contention under stress" so far
rests on a window that was never separated. What is unlocated is which code holds proc_lock
that long, and the next step is not more candidate hunting but giving the counters a reset, or
differencing two snapshots, so the boot window and the stress window can be told apart. Until
then no attribution from this gate is trustworthy.
9a4024c8e6be748fb98e3f7509e7c2b194a3a100:
test(smoke): separate the boot window from the stress window and answer the question

The lock counters have no reset entry point, so they accumulate from boot.
Every reading of "contention under stress" so far therefore rested on a
window that was never separated, and the doc speculated that the 905K-1.37M
spin maximum had happened during boot.

No kernel change is needed to separate them: read /proc/a20/lock_contention
before and after the stress and difference the two. proc_lock is registered
first at proc.c:365 and lock_counters_format() iterates in registration
order, so each block's "^proc: " line is a reliable delimiter.

The measurement refutes the boot-artifact hypothesis, twice:

  boot    2544 acquires / 2267465 spins   mean   891
  stress   103 acquires / 1256900 spins   mean 12202
  boot    1786 acquires / 2840455 spins   mean  1590
  stress    62 acquires /  797794 spins   mean 12867

The stress phase is 8-14x heavier per contended acquire, so the long holds
really are in the stress phase. That further weakens the four file/MM
candidates from the previous commit, since net_stress_test is pure network:
its read() and write() are socket calls.

Two defects in my own first attempt at this are fixed rather than papered
over. The shell arithmetic subtracted from an empty field when the
post-stress read was dropped -- the console tail command does get lost under
load -- producing negative spin counts while the gate still reported PASS. It
is now a single self-validating awk that prints an explicit UNAVAILABLE
instead. And the per-site invariant was passing vacuously, because
site_acq == 0 satisfies it, so a run with no stress-window lwip attribution
looked identical to a checked one; the gate now says so explicitly.

The cause is still unlocated, but it is now correctly scoped to which code
holds proc_lock for milliseconds during the network stress phase.
92bb8788e9c5b456de83c9a03e3c641bf7e5215e:
docs(server-readiness): name the structural limit and withdraw the clock-free attribution

Calling the four whole-task-list candidates "cold" for this workload understated it. Every
caller of proc_first_task_locked() lives in kernel/mm/, kernel/proc/ or kernel/fs/, and
kernel/net/ has zero hits. Since the stress workload is pure network, with net_stress_test's
read() and write() being socket calls, those sites are not merely unlikely, they are not on the
call path at all. The traversal explanation is dead.

Differencing the boot window against the stress window per callsite also corrects where the
earlier cumulative numbers came from. The boot window is dominated by proc_sched_tick+0x30 at
1576889 spins, and that single site is what inflated every total read so far. The stress window
has a different profile: proc_clone_impl+0x64 with 163315 spins from only 2 contended acquires,
whose max equals its total, i.e. one hold of roughly 1.6ms, plus sys_wait4+0x36 at 70750 and
proc_task_first_entry+0x30 at 92972.

The important caveat is recorded rather than glossed: those labels name the waiter, the side
that called acquire and spun, not the holder. proc_clone_impl spinning 163315 times says only
that someone else held the lock for a long time.

The claim that waiter-side data cannot in principle identify the holder is then softened to
what is actually true. Checking the lock shows why: spinlock_t.owner_ra is written with the
acquirer's return address on acquire, at lock.h:197 for spin_lock_at and lock.h:232 for the
irqsave variant, and cleared only on unlock at :206. The holder's identity is therefore visible
for the entire hold, and the existing [LOCK-STALL] diagnostic at lock.h:158-163 already prints
owner_ra alongside waiter_ra, so the plumbing demonstrably works. The real obstacles are
narrower: the per-callsite table records only the waiter, and the spin loop samples every 2^20
iterations at lock.h:154, which is above the observed hold magnitude of roughly 512K-1.37M
spins, so some holds fall below the threshold and would never be sampled at all. That made the
next step look concrete and clock-free: sample lock->owner_ra once a waiter passes a threshold
well below those figures, and attribute by holder. The state needed already exists; only the
sampling and the attribution were missing.

That promise was withdrawn along with the code, because it was implemented and it does not
work. Two attempts, both discarded. Charging all remaining spins to a single mid-wait sample
blames whichever task happened to hold the lock at that instant, which is wrong whenever the
lock passes between short holders. Charging per 2^16 window fixes that but introduces a worse
problem: each window contributes the same 65536 spins whether the holder held for a microsecond
or for a millisecond, so the metric measures who holds the lock while contended, weighted by
frequency, and cannot answer who holds it for a long time. That is precisely the question being
asked. Measured: about 5% of spins were attributable, across only 2 callsites with exactly one
window each, and hmax was pinned at the window size, making it useless as a longest-hold
figure. The callsites it did name were frequent brief holders, proc_sched_tick and idle_loop.
The first version named proc_task_first_entry, which turns out to be the idle task's
trampoline: it is written into the initial ra at proc.c:423 and proc.c:454 and is not a
lock-taking function at all. A real bug was introduced and then fixed along the way: the holder
path indexed lock->samples without the NULL check the waiter path has, which faulted in the
kernel for any lock not registered for callsite sampling.

The net conclusion is a limitation rather than a result: identifying a long-duration holder
requires measuring duration, which needs a real clock. On QEMU that means real hardware or
-icount. The cause stays unlocated, narrowed only to a millisecond-scale hold near fork/clone
and wait-for-child during the stress phase.
227015504da5df775e7f56c3b0235c59ac5539a2:
merge(net): merge the server-hardening branch and the proc_lock contention work

46 commits in four parts:

1) Infrastructure fixes
   - PCI: pci_scan_current() went from a flat bus range to worklist traversal,
     following the secondary and subordinate buses of header-type-1 bridges,
     which fixes devices behind a bridge being invisible on narrow-bus
     platforms
   - ext4 journal, virtio-blk flush, AF_ALG, reboot permissions, the pagemap
     gate, fail-closed setsockopt, rlimit/getrusage/PSI and more

2) Networking
   - Enabled the lwIP TCP window scaling switch, since LWIP_WND_SCALE was
     compiled off, sized it to pbuf pool capacity and added compile-time
     assertions
   - New /proc/a20/netmem exposing pbuf and TCP memory pool watermarks
   - Gated the poll on the read path: a blocked reader used to take the global
     lock on every loop iteration to confirm there was nothing to do

3) Gates and observability
   - New smoke-pci-bridge, smoke-lwip-memp and smoke-smp-lock-contention
   - net_stress_test: 4-way concurrent TCP load
   - Fixed the site spin count in spin_lock_at() that duplicated the acquire
     count
   - Counters accumulate from boot, so the gates now read once before and once
     after the stress and take the difference, separating the boot phase from
     the stress phase

4) Locating proc_lock contention, mostly by disproving hypotheses
   - Disproved TLB convergence as the cause: flushes == waits, with no repeated
     convergence
   - Disproved "the holder got preempted": all 69 acquisitions are
     spin_lock_irqsave and there is no sched() or proc_yield() in the critical
     sections
   - Disproved a whole-system walk as the cause: the proc_first_task_locked
     call site is not on the net/ path
   - Disproved "the extreme happens during boot": each contention during the
     stress phase is 8-14x worse than during boot
   - Two attempts to attribute the lock holder, via rdcycle and windowed
     sampling, were withdrawn because they did not hold up. The conclusion is
     recorded in docs/server-readiness.md: naming a long holder needs a real
     clock

Verified with -Werror on 4 architectures; smoke-abi-linux,
smoke-sched-stress, smoke-network-suite, smoke-riscv64 and
smoke-smp-lock-contention pass; check-concurrency-foundation,
check-process-lock-split-boundary, check-honesty-policy and check-doc-drift
pass.
e72848033ce04633554af92febb26a825ffa666f:
fix(ipc): correct the SysV message and shared-memory ABI layouts

shmctl(SHM_INFO) copied 64 bytes into musl's 48-byte `struct shm_info`, so
every call wrote 16 bytes past the caller's buffer. musl's layout is
`int __used_ids` plus five unsigned long -- 4 + 4 pad + 40 -- and glibc agrees,
so both were overrun. Replaced the raw `char zero[64]` with a named struct and
a compile-time check on its size.

msgctl(IPC_STAT/MSG_STAT) had the mirror-image problem: it wrote 96 bytes into
musl's 120-byte `struct msqid_ds`, so msg_lspid, msg_lrpid and the trailing
__unused pair were never written at all. That one is nastier than an overrun
because it cannot fail -- the syscall returns 0 and the caller silently reads
whatever its own uninitialised buffer held. The kernel already tracks lspid and
lrpid (msg_send/msg_recv maintain them), so they are now reported instead of
left at zero.

Both structs are now named and asserted rather than hand-computed offsets.
The msg reply had six `((unsigned long *)(ds + N))[0] = ...` stores encoding
the layout positionally; that is exactly what let the size drift to 96 while
the comment above it claimed a different one. Named fields plus STATIC_ASSERT
means a future layout change fails the build instead of the guest.

The kernel builds as -std=gnu99, so C11 _Static_assert is unavailable. The
STATIC_ASSERT macro in core/types.h uses an extern array with a negative bound
when the condition is false; a file-scope typedef would pass silently, which
would defeat the point. Verified load-bearing: changing the shm_info assert
from 48 to 47 fails the build with "size of array ... is negative".

On the missing IPC_64_BIT mask in msgctl: the original diagnosis was wrong, and
the disassembly says so. musl's IPC_CMD() is `((cmd) & ~IPC_TIME64) | IPC_64`,
but its syscall_arch.h sets IPC_64 to 0 on all four 64-bit targets and ipc.h's
#ifndef guard respects that, so cmd is passed through untouched -- the built
wrappers contain no `or $0x100` at all. I still added the mask, because
shmctl and semctl both have it and one ctl path disagreeing with the other two
is how this class of bug gets reintroduced; it is inert today and the comment
says so rather than implying a live fix.

Also checked and found already correct, so left alone: semid_ds (88, matches
musl), seminfo (40, matches), shmid_ds (112, matches), and the semctl
SEM_UNDO/SEM_INFO paths. IPC_SET read 96 of 120 bytes, which is an under-read
and therefore memory-safe, but it now uses the same checked type as the write
path so the two cannot disagree.

Four architectures build; the 20 source gates stay at the 16/4 baseline and
the three generator gates still pass.
926382b3e6d52b991b68f50543878d275d9a69af:
test(a20): gate QEMU launches on host resources and wait when they are short

A `tools/a20 run` on a 4 GiB GUI instance can starve the host: QEMU takes
the guest's RAM and vCPUs while the build writes a 4 GiB image. The result
is rarely a clean failure. More often the host gets OOM-killed mid-build,
or the guest's time-sensitive gates start failing for reasons that have
nothing to do with the code under test -- which then gets recorded as a
flaky result and re-investigated as if it were a kernel bug.

So the launch path now samples the host first and, when the instance does
not fit, waits for the resources to come back. Waiting rather than failing
is deliberate: the usual cause is a co-tenant or another build finishing,
which resolves on its own, so refusing immediately only relocates the
retry onto the human. A20_PREFLIGHT_TIMEOUT bounds the wait (0 reports
without waiting), A20_PREFLIGHT=0 bypasses the gate, and
A20_PREFLIGHT_VERBOSE=1 logs the sample when it passes.

The sizing policy lives in a20_preflight rather than in the launcher so it
can be reasoned about and tested without booting anything. It mirrors three
Makefile defaults, which is duplication and therefore drift-prone, so
`a20 check` now re-reads the Makefile and fails if the copies disagree.

The gate is checked on the run/debug/test paths only: build, package and
flash do not launch a guest and must not be blocked by it.
ae01fe5850083472bd80463e54674e6c35c0afba:
feat(tools): build a host virglrenderer new enough for a current mesa

GPU_3D=1 makes the guest attach a virgl-capable virtio-gpu, but the renderer
that actually executes the command stream is on the host: QEMU dlopen()s
libvirglrenderer. So guest 3D availability is gated by the host's renderer
version, and no guest kernel change can move it. A renderer too old to build
the offscreen desktop-GL context that virgl_renderer_get_capset() needs
makes Mesa's virtio_gpu_dri.so attach fail with ERR_INVALID_PARAMETER, which
is exactly the failure this project has been recording as a dead end.

Distributions still ship 1.1.0 from 2020 on some releases -- Debian trixie
offers no newer candidate -- so the only route is to build it. That needs
root, so it is a script an operator runs on purpose rather than something the
build does behind their back, and it does not touch the system install: the
result lands under tools/virgl/install and is picked up from there.

The Makefile now looks for that prefix and, when present, runs QEMU with
LD_LIBRARY_PATH pointing at it. It uses an env prefix rather than QEMU's -L
because -L is the *data* search path, not the shared-library path, so -L
would silently do nothing. With no prefix present the QEMU command line is
byte-for-byte what it was before.

`check` reports host QEMU, both the distro and any local virglrenderer, and
whether /dev/dri/renderD128 is actually accessible -- a node that exists but
is not readable produces a QEMU failure that reads like a driver bug. The
build step closes by naming the falsifiable check: a modern renderer reports
a capset of kilobytes, so a guest log showing 308 bytes means the old library
is still being loaded and the build did not take effect.
58171df677112dc958f4fb760f7c9f66fa01426b:
feat(drm): model KMS objects and validate the ioctl ABI against Linux

Presenting without recording what was presented is the root defect here. The
CRTC kept no framebuffer binding at all: SETCRTC copied pixels to scanout and
returned 0 without storing anything, so GETCRTC reported fb_id 0 forever and
GETPLANE hardcoded 0. A client cannot tell that apart from "nothing is on
screen", and wlroots reads the primary plane's fb to decide whether it still
owns the display. The CRTC now holds the binding, GETCRTC reports it and
writes back the connector list the way Linux does, and the primary plane
mirrors that single binding rather than keeping a second copy that can drift.

mode_valid stays 1 with fb_id 0 on purpose. It means "the CRTC/connector pair
has a programmed mode", not "a framebuffer is bound"; the connector here is
permanently connected. Reporting 0 tells wlroots the output has no mode and it
abandons the output during backend init.

PAGE_FLIP resolved pf.fb_id as a GEM handle. Framebuffer ids and GEM handles
come from independent counters, so that only works while the two happen to
coincide and otherwise presents the wrong buffer. It goes through the
framebuffer now, like SETCRTC already did.

Three ioctl numbers and two struct layouts did not match the Linux UAPI, and
none of the mismatches could have been found by reading the code:

  MODE_GETFB2  was 0xc04864ca, Linux is 0xc06864ce -- wrong size field *and*
               wrong command number, so drmModeGetFB2 returned EINVAL
  MODE_RMFB    was _IOW where Linux uses _IOWR, so drmModeRmFB never matched
  GEM_OPEN     was 0xc0186410; Linux puts it at 0xc010640b
  drm_gem_open had the handle at offset 8; Linux returns it at 4, so every
               GEM_OPEN read the handle from the wrong field
  GEM_GET_HANDLE was a 12-byte struct where Linux's GEM_FLINK is 8

Worse, DRM_IOCTL_GEM_MMAP was defined as 0xc010640b -- which is Linux's
GEM_OPEN. A guest calling the real GEM_OPEN was served by the mmap handler.

The Linux UAPI also has no GEM_CREATE, GEM_MMAP or GEM_GET_HANDLE at all:
userspace buffer creation goes through MODE_CREATE_DUMB, and naming a handle
for import is GEM_FLINK. So those three had no upstream number to match, which
is how they ended up shadowing real ioctls. GEM_FLINK is now implemented as the
real ioctl, and the two that remain are A20-private, parked outside the Linux
range where they cannot shadow anything.

GETFB2 was a stub that zeroed the struct and returned success, so every lookup
of a real framebuffer looked like a lookup of framebuffer 0 with no geometry.
It now answers from the backing GEM.

EXECBUFFER ignored bo_handles, so a command stream naming a texture or vertex
buffer reached the host with no memory mapped and rendered into nothing. The
kernel is the only place that can resolve those handles, since the stream
carries them rather than resource ids, so it now publishes any backing that is
missing before submitting. VIRTGPU_WAIT likewise validated nothing, which turns
a caller waiting on the wrong resource into corruption that surfaces much later.

There is also a lifetime bug: a 3D resource stays mapped by the host after
userspace drops its handle, because the host writes results straight into those
frames. Releasing the VMO first returned them to the allocator while the host
could still write. Reclaim now drops the resource before the pages.

tools/check-drm-abi.sh is the gate for all of the above. It compiles a probe
against the installed UAPI headers and compares every number, and it lifts the
local struct definitions out of drm.c to measure the layouts A20OS actually
uses -- a correct ioctl number does not protect against a wrong struct. Both
directions are verified to fail: perturbing MODE_RMFB and dropping one field
from drm_mode_fb_cmd each make it exit 1.
4fb9171f3c023c3552d906b134795bbbf75a5d60:
fix(net): fix a double free on the raw-socket receive path and add a pbuf canary

The raw recv callback frees the pbuf and then returned 0. lwIP reads that
return as an "eaten" flag: non-zero means the callback took the packet and
the caller must not free it, zero means it is still the caller's. So the
caller freed a pbuf the callback had already freed -- on the path that
leads straight back into ip6_input/icmp6_input, which is the shape of the
`pbuf_free: p->ref > 0` assert that has been killing the desktop session
after ~55s.

raw_recv is registered for both AF_INET and AF_INET6 SOCK_RAW, so IPv6 raw
sockets reach the same callback. This is the receive-side mirror of the
send-side double free already fixed, and the receive side was missed.

Why this was so hard to see: memp's free list is a plain pointer chain
threaded through the freed blocks themselves, so a single double free does
not just corrupt one refcount -- it re-links the block and memp_malloc then
hands the same memory to two live pbufs. After that every refcount reading
is meaningless, and "double free" versus "a neighbour was overwritten"
stopped being distinguishable. Both explanations were recorded as
conclusions in known-issues.md; neither survived, and the symptom being
IPv6-only is still not fully explained -- boot IPv6 traffic (RS/NS/NA/DAD,
MLD) is simply far higher volume than boot IPv4 traffic on the same paths,
which is enough to surface a latent race that IPv4 load hides.

MEMP_OVERFLOW_CHECK is now available as CONFIG_LWIP_MEMP_OVERFLOW_CHECK=1.
It is the cheapest way to catch the *first* imbalance rather than the one
that trips the assert, and the pool currently has no canary at all. Off by
default because it costs a comparison per pool operation.

Also recorded what has been ruled out, so it is not re-derived: lwIP itself
is unpatched apart from one board-guarded diagnostic printf, the RX seam
allocates a fresh single-element pool pbuf per frame and the virtio driver
clamps both pkt_len and used_len, so one frame's pbuf cannot be double
freed at the seam. The offending free therefore happened on an earlier
packet.
e1b286795ed3d7bfbcc40fab5e9ef25e8cabb8b8:
feat(xfce): run minecraft on the Wayland backend instead of the broken XWayland one

Minecraft reached its main menu and then showed nothing, which looked like a
3D-driver problem. It is not. GLFW 3.4.0 selects its backend in
_glfwSelectPlatform, and with both backends compiled in and no
glfwInitHint(GLFW_PLATFORM, ...) -- which Minecraft never calls -- it
honours XDG_SESSION_TYPE=wayland together with WAYLAND_DISPLAY, and
otherwise falls back to trying Wayland and then X11. Landing on X11 means an
XWayland window, and labwc's xwm never presents those on A20OS.

So the game was being handed to a presentation path that is known-broken,
while the native Wayland path is already proven: es2gears_wayland reported
EGL 1.5 and GLES 3.2 on llvmpipe and kept running. Setting the session type
takes the working branch before any detection happens, so DISPLAY being set
no longer matters.

The premise this replaces was wrong in a way worth recording. There is no
GLFW_PLATFORM environment variable -- not in 3.4.0 and not in current GLFW;
it is an init hint only, and the string is absent from the shipped
libglfw.so. The image also carries LWJGL 3.3.3, not 3.3.6. The conclusion
holds anyway because that LWJGL build bundles GLFW 3.4.0, but the reasoning
that reached it did not.

The guard is deliberately loud. Without WAYLAND_DISPLAY and XDG_RUNTIME_DIR
the Wayland branch is not taken at all and GLFW quietly goes back to X11,
which is the exact failure being fixed -- so refusing to start beats
reproducing it invisibly.

Not needed, and confirmed rather than assumed: the Wayland backend binds no
zwp_linux_dmabuf_v1 and no wl_drm, so llvmpipe's wl_shm path suffices. The
fake connector is 1024x768 against Minecraft's 854x480 default, and GLFW
only rejects non-positive dimensions, so window size is not a constraint.
61096de81276eb7cd7c0c2ed981fede1e06c8ab5:
feat(virtio-gpu): negotiate CONTEXT_INIT and adopt the host scanout geometry

Two protocol fields were observed rather than acted on.

VIRTIO_GPU_F_CONTEXT_INIT was read from the device feature bits into
inst->context_init but never added to the driver's own feature set, so the host
never saw it negotiated.  GETPARAM still reported CONTEXT_INIT=1 while every
context was created the legacy way, a capability the driver claimed and was not
using.  The bit is now echoed into driver_lo, and the three inst-> flags are
derived from driver_lo rather than from the device bits, so they describe what
was actually agreed.

VIRTIO_GPU_CMD_GET_DISPLAY_INFO was defined in the UAPI header from the start
and never sent.  The guest therefore advertised a hardcoded 1024x768 to the
compositor regardless of the window QEMU was actually showing, which is the
kind of mismatch that shows up as a scaling or stride bug and gets attributed
to the DRM layer.  The driver now queries scanout 0 and adopts the host's width
and height when it reports a usable pair, keeping the old values as the
fallback for a headless host or a zero-sized window so a GET_DISPLAY_INFO that
fails cannot turn into a zero-area scanout.

Both commands now have a real caller, which is why they were dead weight
before: nothing exercised them, so nothing could have noticed they were wrong.
4971cb6c69665e2220e406acd04dd05b0204cee7:
test(gates): run the DRM UAPI check as a gate rather than a manual step

The ioctl numbers and wire struct layouts were reviewed by eye and had
already drifted from the Linux UAPI, so a gate is the only thing that keeps
them honest. check-drm-abi skips cleanly where no UAPI headers are installed,
so it does not become a new way for the build to fail on a machine that is not
a Linux host.

Verified to fail in both directions: perturbing MODE_RMFB back to its old
value makes the target exit non-zero, and restoring it exits zero.
ba6aae70894bb7f4ab4b3cbc8b28a9a17c0bf84d:
feat(a20): refuse to boot a guest image that a previous run left dirty

The guest images are built without a journal, and the desktop instances are
booted under a timeout and then killed rather than shut down, so a run leaves
on-disk metadata dirty. The next boot starts from a filesystem with invalid
group descriptor and inode checksums, an orphaned inode list, and directory
entries pointing into the unused inode area.

That does not look like a filesystem problem. It looks like the kernel being
broken: udev workers time out and get killed, cairo fails to create scaled
fonts, applications refuse to start. docs/distro/known-issues.md already warns
that a corrupt rootfs fabricates kernel bugs and tells you to run e2fsck before
testing, but nothing checked, so the advice depended on remembering it -- and
the symptom then gets investigated as a driver bug instead.

The check runs e2fsck -fn, which answers "what is wrong" without touching the
image, and reads the output rather than the exit status, because e2fsck's
status alone does not separate a clean filesystem from one it could not fully
check. A dirty image is refused outright rather than waited on: no amount of
waiting repairs it, and rebuilding is a deliberate act.

Verified in both directions. A freshly built image passes all five e2fsck
passes and the launch proceeds. Overwriting the group descriptor table of a
copy makes it refuse, naming the errors. A20_PREFLIGHT_SKIP_FSCK=1 boots it
anyway for when the dirty image is the thing under test.
57668a782097ec9113853e83cb121a1c4a82056e:
docs(graphics): prioritize current 3D blockers and correct stale status claims

The roadmap's premise was wrong in a way that misdirected the work. It read as
a plan to develop shaders, and put the effort on the GPU transport subsystem --
which is now largely done -- while the two cheapest high-value items sat at the
end of the list and the real blockers were not on it at all.

The reframe: guest GLES 3.2 already works today, on llvmpipe, on the Wayland
path. es2gears_wayland reported EGL 1.5 and GLES 3.2 and kept running. So 3D
games are not gated on GPU work; they are gated on presentation and on speed.
Those are two different milestones with two different bodies of work, and
conflating them is what made the plan misleading. The document now separates
them and states which one is done.

Also made load-bearing, because estimating work without it is guesswork: the
entire graphics stack is stock Alpine apk under the Linux syscall ABI. There is
no vendored Mesa, libdrm, EGL, GBM, wlroots, labwc or Xwayland. Two facts
derived from this were being cited backwards -- user/external/mlibc's
sysdeps/managarm/generic/drm.cpp is not in the build at all (A20OS configures
mlibc with sysdeps/a20, which has no DRM code), and user/cmds/core/egl_test.c
is filtered out by user/Makefile:200 and has never been built.

The section added on the ABI defects is the most transferable thing here. A
wrong ioctl constant is invisible: it never matches the switch, falls through
to the default arm, and userspace sees EINVAL, which reads as a Mesa or libdrm
bug. Five were live -- GETFB2 had both a wrong size field and a wrong command
number, and the private GEM_MMAP was sitting on the number Linux uses for
GEM_OPEN, so a guest calling the real GEM_OPEN was served by the mmap handler.
tools/check-drm-abi.sh now gates both the numbers and the struct layouts.

The order is now argued rather than listed, and the two items that need no
kernel change at all -- building the host virglrenderer, and getting the
compositor to present -- are marked as such, with the first flagged
operator-only because it needs root.

The verification record binds every runtime claim to a command, a
configuration and a commit, and states plainly that the virglrenderer build has
never been run, so there is still no evidence either way about whether stock
Mesa attaches.

new file real-hardware-gpu.md exists because "real device support" was being
treated as one project. Scanout is a 2-4 week job against a 2207-line upstream
driver; 3D is not feasible on x86 and on RISC-V depends entirely on which
silicon, with the VisionFive 2's BXE-4-32 absent from the mainline PowerVR
binding and its replacement blob non-redistributable. The redistributability
constraint is called out as a hard requirement, not a preference.

known-issues.md now states the pbuf situation unambiguously: a real double
free was found and fixed on the raw receive path, whether it was the trigger is
unproven, the IPv6-only correlation is still unexplained, and the "double free
versus neighbour overwrite" pair was never actually distinguishable because
memp's free list is a pointer chain through the freed blocks, so one double
free hands the same block to two live pbufs. The entry stays under unresolved
for that reason. The managarm citation there was invalid and is corrected.
7bdaaaac7931b854d909fb2afd3fef629c937d1f:
test(a20): keep the image check out of the resource gate and document both in the gate list

The image-hygiene check was placed after the A20_PREFLIGHT=0 early return,
which made a flag named after resource pressure silently disable a correctness
check. Booting a filesystem the last run left dirty is never what anyone wants,
and conflating the two is how a corrupt rootfs ends up being investigated as a
kernel bug -- which is the whole reason the check exists. The check now runs
first and its own opt-out is A20_PREFLIGHT_SKIP_FSCK.

Verified: with A20_PREFLIGHT=0 the dirty image is still refused, and
A20_PREFLIGHT_SKIP_FSCK=1 boots it.

testing-gates.md gains entries for this and for check-drm-abi, including what
each one is for and what a failure means. A gate nobody can find is not a gate,
and the DRM one in particular fails with a bare hex difference that is only
meaningful once you know a wrong constant presents as a Mesa bug.
4ddb1bd59d0fb621deb8007902116d1d6371ad42:
feat(drm): clip presents to the scanout instead of demanding an exact full-screen match

A framebuffer had to match the scanout's width and height exactly or SETCRTC
and PAGE_FLIP returned -EINVAL. That made a perfectly legal commit fail: a
client that allocated for a mode the display has since changed cannot commit
at all, and the failure arrives as a compositor error rather than as a clipped
blit, which is what it is.

The buffer may now be smaller than the scanout and positioned anywhere inside
it. The copy is clipped to the scanout and only the rectangle actually written
is flushed, since the rest of the host's copy still holds what the previous
present put there -- which is what a partial present means. The strict
requirements that were load-bearing stay: 32 bits per pixel, a pitch that
actually covers the width, and a destination at least as large as the mode.

Position follows Linux's model. x and y are CRTC state that SETCRTC sets, so a
subsequent page flip presents at the recorded position rather than at an
implicit zero; before, a flip at a non-zero position would have been clipped
away to nothing.
346575c0b703b4ec99893f2594cab66b6bde6d36:
feat(gpu3d): retire the private 3d transport ABI and make GETPARAM tell the truth

A20_GPU_IOCTL_CTX_CREATE / CTX_DESTROY / RES_CREATE_3D / RES_UNREF /

ab6dea3bde1a4519b952267d7bdb093eb4fd7d81:
docs(graphics): record why RESOURCE_BLOB 0 is the right answer and ship strace for GBM

The roadmap listed VIRTGPU_RESOURCE_CREATE_BLOB as "defined but not
dispatched", which reads as a gap to be closed. QEMU's own virtio-gpu
documentation says the opposite, and the distinction matters:

- OpenGL pass-through over virgl works *without* blobs. The documented host
  requirement is "any Linux version compatible with QEMU if not using host
  blobs feature".
- Blobs raise guest OpenGL from 4.3 to 4.6. They are a capability level, not a
  precondition for attaching.
- Venus and DRM native context *do* require blobs. So Vulkan is not merely
  unimplemented here, it is blocked on host configuration.
- A20OS's QEMU command line configures no memory-backend-file, no vhost-user
  and no hostmem=, so there is no blob memory window on the host at all.
- There is no virtio feature bit for blobs -- it is a device property -- so
  the guest cannot detect it. Reporting 0 is the only honest answer; reporting
  1 would send Mesa down RESOURCE_CREATE_BLOB and into a host-side failure.

Adding the dispatch would therefore make things worse, and the section now
says so with the exact cost and benefit of changing it instead.

The DMA-BUF row is corrected too, and in the other direction. It said "from
scratch", which is too heavy: memfd already holds a pfn_t array of physically
allocated pages and mmap maps those same PFNs into the VMA, so it is already a
multi-process shareable memory object. What is missing is an fd backed by a
GEM's VMO -- DRM maps the VMO directly today with the handle encoded in the
offset -- plus fd lifetime and refcount wiring. Still its own project, but not
greenfield.

The GBM investigation log repeatedly says the next step is strace in the guest
and then notes the world does not have it. It does now: strace is in xfce.world,
present in both v3.23 and edge, so the five places that said "prepare a static
musl build offline" are corrected.

02fb8478d951c65077c3f05f1e6970a278f3c218:
docs(distro): identify pbuf pool corruption as the panic cause

The investigation log had gone back and forth and settled on "the two
hypotheses were never actually distinguishable", because memp's free list is
a pointer chain through the freed blocks, so one double free hands the same
block to two live pbufs and every later refcount reading becomes meaningless.

That reasoning was right about memp and wrong about distinguishability. The
pbuf pool canary distinguishes them directly, and CONFIG_LWIP_MEMP_OVERFLOW_CHECK
was added for exactly this. Running the x86_64 desktop with it reports:

    lwIP assertion failed: detected mem underflow in pool PBUF_POOL
    mem_overflow_check_raw <- do_memp_malloc_pool_fn <- pbuf_alloc
                           <- a20_lwip_process_netif_rx_tx_locked

not `pbuf_free: p->ref > 0`. So three things are now settled, and all three
contradict what this file previously said:

- It is an out-of-bounds write into the pool, not a double free. A double free
  would trip the refcount assert with the canary intact; the canary was not
  intact.
- It is an underflow, not an overflow. The pool is an ascending array of
  struct pbuf, so writing before element N lands in the tail of element N-1 --
  the corrupting buffer overran its low end.
- It is detected on the allocation path, so the corruption predates that
  pbuf_alloc and has nothing to do with IPv6 parsing. IPv6 is traffic shape:
  it pushes packet count and length distribution into the range that hits it.

The double free that was fixed in socket_inet.c was a real bug and stays
fixed; it simply was not this panic. That is now measured rather than assumed.

What the canary does not say is which buffer overruns. It gives a direction,
not an identity, so the next step is bounded: compare pool element size against
PBUF_POOL_BUFSIZE and find what writes with a stride above 1536 near the pool.

The roadmap's verification record gains the same row and flags it as the only
measurement this round that overturned an existing documented conclusion.

9de518ff0c312d10a256e633e0c1f7b1f621a1f7:
feat(mm): add P0/P1 page table descriptors and per-PTE state zero overhead

The authoritative representation of mapping state follows the single-level
model from SOSP'25 CortenMM: the state of each virtual page lives in a per-PTE
metadata array hung off the page table page that covers it, not in a range
structure like a VMA, and the only entry point to the programmatic MMU is a
transactional cursor.

State cannot go into PTE software bits:

- riscv32 and arm32 have no free software bit at the root level, PPN already
  fills it
- loongarch64 maps PTE_R/W/X onto the LA_PTE memory attribute bits, leaving no
  room
- the existing PTE_SWAP already steals one hardware-meaningful bit per
  architecture, which is exactly the risk a general state encoding multiplies

So the sidecar array described in the paper is used instead: one state byte with
class in [7:4], COW shared in [3] and R/W/X in [2:0]. The physical frame of a
mapped page is not stored again, since the PTE already has it, and the
reference count lives in pfa.meta[].refcount.

Zero memory overhead: the descriptor pointer goes into the prev/next union of
frame_meta_t that is only valid on the free list, so frame_meta_t stays 16
bytes, pinned by a _Static_assert. pt_meta_t blocks are allocated on demand
per page table page and released with that page. The lock-free traversal in
the ADV protocol needs the descriptor on the hottest path, reading stale and
taking the covering node lock, and one indexed load beats a slab or hash probe;
pfa.meta is already a resident direct-mapped PPN index array.

What landed:

- kernel/include/mm/pt.h: the state encoding, pt_meta_t, the cursor and the
  audit interface, plus the MM_AS_MODEL and MM_AS_CURSOR_ONLY_ENTRY contracts
- kernel/mm/pt.c: descriptor lifecycle, the MCS queue lock with nodes
  allocated per cpu and depth so that no allocation happens on the lock path,
  the transactional cursor (lock/query/map/mark/unmap), and an auditor that
  walks the page tables and the metadata independently and compares them entry
  by entry
- kernel/mm/mm.c: metadata is synchronised at every page table write point.
  pt_create and pt_free_table attach and detach descriptors, pt_walk and
  pt_map_huge register intermediate nodes, pt_map_cls records leaf state,
  pt_unmap and pt_unmap_leaf clear state and reclaim descriptors, pt_clone
  copies the state array, and pt_map_kernel marks the shared kernel half as
  PT_NODE
- pt_map_cls is the explicit-state variant of pt_map, so file mappings, fork
  shared pages and VMO pages can register their real class and later faults
  need not look up a range again

mm_addrspace_lock now rejects, in code rather than in a comment, any range that
touches the shared kernel half. Those nodes are shared between all address
spaces, so taking a write lock on them serialises globally and releasing them
is a system-wide use-after-free.

Not landed here, recorded honestly in MM_AS_MODEL: page faults are still
resolved through mm_find_vma, the VMA list is still a live second
representation, and the auditor guarantees the two agree for now, so the cursor
is not yet the only entry point.
8ec42af4cc3fede0515ee4954510c7e13ee6f00f:
feat(mm): make the single-level model machine-provable via shutdown audit

The value of P1 is that the equivalence is machine checkable rather than a
big-bang rewrite: the metadata is shadow state, and the auditor walks the
hardware page tables and the per-PTE metadata independently and reports every
divergence. The audit is therefore attached to the existing shutdown audit
point next to pfa_audit_lists, so whether the two representations agree is
proven once at the end of every smoke workload rather than at one sampled
instant.

mm_pt_audit_all() follows the existing traversal pattern of
mm_sync_shared_dirty_for_vnode (proc_lock + proc_first/next_task_locked +
mm->lock) and audits every live address space, with an extra VMA cross check. A
VMA is a range assertion and the metadata is per-page, so the two have
different granularity and the consistency rule cannot be derived from either
side alone: every VMA must have at least one page known to the metadata, and a
mutator that updates one representation and forgets the other shows up here
first. An audit result of 0 is a factual record of the current state, not an
assertion.

Gates: check-mm-lock-model gained the MM_AS_CURSOR_ONLY_ENTRY,
mm_pt_note_present|absent and mm_pt_audit_all markers, so the gate actually
enforces the new model instead of rotting along with the implementation. The
existing MM_LOCK_MODEL and friends are unchanged, because the mutators that
have not been converted yet are still governed by them. MM_AS_MODEL went into
vm.h, describing the target model, why state does not go in the PTE, and how
far the migration goes.

Measured on riscv64:

- smoke-mm-stress         PASS, audit pt_pages=6 entries=2048 all 0
- smoke-mm-fork-exec-race PASS (smp8)
- smoke-abi-linux         PASS against real musl userland
- check-mm-lock-model     PASS
- builds of riscv64, aarch64, x86_64, loongarch64, ppc64le plus riscv64 and
  aarch64 NOMMU all OK

acad00488c5345cd1de0e50ea34bcdb829e2e70a:
docs(roadmap): design the single-level model migration and the P0-P9 plan

The full rationale for migrating the A20OS MM to the CortenMM-style
single-level model, written down so later phases can execute it:

- The target model: per-PTE state as the only authoritative representation, the
  transactional cursor as the only MMU entry point, and the page table page
  lock as the writer mutual exclusion unit
- Why state does not go into PTE software bits, with a per-architecture
  software bit budget table (0 on the riscv32 and arm32 root levels,
  loongarch64's PTE_R/W/X occupying LA_PTE_MAT1) and the existing risk that
  PTE_SWAP already steals a hardware bit per architecture
- Why ADV rather than RW: RW requires a fully populated page table while pt_walk
  allocates lazily, and fully populating a 4-level 512-entry architecture needs
  2 MB of scaffolding per address space
- The reasoning behind inlining the descriptor into the frame_meta_t union at
  16 bytes for zero overhead, and the alternatives that were rejected
- The shared kernel half constraint: all address spaces use the same physical
  pages, so the cursor must be refused in code
- Per-feature conclusions for the things the paper does not cover
  (brk/mseal/madvise/mlock/THP/NUMA//proc maps/fork-COW/VMO/swap/fault-around),
  including the honest conclusion that the VMA list stays forever as a derived
  index
- The P0-P9 stage table, each stage with the invariant that holds at its end
  and the verification gate
- The risk ranking: PT pages and frames freed too early, the shared kernel half,
  TLB-IPI deadlock, COW ordering, swap check ordering, the la32r software TLB
  refill, PTE bit aliasing
- The 8 things explicitly not promised, so that "degraded" is not reported as
  "removed"
- A record that the smoke-mm-stress gate decides by grepping markers printed
  before shutdown, so a panic on the shutdown path does not fail it and the
  audit line has to be checked alongside the PASS marker

Also recorded: riscv32 already fails to build on main (kexec.c pointer
conversion) and arm32 lacks the arm-linux-gnueabihf toolchain, both unrelated
to this work.
1c2bec2472c9e998b35a38e9a06958e1d1330d1b:
feat(mm): route P2 fault PTE writes through the cursor and cache the descent

Every PTE write on the page fault path now goes through the cursor, so the
per-PTE state and the hardware page table entry necessarily update in the same
step and no path can update only one of them.

The cursor now caches the descent path (path[]). This is not an optional
optimisation: if every operation re-walked the page table, a transaction would
be slower than the pt_walk it replaces, and once mm->lock goes away in P5 a
re-descent could read a path that a concurrent unmap has already detached.
Caching is what makes the cursor a single-descent primitive, and it is why the
lock must cover the whole subtree (P3).

The lock range calculation is corrected to take the lowest level that fully
covers the range. The old implementation hit from the top, so a single-page
fault returned the root node, which meant modifying unlocked descendants while
holding only the root lock. A single page belongs at level 0.

mm_addrspace_lock can now allocate missing intermediate nodes on demand, under
the parent's lock, which matches pt_walk's lazy allocation and is the concrete
reason the RW protocol is unavailable here. A stale node makes the whole
attempt retry, since the subtree may have been detached during the descent.

Every fault-path PTE write point is now a cursor call and passes the real
class: shared file pages FILE_SHARED, private file pages FILE_PRIVATE, VMO
pages VMO, and anonymous plus brk and stack growth ANON_MAPPED. The
fault-around window is covered by a single cursor for the whole window, one
lock acquisition and one descent instead of one per page, which is what the
single-level model buys.

New mm_cursor_replace() installs the mapping and hands back the replaced frame
but does not free it. The COW path must release the old reference only after
the remote TLB shootdown, and its rc==1 branch already runs under pfa.lock, so
calling frame_put inside a combined map would self-deadlock. mm_cursor_map() is
the owning version, replace plus frame_put.

A real defect was fixed along the way: fault-around passed the pfn straight to
mm_cursor_map as a physical address, so a PTE with an invalid physical address
was installed, which shows up as CAUSE_STORE_FAULT, a store fault rather than
a missing page, and a SIGSEGV. C cannot catch this kind of type mismatch.

Measured: smoke-mm-stress (smp1 and smp4), smoke-mm-fork-exec-race (smp8),
smoke-abi-linux and check-mm-lock-model all PASS with the shutdown audit all 0;
builds of riscv64, aarch64, x86_64, loongarch64, ppc64le plus riscv64 and
aarch64 NOMMU are OK.
048bc9a4bd509f37f8408263acaf427a824499b6:
feat(mm): make P3 page-table locking exclude concurrent writers

From here on, mutual exclusion for every page table write rests on the page
table page's own MCS lock rather than on "mm->lock happens to be held
outside". This is the precondition for parallelising in P5: only once the page
table page lock itself excludes writers can mm->lock come off the fault path.

MCS nodes are allocated per (cpu, depth). One transaction can hold the covering
node while also holding several descendants, so a single CPU needs one node per
nesting depth. The node pool is preallocated once at mm_init, sized for the
worst DFS width, a level-1 node with all 512 level-0 children filled, and its
size is fixed. The lock path runs with preemption disabled and must never call
the allocator.

The mutual exclusion unit is the covering node itself, not the whole subtree. A
cursor only modifies nodes below its cached path and at or under the covering
node, and any other cursor that could touch that path must first take the same
covering node lock, so that granularity is sufficient and finest, and cursors on
disjoint ranges really do run in parallel. The "lock all descendants" step from
the paper's ADV protocol belongs to the lock-free traversal plus RCU read side
plus revalidate design (P4). Without RCU, taking a subtree lock by DFS first
would serialise unrelated ranges and would also take the same node twice
through aliasing, which self-deadlocks. That is exactly what hung the evict
phase of mm_stress in the first implementation.

A real deadlock was fixed: the cursor's rollback loop and mcs_unlock both
decremented the per-CPU depth, so one release subtracted twice, the depth
underflowed, stack discipline broke, and it then self-deadlocked on the same
node, which the kernel reported as LOCK-STALL with waiter=4 owner=4 at the
same address. Depth now has a single owner in each direction: mcs_lock pushes,
and the rollback loop in mm_cursor_unlock pops.

MCS spinning is also bounded. A page table lock must never be held across a
blocking operation, so a long wait means a lock ordering bug rather than
contention, so exceeding the bound panics and prints the number of nodes the
waiter already holds, to avoid a failure that only ever shows up as a hang.

Measured: smoke-mm-stress (smp1 and smp4), smoke-mm-fork-exec-race (smp8) and
smoke-abi-linux all PASS with the audit all 0; builds of riscv64, aarch64,
x86_64, loongarch64, ppc64le plus riscv64 NOMMU are OK.
2f809897adb0f3787f3d869393fec86f577390ee:
feat(mm): add P4 deferred page-table reclamation with read-side counting

The cursor caches physical page table pointers during its descent, so if a
concurrent unmap freed the page immediately the cursor would keep operating on
memory that has already been reused. That is the shape of the 0x63636363 style
corruption this project has hit before. Detaching a subtree therefore no longer
frees immediately: the subtree is marked stale, detached, and queued on the
address space's TLB invalidation barrier, and is only really reclaimed once the
shootdown has completed and the read-side critical sections are empty.

Read-side counting: mm->pt_readers, entered before the cursor descends and left
in unlock, including on every error return. Deferred release reuses the
existing per-mm tlb_holds queue with a new MM_TLB_HOLD_PT kind, drained in
mm_tlb_invalidate_finish only after the remote shootdown and only after the
read-side count reaches zero. That reuses the all-CPU barrier A20OS already has
instead of starting a second grace period.

Stale: the detached subtree is marked stale as a whole, and a cursor that gets
it retries the entire descent.

This change only lands the mechanism and does not change when detaching sites
release. Every cursor still holds mm->lock today, and every pt_unmap and
pt_unmap_leaf caller holds mm->lock too, so the two are serialised by the same
lock and releasing immediately is still safe. Actually wiring deferred release
into the detach path has to land in the same commit as P5, taking mm->lock off
the fault path, because that is the step at which the danger becomes real.
Committing the mechanism and the switch separately is what makes the P5 switch
revertible on its own.

Measured: smoke-mm-stress PASS, audit all 0.
92a7dc54628b774ca4b142f91214ec13afc9d3c7:
perf(mm): add the mm_pt_scale parallelism benchmark as a falsifiable gate

The single-level model's performance claim is precise: two transactions with
different covering nodes do not serialise. This benchmark turns that claim into
a falsifiable acceptance criterion instead of an assertion.

Method: each thread mmaps a fresh anonymous range per round, so the first touch
is a real demand fault and the page table path's scalability is what gets
measured, since reusing hot pages would only measure memcpy and prove nothing.
Multiple threads touch disjoint address ranges concurrently and throughput for
1T through 4T is measured. The kernel's own page table lock counters
(mm_pt_lock_acquires/contended, mm_cursor_open, stale_retry) are read at the
same time, so the result is attributable rather than just timed.

Current measurement: on smp4, 1T=0.835s and 4T=3.07s, speedup=1.09x, so there
is no parallelism yet. The reason is clear: the fault path still holds the
global mm->lock, which serialises the whole address space. The benchmark
therefore records the current state faithfully and points at P5, taking
mm->lock off the fault path and giving writer exclusion entirely to the page
table page locks, as the step that actually delivers the performance win.

New kernel counters: mm_pt_lock_acquires, mm_pt_lock_contended,
mm_pt_lock_waits, mm_cursor_open and mm_pt_cursor_stale_retry, exposed through
/proc/a20/perf. The contended/acquires ratio is a direct measure of how often
disjoint ranges collide.

Note: the /proc/a20/perf counters are disabled until first read
(a20_perf_enabled), so this benchmark sees the tail rather than the whole run,
which does not affect the timing conclusion.
fe3fef39fd958a21c26a41de4015003caee83102:
docs(roadmap): record P0-P4 and measure the P5 parallelism baseline on KVM

This records what actually landed in this round and one experiment that
measured P5's precondition out.

P0-P4 are complete and verified, with the evidence table in the design
document's section 8.1. P4 only lands the mechanism without changing when
detaching sites release, because every cursor still holds mm->lock today and
the danger is not yet real. The wiring has to land in the same commit as P5
removes the lock.

The P5 measurement, on smp4 with mm_pt_scale where each thread mmaps a fresh
region per round to produce real demand faults, gives a baseline of 1T=0.807s
and 4T=3.137s, speedup=1.03x, so no parallelism. The cause is located: faults
still take the address-space-wide mm->lock and must also look up the VMA, which
has no reference count and can be freed by a concurrent munmap, so every fault
still queues on that lock.

A useful failed experiment: a fast path that snapshots the VMA under the lock
and installs the PTE with a cursor outside it, for anonymous write faults,
measured slower, with 1T going from 0.835s to 1.423s and 4T still around 1.0x.
As long as faults still look up VMAs, removing mm->lock buys no parallelism and
only adds overhead. It was rolled back, and that result is the evidence that P6
has to come first.

The document gives P5's architectural fork and explicitly does not pick for the
reader: (a) on-demand tagging of large address spaces, (b) paper-style eager
leaf page table allocation, where a 1GB mapping needs 2GB of page table memory,
or (c) a reference count or snapshot for VMAs, the general Linux approach. All
three trade memory against compatibility and should not be settled in passing.

Also recorded as hard requirements for wiring P5: removing the lock and P4's
deferred release wiring go in the same commit, the remote TLB shootdown must be
dispatched after all page table locks are released, COW's 0x63636363 ordering
is preserved verbatim, the verification checklist for each commit, and the fact
that the QEMU smoke gate can fail spuriously because a leftover QEMU holds port
5555, which NET_HOSTFWD can work around.
6c9148d74164a323f9aedaacafa11dd33b332f14:
fix(mm): fix the MCS depth leak and add the cpu_scale TCG sanity probe

Two root causes, one real defect and one measurement error.

The defect: while fixing the "rollback loop and mcs_unlock both decrement
depth" problem in P3, depth-- was removed from mcs_unlock, but the descent
loop in mm_addrspace_lock calls mcs_lock(pm) and mcs_unlock(pm) as paired
inline calls and relies on mcs_unlock to decrement the depth. So every descent
that needed to allocate an intermediate node leaked a depth slot. Depth now
has a single owner in each direction: mcs_lock pushes and mcs_unlock pops, and
the rollback loop in mm_cursor_unlock no longer pre-decrements itself, only
popping on behalf of a slot that recorded no node. The defect was masked by
riscv64's TCG testing until the MCS deadlock detector caught it in a genuinely
parallel x86_64/KVM configuration.

The measurement error, which matters more: mm_pt_scale on riscv64/TCG had
reported speedup=1.03x, and the conclusion "the fault path is serialised by
mm->lock" was drawn from it. That conclusion is void. A riscv64 guest on an
x86_64 host only has TCG, there is no usable multi-threaded TCG across
architectures, and the vCPUs are themselves serialised. The new
user/cmds/stress/cpu_scale.c, pure integer arithmetic with no memory traffic and
no kernel locks, manages only 0.89x-0.96x in the same TCG configuration, which
proves the environment cannot show parallelism at all and that no memory
management change can display a speedup there. The same probe reaches 3.93x
under x86_64/KVM.

A valid baseline was therefore retaken under x86_64/KVM: an environment ceiling
of 3.93x and 1.48x-1.53x for mm_pt_scale with real demand faults. The fault
path really does lose about 2.4x of parallelism, so P5 is worth doing, and this
time there is real evidence behind it instead of a TCG illusion.

Going forward, parallelism must be measured under x86_64/KVM; riscv64/TCG is
only good for functional correctness.
b971fc4cfea362da11d49d77614f6747fb549946:
docs(mm): retract the P5 parallelism claim based on TCG measurements

The old section 8.2 measured mm_pt_scale speedup=1.03x on riscv64/TCG and
concluded that faults are serialised by mm->lock. That conclusion is void: a
riscv64 guest on an x86_64 host only has TCG, there is no usable multi-threaded
TCG across architectures, the vCPUs are themselves serialised, and no memory
management change can display a speedup in that environment. The new cpu_scale
probe confirms it: pure integer computation that touches neither memory nor
kernel locks manages only 0.89x-0.96x in the same TCG configuration, while the
same probe reaches 3.93x under x86_64/KVM.

The rewritten valid baseline is taken under KVM: an environment ceiling of
3.93x and 1.48x-1.53x for real demand faults. The fault path really does lose
about 2.4x of parallelism, so P5 remains justified.

The "the bottleneck is mm->lock" attribution is also withdrawn. That workload
mmaps a fresh region every round, and mmap itself takes mm->lock for range
allocation and VMA insertion, and every fault also calls pfa_alloc_page(),
which goes through the buddy global lock and a whole-page memset. Until those
three costs are separated, the bottleneck cannot be attributed.

Parallelism measurement is henceforth done only under x86_64/KVM; riscv64/TCG
is only for functional correctness.
96778c717c5f7d0fda4977c440b8ca3bdfd46819:
perf(mm): add mm_fault_cost to attribute the parallelism loss

mm_pt_scale only gives an end-to-end number, cannot say where the serialisation
comes from, and its workload mixes three kinds of cost. mm_fault_cost uses the
same thread count, the same shared address space and the same disjoint ranges,
and runs each phase on its own:

  A mmap   : mmap + munmap only, never touching a page  -> address space lock
  B fault  : one mmap, then first touch page by page    -> demand fault path
  C mem    : repeated writes after pre-touching         -> memory path ceiling

Measured on x86_64/KVM smp4 with 2 threads:

  mmap   1T=0.168s  2T=0.275s  scale=1.22x
  fault  1T=0.091s  2T=0.126s  scale=1.44x
  mem    1T=0.047s  2T=0.052s  scale=1.78x

Attribution:

- The memory system is not the bottleneck, since 1.78x is close to the ideal
  2x, so P5 has real headroom
- The main source of serialisation is mm->lock. The mmap/munmap path is worst
  at 1.22x, because range allocation and VMA insertion are entirely inside the
  lock, and the fault path follows at 1.44x, where the gap below the 1.78x
  ceiling is the MM-side loss
- So "the bottleneck is mm->lock" is confirmed independently for the first
  time, instead of being inferred from end-to-end numbers as before

One trap: the iteration count of the mem phase has to be much larger than the
number of pre-touched pages, otherwise what gets measured is still fault cost
rather than memory cost. The first version fell into exactly that, with 1024
pre-touched pages worth about 10ms being the same order as the write loop,
producing a bogus 1.13x. MEM_ROUNDS=4096 is used now so the write loop
dominates the pre-touch.
b2fb49c485eb186b62f76a105dcf0b8d323b9394:
docs(roadmap): record the cost attribution mm- lock serialises mmap worse

The three phases of mm_fault_cost on x86_64/KVM smp4 give mmap=1.22x,
fault=1.44x and mem=1.78x. This confirms independently, where before there was
only an end-to-end inference, that the main source of serialisation is mm->lock
and that mmap/munmap is worse than the fault path, since range allocation and
VMA insertion are entirely inside the lock. That widens P5's scope from "only
the fault path" to mmap/munmap as well and gives an upper bound on the gain,
1.44x to 1.78x on the fault side and 1.22x to 1.78x on the mmap side, rather
than an order of magnitude.

The measurement trap is recorded too: the iteration count of the mem phase must
be much larger than the number of pre-touched pages, otherwise what gets
measured is still fault cost. The first version's 1.13x was an illusion and
raising MEM_ROUNDS to 4096 gives a credible 1.78x.
7d153bc82706a00cb17adedfdc3ebf3b7c0c3133:

syscall_smoke on the x86_64 target reports `renameat errno=22`, and the same
