89d9dcb8cb41449bfceaf271dba4223e85a01a2e:
feat(mm): abort the MCS watchdog only on self-deadlock

The old watchdog panicked unconditionally once spinning exceeded a fixed
bound. That judgement does not hold under KVM: the lock holder can be scheduled
out by the host, so a perfectly legal cross-CPU wait gets mistaken for a
deadlock, which was actually observed as a "phantom deadlock" with cpu=1
holding at depth 0 yet timing out. Killing a correct but slow kernel is worse
than not aborting at all.

It now aborts only on the self-deadlock signature, where the node being waited
on is the one this CPU already holds, pool->held[depth-1] == m. That is the
genuinely hopeless case. A remote holder resets the count and keeps waiting.
The diagnostics changed from "number already held" to the node address, level
and depth, which is more useful for locating the problem.

This is not the P5 implementation. The lock-free fast path for the fault path
without mm->lock failed in four attempts and was rolled back in full; see
section 8.7 of the design document.
552c3e916dc61a1c7cafbf705867d547d9feb1a0:
docs(roadmap): record four failed P5 fast paths and the precondition they expose

The four attempts hit, in order: a PFN used as a physical address, a double
free in the revalidation branch, an MCS depth slot leak, and remote TLB IPIs
being obstructed by a CPU holding a page table lock. The third is a real
defect and was fixed in its own commit (91f3eafc); the rest went away with the
fast path rollback.

The fourth is a hard precondition for the next step. Removing mm->lock also
requires rebuilding the TLB transaction boundary, which today is built around
mm->lock, and MM_LOCK_MODEL already records that a remote CPU spinning with
interrupts disabled must still be able to exit so that it can respond to a TLB
IPI. Without that, new TLB-IPI deadlocks appear. So P5 has to be designed,
implemented and verified together with the P4 deferred release wiring, the TLB
boundary rebuild and the VMA lifetime scheme; piecemeal versions will keep
tripping over the same ground.
5e61fad702bcb8eeddb6f345017934dec8268732:
docs(roadmap): report no measurable P0-P4 performance change

On x86_64/KVM smp4, four mm_fault_cost samples were taken on main and on
cortenmm and averaged: mmap 1.098x to 1.118x (+1.8%), fault 1.413x to 1.405x
(-0.5%), mem 1.633x to 1.650x (+1.1%).

The noise floor is given by the `mem` phase. It produces no page faults and no
mmap churn, so a change cannot affect it in principle, yet on the same port it
spans 0.28x, from 1.50x to 1.78x. All three differences fall inside the noise.
P0-P4 therefore brings no measurable performance change, and the earlier
1.22x/1.44x/1.78x seen in single samples was the top of the noise band.

That matches the expectation: parallelism only pays off once mm->lock no longer
serialises faults and mmap, which is P5/P6. What P0-P4 actually delivers is
structure and correctness, namely authoritative per-PTE state, page table page
mutual exclusion, the deferred reclamation mechanism in place, zero per-frame
overhead and a shutdown audit that is all 0. Those are the preconditions that
make P5 possible.

Methodological lesson: a single sample is meaningless in this environment, where
the noise floor is plus or minus 9%. Any future performance claim must be taken
on x86_64/KVM with several samples for both the control and the experiment, and
must report a control phase that the change cannot affect in order to establish
the noise floor.
40538662998d88f37d53bf403206fc114e845c7e:
feat(mm): add VMA reference counting so faults can read vmas unlocked

P6's precondition is that the page fault path stops depending on mm->lock: to
realise the single-level model's parallelism, faults must not be serialised
within a process by a single address space lock. But once the lock is gone the
vm_area_t pointer itself is unprotected, and after mm_find_vma() returns, munmap
can unlink it and free it. So VMAs get a reference count, and the fault path
takes a reference and drops it when it is done.

Ownership rule: the address space list holds the reference created at
allocation, unlinking drops it, and the last holder, which may be a fault
holding no lock at all, is responsible for arranging the release. That matches
the intent of the existing deferred list, it just makes "who holds it"
explicit.

The key constraint and two non-obvious corrections:

1. The deferred list now uses its own vma_ref_lock instead of continuing to
   borrow mm->lock. Otherwise a fault that has just escaped mm->lock would have
   to reacquire the lock it just released in order to drop its reference, which
   makes the fast path pointless. That lock only guards list push and pop and
   never spans vma_release(), which reaches vfs_close and can sleep. A
   deferred_next field was added as well to avoid sharing with mm->mmap's next.
2. Two inherited states have to be reset on the fork path: `*child = *parent`
   copies the parent's vma_ref_lock state along with everything else, and a
   cloned `*cv = *pv` inherits the parent VMA's reference count. Both are now
   reset explicitly, otherwise the child either uses a lock carrying the
   parent's lock state or shares one reference count.

Invariant: any VMA that has entered mm->mmap is no longer kfreed directly, only
unlinked through vma_put. Every remaining direct kfree sits on a
pre-publication rollback path where the reference count is 1 and the VMA was
never visible to another thread, including the half-built mirror rollback in
elf_discard_vmas. mm_destroy's existing vma_release() plus kfree() was also
changed to a vma_put() plus a flush, with the semantics unchanged.

Verified with a riscv64 kernel-only build; smoke-mm-stress,
smoke-mm-fork-exec-race and check-mm-lock-model pass; mm_stress under
x86_64/KVM smp4 is all green (MM_STRESS: PASS, including the vma-deferred-race
subtest), the shutdown audit is pt_pages=10 entries=2560 missing_meta=0 with
present/absent/prot/cow/vma all 0, and there were no panics and no watchdog
aborts.

This is not the P6 implementation. Only the VMA lifetime mechanism lands here;
the fault path still does not read VMAs without the lock. The next step is take
a reference, install outside the lock, revalidate, drop the reference,
together with rebuilding the TLB transaction boundary and wiring in P4's
deferred release as the earlier conclusion requires.
95289405dfa7f86107ddb7770b5569d2491cedfb:
docs(roadmap): record the VMA refcount and pin the P5 deadlock to an instruction

Section 8.9 records the VMA reference counting from b10b267b: the ownership
rule, the two fork state inheritance corrections, the invariant that a VMA which
has entered mm->mmap is never kfreed directly, and the all-architecture build
plus x86_64/KVM mm_stress verification results.

Section 8.10 takes the item 4 deadlock from section 8.7 from a symptom
description to an exact cause. mcs_lock() does not itself disable interrupts,
but the page table lock is taken while holding the IRQ-disabled mm->lock, so a
waiter inherits interrupts disabled and cannot receive a TLB IPI, and the
initiator panics after 5 seconds. The target's IPI handler takes no locks, so
the bottleneck is purely in delivery.

That yields a stronger conclusion: removing mm->lock does not by itself solve
the deadlock. As long as the condition "holding a page table lock blocks IPI
delivery" holds, which lock is held makes no difference. The real decision point
is whether spinning on the MCS page table lock can be done with interrupts
enabled. That turns P5 from "move one lock aside" into "redefine the interrupt
semantics of page table writer mutual exclusion", which needs an explicit
design decision.
121368824a4c53f51881bc9581ab1c2b39cd2230:
docs(roadmap): retract the P5 deadlock diagnosis and rule out async generations

The root cause given for section 8.7 item 4 in fdeb3b6f is withdrawn.
Attributing it to "the MCS page table lock is taken while holding the
IRQ-disabled mm->lock, so the waiter cannot receive a TLB IPI" is wrong. The
mistake was treating spin_lock as an interrupt-disabling spinlock. In reality
spin_lock goes to spin_lock_at in core/lock.h, which does not touch the
interrupt state, and the only arch_irqs_enabled() in the function body appears
in the deadlock diagnostic print. Only spin_lock_irqsave calls
arch_local_irq_disable(). Interrupts are therefore enabled while the fault path
holds mm->lock, so it can respond to a TLB IPI and there is no IPI delivery
block.

Verified on the current branch: shootdown has long been issued outside mm->lock
(mprotect.c:154-158 and the COW path in fault.c both do begin, then
lock_irqsave, then the rewrite, then unlock, then finish). The MCS page table
lock does exist in kernel/mm/pt.c and is indeed taken while holding mm->lock,
but the holder has interrupts enabled, so it does not form the blocking loop
described.

The residual real risk is a different class of problem: any writer critical
section that holds mm->lock with spin_lock_irqsave has interrupts disabled, and
a TLB IPI landing in that window cannot be acknowledged, so the initiator
panics after 5 seconds. Under KVM that window can be stretched by the host, in
the same class as the MCS watchdog "phantom deadlock" already fixed, and that
fix does not cover this window. The exact root cause of the panic in section 8.7
item 4 can only be settled with the diff from that time, and is recorded as
unresolved.

That corrects the section 8.7 conclusion: "the TLB transaction boundary must be
rebuilt at the same time" no longer holds as a hard precondition, because the
precondition it rests on, interrupts being disabled while the fault path holds
the lock, is false. The one hard requirement P5 really must satisfy narrows to
this: the mutual exclusion unit that installs PTEs must not span the dispatch
and wait of mm_tlb_invalidate_finish / mm_tlb_shootdown_page.

New section 8.11: ARCH_MM_CONTEXT_ALLOC is covered only for riscv64, every
other architecture takes the default 0U, and x86_64 has no way to set arch_asid
non-zero. The lazy generation correction loop in mm_context_enter is gated
entirely by `if (mm->arch_asid && ...)`, so on x86_64 it never runs and
tlb_cpu_generation is written but never used to repair anything, which means
there is no lazy fallback. If the change were to stop blocking the shootdown,
writing tlb_cpu_generation would be a lie with no reader to correct it and stale
translations would live forever, since a re-mmap at the same address after munmap
would hand the old mapping's data to the new mapping, and the deferred
reclamation would also release data frames before the shootdown had truly
completed. x86_64 must therefore keep the synchronous blocking shootdown, and
the asynchronous design is out.
6359efc1cdb4d791085c02f66d9d1ce14bb3e4f3:
docs(roadmap): record the fifth P5 rollback two self-found bugs and the lesson

The fifth attempt at P5 used prepare outside the lock and commit with
revalidation inside it, unlocked by the VMA reference count. Two real defects
introduced this round were found and fixed during self-review: returning
-EAGAIN after vma_put, which left the caller dereferencing a vma with no
reference held and was a UAF during exec, and hoisting the fast path ahead of
the THP judgement, which was moved behind the guard that excludes
VM_HUGEPAGE.

It still failed after those fixes. smoke-mm-stress hung silently after execve
of mksh, with no panic and no spinlock diagnostics. Instrumentation showed the
fast path being entered 4 times and each returning normally with mapped=1, and
the hang was after that. A stashed control confirmed that reverting fault.c made
the same gate PASS immediately, so this came from the change rather than from a
pre-existing flake.

Structural lesson: handle_demand_fault_locked is an ordered decision chain,
swap, then stack, then brk, then VMA, then permissions, then file, then VMO,
then THP, then anon batch, then the single page. Hoisting a fast path in front
of it changes the priority of those decisions, and excluding one just exposes
the next unmodelled interaction. The right approach is to modify in place,
doing the lock-free prepare at the exact position the original anon batch
occupies and fully preserving the decision order before it. That rewrite was
not completed, so this was rolled back.

The P4 wiring state was also verified and corrected: deferred release of leaf
data frames is wired up (mm_tlb_hold_frame is called from munmap, madvise, oom
and vm.c), but mm_pt_defer_free for page table frames has no caller anywhere in
the tree and is dead code. Freeing page table frames synchronously is still safe
under the current design, since it happens after the mm->lock transaction and a
synchronous shootdown have completed, but it is a hard precondition for P5. The
wiring itself brings no performance benefit while introducing page table frame
lifetime risk, so it is deliberately deferred to land together with P5 rather
than in its own commit.

Two unrelated pre-existing defects in the acceptance environment are also
recorded: the lwIP IPv6 receive path asserts and crashes in pbuf_free
(ip6_input, hit 0 times with -netdev removed, so the mm_* benchmarks must run
without a NIC), and mm_pt_scale's self-reported counters, 0 and 3, disagree with
the live values from /proc/a20/perf during the same run, 23 and 11. The counters
themselves are fine, so their output cannot be used for attribution for now.
The baseline ideal_speedup of 1.06x-1.20x is still below the 1.80x threshold,
which is the quantitative evidence that P5 is not done.
86ce94b605ef61760ad8bc515472644ef3454c8d:
docs(roadmap): record that the in-place rework also fails refuting the 8.12 advice

Section 8.12 concluded that the front-of-line insert was the root cause of the fifth
failure and recommended an in-place rework instead: do the lock-free prepare at the
original anon batch position so the preceding decision order is preserved exactly.  That
advice has now been implemented.  handle_demand_fault_locked() grew a lock_held
parameter, because the three call sites differ in lock state (NOMMU holds no lock, the
swap retry deliberately drops it, the main path holds it), and the post-prepare
re-validation under the retaken lock handles three outcomes: the leaf is already valid,
return 0; the VMA has been unlinked, return -1; otherwise re-validate page by page and
drop the pages somebody else got there first.

Both smoke-mm-stress and smoke-mm-fork-exec-race failed with a signature identical to the
fifth attempt: the log stops silently at line 222 during execve mksh, with no panic, no
assertion and no spinlock diagnostic.  The change has been reverted, so HEAD is back to
a verified state.

Also recorded, so the same ground is not covered twice: reordered decision chains
(ruled out by the in-place rework), THP preemption, the UAF after -EAGAIN, stack growth
bypassing the path (VM_STACK is indeed set by elf.c), and the pfa.lock to mm->lock lock
order inversion (frame.c releases pfa.lock before it calls oom_try_reclaim).

The clue still not ruled out and most worth chasing: the only thing the fifth and sixth
attempts share is moving pfa_alloc_page and its cg_mem_charge/memset out from under
mm->lock.  A silent hang rather than a panic fits lock wait.  The next step should be to
read the held-lock stacks at the hang to see which locks each CPU holds, rather than
keeping editing the fault path.  P5 is still unfinished, and the kernel remains in the
"correct but serialised fault path" state.
7f4341dc667ffaafe7604e95a1183645238eac15:
fix(mm): fix the missed VMA refcount init prepare anon faults unlocked

This commit has two parts, and the first is the precondition for the second.

One, fix the missed refcount initialisation (a real defect from b10b267b).  b10b267b
located allocation sites with `grep sizeof(vm_area_t)` and missed four sites written as
`sizeof(*vma)`: munmap.c:262, udriver.c:183, framebuffer.c:181 and :363.  Those VMAs
kept the refcount of 0 that kcalloc gave them.

The defect was latent in b10b267b: with nothing calling vma_get/vma_put, a refcount of 0
only cost one extra free at munmap, a leak, not a fault.  Once P5 made the fault path
really do vma_get -> vma_put, the 0 -> 1 -> 0 transition would free the VMA while it was
still linked on mm->mmap, turning the list pointers into dangling garbage.

The observed symptom was smoke-mm-stress hanging silently after execve mksh, the log
stopping at line 222 with no panic, assertion or spinlock diagnostic, and nothing to do
with how fault.c was written.  Adding a step bound to the list fallback in mm_find_vma
located it immediately:

  [VMAWALK] CYCLE steps=100001 head=0xffffffc0bf12ecc0
  mm_find_vma: VMA list cycle

The "address" being walked was 0x6e69746c69756000, which is ASCII text, so the walk had
entered memory that had been freed and reused.  The triggering site, munmap.c:262, builds
exactly a VM_ANON|VM_READ|VM_WRITE brk VMA, which is precisely the class the P5 fast path
matches.

The lesson: grepping for allocation sites by type name is unreliable, since equivalent
spellings such as `sizeof(*vma)` have to be covered too.  All 14 sites have now been
re-checked.

Two, P5: move the prepare for anon fault-around out from under mm->lock (the in-place
rework).  handle_demand_fault_locked() gained a lock_held parameter, since the three call
sites differ in lock state (NOMMU holds no lock, the swap retry drops it on purpose, the
main path holds it).  The rework happens at the original anon batch position rather than
in front of the chain, so the swap -> stack -> brk -> VMA -> prot -> file -> VMO -> THP
decision order is preserved in full.  pfa_alloc_page + cg_mem_charge + a 16KiB memset run
outside the lock, and after retaking the lock there are three outcomes to re-validate:
the leaf is already valid (somebody else populated it, return 0), the VMA has been
unlinked (return -1 and retry), or page by page re-validation and dropping the pages
somebody else got to first.

But it brought no measurable performance win.  x86_64/KVM smp4, no NIC, 3 samples:
1.01x / 1.12x / 1.12x, no different from the 1.06x to 1.20x baseline before the change and
still below the 1.80x threshold.

The reason, verified: mm->lock is not the bottleneck of the anon fault path.  Outside the
lock the path still goes through two *global* serialisation points:

  * cg_mem_charge() -> spin_lock_irqsave(&node->lock), a per-cgroup-node lock shared by
    every fault in the same cgroup;
  * pfa_alloc_page() -> pfa.lock, where `extern pfa_t pfa` is a single global allocator
    (one spinlock_t guarding all mutable fields) and the per-CPU batch is refilled under
    the same lock.

Dropping mm->lock only moved the serialisation point from the address space lock to these
two, so the four threads still queue behind each other.

The hypothesis that P0 to P4 plus P5 would cash out parallel speedup therefore does not
hold: the real bottleneck is the allocator and cgroup charging, not the address space
lock.  Raising fault parallelism has to address those first, for example a lock-free
per-CPU allocator, batched charging, or moving charge out of the per-page path.

The step bound in mm_find_vma is kept as a failure guard: a corrupted list used to spin
silently forever (it did here, and it took six attempts to find), now it panics
immediately and names the problem.

Verified: riscv64 kernel-only; smoke-mm-stress, smoke-mm-fork-exec-race and
check-mm-lock-model pass, the shutdown audit reports pt_pages=6 entries=2048
missing_meta=0 with present/absent/prot/cow/vma all 0; no panic on x86_64/KVM.
6188a00cb231a9e99a3f05a224839b5484c74535:
docs(roadmap): identify VMA-refcount initialization behind the six P5 failures

Section 8.16 suggested instrumenting the held-lock stacks, but the run never got that
far, because it was not a lock deadlock at all.  Adding a step bound to the list fallback
in mm_find_vma immediately showed the VMA list had become cyclic, and the "address" being
walked, 0x6e69746c69756000, is ASCII text, which proves the walk had entered memory that
had been freed and reused.

The root cause is a real defect from b10b267b: the allocation sites had been found with
`grep sizeof(vm_area_t)`, which missed the four sites written as `sizeof(*vma)`
(munmap.c:262, udriver.c:183, framebuffer.c:181 and :363), leaving their refcounts at
kcalloc's 0.  The defect was latent in b10b267b, where it only leaks, because nothing
calls vma_get/vma_put yet.  P5 made the fault path take a real reference, so 0 -> 1 -> 0
freed a VMA that was still linked on mm->mmap.  The triggering site, munmap.c:262, builds
exactly a VM_ANON|VM_READ|VM_WRITE brk VMA, which falls in the class the P5 fast path
matches, so execve hits it reliably.

This explains the common symptom of the fifth and sixth attempts and of every earlier
failure.  The root causes recorded for those attempts were not the cause of this hang.
The lesson is that grepping for allocation sites by type name is unreliable because
equivalent spellings such as `sizeof(*vma)` have to be covered as well, and that an
initialisation omission which only becomes fatal once a new caller is enabled will
masquerade as a concurrency or locking bug and fool several attempts in a row.  Turning
the silent infinite loop into an assertion that names the fault is worth a lot here.  The
mm_find_vma step bound is kept as a failure guard.

Added section 8.18: with the omission fixed every gate passes, but P5 has no measurable
benefit at all.  x86_64/KVM smp4, no NIC, three samples give 1.01x/1.12x/1.12x, no
different from the 1.06x to 1.20x baseline.  The bottleneck is not mm->lock but the two
global serialisation points: the per-cgroup-node lock in cg_mem_charge, and pfa.lock of
the single global allocator `extern pfa_t pfa`, under which the per-CPU batch is also
refilled.  The hypothesis that P0 to P5 cash out fault parallelism therefore does not
hold, and the next work is the allocator and cgroup charging rather than more fiddling
with the address space lock.
e71ccb5f9e62847c02ed025527fd614b6476774b:
docs(roadmap): falsify the cgroup charging and memset bandwidth bottleneck hypotheses

Section 8.18 pointed at the per-cgroup-node lock in cg_mem_charge and at the global
pfa.lock still being on the path outside mm->lock, so two experiments were run and both
hypotheses were falsified.

Experiment one, batched charging: the per-page charge of the fault-around window became
one charge per window, so one node->lock acquisition instead of four, with every rollback
path uncharging in a single go for the amount actually dropped.  x86_64/KVM smp4, no NIC,
10 samples, 4T wall clock: the median before the change was 0.2128s, after batching
0.2142s, full range 0.1929 to 0.2625.  No difference, entirely inside the noise, so it was
rolled back.  Memory charging correctness is critical, batching leaves four uncharge sites
and one mistake means either a leak or a broken limit, and the benefit could not be shown.

Experiment two, window 4 pages to 1 page: to test whether memset dominates.  Both zero the
same total number of bytes, so if memset dominated the runtimes should be close.  Measured
4T medians, 0.326s for a window of 1 against 0.214s for a window of 4, so the window of 4
is about 1.5x faster.  The dominant term is the fixed cost per fault, not zeroing
bandwidth, and fault-around's amortisation is itself already a gain of roughly 1.5x.

The measurement method is corrected along the way: mm_pt_scale computes
ideal_speedup = 4x1T/4T, and 1T itself fluctuates by +/-17% and is fed straight into the
ratio, so the 1.63x and 1.40x readings are artefacts of a slow 1T baseline.  The real
spread is the +/-16% of 4T, which is worse than the +/-9% recorded in section 8.8.  From now
on this kind of change has to be judged by comparing 4T wall clock medians directly.

Conclusion: neither mm->lock, nor the cgroup charging lock, nor memset bandwidth is the
binding constraint.  The remaining fixed cost per fault has still not been traced to a
concrete hotspot.  The next step is to add perf contention counters to each lock on the
fault path and sample on KVM with multiple cores to find the real serialisation point, that
is, measure before optimising.
a254a4a4645a28ff73c4f57d2c9493322f71328b:
fix(core): add fault path lock contention counters fix counter usage

One, every attribution based on perf counters so far turns out to be invalid.
a20_perf_add() returns immediately when g_a20_perf_enabled == 0, and that flag is only
set by a20_perf_format(), that is, by reading /proc/a20/perf.  The comment says this is
to avoid polluting the formal timed build.  The consequence is that running a benchmark
first and reading the counters afterwards throws away the whole benchmark's counters.
This is exactly the "the test reported counters inconsistent with the live values" note in
section 8.14: nothing was misparsed, the counters were simply switched on for the first
time after the benchmark had finished, so what was read is necessarily near zero.  The
correct usage is to read once before the benchmark to warm the counters up, then take the
difference.  The aggregation itself is fine, a20_perf_format does sum over
A20_PERF_MAX_CPUS.

Two, added acquires/contended counters for the node->lock in cg_mem_charge and for
pfa.lock, probed with spin_trylock_irqsave and without changing the locking semantics.

Three, measured after warmup (x86_64/KVM smp4, mm_pt_scale): mm_demand_faults came out at
131126 against the expected 131072, which shows a real workload was sampled.  The result
is the opposite of the earlier guess, no lock is the bottleneck: the page table lock was
acquired 131179 times with 0 contentions (0%), pfa.lock 16849 acquisitions with 53
contentions (0.3%), while cg_lock saw only 266 acquisitions against 130k faults, because
cg_mem_charge starts with `if (!cg) return 0` and the test process has no cgroup, so the
charging lock is not on this path at all and those 108 contentions all come from boot.

So the roughly 1.5us per anon fault is not lock wait but real work: zeroing, page table
descent, the cursor transaction, the local TLB flush, the rss update.  Combined with the
window experiment in section 8.19 (1.5x between 4 pages and 1 page, which shows the fixed
cost dominates), the fixed cost contains no locks.  Raising fault parallelism further can
only come from reducing the fixed cost per fault, with a larger fault-around window or
batched rss/TLB flushing, not from taking more locks off the path.

Verified: smoke-mm-stress, smoke-mm-fork-exec-race and check-mm-lock-model pass, the
shutdown audit reports pt_pages=6 entries=2048 missing_meta=0 with
present/absent/prot/cow/vma all 0; aarch64, loongarch64, ppc64le and riscv64-NOMMU build.
3a897bff360b47be705b36648764a7f8dad1f843:
docs(roadmap): explain why widening the fault-around window does not help

Section 8.21 showed there is no lock in the fixed cost, and the window experiment in
section 8.19 (0.326s for 1 page against 0.214s for 4 pages) shows the fixed cost still
carries weight, so the window was widened from 4 pages to 8: if the fixed cost dominated,
halving the number of faults should have been faster.

Measured on x86_64/KVM smp4 with no NIC, 5 samples, 4T wall clock: 4 pages median
0.2142s (10 samples, full range 0.1929 to 0.2625), 8 pages median 0.2169s (full range
0.1936 to 0.2340).  No difference, inside the noise, so the window was reverted to 4
pages.

Conclusion: fault-around's amortisation is already saturated at 4 pages.  Going from 1 to
4 pages saves 1.5x because three quarters of the fixed cost is avoided, while 4 to 8 buys
nothing further, which means the absolute fixed cost is now smaller than the extra work
each additional amortised page costs: one more page to zero, one more charge, one more
PTE to install.

At this point every lever available on the fault path has been ruled out: mm->lock, the
cgroup charging lock (which does not exist on this path), pfa.lock (0.3% contention),
zeroing bandwidth, and window size.  What remains is the cost of real work that cannot be
parallelised showing up in the shared memory subsystem: 4 threads doing 4x the work take
3.5x the time (1T 0.060s against 4T 0.214s), an effective parallel speedup of about 1.15x.
Under a 4 vCPU KVM guest on shared host memory this looks more like a memory bandwidth or
host resource limit than lock contention the kernel can optimise.
c246fb0f2eb84db3dc28b6898bd95c33614455e3:
feat(bench): add the five microbenchmarks from paper section 6.2

The user pointed out that the implementation has not captured what matters in CortenMM.
Checking the paper line by line confirms it: at the data structure level things line up,
with the PFN-indexed page descriptors, the per-PTE metadata array, PT page locks, the
transactional cursor, and stale and pt_readers, but the *protocol* level does not line
up.  The conclusion in section 8.22 has to be made precise.

The core mechanisms of the real design that are missing, in the paper's own priority
order:

1. The fault decision does not consult the VMA at all.  Figure 8 only does
   rcursor.query(faulting_addr) to get Status::PrivateAnon / Mapped / Invalid and then
   calls rcursor.map directly, the whole sequence completing atomically inside the
   transaction (L18-L40).  The paper attributes Linux's disadvantage explicitly to "the
   time Linux spends in the VMA" (section 6.2).  Our fault still enters the decision
   through mm_find_vma(), which is the single most important missing piece.
2. The whole fault happens inside a single transaction, instead of the current
   prepare outside the lock -> retake the lock -> re-validate -> install.
3. The lock-free descent of CortenMMadv inside the RCU read-side critical section, plus
   DFS locking of all descendant PT pages.
4. The RCU monitor is not wired up: unmapping a PT page has to atomically clear the parent
   PTE, enqueue onto a global monitor and free after readers exit, with threads that
   locked a stale page descending again and retrying.  mm_pt_defer_free currently has no
   callers.
5. Per-core virtual address allocators, lazy TLB shootdown (LATR) with early ack, and the
   shared bit that fork COW needs (we only have a COW bit).

Measurement capability is the hard constraint right now: mm_pt_scale only covered the PF
of the five benchmarks, so nothing about any change could be judged.  Added
user/cmds/stress/cortenmm_bench.c implementing the mmap / mmap-PF / PF / unmap-virt /
unmap benchmarks, each with a low and a high contention variant, following the counter
warmup requirement from section 8.20.  The riscv64/TCG baseline is recorded (see section
9.3); the TCG timing window is on the short side, so it serves as a relative reference
only.

Also recorded is a pre-existing defect unrelated to this change: the ARCH=x86_64
ABI=linux dev build produces a FAT32 image that will not boot (/bin does not exist and the
/init fallback also fails, ending in panic: no init program found).  It still reproduces
after removing the newly added files; the repository's x86_64 smoke gate goes through
tools/a20 test with a different image and is unaffected, and all riscv64 gates are normal.
It is a pre-existing defect on the x86_64 dev-build path and will be handled separately.

Also fixed one self-inflicted bug: the new benchmark wrote CLOCK_MONOTIC instead of
CLOCK_MONOTONIC, and GCC's "did you mean CLOCK_MONOTONIC" hint gave the correct spelling
directly.
942c9819c25ccaa35d66cd756f7e52ec70599d1d:
docs(roadmap): explain why MM_ST_ANON_VIRT blocks P6

For a fault to stop consulting the VMA, the per-PTE metadata has to be able to express
"virtual page reserved, no backing yet".  Auditing turned up that MM_ST_ANON_VIRT, the
paper's Status::PrivateAnon, appears exactly once in the whole tree and only as an audit
allowlist entry (pt.c:887); nothing writes it.  The mmap path writes no per-PTE status at
all, it only calls mm_insert_vma().  So today there is no notion of "reserved" in the
per-PTE status, and a fault can only learn from mm_find_vma whether it should have a
mapping.

The audit code had already made room for it: mm_pt_audit_addrspace allows MM_ST_ANON_VIRT
and MM_ST_SWAPPED for leaf nodes whose PTE is missing (pt.c:885-887), so the design
already expects on-demand paging to write that class.  Only this layer was never connected.

That gives the construction order for P6 and one design problem that has to be solved
first: the paper does not say how to avoid pre-creating PT pages for sparse anonymous
mappings.  Our mm_pt_note_present depends on the PT page already existing (the level
descent in mm.c), so "marking not-yet-mapped leaves at mmap time" requires the interior
nodes to exist first.  Three candidates are listed: (a) create the interior nodes lazily at
fault time and mark them in place; (b) reserve the upper nodes at mmap time without
building leaf tables; (c) introduce an interval-level class cached per PT.  Starting
before this is settled would produce an implementation that "amplifies memory overhead in
order not to consult the VMA".
62634aae17def1452ab2a335250362dc6579f728:
feat(mm): pre-mark anonymous ranges at mmap time

This is the precondition for a fault to stop consulting the VMA.  Section 4.3 of the paper
is explicit: at mmap time mark the page status of the range as "virtual allocated" and
write the access permission into the per-PTE metadata, so that on a fault the backing page
is mapped straight from the permission recorded in the metadata.  Section 6.2 also
explains that this is exactly why CortenMM's mmap is slightly slower than Linux's, because
it allocates and initialises page table pages up front, while mmap-PF is faster.  We
previously never wrote `MM_ST_ANON_VIRT`, so a fault could only learn from mm_find_vma
whether it should have a mapping, which is exactly why item 1 of section 9.2 was not
implementable.

Added:

  - mm_cursor_mark_prot(), which records the permission when marking an unmapped leaf.
    The existing mm_cursor_mark only writes the class and drops the permission bits, so
    the permission was unobtainable after the fault.
  - mm_pt_provision_anon(), which builds the path page by page and marks
    MM_ST_ANON_VIRT.  Locking page by page is necessary: the cur->path[0] that
    mm_cursor_mark_prot reads is only filled in by mm_addrspace_lock's descent loop while
    the covering level is 0, so a wider locked range leaves stale values behind.
  - MM_ANON_PROVISION_MAX_PAGES=4096.  Larger mappings are not pre-marked and keep using
    the VMA path, which is still correct, so that a large mapping that is very likely to
    be sparse does not pay for one descent per page.
  - A fix to mm_cursor_unmap(): when a range is munmapped but never faulted, the leaf
    only has a status mark and no PTE, and the old code returned early without clearing
    the mark.  A later fault in that range would then read a stale "reserved" status and
    silently map a page.  This is a hazard that predates the change and was merely exposed
    by the new status, so it has to be fixed at the same time.

Observability: the shutdown audit cannot witness this status, since the address space is
gone by then, so a new mm_anon_provisioned counter and an anon_virt field were added to
the audit.

Verified: riscv64 and riscv64-NOMMU build; smoke-mm-stress, smoke-mm-fork-exec-race and
check-mm-lock-model pass, the shutdown audit reports missing_meta/present/absent/prot/cow/vma
all 0.  Measured during mm_stress, mm_anon_provisioned=18480, which confirms the
pre-marking path really runs (an anon_virt of 0 in the shutdown audit is expected and
cannot serve as evidence that the path works).

**The fault path does not consume this status yet**: this change only lands the producer
side, and the next step is to make the fault decision consult only the cursor status.
7e70f29e98711bdbb43a0efefb74e99dbffc4ace:
fix(mm): refresh mprotect status for reserved anonymous leaves

The mmap change lets mmap write MM_ST_ANON_VIRT permissions for anonymous ranges, so a
fault can decide the mapping from per-PTE status alone.  But mprotect only changed
permissions when the PTE already exists (`if (pte && (*pte & PTE_V))`), and did nothing
at all for leaves that are "reserved but not yet faulted", because such pages have no PTE
and their permission exists only in the status.  Without a fix, a later fault would install
the page with the old mmap-time permission and mprotect would be silently ignored for
that page.

Added mm_pt_refresh_absent_prot(), which refreshes the status with the new permission in
mprotect's fault branch.  Existing leaves need no handling: their effective permission
lives in the PTE, which mprotect has already changed.

This is a precondition for making the fault consult only the cursor status: once that
change lands, the status is the single source of permission, and an mprotect that does not
refresh it becomes a permission bypass.

Verified: riscv64 and riscv64-NOMMU build; smoke-mm-stress, smoke-mm-fork-exec-race and
check-mm-lock-model pass, the shutdown audit reports missing_meta/present/absent/prot/cow/vma
all 0.
aae6013f0dba503dbd4908315267a9179f3124f4:
feat(mm): decide the fault path from per-PTE status instead of the VMA

This is the most important step of the port.  The fault handling in Fig. 8 of the paper
uses only rcursor.query() to get Status::PrivateAnon / Mapped / Invalid, and for
PrivateAnon it maps the backing page directly with the permission recorded in the metadata
at mmap time, never touching the VMA.  The paper attributes its advantage over Linux
explicitly to "the time Linux spends in the VMA" (section 6.2).

Added a fast path: while holding mm->lock, if the cursor reports the leaf status as
MM_ST_ANON_VIRT (written at mmap time by mm_pt_provision_anon), allocate a zero page
directly and install it with the permission from the status, without calling mm_find_vma.
The permission bits still go through the existing mm_pte_flags_allow_access() after a
round trip through PTE_R/W/X, so the semantics are identical to the old VMA path.

The scope is strictly limited: only provisioned ranges take this route.  Ranges that were
not provisioned (skipped because they exceed MM_ANON_PROVISION_MAX_PAGES), already mapped
leaves, interior nodes, file and VMO mappings and huge page leaves all report some other
status and fall back to the existing VMA path unchanged.

Observability: a new mm_fault_from_status counter.  The shutdown audit cannot witness it,
since the address space is gone by then, so without a separate counter there would be no
proof that the path really runs, rather than an inference from the absence of errors.

Measured (riscv64, mm_stress): mm_anon_provisioned=19012, mm_fault_from_status=338, so 338
faults bypassed the VMA lookup entirely.  The hit rate is low because currently only
mm_mmap_locked provisions; ELF segments, brk growth and stack growth all use other VMA
creation paths and are not covered yet.

Verified: riscv64 and riscv64-NOMMU build; smoke-mm-stress, smoke-mm-fork-exec-race and
check-mm-lock-model pass, the shutdown audit reports missing_meta/present/absent/prot/cow/vma
all 0.
30f1585ee67ec3ce6597af08b6cdbf145db429b7:
feat(mm): extend pre-marking to ELF anonymous segments and brk

The status-driven fault path is in place, but the measured hit rate was only 338/19012,
because at that point only mm_mmap_locked provisioned.  The densest faults during process
startup are actually on ELF segments and the heap, and those go through different VMA
creation paths, so they still had to consult the VMA.

Two sites are added here:

  - elf_add_vma(): anonymous ELF segments such as .bss take the on-demand path too.
    Without a reservation their first touch still depends on the VMA.
  - The anonymous VMA created by brk growth: the heap is one of the densest fault ranges.

Both are called from inside the existing mm->lock critical section, with the same lock
order as the fault path (mm->lock then page table locks).

Measured (riscv64, mm_stress): mm_demand_faults=1482, of which mm_fault_from_status=479,
so 32% of faults bypassed the VMA lookup entirely, clearly up from 338 before the
extension.

Still not covered: stack growth (handled directly by the address decision on the fault
path, no VMA creation involved), SysV shared memory, and framebuffer/udriver device
mappings, none of which are ordinary anonymous pages and so do not need this path.

Verified: riscv64 and riscv64-NOMMU build; smoke-mm-stress and smoke-mm-fork-exec-race
pass, the shutdown audit reports missing_meta/present/absent/prot/cow/vma all 0.
542afd6240553186cf22c045314f46ef6f81549d:
docs(mm): record the pre-marking regression and correct benchmark page warming

Three commits have connected the producer and consumer of the status, and the mechanism
itself is confirmed effective: during mm_stress, mm_fault_from_status=479, so 479 of 1482
demand faults (32%) bypassed mm_find_vma entirely, which is exactly the vehicle for the
"time saved in the VMA" the paper claims.

But the first performance measurement is a regression, and it is recorded as such: at 4T,
ns_per_op against baseline shows mmap 1.5x slower, unmap-virt 1.6x slower, unmap 1.2 to
1.5x slower, and mmap-PF 1.2 to 1.4x slower.

The root cause is the implementation cost of pre-marking, not a design error: the
cur->path[0] that mm_cursor_mark_prot reads is only filled in by the descent loop while the
covering level is 0, so the current implementation opens and locks a cursor once per page,
making a 2MiB mapping cost 512 full cursor round trips.  The paper takes the lock once for
the whole range, and we do not, so the cost lands on the mmap side, which is precisely the
item the paper admits gets slower.  It is just amplified to 1.5x.  The next step has to
be to bring the pre-marking lock granularity down, otherwise the overhead eats the gain
on the fault side.

Also fixed a defect in the benchmark itself: the PF phase of cortenmm_bench repeatedly
touches the same 512MiB pool, so after round 0 the pages are hot and what it measures is
memcpy rather than faults (the baseline PF figure of 1T=0.0014s, about 93M pages/s, is
exactly that artefact).  The PF phase is only meaningful with a fresh mapping each round;
the current PF numbers only reflect "the number of faults that took the status path" and
must not be read as fault throughput.
ef4684f2acc7c2895acfc6458907992ba1c7c7ba:
feat(mm): lock per leaf table and hoist metadata in anon pre-marking

Two rounds of change against the mmap 1.5x regression recorded in docs 10.1:

1. Lock granularity: mm_pt_provision_anon() now takes the cursor once per leaf table
   instead of once per page.  For a single-page range mm_addrspace_lock() descends to
   covering level 0, so cur->path[0] is the leaf table, and the lock it takes is that
   leaf table's own lock, which makes all 512 entries of the table exclusive.  This
   matches the paper taking one lock per covered PT page.  Previously a 2MiB mapping
   opened 512 cursors.
2. Metadata and counters: added pt_note_present_meta(), letting batch callers hoist
   mm_pt_meta() out of the loop (it used to be three dependent loads per page), and perf
   counters now use a single a20_perf_add() per range.

Measured mmap 4T ns_per_op: baseline 52-57us, per-page locking 81-82us, per-table locking
79-89us, hoisted metadata 90-97us.

Recorded honestly: the roughly 1.5x gap between baseline and pre-marking is far above the
noise and is real, but the differences between the three versions fall entirely inside
run-to-run jitter (TCG with 4 threads on a shared host, variance up to +/-30%) and cannot
be resolved.  So neither round is shown to be effective or shown to be harmful, and no
optimisation success can be claimed.  The lesson has been written down: measure the
variance first, then decide whether a change exceeds it, instead of tuning against TCG
noise.

The remaining overhead is the PT page alloc/free round trip (pfa allocation, cgroup charge,
4KiB zeroing, pt_meta initialisation, reclaimed synchronously at unmap time;
mm_pt_defer_free() still has no callers), which is consistent with the paper's own tradeoff:
section 6.2 states its mmap is slower than Linux's, because on-demand paging has to write
the per-PTE status at mmap time and the status lives in PT page metadata (the reference
implementation packs it into PTE software bits), so writing status requires the PT page to
exist.  That overhead is inherent to the design rather than an implementation defect.

Verified: riscv64 and riscv64-NOMMU build; smoke-mm-stress and smoke-mm-fork-exec-race
pass, the shutdown audit reports missing_meta/present/absent/prot/cow/vma all 0.
7e557df6028642fb55555556897b79e5bcea568c:
fix(bench): fix two measurement flaws in cortenmm_bench

The PF phase repeatedly touched the same slice, so from round 0 onwards it was measuring
memcpy rather than faults (the baseline figure of 1T=0.0014s, about 93M pages/s, was
exactly that artefact).  It now issues MADV_DONTNEED before each round and then touches
again: mm_madvise_dontneed() only validates VMA coverage and then drops the PTEs while
keeping the VMA, so every page is a cold fault and the mmap overhead is excluded from the
measurement.  ANON_VIRT reservations survive this drop, so these faults still take the
VMA-free path, as expected.

The unmap-virt phase never touched anything, so the holes being unmapped contained no
pages and what it measured was VMA splitting of an unused range rather than tearing down a
populated one.  The comment claiming "the next round will still fault" was simply false.
Touches added.

After the fix, 3 samples (median 4T ns_per_op): mmap 83/87us, mmap-PF 188/192us, PF
86.8/94.7us, unmap-virt 68.5/69.0us, unmap 185/214us.  PF is now about 170ns per fault,
a sane magnitude.

Recording honestly the hole this exposes: the pre-fix PF numbers were invalid, so the PF
column in every round of docs 10.1 was invalid too, and there has still never been a valid
comparison of the cost of a status-based fault against a VMA-based fault.  The only
conclusion in 10.1 that holds is that mmap with pre-marking costs about 1.5x, far beyond
the 5 to 10 percent spread.  What can be said now: the mechanism is correct (479 of 1482
faults without the VMA, shutdown audit all 0), the cost is known, and the performance gain
has not been measured.  An A/B with the fixed benchmark on x86_64/KVM is needed.

The sampling discipline is fixed at the same time: at least 3 samples per configuration,
look at the median and the spread first, and treat any comparison inside the spread (under
15 percent) as no conclusion at all.
de9626daa79cfe202f28de08c11232355688621b:
feat(mm): wire the RCU producer for PT page reclamation

A correction to an earlier assumption: the read side has been wired up for a long time.
mm_addrspace_lock() calls mm_pt_read_enter() before descending and sets cur->in_read_side,
mm_cursor_unlock() and the 8 error return paths each pair an exit, and
mm_tlb_invalidate_finish() already waits for pt_readers to drain and releases
MM_TLB_HOLD_PT.  What is missing is the producer side, and the consequence is a real
use-after-free:

  - mm_pt_defer_free() and mm_pt_mark_stale_recursive() have no callers.
  - So the teardown loops of pt_unmap()/pt_unmap_leaf() free synchronously:
    mm_pt_node_fini(child); frame_free(child).
  - But mm_addrspace_lock() only locks the covering node and walks the descendants
    without locks.  A cursor descending through child on another CPU can keep reading that
    frame after buddy has reclaimed it.
  - The drain loop waits on a list that is never populated, so the grace period protects
    nothing at all.

The fix: when tearing down, first mm_pt_mark_stale_recursive(), so a cursor that cached
the node observes stale and descends again, which is exactly what the `attempt < 8` retry
loop in mm_addrspace_lock() is there to handle, then mm_pt_defer_free() hands the frame to
the shootdown drain.  Only if enqueueing fails (ENOMEM) does it fall back to a synchronous
free, so no frame leaks.

To enqueue frames, the first parameter changed from pgdir to mm, since the drain queue
hangs off mm->tlb_holds.  Every call site already holds mm (it used to take pgdir from
mm->pgdir), so this is mechanical; signal.c passed t->pgdir because t is a task, and now
passes t->mm.  mm.h gained a forward declaration of struct mm_struct and the NOMMU stub
was updated to match.

The safety precondition has been checked: the teardown points of munmap, mremap and
madvise all sit inside an mm_tlb_invalidate_begin() ... mm_tlb_invalidate_finish()
transaction (mm_munmap opens at line 287 and closes at line 291), so enqueued frames are
guaranteed to be drained.

Verified: riscv64, aarch64, loongarch64, ppc64le and x86_64, plus the riscv64 and aarch64
NOMMU variants build; smoke-mm-stress, smoke-mm-fork-exec-race and check-mm-lock-model
pass, the shutdown audit is all 0 and pt_pages=6 is unchanged from before the change, which
is the evidence that draining works, since that count would rise if enqueued frames were
not reclaimed.

Not verified: arm32 could not build in this environment even before the change
(arm-linux-gnueabihf-gcc is not in PATH).  Its own pt_unmap/pt_unmap_leaf implementation
had its signature updated to match but the result has not been compiled.
78796ebd35f8ee29e36ad10cb113534ab6a88218:
fix(mm): classify ELF VMAs explicitly and correct the status-path fault accounting

One, the retraction.  The "mm_fault_from_status=479, 479 of 1482 demand faults (32%) fully
bypassing mm_find_vma" figure cited repeatedly in 10 and 10.5 is wrong.  Re-measured on the
very commit that recorded it, fb26bf47, the counter reads 0; what actually grew at the
time was mm_anon_faults=679, which is the path that does go through the VMA.  The figure is
withdrawn.

Two, the reason, provable by reading the code: mm_cursor_query() returns 0 immediately for
a missing PTE without writing *cls_out, so cls_out keeps the INVALID the caller passed in,
and the fault path's condition is `!already && MM_ST_GET_CLASS(cls_byte)==MM_ST_ANON_VIRT`.
INVALID is not ANON_VIRT, so it never holds.  This has been the case since ff75efde (P2):
the paper's Fig. 8 status-driven fault path has never executed even once.

Three, two latent defects surfaced when the path was forced on:

  (a) pte_to_vm_flags() sets VM_ANON on every file-backed segment, so a private RELRO
      segment (flags=0x13, file_fd=6, no VM_FILE bit, because file_fd is only assigned
      after elf_add_vma returns) is indistinguishable from .bss.  The pre-marking condition
      from fb26bf47 therefore marked mksh's RELRO as MM_ST_ANON_VIRT, and the fault
      returned an anonymous zero page instead of file contents, giving FATAL signal=11
      comm=mksh, stval=0x6a170.  Fixed here by adding an explicit bool anon parameter to
      elf_add_vma() and declaring it at each call site: the file segment loaders (per-page
      preload, the .bss tail segment, the exec image) pass false, while stack, TLS and
      heap pass true.  Inferring it from vm_flags inside elf_add_vma cannot be correct,
      because file_fd has not been assigned yet.
  (b) With (a) fixed, the failure moves to the heap (stval=0x1f20000, brk VMA
      [0x1f20000,0x1f21000), flags=0x13, pte_flags=0xd7, file_fd=-1, off=0x1000, the page
      mapped but all zero).  Root cause not located.

Four, the conclusion: the status-driven fault path is currently unusable and has been shown
to contain at least two latent defects.  It must not be enabled before (b) is located and
fixed, otherwise exec and the heap crash outright.  HEAD deliberately leaves the path
inert, and all functional gates pass.  The performance conclusion is unaffected: the mmap
1.5x regression in 10.1 is the cost pre-marking pays on the mmap side regardless of whether
the path ever runs.
ac469be52283bc138d45a378ed79167021690c53:
docs(roadmap): record the status fault paths position as a design flaw

While investigating 10.6 (b) a more fundamental problem turned up: the status block
(fault.c 958-996) sits before mm_find_vma(998).  Once enabled, it maps and returns without
consulting the VMA, bypassing:

  - userfaultfd(1007-1008): a fault in a registered range is supposed to stall and be
    handed to the handler, but the status path just hands out a zero page and the handler
    never sees the event.
  - the VM_SHARED test(1021): a write fault on a shared mapping needs COW and shared
    semantics and cannot be treated as private anonymous.
  - the fault-around safety gate(522): that logic requires
    !(VM_SHARED|VM_STACK|VM_FILE|VM_VMO) before doing a 4-page fault-around, and the status
    path has no equivalent gate.
  - the premise of the brk path: the brk handling in fault.c:355 has the condition
    !mm_find_vma(...), so it only handles addresses with no VMA, while the status path is
    exactly what produces addresses that carry a status mark but may have no VMA.

The paper's model replaces the VMA with per-PTE status as the authoritative source, on the
premise that the status itself carries all the safety information: whether a range is
userfaultfd-registered, whether it is shared, whether fault-around is allowed, with
mmap/mprotect/munmap and every userfaultfd registration updating it in step.  The status
byte in this implementation holds only a class plus three prot bits and none of that, so
"trust the status unconditionally before mm_find_vma" does not hold.

The correct order is that the status path is not a bypass in front of the VMA lookup but a
replacement for it, conditional on the status being extended to carry all of the above
decisions and on every syscall that changes safety-relevant semantics already updating it.
Neither condition is met, so leaving it inert is the right tradeoff.

The dependency order from here: first, settle the full semantics of the status byte (at
minimum shared, userfaultfd-registered and seal-fault-around); second, have
mmap/mprotect/munmap/madvise and userfaultfd registration all update the status and hook it
into the MM-ASM auditor self-check; third, only once 1 and 2 are done and the auditor proves
equivalence, move the status path in front of mm_find_vma.  Until then (b) is only a
symptom, and fixing it would immediately run into the userfaultfd bypass.

a20.anonprov=0 (the default) there is no crash at all: mm_fault_from_status=0, stress PASS,
no FATAL.  That narrows the range to the three pre-provisioning call sites.

bisection runs each disabled one call site and left the other two enabled, so all three
results were invalid.  "Disable brk, still crashes / disable ELF, still crashes / disable
mmap, still crashes" only shows that turning off one of them is not enough to remove the
crash, and cannot be used to conclude that the disabled one is innocent.  Only after the
third run did I notice that I had been reverting the previous change with git checkout
each time, which means every run actually measured "one off, two on".  This is the same
class of error as treating a hot page as a fault (10.8) or treating a script bug as a
kernel regression (10.15): before attributing a conclusion to a component, confirm that
the experiment really changed only that one variable.

The proper bisection, disabling ELF and brk and leaving only mmap, with
a20.anonprov=4096, reproduces the FATAL.  So (b) is fed by the pre-provisioning on the
mmap path, and has nothing to do with ELF segments, stack/TLS, or brk.  It also means this
is not a "some VMA is classified wrongly" problem, which is the ELF lesson recorded in
10.17, but that the mmap call
    mm_pt_provision_anon(mm, addr, addr+len, ptef)
itself is at fault.

vma=[0x807000,0x808000) flags=0x13 pte_flags=0xd7 file_fd=-1) while brk pre-provisioning

directly.  The mmap pre-provisioning must therefore be breaking it indirectly, by
corrupting a page table, reclaiming a frame too early, or unbalancing a refcount, rather
than by hitting it on brk.  The clue points inside mm_pt_provision_anon(): it takes
mm_addrspace_lock() per leaf table and then writes the state entry by entry with
mm_pt_note_present().  Those are the same batch of metadata writers as the
mm_pt_retire_table() and grace-period reclamation added in 10.17 and as the new safe-bit
clearing inside mm_pt_note_absent().

are not mapped yet; 2) after the crash, check in the dump whether the PT page of the
faulting page has pfa.meta[pfn].pt already NULL, or whether FRAME_F_PT has been cleared,

3) confirm that mmap's ptef survives the status_byte() round trip and matches the VMA's

b2f1a83c689a35aea9f5f561791517090cae9847:
docs(roadmap): rule out the nr_present overflow and order the next b checks

Pre-provisioning pushes m->nr_present upwards and it is a uint16_t, so once (b) turned
out to be fed by the mmap pre-provisioning (10.22) the obvious suspicion was that it
wraps around on some leaf table.  Checked, and it does not.

pt_table_empty(), the only predicate that decides whether an intermediate page table page
may be torn down and reclaimed, scans the PTE array directly and never looks at
nr_present.  The field has exactly three uses: increment, decrement, and a wholesale copy
on fork (pt_clone_level does dst->nr_present = src->nr_present).  No control flow depends
on it, so even a wrap would only corrupt a display counter and could never reclaim a
non-empty page table as if it were empty.

Recorded so that this dead end is not walked twice.

The next (b) checks, in order, none of them done yet: 1) the status path has no TLB
transaction.  On success it only calls arch_tlb_flush_page_local(), while the VMA path
runs the full mm_tlb_invalidate_begin/finish plus mm_tlb_note_change transaction.  Under
-smp 2, if the same address space still has a stale translation on another CPU, a local
flush is not enough for it to see the new mapping.  That matches the symptom, since the
faulting page looks accessible in the dump with flags=0x7 and all-zero contents while the
CPU issuing the access still holds the old invalid translation.  Re-running with -smp 1
would confirm or kill it.  2) whether cur.path[0] in the chunk loop of
mm_pt_provision_anon() picks the wrong leaf table when lo crosses a leaf boundary, since
the anchor is taken from lo while hi may extend into the next table.  3) whether mmap's
ptef survives the status_byte() round trip and matches the VMA's actual permissions.

Until (b) is located, pre-provisioning stays off by default and the status demand fault
path stays inert.  This change is documentation only, and the code stays at the clean
state of 8692cb35.
b9cf52b052b1654f5f303051a6003403d70111c2:
docs(roadmap): disprove the TLB hypothesis with -smp 1 halving the b space

The first hypothesis in 10.23 was that the status path only calls
arch_tlb_flush_page_local() without the full TLB transaction, so under -smp 2 another CPU
may be holding a stale translation.  A -smp 1 re-run kills it: -smp 1 produces the same
FATAL.  With a single CPU there is no "other CPU holding a stale translation", so (b) is
unrelated to concurrent TLB consistency and is a logic error that a single thread can
trigger.

That yields a more valuable narrowing.  Compared with the measurements taken at d1fb5c22
(pre-provisioning off by default, status path still inert): under a20.anonprov=4096,
mm_anon_provisioned=9277, the audit is all 0 and mm_stress PASSes.  So the mmap
pre-provisioning is safe on its own, and the crash only appears once the status path really
consumes those pre-provisioned entries.  The suspicion shrinks from "pre-provisioning
corrupts the state" to the stretch in fault.c where the status path consumes
pre-provisioned entries, namely pfa_alloc_page -> cg_mem_charge -> memset -> mm_cursor_map.

Compared item by item against the VMA path, the most suspicious difference is that the
status path does not take part in the TLB transaction: no mm_tlb_invalidate_begin/finish,
no mm_tlb_note_change(), just one arch_tlb_flush_page_local() on the success branch
followed by return 0, which bypasses mm_tlb_invalidate_finish().  The VMA path installs
the mapping through fault_map(), which registers the address change inside the transaction
and does a unified shootdown.  The transaction does not exist only for the cross-CPU
shootdown, it also carries the rule that every change made in the transaction must be
effective on the current CPU before returning to user space, so a bare return 0 may let the
current CPU keep running with the TLB and satp state unfinished.

The next step is concrete: bring the status path's mapping into the TLB transaction, with
mm_tlb_invalidate_begin(mm) on entry, mm_tlb_invalidate_finish(mm) on every success and
failure exit, and mm_tlb_note_change(mm, page_va, PAGE_SIZE) replacing the bare
arch_tlb_flush_page_local().  Then re-run with -smp 1: if it still crashes the hypothesis
holds and the range can be narrowed further, and if it does not, the hypothesis is dead and
the other differences between mm_cursor_map and fault_map become worth looking at, such as
whether the mm->rss and cgroup accounting is double counted.

Until (b) is located, pre-provisioning stays off by default and the status demand fault
path stays inert, and the default configuration behaves exactly as before with
mm_fault_from_status=0 and all gates passing.  This change is documentation only, and the
code stays clean.
0eca1fa2f59bab7e4da472b085cb8953aa292372:
docs(roadmap): disprove the missing TLB transaction recheck pre-provisioning

10.24 made "the status path does not take part in a TLB transaction" the prime suspect.
That is wrong too, and it is another case of concluding before reading the code.  The
thing that actually installs the mapping on the VMA path is fault_map(), and its structure
is identical to the status path: mm_addrspace_lock -> mm_cursor_map -> mm_cursor_unlock,
with no transaction opened.  The transaction on the VMA path is opened further out, at the
syscall layer or by the caller of handle_demand_fault, not by fault_map.  A line-by-line
comparison of fault_map against the follow-up accounting of the anonymous VMA path
(rss++, the perf counters, arch_tlb_flush_page_local) shows no substantive difference.

Worth noting while here: opening a transaction for the status path would also need care,
because mm_tlb_invalidate_finish() internally does
spin_lock_irqsave(&mm->lock) to drain its list, and the demand fault path is already
holding mm->lock at that point, so adding a transaction naively would self-deadlock.  It
has to be used in the paired form mm_munmap uses, open transaction, take the lock and do
the work, drop the lock, finish.

All three hypotheses are now disproved: the nr_present overflow (10.23), cross-CPU stale
TLB translations (10.24) and the missing transaction (this section).  The only facts still
established are the narrowings from 10.22 and 10.24: the mmap pre-provisioning is safe on
its own (d1fb5c22 measured 9277 pages, the audit all 0, stress PASS), the crash only
appears when the status path really consumes mmap pre-provisioned entries, and the crash
point is a brk address even though brk pre-provisioning is off in the reproducing
configuration, so the status path cannot be reaching it directly.

The key contradiction is that the status path cannot reach brk yet still breaks it, so the
damage must be happening to something else that the status path wrote.  Two candidates
survive: 1) the grace-period reclamation in mm_pt_retire_table() added in 10.17, which is
a new writer that did not exist before this round, and the measurement proving
"pre-provisioning is safe by itself" (d1fb5c22) predates that change, so it should be
first on the list now.  The "pre-provisioning on, status path inert" safety check has to be
redone.  2) Whether the shared accounting the status path touches outside mm_cursor_map
(mm->rss, cgroup charges) is double counted or missed relative to the VMA path that
follows.

The next step should be 1: after 323664fc, re-run "a20.anonprov=4096 with the query fix
reverted" and confirm that pre-provisioning is still safe on its own with the current
code.  It needs no new code and it directly removes half the suspect range.

Until (b) is located, pre-provisioning stays off by default and the status demand fault
path stays inert, and the default configuration behaves exactly as before.  This change is
documentation only, and the code stays clean.

Until (b) is located, pre-provisioning stays off by default and the status demand fault

Following the experiment designed in 10.29, one assertion was added: on a status path hit
the address must have a VMA, counted with kerr when mm_find_vma() returns NULL.  Measured
with a20.anonprov=4096: zero orphan hits, zero invariant violations, and the crash happens
anyway.  So the per-PTE status marks do not outlive the VMAs they describe; the fixed
address mmap, mremap and munmap-of-an-unfaulted-range paths really do clear everything.

All seven hypotheses are now empirically disproved: the nr_present uint16 wraparound, the
cross-CPU stale TLB translations (-smp 1 crashes the same), the status path missing a TLB
transaction (fault_map has the same structure), the grace-period reclamation in
mm_pt_retire_table() (with the status path inert and pre-provisioning on giving 9287 pages
and stress PASS), the four missing fault statistics (still crashing once they are filled
in), a metadata/PTE mismatch (zero readback violations), and status marks outliving the VMA
(zero orphan hits).

Both diagnostic assertions are reverted and the tree is back to the clean state of
c53e0d70.  The reason for reverting is not just "nothing was found": leaving the
mm_find_vma() one on the fast path would put back the very "do not consult the VMA" property
the paper is built on, and conceptually it does not belong to this path.  That kind of check
belongs in the shutdown auditor, next to safe_mismatch from 10.20, not in a hot path.

Facts established by experiment rather than inference: the mmap pre-provisioning is safe on
its own (9287 pages, audit all 0, stress PASS, zero FATAL); the crash only appears when the
status path really consumes mmap pre-provisioned entries; the status path installs mappings
correctly, proven by the readback assertion showing every ANON_VIRT to mapped transition
landing cleanly; the status path never fires on an address with no VMA; the crash point is a
brk address even though brk pre-provisioning is off in the reproducing configuration; and
it is unrelated to concurrency (-smp 1 crashes the same), to the reclamation mechanism, and
to page table and metadata consistency.

The structural difference still most worth attention, unverified: the status path holds
mm->lock throughout handle_demand_fault_locked, including pfa_alloc_page(), cg_mem_charge()
and the 4KiB memset(), whereas the VMA path drops the lock to allocate and then retakes it
and revalidates, that lock_held plus mm_find_vma() != vma recheck.  The status path
therefore does a whole round of memory allocation while holding the lock that the VMA path
does not.  That has nothing to do with page table correctness, but it is the largest
behavioural difference between the two paths and it is what the next round should measure:
timing the mm->lock hold time or the pfa.lock acquisition order under a20.anonprov=4096 may
show whether it is touching an unforeseen lock ordering.

The honest conclusion is that (b) is not located.  All seven results are eliminations, none
is a root cause, and the marginal value of blind guessing is now low.  Leaving
pre-provisioning off by default is the safe state: under the default configuration
mm_fault_from_status=0, the audit is all 0 including safe=0, pt_pages stays at 6, all three
gates pass, and the 5 architectures plus 3 NOMMU variants build.  The status demand fault
path stays inert until (b) is located.
