6be678fd5192bb61e80d83602c4bcde4a0634ac4:
build(build): add EXTRA_CFLAGS and a build-time pre-provision default

Since x86_64 cannot get a command line (10.31/10.32), the Makefile gets an EXTRA_CFLAGS
escape hatch and the pre-provisioning limit gains a build time default via
-DCONFIG_ANON_PROV_DEFAULT=<n>.  On architectures that do get a command line,
a20.anonprov=<n> still overrides it at run time.  That makes it possible to build two
images on x86_64 and alternate between them, giving the same time-adjacent A/B as on
riscv64.  Both switches were verified, each building across 5 architectures plus NOMMU:

    DEFAULT=4096 -> mm_anon_provisioned=53, mm_fault_from_status=12, mm_stress FATAL(signal=11)
    DEFAULT=0    -> 0, 0, PASS

Conclusion one: PTE_U is necessary but not sufficient.  The status path really does run on
x86_64, 12 times, so the U bit fix works across architectures, and it still crashes
afterwards.

Conclusion two: the permission round trip is architecture specific, and having got it
working on riscv64 I did not check any other architecture.  On riscv64
PTE_R=1<<1, W=1<<2, X=1<<3 and U=1<<4, so adding U is enough, but on x86_64:

    PTE_V=1<<0, PTE_R=1<<0 (the same bit as V), PTE_W=1<<1, PTE_U=1<<2,
    PTE_X=1<<11 (a software bit), PTE_USER=(PTE_V|PTE_W|PTE_U|PTE_NX|PTE_LEAF)

The status path rebuilds allow using only MM_ST_PROT_R, MM_ST_PROT_W and MM_ST_PROT_X, so
it drops PTE_NX and PTE_LEAF.  The pages it installs on x86_64 are therefore executable
(missing NX) and lack the leaf marker, which matches faulting immediately on a freshly
installed page and is the most likely reason x86_64 still crashes after the PTE_U fix.

The underlying lesson, the third of its kind in this project: the essence of the PTE_U bug
was treating one architecture's PTE semantics as universal.  The fix was only verified on
riscv64, the one architecture where the command line works, with no cross-check on a second
architecture, so "fixed" only held on one architecture.  Any change to the page table
abstraction layer has to be verified on at least two architectures with different semantics,
which is precisely the reason this repository carries riscv64, x86_64 and aarch64.

An unrelated problem turned up along the way: mprotect.c:141 calls
mm_pt_refresh_absent_prot(pte - idx, idx, ptef), which UBSAN reports as a pointer overflow
because it back-computes the table base from an entry inside the table and does pointer
arithmetic outside the object bounds, 35 times in one x86_64 run.  This has nothing to do
with (b), being a UBSAN diagnostic rather than the cause of a FATAL, but it shows that
back-computing a table base from an entry pointer is always out-of-bounds arithmetic as far
as a pointer sanitizer is concerned, and the table base should be passed explicitly instead.

State: the follow-up to (b) on x86_64 is not fixed.  The missing PTE_NX and PTE_LEAF are
the clear next target, but that needs a cross-architecture representation for the permission
round trip, since the current 3-bit MM_ST_PROT_* cannot express NX or LEAF on x86_64.  It
is another extension of the status byte format and runs into the same constraint recorded
in 10.18/10.19, that all 8 bits are already used up.  Get the cross-architecture permission
round trip right on riscv64 first, then re-measure on x86_64.
da49c364cd862520a9e8e4df983f5f1fba10b967:
feat(mm): route the status path through mm_prot_to_pte_flags

10.35 guessed that x86_64 still crashing meant the status path was hand-rolling PTE bits
and dropping PTE_LEAF and PTE_NX.  That guess is wrong, because the repository already has
the right interface, mm_prot_to_pte_flags().  It lays down the bits an architecture
requires (PTE_V|PTE_U|PTE_A|PTE_MAT1|PTE_LEAF) and then adds R, W and X according to prot,
and it encodes the W implies R dependency.

The status path used to hand-roll PTE_R|PTE_W|PTE_X|PTE_U.  It now turns the three prot bits
from the status back into a prot mask and hands that to mm_prot_to_pte_flags().  Every
architecture's required bits and the W implies R dependency are then the architecture's own
business and the call site knows nothing architecture specific, which promotes the
architecture-specific "add PTE_U" patch from 10.33 into the architecture-neutral correct
form, and allow |= PTE_U goes away with it.

Verification.  On riscv64 with a20.anonprov=4096: mm_fault_from_status=2836, stress PASS,
zero FATAL, MM-ASM all 0, matching the 2842 from before the refactor with no regression.  On
x86_64 with CONFIG_ANON_PROV_DEFAULT=4096: still FATAL, with pc=0x1e2e2, signal=11, pid=6
and 35 UBSAN reports, byte for byte identical to before the refactor.

The conclusion has to be stated plainly: this refactor is right, since it is the
architecture abstraction, it removes an architecture-specific patch, and there is no
riscv64 regression, but it is not the cause of the x86_64 crash.  The 10.35 inference about
missing PTE_LEAF and PTE_NX is disproved.  The crash address, the signal and the UBSAN count
are identical before and after, which shows that path is never even reached.

The x86_64 crash is still not located.  What is known: the status path really does run 12
times on x86_64, mm_fault_from_status=12, and then mm_stress crashes at pc=0x1e2e2.  The
shutdown audit is all 0, with pt_pages=9, every mismatch at 0 and safe=0, so the metadata
and the PTE have not diverged.  The same run also has 35 UBSAN pointer overflows from
mprotect.c:141.

pc=0x1e2e2 is in mm_stress user space.  The next step is to resolve that pc back to a
source line rather than continuing to guess at permission bits, which is the forensics
approach warranted after three consecutive wrong guesses about permissions, accounting and
reclamation in a row.
30d91b6ca3abb1a496934bb767bc4a580e50ddf2:
docs(roadmap): find the PTE/VMA permission split pointing at mprotect.c 141

Following the forensics approach from 10.36, no more guessing, pc=0x1e2e2 was resolved
back to source:

    pc=0x1e2e2 -> __copy_tls + 0x72 (glibc)
    1e2db: mov 0x5ea6(%rip),%rax
    1e2e2: mov %rax,0x0(%r13)     <- the faulting instruction

%r13 is the thread pointer TBLOCK, so this is a write through the thread block.  The crash
dump gives the decisive information:

    stval=0x108369f20
    pte value=0x800000007ee92425   <- bit63 = NX
    leaf flags=0x425               <- no RW bits, so read only
    vma=[0x108349000,0x10836a000) pte_flags=0x467  <- contains W, so writable

The core contradiction is that the VMA says the range is writable while the PTE is read
only.  A user mode write, __copy_tls writing to the thread block, lands on a read only page
and faults.  The kernel correctly refused an out-of-bounds write; what is wrong is that the
mapping itself disagrees with the VMA.

That points at mprotect.  The same run has 35 UBSAN pointer overflows, all of them at
kernel/mm/mprotect.c:141 in mm_pt_refresh_absent_prot(pte - idx, idx, ptef), a line in
mprotect's "reserved but never faulted" branch.  And the symptom here is exactly "the VMA
has become writable while the PTE is still read only": mprotect updated the VMA and not
the PTE.

The most likely mechanism is that mprotect back-computes the table base with pte - idx from
a leaf entry, doing pointer arithmetic outside the object bounds, which UBSAN reports every
time.  If the base is computed wrong, mm_pt_refresh_absent_prot() writes to the wrong slot,
the PTE of the page that should have changed is never updated, and the VMA side updates as
usual, so the two diverge.

That replaces "guessing at permission bits" with "one identifiable inconsistency", but the
root cause is not finally confirmed yet.  Still missing is whether mprotect takes a
different branch for already mapped pages, and whether those 35 UBSAN reports happen to
land on this faulting page.  The verification for the next step is to add counters and
warnings to both the "already mapped" and the "reserved" branches of mprotect, and to print
the table base computed by pte - idx alongside the table pointer returned by
pt_lookup_leaf().

This is not the same place as the PTE_U fix from 10.33.  That one was "the installed page
is missing the user bit", whose symptom was faulting immediately after installation.  This
one is a divergence between the PTE and the VMA permissions, and it does not reproduce on
riscv64, which completes 2836 status faults with stress PASS and the audit at 0.

The x86_64 crash is still unfixed, but it has narrowed from an unobservable FATAL to one
concrete contradiction: mprotect makes the PTE and the VMA permissions diverge, together
with the out-of-bounds pointer back-computation at mprotect.c:141.  The riscv64 functional
and performance conclusions are unaffected.
1d51c7696a7741beea80ba874a7acd9d40d4c571:
fix(mm): fix the NULL pointer arithmetic in mprotect

This is a real UB fix, but it does not fix the x86_64 crash.

10.37 found that in mprotect's "reserved but never faulted" branch:

    } else {
        int idx = arch_pt_vpn(va, 0);
        mm_pt_refresh_absent_prot(pte - idx, idx, ptef);
    }

The branch condition is !(pte && (*pte & PTE_V)), so pte can be NULL when the address has
no leaf table at all, and the code does pte - idx unconditionally, which is pointer
arithmetic on NULL.  The consequence chain: pte - idx yields a wild pointer from NULL, which
UBSAN reports as a pointer overflow every time; mm_pt_meta() inside
mm_pt_refresh_absent_prot() computes a pfn from that wild address that does not satisfy
pfn_valid(), so it silently does nothing; the per-PTE state therefore keeps the old
permissions while v->pte_flags at the end of the loop is updated to the new permissions as
usual; and the status demand fault path then installs a frame from the stale state, so the
PTE and the VMA permissions diverge.

The fix is that with no leaf table there is no metadata and therefore no state to refresh,
so it is simply skipped:

    if (pte) { int idx = arch_pt_vpn(va, 0);
               mm_pt_refresh_absent_prot(pte - idx, idx, ptef); }

Verified on x86_64 with CONFIG_ANON_PROV_DEFAULT=4096:

    before: UBSAN=35, mm_stress FATAL(signal=11, pc=0x1e2e2)
    after:  UBSAN=2,  mm_stress FATAL(signal=11, pc=0x1e2e2)

UBSAN dropping from 35 to 2 proves that this NULL pointer arithmetic existed and has been
removed.  The crash is unchanged and pc has not moved by a single digit, so the causal
chain from 10.37, stale state leading to installing the old permissions leading to a
PTE/VMA divergence leading to the fault, is disproved.  It is a correlate on the symptom
chain rather than the cause, or at least not the only cause.  The PTE/VMA permission
divergence is still real and still a genuine inconsistency, but the mechanism producing it
is something else.

This is an honest "fixed a real defect but did not fix the crash" change.  It is kept
because that NULL pointer arithmetic is unambiguous UB and deserves fixing whether or not
it is what caused this crash.

The x86_64 crash is still not located.  Ruled out so far: the permission bit set (identical
byte for byte before and after the 10.36 refactor), PTE_U (already solved on riscv64),
state and PTE divergence (zero readback assertion violations), state outliving the VMA
(zero orphan assertion hits), and mprotect's NULL pointer arithmetic (fixed here, crash
unchanged).  What still holds from the scene: after 12 status path hits on x86_64,
mm_stress crashes in __copy_tls+0x72 writing to the thread block, the faulting PTE is read
only while its VMA is writable, and the shutdown audit is all 0.

The forensics for the next step, since further guessing has a low marginal value and the
approach has to become systematic: at the address where __copy_tls faults, dump together
who installed the page, the permissions it was installed with, and the permissions of the
corresponding VMA, meaning the page table entry, the VMA, and the class/prot bytes in
pt_meta, so that a single pass decides whether the status path installed it wrong, mprotect
changed it wrong, or something else did.

The riscv64 side is unaffected: 5 architectures plus 2 NOMMU variants build, all three
gates pass, and the audit is at 0.
e932d1c8ba8b6e99d7539b6380aa5ae199390266:
docs(roadmap): find that mprotect updates one PTE but the whole VMA

Following the forensics method from 10.38, the page table entry, the VMA and the per-PTE
status were dumped together on the "PTE present but the access was refused" branch, once.
The diagnostic code has since been removed:

    [MM-PERM] va=f9374f20 acc=1 pte=800000007eecb425 leaf=1 U=1 W=0
              vstart=f9354000 vend=f9375000 vflags=13 vpte=467
              cls=2 prot=1

That is a qualitative result.  Reading the three columns side by side: the PTE
(flags=0x425) has read but no write, the per-PTE status (cls=2 ANON_MAPPED, prot=1=R) has
read but no write, and the VMA (vpte=0x467) has both.  So the PTE and the status agree with
each other, both read only, and only the VMA is writable.  The problem is therefore not
"who installed this one page wrong" but "someone made the VMA writable without changing
the PTE along with it".  acc=1 is a write access, on the path of __copy_tls writing to the
thread block, and it is correctly refused, giving a SIGSEGV.

The mechanism is in mprotect's page loop in kernel/mm/mprotect.c.  The loop body only
modifies the single leaf entry returned by pt_lookup_leaf() and then does
va = base + size once, which skips all of that leaf's entries.  As long as such a large
leaf falls entirely inside the VMA, so that no downgrade is triggered, none of the entries
in between is changed, while v->pte_flags outside the loop has already changed the
permissions of the whole VMA.  The result is exactly the shape observed: the VMA is
writable and the skipped pages are still read only.

It does not reproduce on riscv64, where mm_stress's mprotect range does not happen to
enclose an un-downgraded large leaf, or where the leaf geometry differs, so every page
reaches the *pte update step.

The fix, not done yet, has to handle the large leaf as well: the loop must walk every entry
inside that leaf instead of only the first one.  The minimal safe version is to turn
va = base + size into va += PAGE_SIZE, or to downgrade first and go page by page whenever
level > 0 and the leaf lies entirely inside the VMA.  The current "do not downgrade unless
it crosses a boundary" optimization is the source of the hole.

This is the fourth lesson in this project about verifying on only one architecture or one
path.  The first three were treating a hot page as a fault (10.8), treating a script bug as
a kernel regression (10.15), and treating riscv64's PTE semantics as universal
(10.33/10.36).  What they share is passing off single platform, single path success as
correctness.

The safe state right now: the riscv64 side is unaffected, with 5 architectures plus 2
NOMMU building, three gates passing, the audit at 0 and 2836 status path faults working.
The x86_64 crash is still unfixed, but it is now pinned to a definite code defect rather
than a vague symptom.
7ff00fe671062bda947e5ef5b4d750e5e573d920:
fix(mm): split large leaves before applying mprotect

A real defect, but it does not fix the x86_64 crash.

The mechanism found in 10.39 is that the page loop only changes the single leaf entry
returned by pt_lookup_leaf() and then does va = base + size once, skipping all of that
leaf's entries, while v->pte_flags outside the loop changes the permissions of the whole
VMA.  The original downgrade condition only triggered when a large leaf crossed the VMA
boundary, so a large leaf lying entirely inside the VMA was never split and every page but
the first one kept its old permissions.

The fix is to downgrade first whenever level > 0, which makes size a single page so that
the va = base + size advance is correct.

Verified on x86_64 with CONFIG_ANON_PROV_DEFAULT=4096:

    before: FATAL, counters 53/12, UBSAN 2
    after:  FATAL, counters 53/12, UBSAN 2

The crash is unchanged and not one counter has moved, so the causal chain from 10.39,
skipped entries leading to a VMA/PTE divergence leading to the fault, is disproved.  The
PTE/VMA permission divergence is real, but it does not come from this skipping.

This is an honest "fixed a real defect but did not fix the crash" change, of the same kind
as 10.38: skipping entries is an unambiguous logic error that deserves fixing regardless of
whether it is the root cause, and it is not the root cause of this crash.

The x86_64 investigation stops here, because it has now been wrong four times in a row:
1) the permission bit set is wrong, missing PTE_LEAF and PTE_NX, and the crash is identical
byte for byte before and after the 10.36 refactor; 2) PTE_U is missing, and fixing it
makes riscv64 completely healthy (10.33); 3) the state was not refreshed so the old
permissions were installed, through the NULL pointer arithmetic, and fixing it drops UBSAN
from 35 to 2 while the crash stays (10.38); 4) mprotect skips the rest of a large leaf, and
fixing it does not move a single counter (this change).

What is still certain, all of it from experiment: the status path really does run 12 times
on x86_64 before the crash, while riscv64 runs it 2836 times with no problem; the scene is
a write access landing on a read only PTE whose per-PTE status is also read only
(cls=2 ANON_MAPPED, prot=1), with only the VMA writable (vpte=0x467); the shutdown audit
is all 0 including safe=0, so the metadata and the PTE have not diverged; and it is
unrelated to concurrency, since -smp 1 crashes the same, and unrelated to pre-provisioning
itself, since with the status path inert and pre-provisioning on it is a PASS.

So of the PTE, the per-PTE status and the VMA, two agree and one, the VMA, differs.  The
first two fixes touched the state refresh and the entry walk respectively, and neither
changed that shape, which means whatever produced the difference is not in those two
places.  If the investigation continues, the next step is to add assertions at every place
that writes a VMA pte_flags, confirming alongside any place that makes a VMA writable that
the corresponding leaf has been updated, and to work backwards from "who changed the VMA"
rather than guessing from the PTE side again.

The safe state right now: the riscv64 functional and performance conclusions are completely
unaffected, with 5 architectures plus 2 NOMMU variants building, all three gates passing,
the audit at 0, 2836 status path faults working, and pre-provisioning performance neutral
both on and off (10.34).  All x86_64 investigation runs under
EXTRA_CFLAGS=-DCONFIG_ANON_PROV_DEFAULT=4096.

28b5acf7c441dc6363bbb10e5d0b448526505b68:
test(mm): distinguish declined from refreshed and add the MM-DIV probe

The experiment designed in section 10.48 hit.  mm_pt_refresh_absent_prot() now distinguishes
"did not flush" from "flushed", returning 1 to mean declined, and mprotect reports [MM-DIV]
when it widens to RW but the flush is declined.

The observation:

    [MM-DIV] widened v[158d51000,158d72000) to RW but status NOT refreshed at va=158d51000
             (pte=0) ... 33 times in total, one per page
    SIGSEGV: pid=6 code=14 sepc=0x1e2e2 stval=0x158d71f20 abi=0
    vma_file=/bin/mm_stress
    FATAL: pid=6 signal=11 pc=0x1e2e2 comm=mm_stress path=/bin/mm_stress

The correlation is solid, not a coincidence.  stval=0x158d71f20 falls inside
v[0x158d51000,0x158d72000) at offset 0x20f20, which is page 32 of 33, the very last page of
that VMA, and it lines up with the last [MM-DIV] at va=158d71000.  There are exactly 33
[MM-DIV] lines, one per address, and pte=0 means there was not even a leaf table at the
time.  code=14 maps to the x86_64 error code 0xE, present plus write plus user, so "the
page is mapped and the access is a write".  And vma_file=/bin/mm_stress, so this VMA is the
executable's own file mapping, not the heap and not brk.

That refutes the premise the previous eight investigations rested on.  For a file backed
private VMA, mprotect deliberately leaves the PTE read only and sets PTE_COW, at
mprotect.c:120-133 with the comment "Keep the canonical cache page read-only. The first store
will copy it in handle_cow_fault()."  So "a read only PTE under a writable VMA" is the
correct state by design for such a VMA, with handle_cow_fault() finishing the job on the
first write.  The 10.45a guard, which reports when a writable VMA contains a mapped read
only page, was therefore measuring the wrong thing: for a file private COW range this is
exactly what should happen and the guard ought to stay silent.  Reading its silence as
"mprotect is not involved" mistook behaviour that matches the design for a defect, and the
reasoning built on that conclusion in 10.47 and 10.48 is invalidated along with it.

The cls=2 (MM_ST_ANON_MAPPED) read at the scene in 10.39 is also an artifact:
mm_pt_query() synthesises MM_ST_ANON_MAPPED when MM_ST_GET_CLASS(byte)==MM_ST_INVALID
(pt.c:1097), so a file page with no status record reads back as ANON_MAPPED.  The judgement
"this is an anonymous page" was fabricated by the query function from the start.

The real problem is therefore one sentence: the write fault landed on the last page of a
file private COW range and handle_cow_fault() did not take over, turning straight into a
fatal SIGSEGV.  That is a different class from the previous eight hypotheses: not "who broke
the permissions" but "the COW finishing path was never reached".

And the pte=0 in the [MM-DIV] lines is the key clue.  When mprotect ran this stretch, these
pages did not even have a leaf table yet, so mprotect's already mapped branch, which contains
the PTE_COW code above, never ran even once.  These pages were installed later by the fault
path.  So the likely real defect is that PTE_COW is only set in mprotect's already mapped
branch, while a file private page first installed by the fault path carries no COW mark, so
its first write never reaches handle_cow_fault() and goes straight to fatal.

The next step is single pointed and verifiable: read the trigger conditions of
handle_cow_fault() and find out what it uses to recognise a write fault that needs COW,
whether it looks at the PTE_COW bit or at the VMA's VM_FILE && !VM_SHARED, then check
whether the path that installs a file private page on a fault sets PTE_COW.  If it does not,
add it, which is both the minimal fix and the explanation for why the first eight were all
wrong: they were all asking where the read only PTE came from, when the answer is that it was
always supposed to be read only and what is wrong is that it never gets its COW finishing
pass.

The diagnostics here are temporary instrumentation and should be removed from
kernel/mm/pt.c and kernel/mm/mprotect.c once the conclusion is settled.

The riscv64 side is completely unaffected: 5 architectures plus 2 NOMMU variants build, all
three gates pass, the shutdown audit is all 0 including safe=0, 2836 status path faults
work, and pre-provisioning is performance neutral both on and off (10.34).
9280734ab9fd8ac71d58f4e381d77df9a21a0560:
docs(roadmap): explain why private file faults install read-only pages without PTE_COW

Three pieces of code together close the loop.

First, the faulting page's PTE is 0x425 while PTE_COW = 1UL << 9 = 0x200
(x86_64/include/page_table.h:26), and 0x425 & 0x200 == 0, so PTE_COW is not set.  The page
is present, user, leaf and read only.

Second, handle_cow_fault_locked() recognises only two situations, from fault.c:150:

    if (*pte & PTE_COW) { ... copy ... }
    if (*pte & PTE_W)    { ... add PTE_D only ... }
    return -1;                       /* neither COW nor writable -> give up */

Our page has neither PTE_COW nor PTE_W, so it falls through to return -1, no one takes over
the write fault and it goes straight to fatal.  That matches the observation exactly, with
code=14 giving the error code 0xE, present plus write plus user, so the page really is there
and it really is a write.

concept of COW at all.  It memcpy's a private copy and then installs the page with

moment handle_cow_fault() is triggered.  What was missing was never "who makes it writable"

0bf1403e91ed657af007ed89ad4753720d211502:
docs(mm): record the first evidence-backed root cause of the status bug

Instrumented every install inside mm_cursor_replace() with an [MM-INS] va= cls= flags= W= cow=
line.  One run, 29 installs: 28 of them all carry flags=467 W=1 cow=0, and only the last one
is va=abd17000 cls=2 flags=425 W=0 cow=0.  The page base of the SIGSEGV, stval=0xabd17f20, is
0xabd17000, so the last install record is the page that faulted.

The trace nails down three things at once.

(1) It is not a PTE_COW problem.  The page has cow=0 and W=0, but the root cause is that the
    permission bits themselves are missing PTE_W: all 28 sibling pages of the same VMA were
    installed with flags=0x467, which includes PTE_W, and only this one with 0x425.  Since
    0x467 & ~0x425 == 0x42, the only difference is PTE_W (0x2) and 0x40.  The whole PTE_COW
    thread of investigation in 10.50/10.51 was an unrelated branch, an artifact of being
    misled by the return -1 in handle_cow_fault().

(2) It was installed by the status path (per-PTE status), not the VMA path.  The status path is
    the only place in the tree that takes permissions from something other than the VMA: it
    loops the recorded status byte back into PTE permissions (fault.c:968-980, prot ->
    mm_prot_to_pte_flags(prot)).  mm_prot_to_pte_flags(1), read-only, is exactly 0x425.  The
    other 28 pages were all installed by the VMA path with 0x467.  mm_fault_from_status=12 is
    consistent with the one and only W=0 install coming from the status byte.  A strict
    confirmation only needs an independent marker in the status path, at the cost of one run.

(3) So the real fork is this: the per-PTE status for this page records read-only, while the VMA
    it lives in is writable.  The status path faithfully installed a read-only page from the
    status.  It is not at fault; the status is.

The problem therefore collapses into a single one, with a single candidate: who turned this
page's status into read-only without updating the VMA?  Only one function in the tree writes
status permissions, mm_pt_refresh_absent_prot() (pt.c:857), and it is called only from mprotect's
"page not yet mapped" branch.  mprotect then unconditionally runs v->pte_flags =
mm_pte_flags_apply_prot(...) after the same branch.  Both get the same ptef, so a single mprotect
cannot fork; the fork can only come from two mprotects: the first flushes the status to
read-only, the second widens the VMA back to writable but fails to refresh the status.  It has two
ready-made "cannot flush" paths, and [MM-DIV] has already proven one of them happened 33 times
in this run (pte=0, that is pt_lookup_leaf returned NULL and the call site skipped the refresh
entirely):

  - pte == NULL, so the call site's if (pte) is false and the refresh is never called
    (mprotect.c:162-165)
  - cls != MM_ST_ANON_VIRT, so the refresh function itself returns 1 early (pt.c:867)

Fix direction (the evidence is sufficient, but it is not done in this round): the real problem is
that there is no consistency constraint between the status and the VMA.  The status path trusts
the status byte to the point of never consulting the VMA, and the status byte is only refreshed
by mprotect on a fault, where a failed refresh reports nothing.  Two candidate fixes:

  - A (symptomatic, minimal): when mprotect widens a page to writable but fails to refresh the
    status, do not just kerr.  Rewrite the page's status to the VMA's permission, or set the
    status to INVALID so the next fault falls back to the VMA path.  Semantically this is "the
    VMA is authoritative and the status is only a cache", which matches Linux.
  - B (root cause): have the status path cross-check against the VMA on an ANON_VIRT hit and
    fall back to the VMA path when they disagree.  The cost is one extra VMA lookup per status
    fault, which contradicts the paper's "no VMA lookup" claim and conflicts with the project
    goal.  Not recommended.

A is recommended: it accepts the "VMA authoritative, status is a cache" convention that should
have held from the start, and turns today's silent fork into an impossible one.

Follow-up that was not done, to be done first next time, at negligible cost:

  1. Add an independent marker to the status path (around fault.c:993) to confirm that the
     0x425 install really came from it.
  2. Remove all TEMP instrumentation: pt.c ([MM-INS], declined distinction), mprotect.c
     ([MM-DIV]), fault.c ([MM-FP]).  All three are hot-path kerr and must go once the fix
     verifies.
  3. Re-run after applying A.  Expected: x86_64 mm_stress PASS, mm_anon_provisioned=53,
     mm_fault_from_status>0, MM-ASM all 0; then re-check the three riscv64 gates and the
     five-arch build.

riscv64 is completely unaffected: the 5 arch plus 2 NOMMU variants build, all three gates pass,
the shutdown audit is all 0 including safe=0, the status path's 2836 faults behave normally, and
the pre-marking on/off performance is neutral (10.34).

10.61 explicitly noted that having no targeted regression test is this fix's weak point.  The test
is written, as test_uffd_double_registration() in syscall_ext.c: register the same page once on
each of two uffds, unregister one of them, trigger a read fault from another thread, check that it
is still parked with read() returning UFFD_EVENT_PAGEFAULT, resolve it with UFFDIO_COPY on the
surviving uffd, and verify the contents.  If unregister still cleared the range in one shot, the
page would be satisfied in place by the status fault path, read() would never return, and the test
would hang and fail.

The test itself passes: two runs printed no uffd2 ... failure line, and pthread_join returned
normally, so park, resolve and content verification are all working.

But it exposed a separate pre-existing problem.  With the test enabled, a later uffd-unrelated test
failed:

  MM_STRESS: evict start
  [BCACHE] no evictable page page=5772 valid=2000 dirty=1879 referenced=0 total_refs=0 max_refs=0
  MM_STRESS: evict-mmap start
  MM_STRESS: FAIL evict-mmap-verify-mapped errno=17      <-- 17 = EEXIST

evict-mmap-verify-mapped asserts that a hinted mmap succeeds, and EEXIST means the hint address was
already taken.  An isolation experiment confirmed the causality: with the new test enabled,
MM_STRESS fails on evict-mmap-verify-mapped with errno=17; with MM_SKIP_UFFD2=1, skipping the new
test, it
passes.  So this is not a defect of the new test, it is that evict-mmap is sensitive to address
space layout and page cache state: the new test creates one more thread and does a few more
mmap/munmap calls, which is enough to make evict-mmap's hint address collide.  The preceding
[BCACHE] no evictable page line also hints that the reclaim path was already under pressure at that
moment.

Decision: do not land the test in this round.  The default mm_stress must not go red, and
committing a test that makes an existing test fail is worse than not having the test.  syscall_ext.c
has been reverted to the state of 72117795 with git checkout, the working tree is clean and the
build has 0 errors.  The per-page UFFD clear itself has been merged and verified (10.61); the only
thing missing is the targeted case.

The next round's explicit tasks, in order:

1. First find out why evict-mmap-verify-mapped uses a hint address and why it can get EEXIST.  That
   is itself an existing defect, unrelated to UFFD, and should be fixed on its own rather than
   worked around by a new test.
2. Then land test_uffd_double_registration(), reusing this implementation directly: double
   registration, unregister one, assert the other still receives a fault, resolve with COPY,
   verify contents, and confirm on landing that it no longer has a layout coupling to evict-mmap.

Methodological note: this cycle of "wrote a test, the test passed, something else turned out to be
broken" is the other face of the same lesson as the ten investigations of 10.39 to 10.56.  A new
test that changes address space state is enough to wake a previously masked defect.  A passing test
does not mean the surroundings are fine, and a failing test is not necessarily the test's own fault.
8647149335d4b0ed2a5e855224f26f5274971656:
docs(roadmap): correct the 10.62 misreading it is data loss not an address clash

10.62 read `MM_STRESS: FAIL evict-mmap-verify-mapped errno=17` as "a hinted mmap returned EEXIST"
and set the next round's task to "investigate the hint address collision".  That reading is wrong.

The fail() at user/cmds/stress/mm_stress.c:15 takes only a string and prints whatever errno
happens to be left in the environment:

    static int fail(const char *what)
    {
        printf("MM_STRESS: FAIL %s errno=%d
", what, errno);
        return 1;
    }

and this call site is return fail("evict-mmap-verify-mapped"); (mm_stress.c:1416), which passes no
errno.  So the errno=17, EEXIST, is a leftover from some earlier unrelated syscall and has nothing
to do with the failure.  The whole causal chain 10.62 built on it, "the hint address was taken", is
void.

The real nature of the failure: the loop at mm_stress.c:1404-1416 is a page-by-page content
verification.  It writes a predictable pattern page by page into a file mapping, fsync(fd_b), then
reads it back through the mapping and compares byte by byte.  A mismatch means the mapping's
contents differ from what was just written, that is data loss or corruption.  That is much more
serious than the "address clash" of 10.62: it is not that the mapping could not be created, it is
that data already written comes back changed, and it happens under memory pressure with reclaim in
play.  The message right before it points at the reclaim side:

    [BCACHE] no evictable page page=5772 valid=2000 dirty=1879 referenced=0 total_refs=0 max_refs=0

valid=2000, dirty=1879, and yet "no evictable page": at a moment when there should obviously be
evictable pages, the reclaim path reports finding no candidates.  The mapping's contents are
inconsistent right after that.

Established so far: the failure is a data inconsistency, not a failed syscall; the errno field has
no diagnostic value here; the failure occurs under the combination of file mapping, memory pressure
and reclaim; and the reclaim side had just reported finding no evictable page.  Not established,
and not investigated this round: the exact mmap flags of that mapping, MAP_SHARED or MAP_PRIVATE
and whether MAP_NORESERVE was set; whether the content is lost in dirty writeback, in reclaim, or
in remap; and whether the "no evictable page" verdict itself is simply wrong, for example whether
referenced=0 total_refs=0 means the reference accounting is not maintained on the drop path.

The next round's tasks are corrected accordingly, replacing item 1 of 10.62:

1. Read the mmap call in the evict-mmap test and confirm the mapping type.
2. Trace back along the conditions of [BCACHE] no evictable page and find out why valid=2000 is
   still judged as having nothing to evict.
3. Then follow with item 2 of 10.62, landing the UFFD double-registration test.

This also exposes a design problem in fail(): it prints errno unconditionally, so a great many
assertion failures that have nothing to do with errno carry a misleading errno string.  This time it
nearly sent the whole investigation down the wrong path, since a full section was spent believing
the EEXIST.  Either it should distinguish a syscall failure from an assertion failure, or it
should not print errno for assertion failures at all.  That is a small defect worth fixing on its
own.

the MAP_SHARED mapping reads back content that does not match.  The defect was always there, the
default test sequence just did not apply enough pressure to reach it.

makes evict-mmap fail", is wrong and is corrected here: it was not a perturbed address layout, it
was applied memory pressure.  The misleading EEXIST errno is void along with it, see 10.63.

55bf71e560c72d4b90fc6c8fda7e01cb8001707d:
fix(mm_stress): stop printing the environments errno in fail

The defect recorded at the end of 10.63, that fail() prints errno unconditionally, is fixed here.

fail() in user/cmds/stress/mm_stress.c was:

    static int fail(const char *what)
    {
        printf("MM_STRESS: FAIL %s errno=%d
", what, errno);
        return 1;
    }

All 171 call sites pass a single argument, and the overwhelming majority of them,
fail("mseal-mmap"), fail("mseal-seal"), fail("mseal-mprotect") and the rest, are assertions or
ret < 0 checks with
nothing to do with errno.  So every such failure carried a leftover errno from the environment that
was unrelated to the cause.

It has already caused concrete misdirection, in 10.62 and 10.63: a content comparison failure was
printed as FAIL evict-mmap-verify-mapped errno=17, EEXIST, and a full section was spent chasing a
hint address collision that did not exist, while the real cause was page cache reclaim failure
under memory pressure.  By contrast syscall_ext.c's own fail(what, e) takes two arguments, passes
errno explicitly, and has 188 call sites with none of this problem, so two different fail
semantics in one tree contributed to the confusion.

The change is that fail() no longer prints errno:

    static int fail(const char *what)
    {
        printf("MM_STRESS: FAIL %s\n", what);
        return 1;
    }

On the trade-off: a fail_ex(what, e) was deliberately not added with all 171 call sites classified
and migrated one by one.  That would require judging at each site whether the failure really comes
from a syscall, which is an independent change needing point-by-point review, and at the end of a
round, guessing at the classification is worse than not doing it, since turning a site that should
report an error into one that does not is also wrong.  The certain harm, the false signal, is
removed first.  The few sites that genuinely need errno should pass it explicitly when they are
next modified rather than depending on a leftover environment value.  The convention is written
down in the comment.

Verification: x86_64/KVM ON arm mm_stress PASS, 0 FAIL, 0 FATAL, no evictable page = 0, MM-ASM
audit all 0; build with 0 errors and no unused-function warnings.

    normal.
  - the mark survives: the !mm_cursor_safe_test(... MM_SAFE_UFFD) at fault.c:974 is false, so the
    status path is skipped and it falls back to the VMA path, which also does not park and also
    installs the frame from the VMA.

Neither case parks, and both complete the fault correctly, because at that point the page really
is covered by no remaining registration, so "not parked" is the correct behaviour anyway.  The only
difference is speed: a surviving mark means this page can never take the per-PTE status fast path
again, costing one extra VMA lookup per fault, which is a performance problem and not a correctness
one.  So the assertion "the page should no longer be parked" is always true and has no power to
discriminate.

There is exactly one direction that can actually fail, and it is already covered: the mark being
over-cleared, meaning a page still covered by another registration had its mark cleared because
someone else unregistered, so a fault that should have been parked was not and the handler never
receives the event.  That is precisely the side test_uffd_double_registration() asserts, unregister
one side and check the other still gets UFFD_EVENT_PAGEFAULT, and it has really run and passed on
both platforms' ON-arm builds.

One more thing: mm_pt_note_absent() at pt.c:312-323 clears MM_SAFE_MASK along with the class, and
its comment gives the reason, otherwise a reused slot would inherit stale UFFD/NO_FA flags.  So
the mark cannot outlive the mapping it describes, and cross-mapping leakage cannot happen either.

Conclusion: the fix and the test coverage for UFFD over-clearing are complete.  The dangerous
direction has an assertion and it passes, the harmless direction has no assertion and also has no
failure mode.

aa2e7eacfcde71c53f1539d7c36a3da2f3a0977a:
docs(roadmap): identify mm->lock removal as the next status-fault step

Current state verified: kernel/mm/fault.c takes spin_lock(&mm->lock) at line 800 and only releases
it at line 1119, and the status fault path that never touches the VMA, lines 963 to 1010, sits
inside that interval.  So the paper's central claim, that a fault does not take the VMA lock, is
not implemented yet: the status path really does not consult the VMA, but it still runs under the
mm-wide lock, so all concurrent faults on multiple cores and threads queue on mm->lock.  That is
consistent with the "performance neutral" measured in 10.33: the saving from skipping the VMA
lookup is not obtained, because the cost of that lock is still there.

The prerequisite is now understood: the blocker is a data race on mm->rss.

  - mm->rss is a plain size_t (vm.h:227), not atomic.
  - fault.c has 12 rss++ / rss += sites, cow.c has 3 more.
  - The status path itself does mm->rss++ (around fault.c:1010), and it has to do so without
    holding mm->lock.
  - More importantly the read side: cg_mem.c:125 reads t->mm->rss when OOM picks a victim, and
    that code holds only proc_lock, not mm->lock:

        uint64_t pflags = spin_lock_irqsave(&proc_lock);
        ...
        size_t task_rss = t->mm ? t->mm->rss : 0;
        int score = (int)task_rss + t->policy.oom_score_adj;

    That is already a potential data race, a reader under proc_lock and a writer under mm->lock
    which do not exclude each other.  It only holds together today because every writer happens to
    be under mm->lock and the OOM path happens not to run concurrently.  Moving the status path out
    of mm->lock turns it into a real bug immediately.

The order is therefore fixed and cannot be skipped:

1. First make mm->rss atomic and consistently readable, with __atomic_add_fetch and friends, and
   have OOM's read side pick up a consistent value with acquire semantics.  This step is a fix for
   an existing latent hazard in its own right and should be done even without the status path
   change.
2. Then move the status path's critical section from mm->lock to underneath the page table cursor
   lock.  The design has promise here: the status path only touches per-PTE metadata and PT
   entries, which mm_addrspace_lock()'s PT page lock protects, and pt.h:29-43 states exactly that
   contract.  It needs no VMA lock because by design it does not read the VMA list.  What needs
   care is concurrency with munmap and mremap tearing down page tables.  The read-side token in
   mm_pt_read_enter() must cover everything from "decide ANON_VIRT" to "write the PT entry",
   otherwise an already-torn-down leaf could be written back while someone else is unmapping it,
   which is the shape of the PT page UAF in 10.29.
3. Only then does performance verification become legitimate.  mmap-pf can only be re-measured
   after this step, and it must be measured in an environment where the noise can be reduced
   (10.73), otherwise the number is still noise.

What is explicitly not going to be done:

  - No pseudo-lock-free tricks such as a per-mm sequence number in the status path, added to look
    lock-free.  10.30 just proved that a per-metadata MCS node already brings the cursor round-trip
    cost down by an order of magnitude, which says the bottleneck is lock scalability, not the mere
    existence of a lock.
  - No attempt to prove a gain with the current benchmark on a shared host, since 10.72 and 10.73
    have shown it cannot be measured.

Conclusion: this is the most worthwhile engineering step available, and step 1, making rss atomic,
has independent value, low risk, and can be done first.  But it is a multi-stage change, and this
round's context is not enough to complete step 2 safely, which is recutting the critical section
under the page table cursor lock and covering the read-side token against table teardown
concurrency, and then to verify it credibly.  So it stops here, per the discipline established in
10.57, rather than changing things on a guess.
e56ee8d43e6131830af60e57e327bfdfac178cd3:
docs(roadmap): correct the 10.74 underestimate of the rss atomicisation risk

10.74 wrote that step 1, making rss atomic, has independent value, low risk and can be done first.
Counting the sites before starting shows that "low risk" is an underestimate, corrected here to
match reality.

There are 52 `->rss` sites in the whole tree, across 10 files.  The point is that they are not all
the same shape.

(a) Plain add and subtract, doable with a single atomic operation, low risk.  fault.c has 12 sites,
    mm->rss++, t->mm->rss++, t->mm->rss += PMD_PAGE_COUNT and t->mm->rss += mapped, elf.c has
    2, vm.c 1, cow.c 4, mremap.c 1.

(b) Read-modify-write with a clamp, and this is the hard part where a plain atomic operation would
    be wrong:

        mm->rss = (mm->rss > pages) ? mm->rss - pages : 0;   /* munmap.c:125,246 madvise.c:71,91 */
        mm->rss = mm->rss ? mm->rss - 1 : 0;                 /* oom.c:159 */

    These 5 sites must become a CAS loop to be both atomic and underflow-free:

        size_t cur = __atomic_load_n(&mm->rss_atomic, __ATOMIC_RELAXED);
        for (;;) {
            size_t next = cur > pages ? cur - pages : 0;
            if (__atomic_compare_exchange_n(&mm->rss_atomic, &cur, next, 1,
                                            __ATOMIC_RELAXED, __ATOMIC_RELAXED))
                return;
        }

    Taking the shortcut of a __atomic_sub_fetch followed by a clamp introduces an underflow window
    that did not exist before, where a reader has already computed a smaller value and another
    thread subtracts again.  And rss feeds OOM victim selection directly, cg_mem.c:125 as
    10.74 notes, so an underflow makes OOM pick the wrong victim.  That is a real regression in the
    safety direction, not a style question.

(c) Initialisation and zeroing: vm.c:514,709, proc.c:605, exec.c:640, where a release store is
    enough.

(d) Cross-lock reads: fork.c:267, which prints under proc_lock, and cg_mem.c:125, OOM victim
    selection, also under proc_lock.  Both must read a consistent value with acquire semantics,
    otherwise all that changes is trading a non-atomic race for an atomic but torn one.

So the real shape of step 1 is: add a set of helpers, mm_rss_add, mm_rss_sub_clamped, mm_rss_set
and mm_rss_get, rename the field so the compiler is forced to expose all 52 sites, rewrite each
site according to (a), (b), (c) or (d), then verify across all architectures and all gates.

This should be a separate change with a reviewer rather than something slipped in at the end of a
performance session.  The reason is that it touches the safety-critical path that picks OOM
victims and needs correctness verification across 10 files, and in an environment with no slack to
check each one line by line, the risk is out of proportion to the benefit.

It is still worth doing and it is still step 1, because it fixes a race hazard that already exists,
a writer under mm->lock and the OOM reader under proc_lock with no mutual exclusion, and it is only
not yet a real bug because every writer happens to hold mm->lock.  The order is unchanged: first
(d) plus rss atomicisation, then move the status path out of mm->lock, and only then performance.

                            (struct is 120 bytes)

so the test detects exactly the two defects it was written for, rather than
just passing.

While enumerating the musl-reachable shmctl commands I found SHM_STAT (13)
unhandled: musl defines it, and the kernel fell through to `return 0` without
writing the buffer, the same silent-underscore shape as the msgctl tail.
Now handled alongside IPC_STAT and SHM_STAT_ANY. This also removes the last
musl-reachable shmctl command that returned success without doing anything --
except IPC_SET, which is a real gap but not a one-liner: sysv_shm_t does not
track uid, gid or mode at all, and the IPC_STAT reply hardcodes 0/0666, so
supporting IPC_SET means first deciding what ownership A20OS claims to
enforce. Left alone deliberately rather than half-implemented.

smoke_cases.py regenerates byte-identical: smoke_extract.py only extracts
targets that call tools/smoke.py, and this one is raw shell like the existing
smoke-fsync-durability, so it is outside both directions the audit checks.
check-smoke-cases still reports 73 reachable cases, no orphans.

Four architectures build, user_apps build for riscv64 and x86_64, the 20
tracked source gates hold at the 16/4 baseline, and the build-matrix and
generator gates pass.
9d5ea534776c4017f037967a0518a4ca02f29d97:
fix(mm.ipc.fs): fix the futex cross-process wake loss and unblock riscv32

futex: task_spawn() gives the child a fresh, independently ASLR-randomised
mm, so a MAP_SHARED futex word is the same physical page under two different
virtual addresses.  The bucket index came from the caller's virtual address,
so a home-bucket-only search could never observe the peer and the wake was
lost.  On a miss, and only when the caller supplied a physical key (a SHARED
futex), sweep the remaining buckets with the unchanged match predicate.
PRIVATE futxes pass pkey == 0 and short-circuit, so cargo's jobserver and
libc locks pay nothing.  Applied to futex_wake, futex_requeue and
futex_wake_op, since a condvar requeue has the same defect.

shmring: spawn_child() returned the raw task handle, so the channel phase's
"!= A20_OK" check read its own success as failure and that phase had never
run.  Normalise to A20_OK, matching the spawn helper in test_native_debug.c,
and report which stage rejected the child when one does.

mempolicy: mempolicy_set() stored the policy mode in oom_score_adj and
zeroed thp_disabled.  Both are live knobs: oom_score_adj feeds the OOM
killer's victim score and is writable via /proc/<pid>/oom_score_adj, so any
set_mempolicy() silently changed which process got killed under memory
pressure.  The node mask was also discarded and get_mempolicy fabricated
node 0 regardless.  Record both in dedicated fields and reject a mask
naming a node A20OS does not have.

kexec: kexec_load_segments() read struct kexec_segment with a hardcoded
LP64 8-byte stride, so on ILP32 it misread every field.  Read it with the
target's own field widths.

shm_info: the size assert was hardcoded to the LP64 48 bytes; derive it
from the target (24 on ILP32, per musl's riscv32 header).

msqid_ds: the ILP32 layout cannot match musl's.  This struct carries the
IPC64 perm and native-width long timestamps (80 bytes), while musl's
ILP32 struct msqid_ds is 112 bytes because it uses a native ipc_perm and a
64-bit time_t.  Keep the size check for LP64 and report -EOPNOTSUPP on
ILP32 rather than write a reply the caller would read at wrong offsets.

abi: narrow ten uint64-to-pointer casts through uintptr_t, matching the
existing idiom, so riscv32 builds again.

kxan: add the section symbols the W^X split needs to both linker scripts.
Document that loongarch64 is not a pending port but cannot be split via
page tables at all: its kernel space is translated by the LoongArch DMW,
which bypasses the TLB and the walk, so boot_pgdir is empty by design.

docs: drop two server-readiness items that are already done -- /proc/pressure
is a cpu/memory/io directory, and MAX_PROCS is gone.
5177e1b1eda12407db646cc134ef0be8f0b6f8b1:
feat(fs): implement FS_IOC_GETFLAGS on ext4 and refuse SETFLAGS honestly

The ext4 fops had .ioctl = NULL, so FS_IOC_GETFLAGS/SETFLAGS on an ext4
file returned -ENOTTY.  GETFLAGS now reports the inode's real on-disk
i_flags, with the ext4-internal EXT4_EXTENTS_FL bit masked out so it cannot
leak through the ABI word.  The request numbers are size-dependent (the
_IOR/_IOW encoding embeds sizeof(long)), so both the LP64 and ILP32 forms
are matched, the way TIOCGPGRP/PPC64_TIOCGPGRP already are.

SETFLAGS stays refused with -EOPNOTSUPP.  A20OS enforces none of the FS_*
mutation semantics in the write path, so storing the bits would promise
behaviour the kernel does not implement; that is the same position
fileattr.c already takes for the syscall form.

Covered by smoke-vfs-stress, which mounts ext4 at /dev/vdb: it asserts that
GETFLAGS succeeds, that EXT4_EXTENTS_FL does not appear in the result, and
that SETFLAGS is refused with EOPNOTSUPP.  The test found a real bug in the
first cut of the handler -- copy_to_user returns the byte count rather than
0, so returning it directly made a successful ioctl look like a failure to
the caller; the handler now normalises to 0, matching devfs.

never ran, and nothing in the gate output said why.

Add $(ISOFS_IMG) to the dev-build prerequisites.  Verified: dev-build now
emits isofs.img and smoke-vfs-stress goes PASS with no manual step.

d974127cd19075fde3ed645d381dee1d5be22372:
feat(net): expose socket tables, honor socket options, and add netlink writes

The stack carried no TODO markers, but four facilities reported success for
things they had not done, which the honesty policy in docs/security/hardening.md
calls worse than refusing.  Each is real now, and each has a gate written to
fail on the old behaviour.

/proc/net/{tcp,udp,unix} emitted the column header and no rows, so netstat and
ss had nothing to read.  A new socket_table.c walks the registry under
g_net_lock and the procfs renderer emits Linux-format rows.  netstat itself was
a 28-line `cat /proc/net/status` that fell through to printing a directory
listing.  Three bugs in the first cut of it were caught by running it rather
than reading it: data rows are indented, so a first-character header test ate
them too; /proc/net/route orders its hex big-endian while /proc/net/tcp does
not; and Linux numbers TCP states from one, not zero.

FIONBIO returned 0 without touching O_NONBLOCK, so a caller that set it still
blocked forever; it now goes through the same path as fcntl(F_SETFL).
FIONREAD returned -ENOTTY on a socket.  MCAST_JOIN_GROUP returned 0 without
joining.  All three are real now, and IP_TTL, IP_TOS, MSG_PEEK, MSG_TRUNC and
MSG_WAITALL are honoured.  MSG_OOB stays refused with -EOPNOTSUPP: there is no
out-of-band data path to honour it with, and saying so is the correct answer.

The uevent send discarded the caller's message and always emitted "add", so
delete and move could not be delivered.  RTM_NEWLINK, RTM_NEWADDR and
RTM_DELADDR are honoured, and refuse rather than overwrite: with one IPv4 slot
per netif a plain add of a different address is EOPNOTSUPP, because applying it
would replace the primary while answering success.

The new tests found two gaps outside the original scope.  IP_ADD_MEMBERSHIP (35)
and IP_DROP_MEMBERSHIP (36) were unimplemented although MCAST_JOIN_GROUP (42)
was, so the spelling musl programs actually use failed.  SIOCGIFINDEX called
netif_name_to_index() on netif->name, which is a two-character abbreviation
rather than a NUL-terminated name, so every interface answered index 0 while
reporting success; it now uses netif_get_index(), the numbering the netlink
path already used.

MEMP_STATS is pinned on.  It already derived to 1, so the #else stub around
a20_lwip_format_memp() was unreachable dead code, but leaving it to that
derivation turns a silent empty /proc/a20/netmem into a one-line config change.
The column it labelled "avail" is capacity and is now named size.

Covered by smoke-lwip-memp (network_suite 10 passed, 1 skipped, pool err=0),
smoke-smp-lock-contention on 4 cores (net_stress_test, no deadlock) and
check-honesty-policy.  netopt_test (41 checks) and netlink_test (29 checks) are
new and registered in network_suite; the netlink test is weighted towards
non-mutating refusals so it cannot disturb the address the rest of the suite
depends on.

Not addressed: there is still no forwarding table, so /proc/net/route holds only
the default gateway; FIONBIO on a pipe still reports success without setting
O_NONBLOCK; AF_ALG and netfilter NAT remain the documented non-goals.

c936e626e46435fa767c8003958f4e27bdc0857b:
fix(gpu): fix a capset heap disclosure and make the 3d gate falsifiable

The capset path leaked kernel heap and truncated every capset over 4 KiB.
virtio_gpu_get_capset() clamped its DMA receive to a fixed 4 KiB stack
buffer and still reported success, while drm_virtgpu_get_caps() allowed a
userspace caller to ask for 1 MiB into a kmalloc (which does not zero) and
then copied the whole requested length back out.  A caller passing
c.size = 1 MiB therefore read about 1 MiB of uninitialised kernel heap.
The transfer is now sized from the host's own GET_CAPSET_INFO answer, the
ops vtable carries an out_len so callers know how much was really written,
and only that much is copied out of a kcalloc'd buffer.  A driver-side
ceiling bounds the allocation against a bad host answer.

CONTEXT_INIT also discarded its parameters: ctx_set_params is an array of
num_params entries, but only one struct was read and then dropped, so a
client selecting capset 2 silently got capset 1's protocol with no error.
The parameters are now read as an array, and because the host addresses
capsets by index while CONTEXT_INIT names one by id, GET_CAPS resolves the
id back through GET_CAPSET_INFO rather than assuming index == id.

MODE_GETGAMMA returned success without writing its out-parameter, handing
the caller whatever was already on its own stack; it now reports a flat
ramp.

gpu3d_test submitted a 16-byte zero-filled placeholder, reported whatever
the host said as a note, and still printed PASS -- which proved only that
bytes reached the host and made the gate green whatever the host then did.
It now drives a real VIRGL_CCMD_CLEAR against a real surface, mmaps the
resource and compares every pixel, and a rejected stream is a failure.  The
command encoding is transcribed from virglrenderer 1.1.0, the renderer
QEMU loads on the test host, because two details are unrecoverable from
memory: the header also carries an 8-bit object type, and the clear colour
is four float bit patterns rather than uint32.

Because a pixel mismatch has two very different causes, the exit code is
now three-way: PASS, SKIP for a host that cannot produce a capset at all,
and FAIL when virgl is present and the pixels are simply wrong.  Otherwise
a broken host turns a false green into an equally uninformative red.

On the test host the host renderer cannot build its offscreen GL context,
so the context is born in error and every command after the failed surface
create is dropped: the stream is accepted and 4096/4096 pixels stay at the
sentinel.  That is a host fault, and the gate now says so instead of
passing.

Verified: gpu3d gate forward and reverse (both FAIL, the forward case with
the host attributed), smoke-riscv64, smoke-abi-linux, smoke-net-iface,
smoke-network-suite, check-drm-abi, four architectures, drvmod generic.
0dbdecaa924e95fab7895b85c00927563243105f:
docs(distro): record that the pbuf corruption needs IPv6 but is not fragment reassembly

The PBUF_POOL mem-underflow panic has been chased across several sessions
without isolating the writer.  This records what the last round actually
established, so the next attempt does not repeat it.

IPv6 is required: with LWIP_IPV6=0 the xfce desktop runs for nine minutes
with a NIC attached, IPv4 configured, no panic.  Both halves of the
fragmentation hypothesis are now excluded -- the transmission side had
already been tested, and LWIP_IPV6_REASS=0 for the reassembly side still
panics.  The ip6_input fix for the ignored pbuf_add_header_force() return
was implemented, measured, failed identically, and reverted; vendored lwIP
stays unpatched.

The corruption is larger than the 1-8 bytes assumed earlier.  Dumping the
guard shows all 16 bytes overwritten with two adjacent kernel virtual
addresses, which rules out a copy running a few bytes long and points at a
struct with pointer fields landing at the wrong offset.  memcpy cannot be
the writer, and pbuf_add_header_impl() does bounds-check PBUF_POOL properly.

Two dead ends are recorded because both look promising: the loopback netif
allocates PBUF_RAM, so no loopback harness can reach the pool corruption no
matter what it sends -- only the virtio-net driver RX path hands a PBUF_POOL
pbuf to the IP layer.  And QEMU's socket netdev frames a packet as a 4-byte
big-endian length followed by the frame with no flags word; adding a flags
word shifts every frame and the guest sees noise.

The IPv6-off configuration is a verified workaround, not a fix: it costs the
entire IPv6 stack.  It is deliberately not committed here.

aed279c87b055baaad2dd69d2de55ced92144e38:
fix(abi.vdso.mm): stop reporting capabilities A20OS does not have

Five Linux syscalls returned success while doing nothing, and the vDSO
getcpu fast path answered CPU 0 on every core.  Both are the worst kind of
defect here: not an error the caller can see, but a plausible wrong answer.

syslog(2) ignored every argument and returned 0.  It is now backed by the
klog ring for READ_ALL/READ_CLEAR/CLEAR/SIZE_BUFFER/CONSOLE_LEVEL/CONSOLE_OFF,
which is the same buffer /dev/kmsg serves.  CLEAR_BOOT reports
-EOPNOTSUPP because the ring keeps no boot boundary to preserve, and
OPEN/CLOSE and SIZE_UNCLEARED report -EINVAL rather than being invented.

vhangup returned 0 from an empty body.  A20OS has no tty layer: a task
records no controlling terminal and no session, so there is no state to
revoke.  It now reports -ENOSYS.  process_mrelease validated the pidfd and
returned 0 without ever touching the target process; a pidfd here stores a
bare pid and holds no task reference, so there is no detached mm to release
-- the mm is already reaped at exit.  It reports -ENOSYS too, after
diagnosing a wrong descriptor as -EBADF so that error is not masked.

sync_file_range discarded offset, nbytes and flags and flushed the whole
file.  It now rejects unknown flag bits, bounds the range against the inode
size, and reports -EOPNOTSUPP for WAIT_BEFORE alone.  The whole-file flush
stays, because the VFS exposes no range-scoped writeback; that is a
stronger guarantee than Linux asks for, and the comment says so rather than
letting the reader assume the range was honoured.

perf_event_open accepted PERF_FLAG_FD_OUTPUT and the SET_OUTPUT ioctl
accepted an fd and discarded it, so a sampling caller got success and no
data.  Both now report -EOPNOTSUPP, since there is no mmap ring to redirect
into.

The vDSO getcpu stub wrote 0 into *cpu and *node on all five architectures.
It now returns -ENOSYS, which is the one value musl's sched_getcpu wrapper
falls through to the getcpu syscall on -- any other non-zero result is a
hard error to it -- so the caller ends up with the truth by way of one
wasted trap.  A real fast path is not reachable from the vDSO: nothing in
the tree programs IA32_TSC_AUX, so RDTSCP would hand back the reset value
and bits 31:12 would decode as CPU 0 on every core, which is the lie this
commit removes.  The per-architecture reasoning is in the vdso.S headers.

MAP_SHARED_FILE_CACHE_CONTRACT was contradicted by a later comment in the
same file claiming the shared fault path had no writeback coherence.  The
contract is the true one: mm_shared_file_fault() maps the page-cache
page's own frame, and msync reaches mm_sync_shared_dirty_for_vnode() and
page_cache_writeback_vnode().  The wrong comment is corrected, and the real
gap is now stated instead -- anonymous MAP_SHARED, which has no page-cache
identity and so no writeback route, and is served by the VM_VMO path.

arm32 called mm_addrspace_lock() and the mm_cursor_* API from fault.c
outside their ARCH_HAS_PGTABLE_OPS guard, and the Makefile withholds that
macro from arm32, so it compiled with four implicit declarations and
check-arm32-bringup could not build.  Those sites now go through
fault_map_window(), which has a cursor and a non-cursor variant, and every
remaining call is inside the guard.

syscall_coverage.md claimed vhangup and process_mrelease were implemented
and summarised the table as 361 entries with two A20OS extensions;
syscall_table.def registers 366 with seven.  Both are corrected, so the
coverage table no longer asserts capabilities the code does not have.
5e417b1f5351c20bbc8d79bcf1b8bbc88c037d7d:
feat(userland): make ps list processes and ls -r recurse

ps was twelve lines that printed a column header and then called
prctl(99), which the kernel has no case for.  It listed no processes at
all, so the first command anyone runs after login showed an empty table.

It now walks /proc and parses the per-pid files the kernel already
renders.  /proc/<pid>/stat is read positionally, starting after the *last*
')' on the line rather than the first: comm is free to contain spaces and
parentheses, so only the final one is unambiguous.  Field 3 is the
single-letter state and is stepped over rather than parsed as a number.
A row that ends early is a process that died mid-render and is skipped.

TTY is always "?", and that is the honest answer: task_t carries no
controlling-terminal field, so the kernel renders field 7 as 0 for every
task.  A zero tty_nr means "no terminal", not terminal 0, and printing a
device number nobody recorded would be the same fabrication this change
exists to remove.  TIME is utime+stime over the kernel's 100 accounting
ticks per second, the same conversion getrusage applies.  CMD comes from
cmdline, which this kernel renders as the exec path alone with no argv
tail; an empty cmdline falls back to the bracketed [comm] form.

Output is sorted by pid and de-duplicated, because the kernel walks the
task list per getdents() and a task that moves during the scan can be
yielded twice.

ls accepted -R, set a flag, and then discarded it with
"(void)recursive; /* TODO */".  It exited 0 having printed nothing extra,
which is worse than rejecting the flag.  A -R walk now descends, printing
a "path:" header per directory, and collects subdirectories on the same
readdir pass that prints the entries so no directory is opened twice.
Descent uses lstat and never follows a symlink, so a link pointing at an
ancestor cannot make the walk loop; "." and ".." are the walk's own
bookkeeping and are never descended into.  The non-recursive path passes
NULL for the collector and is byte-for-byte what it always was.
7acef128a52dd2fbb5e758bf8ffb2d4585d1c5af:
test(smoke): fail the gate when a declared capability is absent

These gates reported success for capabilities that were not there.  A gate
that cannot distinguish "works" from "does not exist" is worse than no
gate, because it manufactures confidence; the honesty policy in
docs/security/hardening.md:8 says an unimplemented capability must report
"does not exist" and never fabricate output.

vfs_stress treated ENOSYS on a mount, on statx and on chroot as "skip this
subtest" and carried on, so smoke-vfs-stress could pass with all three
filesystems untested.  It now separates three outcomes.  absent means the
capability is not implemented: the subtest prints the errno that gave it
away, the count is tallied, and no PASS marker is emitted, so the gate's
expect pattern goes missing and the gate fails.  skipped means the
capability exists but this run cannot exercise it -- a drive not attached
to this QEMU invocation, no privilege -- and is counted and named in the
summary instead of being swallowed.  failed is everything else.

mount errno triage is the load-bearing part: ENOSYS means the entry point
is gone, EINVAL means vfs_mount() did not recognise the fstype, and
EOPNOTSUPP means the entry exists but refuses the medium, so all three are
absent.  ENODEV, ENOENT, EPERM and EBUSY describe the environment, not the
code, so they stay skips.  chroot reports through distinct child exit codes
so the parent can tell ENOSYS from a missing CAP_SYS_CHROOT.

Proven rather than assumed: with sys_statx forced to -ENOSYS the gate goes
red with "ABSENT statx (not implemented, errno=38)" and coverage
absent=1, and returns to green when the kernel is restored.  A gate that
cannot be made to fail is not a gate, so that round trip is the point.

network_suite printed PASS whenever failed == 0, so a run in which every
subtest skipped still reported success.  It now tallies passed, skipped,
absent and failed separately and emits FAIL rather than PASS when anything
is absent.  netfilter_test distinguished only "the drop counter did not
move", which cannot tell a missing transmit hook from a send that never
reached the wire; it now separates out_packets (the hook was reached at
all) from out_dropped (the rule fired), so a real rule-matching failure is
no longer reported as a skip.  alg_test distinguishes a missing AF_ALG
socket family from a missing algorithm.

smoke-netfilter matched NETFILTER_TEST: SKIP and exited 0, printing "data
plane not reached" as if that were a pass.  Both SKIP and ABSENT now exit
1 with the counter evidence attached.  The current tree still passes it
legitimately -- dropped=3 out_packets=3 -- which is the distinction that
was missing: a proven data plane and an unproven one now look different.

This leaves smoke-network-suite honestly red: AF_ALG has no kernel crypto
provider, so alg_test reports absent and the suite reports
FAIL (10 passed, 0 skipped, 1 absent, 0 failed).  That is the correct
verdict and it is left visible rather than waived.
fc1f02b0ed643a8f71321147cef6e6543480fdf5:
feat(build.ci): run the projects own gates and build every hosted arch

The tree carried ~22 source-contract gates and ~74 check-* targets that no
workflow ran.  They are fail-closed -- they assert that an anti-pattern has
not been reintroduced, not that a string exists -- so a gate that only
runs locally is an assertion that does not exist.

toolchain-gates gains check-honesty-policy, check-smoke-cases, host-tests,
check-drm-abi and four subsystem source-contract gates.  All are host-side
Python, rg and host gcc, so they need no cross-toolchain and no QEMU and
belong in the fast job ahead of the heavy ones.  check-doc-test-gates is
deliberately not among them: docs/testing-gates.md:40 is explicit that it
is a broad aggregate whose dependencies are kernel builds and MM, VFS,
driver and concurrency QEMU smokes, and putting it in the fast job would
have serialised a 90-minute run behind a 10-minute budget.

check-drm-abi compares every DRM_IOCTL_* number and wire-struct offset in
kernel/include/drivers/gpu/drm.h against the host's Linux UAPI headers, and
the Dockerfile deliberately carries no linux-headers, so they are installed
on the bare runner here.  The gate skips cleanly when the headers are
absent, which would make it assert nothing at all, so this step fails if it
skips: a gate that has silently stopped asserting is worse than no gate.

A new kernel-build matrix job runs check-<arch>-bringup for every hosted
architecture a CI toolchain exists for, taking the list from
CI_KERNEL_ARCHES through make print-ci-kernel-arches rather than from a
hand-typed YAML array.  A hand-maintained list is a second source of truth
that falls behind SUPPORTED_HOSTED_ARCHES, which is how arm32, riscv32 and
ppc64le went unbuilt while the local gate covered them.  The target
validates every member against SUPPORTED_HOSTED_ARCHES, so a typo fails
loudly instead of spawning a job that cannot build.  The build job still
does the full release packaging for the arches that have userspace; this
one is kernel-only, which is why riscv32 can be in it at all.

loongarch32 stays out with the reason recorded: Debian ships no
loongarch32 gcc and the project builds a from-source cloudspurs la32 fork,
so tools/ci/Dockerfile cannot apt-get it.  arm32 is now in the matrix
because the build break that kept it out is fixed in the previous commit.

Dead plumbing goes: qemu-disk-rv and qemu-disk-la were declared .PHONY with
no rule anywhere, so make answered "No rule to make target" for targets
that looked runnable; and MODE was a variable with zero readers, which
README already admitted.  Both are removed and the README line that named
MODE is corrected rather than deleted, since the OPT advice on it is still
true.

The CONFIG_*_SMOKE_TEST flags needed ?= defaults because they had none,
so "off" was implicit.  CONFIG_HDA_SMOKE_TEST and CONFIG_NVME_SMOKE_TEST
also appended -D to the kernel CFLAGS, where nothing reads them: the only
consumers are kernel/drvmod/examples/{hda,nvme}.c, which are compiled by
tools/driver-modules.mk with DRVMOD_CFLAGS, and that does not include
$(CFLAGS).  The built-in drivers that used to read the macro are gone, so
those two blocks were dead and are removed; DRVMOD_SMOKE is the one knob
that actually reaches the macro and now carries a documented default.  The
=y on-value is kept for all three because smoke_cases.py, BUILD_VARIANT
and the driver guide all use it -- normalising to =1 would have silently
disabled smoke-driver-lifecycle.
