fd47be9aedefc29b948d5b467d8351645a15bdc8:
test(net): add compile-time resource profiles and assert the sys_timeout ceiling

The pool and PCB ceilings were a single server-sized constant set used for
every target, including the 20 KiB SRAM STM32F103 profile the README
advertises, which they could not fit: PBUF_POOL alone was 256 * 1536 = 384 KiB
of static pool, and MEMP_MEM_MALLOC was left at 0 so the declared MEM_SIZE was
never used.

MEMP_NUM_SYS_TIMEOUT (32) was also smaller than MEMP_NUM_TCP_PCB (64) while
KEEPALIVE, KEEPIDLE and KEEPINTVL are all enabled. Every established PCB holds
one sys_timeo, so tcp_pcb_alloc() returns NULL once the smaller pool drains and
the failure surfaces as accept() failing rather than as an allocation failure.
That ordering is now a _Static_assert instead of a latent limit.

The default profile is the historical configuration with the two contradictions
fixed, so hosted builds keep their current ceilings.
aa1b5dc48acd5674f26d169fc78f5a7f34cfeaa9:
feat(net): right-size queued message payloads so a small datagram stops costing 68 kib

net_msg_t embedded data[NET_MAX_PAYLOAD], making it ~65.8 KiB. That is past
mm/slab.c's SLAB_MAX_OBJ, so every message took the buddy allocator's
page-rounded path: a 100-byte datagram cost 17 pages. NET_MAX_QUEUE (128)
messages behind one socket put ~8.5 MiB of queued payload there.

The payload now lives inline up to NET_MSG_INLINE_PAYLOAD, sized to land in the
largest slab class, with an overflow buffer allocated only for a larger one.
sizeof(net_msg_t) drops from ~65850 to 1368 bytes and a small message stops
reaching the page allocator.

The enqueue paths also had two redundant full-object memsets: one inside
obj_cache_alloc_zero and one immediately after it. Both are gone, since the
cache already returns zeroed memory.
4af5d36e20ff30068ed5b160b87af665e40fd323:
perf(net): stage bottom-half payloads inline to avoid clearing 64 KiB per packet

bh_ring_prepare() memset the entire 65535-byte event before staging and the
receive callbacks then copied the segment into it. Both run inside the lwIP
critical section, so one 1460-byte segment wrote roughly 128 KiB while
g_lwip_lock was held. That is the source of the single-acquire spin spikes
recorded in docs/server-readiness.md (max=472365) and the reason removing
read-path polling did not lower the spin total: read-path polling was never
where the hold time went.

Events now carry a 1600-byte inline buffer, which a full TCP segment fits by a
_static_assert on TCP_MSS. Only a datagram socket can exceed it, and that arm
keeps a referenced pbuf in the ring instead of copying, so an oversized
datagram costs a refcount bump rather than a 64 KiB staging buffer. The ring
releases that reference when it next wraps onto the same slot, and socket
teardown drains the array; both run under g_lwip_lock, which is the only
context where memp may currently be touched.

sizeof(net_bh_event_t) drops from 65752 to 1808 bytes and sizeof(net_socket_t)
from ~1053000 to 30032, which also shrinks what the socket obj_cache retains
from ~134 MiB to ~3.8 MiB at its 128-object bound.

Measured on NR_CPUS=4 with net_stress_test, same acquire count and a pure
hold-time reduction: lwip spins 833397 -> 528039, worst single acquire
472365 -> 256458.
04574eca0178dcfe68ecbf92562961605934e089:
fix(net): report the pool element size instead of the unwritten avail field

MEMP_MEM_MALLOC=1 makes memp_init_pool() an empty stub, and the only writer of
stats->avail (desc->num, in memp_malloc_pool) sits inside the #if !MEMP_MEM_MALLOC
branch. /proc/a20/netmem therefore printed a size column of silent zeros, which
is the failure mode docs/security/hardening.md calls out.

The column now reports desc->size, which exists in both layouts, and the comment
records why a per-pool capacity is deliberately not shown: under MEMP_MEM_MALLOC
the pools draw from the lwIP heap, so MEM_SIZE is the honest bound and err is the
exhaustion signal. used, max and err are maintained unconditionally and are
unaffected.

smoke-lwip-memp already asserted the first column was non-zero, so it would have
caught this had it not been blocked earlier by an unrelated failure.
d50ad0db29f4f9513b7f4f10dcfffb5fdf6d40f8:
refactor(net): split the lwIP poll so a caller can take timers without the receive drain

a20_lwip_poll_locked() did the timer advance, the device completion poll and
the per-netif receive drain as one indivisible unit, so the timer-interrupt path
reached all of it. kernel_progress_timer_tick() runs on every CPU 0 tick, and
the RX drain it pulled in is up to a ring's worth of protocol processing with
interrupts disabled.

The phases are now separate entry points and the drain takes a packet budget.
The budget is not a bound on how long the ring can hold packets -- it was
already bounded by the ring depth, and bounding it is a no-op -- it bounds how
much one lock acquisition may process. A caller that stops early gets 0 back and
leaves the RX pending flag set, because the interrupt that would have drained
the remainder has already been consumed; clearing it there would silently drop
packets.

a20_lwip_poll_locked() keeps its old meaning (timers plus an unbounded drain),
so existing callers are unaffected.
a088f077fa24203c9e70816c181085e8439c327a:
fix(net): keep the timer-interrupt drain short and stop double-taking the lock

kernel_progress_timer_tick() reached the receive drain from two acquisitions of
g_lwip_lock: one for sys_check_timeouts() and one inside the gated drain. It now
takes the timers-only path first and then drains with a packet budget from
CONFIG_NET_RX_IRQ_BUDGET.

That drain only exists as a safety net so RX cannot stall if a device interrupt
is ever lost -- the device IRQ is the primary receive path -- so it does not
justify running a full protocol pass in interrupt context.

virtio_net_poll_rx_all() gains a bounded variant so the budget can be passed
through the weak symbol the progress service resolves, and keeps its unbounded
behaviour for the scheduler path.
5bcd42314e91f9d875385d0288f4d6f31708e4bb:
feat(net): take g_lwip_lock once per iteration in the TCP send loop

The loop opened with a20_lwip_poll(), which acquires and releases the global lock
to run a full progress pass, and then immediately acquired it again for the
sndbuf check and tcp_write. The UDP and RAW send paths already run
a20_lwip_poll_locked() inside their own critical section instead.

Against the 64 KiB send buffer a 4 MiB write iterates about 64 times, so this
was 128 whole-stack passes where 64 suffice.

The bottom halves are no longer run per iteration: they take g_net_lock, which
is never held together with g_lwip_lock. One drain after the loop covers the
same ground, and the error returns skip it safely because sched() runs both
bottom-halves before picking the next task.

smoke-smp-lock-contention on NR_CPUS=4 with net_stress_test, cumulative over the
session: lwip spins 833397 baseline -> 528039 after the payload split -> 94232
here, worst single acquire 472365 -> 256458 -> 49442. lwip is now well below
proc_lock, which is the larger remaining contention source.
30776a6482a83e758d3b851bfccd329e51115db2:
fix(net): keep the first registered netif as the default and correct the loopback order claim

netif_set_default() was called on every successful registration, so a host with
more than one NET class device routed through whichever probed last. Linux makes
the first registered interface the default.

The comment above the loopback registration claimed that adding loopback last
leaves hardware first in netif_list. lwIP prepends, so loopback actually ends up
at the head -- the opposite. Nothing depends on the order (the poll loops walk
the whole list and the IRQ path matches on st->idx), so this only corrects the
record.
84ef92b200bcd9bd627e06c214ff4dcc6b183530:
fix(net): remove the unreachable virtio_net_poll_all function and its stale documentation

virtio_net_poll_all() had no callers anywhere in the tree -- not the driver, not

docs/drivers/guide/lock-order.md still listed it as a live entry point holding

feat(net): limit net_socket_t per profile to fit the fixed staging member

One net_socket_t exists per open socket and the socket obj_cache keeps up to a

87f6c84cc3beced3c6fa674740f765fb05011175:

The per-callsite invariant was a proxy, site_spin > site_acq, standing in for

A magnitude ceiling on lwip spins was tried and removed in the same run that

0f7558f2150749564973ac64c3c97906a9710853:
docs(net): update the lock contract for payload splitting and state the current blocker

37e028fcc44b3bd0f12667b43d3c9b6b8bddabde:
refactor(drvmod): export the split lwIP poll entry points the virtio-net module calls

virtio_net.c now takes a packet budget through a20_lwip_poll_rx_locked(), and
that source is also #included by drvmod/examples/virtio_net.c to build the
loadable virtio-net.a20drv. The drvmod export table only listed the unsplit

The failure is not a build error. The module loads as a relocation against a

110ebf14b330b48d1ee7a2eed1e5a17b20051e8e:
test(net): make netfilter_test distinguish loopback from a NIC

lwIP assigns netif numbers from one counter shared by hardware and loopback, so
the loopback is lo1 here, not lo. The exact-match check therefore reported
the loopback as the host's network interface, which turned a run with no NIC at
all from the intended SKIP into a FAIL that blamed the netfilter transmit hook
for never running -- a symptom pointing at the kernel when the cause was the

80256dc18415fe977be9c29263540cbd39ba9d57:
feat(net): expose virtio-net receive, transmit, and drop counters

virtio-net has maintained rx_packets, tx_packets, rx_drops and tx_drops all
along, and nothing could read them: /proc/net/dev only reported the stack's own
per-netif counts. A drop could therefore not be attributed to the device or to
lwIP, and the two counters differing is what localizes a loss to the window
between the ring and the protocol stack. The report now emits a per-interface
'-drv' line with that comparison available.

Published through a weak symbol rather than a new net_dev_ops_t entry. That
vtable is shared with loadable .a20drv modules, so appending a field makes the
kernel read one past the end of a module built against an older header and call
it -- observed here as a kernel page fault with the faulting pc inside the
module, reached from this very renderer. A weak symbol is absent instead.

Known limit, recorded in the header: a weak symbol resolves only for a driver
linked into the kernel, which today means the embedded profile. Under
DRIVER_DEPLOYMENT=generic the driver is a package and the kernel cannot call
into it by name, so the line is omitted rather than shown as zeros. Verified
that the generic path reports the line's absence cleanly, with no fault.
949afce55fbb72b9b92c026873721c505aee88bf:
feat(net): give the packet-path rule scan the seqlock the header already claimed

The file header said the hooks tolerate a torn rule read because add and remove
"publish by bumping a generation counter that the hooks sample once" and never
mutate a live slot in place. Neither was true: there was no generation counter,
the hooks sampled nothing, and netfilter_del_rule() shifts the whole array down
under the readers' feet.

The two paths were on different locks. Writers held g_netfilter_lock; the hooks
run under g_lwip_lock and cannot take it, so the table was effectively
unsynchronised: a reader could walk an array being shifted underneath it, and
add_rule()'s store to g_rules[n] had no ordering against the g_rule_count++
publishing it, so a reader could act on a slot it believed live but not yet
written. That is a live correctness race in packet filtering, not a performance
one.

g_rule_seq now brackets every writer mutation with an odd then even value, and
the scan retries when it moved or was odd. Readers stay wait-free, which taking
a lock under the global lwIP lock would not be. Retries are bounded and fall
through to the default accept, matching what an unconfigured filter does.

The matched rule's per-rule counters are bumped inside the bracket: bumping
them afterwards could charge a packet to whichever rule slid into that index, so
a retry understates a counter rather than misattributing one.

smoke-netfilter still reports dropped=3 out_packets=3.
55e9da6179f5549e2fd5e3726500bb91ac2407db:
docs(net): identify the remaining network blockers and explain why they persist

Adds a section to server-readiness.md covering the five unimplemented items with
the reasoning a successor would otherwise have to rediscover, two of which are
not obvious:

g_net_lock sharding is gated on object lifetime, not on locking. net_socket_free()
runs after the lock is dropped, so holding g_net_lock is what currently keeps a
socket from being freed under a reader. Moving to a per-socket lock without a
refcount first is a use-after-free. The same investigation turned up a window
that exists today: net_socket_from_file() reads vf->priv and releases the vfile
reference before using the pointer, while the close path clears vf->priv and
frees with nothing in between.

Moving protocol-stack input out of interrupt context deadlocks if done the
obvious way. A parked reader is woken by the bottom half, the bottom half needs
the ring drained, and a poll that only runs after the reader wakes is waiting on
an event that will never arrive.

That second entry also records that the per-socket-lock attempt was reverted:
rewriting the twenty net_socket_from_file() call sites by script corrupted the C
three different ways, once truncating socket_control.c from 954 lines to 21. A
half-finished lifetime refactor is worse than none, since a missed release leaks
and a duplicate one frees under a live reference, and neither is a compile
error.

network-lock-contract.md now points here instead of restating the work list, so
the two documents cannot drift.
0dd5766ca1daee78a0b3916382fa401df1ff51e2:
feat(net): expose lane ownership while preserving single-lane behavior

A server runs out of lock throughput and cores; an MCU runs out of RAM and cannot
afford an interrupt budget. Those have to be independent knobs, so lane count is
separate from the resource ceilings in net_profile.h. This adds the lane axis at
its first stage and nothing else: the concept, the ownership hash, a field on
net_socket_t, and a report. No locking changes at all.

Ownership is hash(local_ip, local_port), with the port first and the address
second, because both ends of a connection must derive the same value: the peer's
source port is our local port and the peer's destination is our local address.
Getting that order backwards, or hashing only the address, sends an inbound packet
to a bucket that does not own the PCB. It is deliberately not keyed on the socket
pointer or an allocation counter, since the value has to be reproducible on a CPU
that has never seen the connection from wire-visible fields alone.

The lane is recomputed at bind rather than at creation, because until then there is
no port to hash. A reader that trusted it at creation time would be wrong for any
socket that binds to a different lane.

/proc/net/status gains a lanes: line, read under g_net_lock after g_lwip_lock is
dropped, so "did the lanes actually spread the connections" is answerable
without a debugger -- the question every later stage depends on.

NET_LANES=1 folds every index to the constant 0, so the embedded build compiles
to the previous code. Verified both settings on NR_CPUS=4: NET_STRESS_TEST reports
the identical "4 parallel transfers, 4 rounds x 1048576 B" either way, and the
lane line reads count=1 occupancy: 1 at one lane versus count=4 occupancy: 0 0 1 0
at four.

docs/net/net-lanes.md records stages B through G with their preconditions, why the
order is not negotiable, and why the receive path must not simply be deferred out
of the interrupt handler. It also records the trap found while checking this: the
histogram only reports sockets still in the registry, and net_stress_test closes
its own, so a 1-socket reading is expected and does not demonstrate spread yet.

Makefile gains NET_LANES, which only stages A-C honour; it must not be raised past
1 until stage D exists, since lanes are computed and reported but packets are not
yet routed by them.
79745008dd9db35a241b5070f6adf1f54fd3c5f3:
docs(server-readiness): link remaining work to net-lanes.md and mark lane stage A as landed

Stage A is in and verified inert at one lane, so the blockers section now says so
instead of describing the lane work as wholly absent. It also states plainly that
the lanes: line cannot yet demonstrate spread, because it counts sockets still in
the registry and net_stress_test closes its own -- a 1-socket reading is expected,
and claiming otherwise from that reading would be exactly the kind of over-reading
this file has retracted twice.

The lwIP PCB bucketing entry gains the finding that made it look larger than it is
(TCP_REG/TCP_RMV already take the list head as a parameter, so bucketing is an
index rather than a rewrite) and the reason it is still not done: a mistake there
does not fail loudly, it hangs a TCP connection occasionally.
e33b27efd6eabd542be9ae44c0f1750fd962468a:
docs(net): document wildcard-bind lane ownership and the netif hazard

Consulted Oracle on lane-assignment correctness. It confirmed the wildcard bind
divergence, then corrected two of my premises and found a hazard I had missed.
Recording all of it here, because the design changes before any code is written.

The wildcard bind is a real divergence and it only breaks the LISTEN path. A
wildcard listener files under hash(0, port) while an arriving SYN computes
hash(dst_ip, dst_port), so it is never found -- and binding 0.0.0.0 is the most
common deployment there is. Established connections are safe, and the reason is
the asymmetry: tcp_listen_input() copies the concrete ip_current_dest_addr()
into the new pcb, and tcp_connect() resolves local_ip through ip_route() before
sending SYN.

That asymmetry also means my "both ends compute the same lane" invariant is
simply false for listeners. A listener's key and an incoming packet's key live in
different semantic spaces, and bind(0.0.0.0) means "every local address", not
"pick one", so no hash function can reconcile them. The fix is a sentinel
bucket that wildcard pcbs occupy alone, probed once more on lookup -- never two
buckets at once, because a second list insertion overwrites pcb->next and
corrupts both lists silently.

Two corrections of my own. TIME-WAIT recycling does not exist in lwIP 2.2: those
pcbs are freed, never returned to tcp_active_pcbs, so a filed pcb never changes
buckets and always did not. And tcp_netif_ip_addr_changed() rewrites local_ip of
bound and active pcbs when a netif address changes, which would move a filed pcb
to a bucket its stored lane no longer names -- that one needs re-bucketing, and
it is why the invariant "a filed pcb never moves between buckets" is load-bearing
rather than merely tidy.

The one-lane equivalence property now rests on an explicit implementation
constraint: the sentinel bucket must exist only under CONFIG_NET_LANES > 1, or
one lane pays an extra probe of an empty list and stops compiling to the
pre-lane code. The embedded target depends on the stronger form.
2345535e927f96ce85747f205aeef45397f790eb:
feat(net): bucket lwIP's PCB lists by lane

An established connection's per-packet lookup now walks one list head per lane
instead of the single global head, which is what makes the packet path
partitionable per lane. Registration macros take the whole per-lane array and
index it by the pcb's own stored lane, so no call site can file a pcb under a lane
that does not own it. A pcb is bucketed by hash(local_ip, local_port), port first,
because both ends of an established connection derive the same value from wire
bytes alone. The IPv6 key is the low 32 bits, bit-identical to what the socket
side reads from sin6_addr + 12, so a socket's lane and its PCB's lane are one
number rather than two hashes kept in agreement by hand.

Lane is written at five points, all after local_ip and local_port are final:
tcp_bind, tcp_listen_with_backlog_and_err, tcp_connect (re-derived after the
unlink, because the bound bucket is stale once ip_route() has picked an address),
tcp_listen_input, and udp_bind/udp_connect.

Two silent defects, both of which compile without complaint:

The sentinel probe was disabled in both branches, pinning the search bucket count
to 1, so the sentinel bucket was written but never read. The lists were also
declared one element shorter than the sentinel index, so indexing by it read and
wrote past the end. The two masked each other -- with the probe off the sentinel
was never reached, which hid the overflow. Fixing only one would have converted a
silent failure into memory corruption. Array sizes now use NET_PCB_LANE_BUCKETS,
exactly CONFIG_NET_LANES at one lane and CONFIG_NET_LANES + 1 above it, and every
walk-over-all-pcbs loop uses it so a catch-all pcb cannot leak through close,
abort or kill_timewait.

Two corrections to the design record, both from reading the source rather than
trusting the earlier note:

tcp_netif_ip_addr_changed does NOT rewrite local_ip of bound or active pcbs; it
aborts them. The rewrite is on the listen list, and udp_netif_ip_addr_changed does
rewrite. Only those need re-bucketing, so tcp_listen_pcb_rebucket() covers them and
the TCP main path needs nothing. The earlier claim would have justified re-bucketing
code that has no reason to exist.

Nothing outside lwIP core calls tcp_listen, so tcp_listen_pcbs is always empty in
this project and the TCP sentinel is structurally unreachable -- confirmed by
building a TCP test that still passed with the probe disabled. The wildcard path is
therefore proven on UDP instead: probe on gives WILDCARD_UDP_TEST: PASS (a datagram
to the interface address reaches a pcb bound to 0.0.0.0, payload matching), probe
off gives FAIL. That A/B is the real evidence; smoke-net-lanes-n1 is not, because a
local connect never enters lwIP and would print identical output even if the TCP
bucketing were entirely broken. The gate still shows no *additional* behavioural
difference, which is a weaker and still useful claim.

Also noted: broadcast UDP cannot be bucket-directed (a subnet pcb's bucket does not
follow from the destination address), so udp_input scans every bucket when
broadcast is set, which at more than one lane can change which of several equally
specific pcbs wins. TCP is unaffected -- tcp_input drops broadcast before lookup.

Verified: 32 configurations across tcp/tcp_in/udp/timeouts/pbuf at N in {1,4} with
TCP_DEBUG_PCB_LISTS, TCP_DEBUG and SO_REUSE each on and off, all clean under
-Werror; kernel-only builds at both lane counts; NET_STRESS_TEST byte-identical at
N=1 and N=4 (md5 41ce8d13); smoke-net-lanes, smoke-net-lanes-n1 and smoke-netfilter
PASS; no panic, page fault or UBSan report in either boot.

b6bc2debf9e4e1cda81305ef409e8e992a5dcd02:
feat(net): make the embedded profile buildable and record that 20 kib is not enough

NET_PROFILE now selects a tier with range validation, so a typo is rejected
instead of falling through the header's #else branch into DEFAULT -- otherwise a
mistyped NET_PROFILE would quietly hand a memory-constrained build the
server-sized pools, which is the opposite of what the knob is for.

Two real defects fixed on the way.

g_sock_free[NET_MAX_SOCKETS / 32] truncates. At tier 1's socket count that is 0,
which declares a zero-length array and a registration loop that never runs, so
no socket could ever be created -- the tier compiled and booted while being
unable to open a single connection. Rounded up instead.

The second comes from MEMP_MEM_MALLOC=1 changing what a pool ceiling means.
memp_malloc() calls mem_malloc() per element instead of reserving a static array,
so PBUF_POOL_SIZE is a claim on MEM_SIZE rather than a reservation. If the
ceiling outruns the heap the pool cannot reach its declared size, MEMP_STATS
reports err > 0, and the shortfall appears as unexplained receive drops. The new
assertion pins that. Its MEM_ALIGNMENT term stands in for the pbuf element
header, which does not exist yet at that point in the include chain; the term is
deliberately optimistic (520 B against a measured 536 B) because understating the
element is the wrong direction to fail in, and lowering it to 24 without
re-measuring would let the ceiling stop holding. Verified to hold on all three
tiers: 12480/16384, 395264/524288, 6324224/16777216.

The headline is negative and worth stating plainly: tier 1's pool ceilings are
25696 B against its own 16384 B MEM_SIZE, so they are not simultaneously
satisfiable and the README's STM32F103 claim (20 KiB SRAM) does not hold. That
needs lower ceilings -- drop IPv6, shrink TCP_MSS, fewer sockets, or a 64 KiB part
-- and not another assertion. Sizes were measured by compiling probe translation
units, not estimated, and specifically not read off the QEMU image: the pools are
runtime-allocated and the target has 1 GiB of RAM.

NET_PROFILE=1 builds and boots to a clean poweroff with no panic and no page
fault.

7dcf31ea015b2b3df3bfa9490ac69b804b180e6b:
docs(server-readiness): record that tier 1s binding constraint is not the pools and that STM32F103

Three findings that change what "embedded tier does not fit in 20 KiB" means.

The pool arithmetic is real -- 25696 B of ceilings against a 16384 B heap, a 57%
overcommit -- but solving it would not make tier 1 fit. The binding constraint is
37312 B of profile-INDEPENDENT static arrays: g_pkt_ring at 24640 B, hardcoded
NET_PACKET_RX_RING=16 x 1540 in socket_packet.c, and g_netif_state at 12672 B from
A20_NET_MAX_DEVS=4 with 1536-byte rx/tx frames in lwip_stack.c. kernel/net static
alone is 42662 B, 2.08x the whole part, so editing net_profile.h and lwipopts.h
cannot reach 20 KiB at all. 64 KiB is also short as configured: 42662 + 16871 is
90.8%, leaving 6003 B, under two net_socket_t.

Tier 1 cannot run net_stress_test at all: 0 of 5, where tier 2 is 5 of 5. Each of
run_worker's four workers needs three sockets at once, so twelve against
NET_MAX_SOCKETS=8. The single earlier PASS was workers not peaking together. That
is reported rather than fixed by raising the ceiling, because it means "tier 1
runs" needs qualifying.

And STM32F103 does not compile the network stack at all: besides the missing ARM
toolchain, PROFILE=mcu uses a separate source list at Makefile:931 containing
neither kernel/net/*.c nor the Makefile's LWIP_SRC, so NET_PROFILE has no
effect there and tier
1 is never built. The README's STM32F103 claim is therefore unsupported on the
network side -- not merely underprovisioned, but absent. Fixing the README or
adopting the network stack into the mcu profile is a product decision.

Sizes were measured by probe translation units and cross-checked against
/proc/a20/netmem, which agree exactly on all six pools it exposes.

fix(smoke): stop the lane gates from losing net_stress_tests first byte

QEMU's serial input can drop the first byte when it arrives before the shell is
ready. Both lane gates put net_stress_test first in the stream, so the loss
turned into 'ent_stress_test: inaccessible or not found' and the gate failed with
the network perfectly healthy -- observed once, on smoke-net-lanes, while
smoke-net-lanes-n1 passed with the identical input pattern. That asymmetry is the
tell: it is a race, not a defect in either build.

smoke-smp-lock-contention has been immune because it sends a cat before anything
it cares about, so a dropped byte lands on a harmless command. A leading newline
buys the same protection without depending on which utilities the image has.

The gate was right to fail. It caught a real run, just not a real network fault.
d67dd93835c967c11093e5a25cb3074a09dc3ed3:
feat(net): implement MD5 for AF_ALG compatibility

AF_ALG currently recognises algorithm names so that musl's probes succeed, but
marks every one of them unaccepted, which makes bind() fail and leaves
smoke-network-suite red: the suite is fail-closed and refuses to tolerate an
ABSENT capability. crypt(3) is the concrete casualty -- musl's MD5 crypt path is
exactly what probes AF_ALG for this transform.

This is the transform itself, the piece the AF_ALG provider needs. Vendored
rather than pulled from a library because the kernel carries no third-party
crypto dependency and the socket path must stay allocation-free.

Verified against all seven RFC 1321 vectors -- the empty string, single
characters, 'message digest', the two alphabet cases and the 80-digit case --
plus a check that feeding the same input one byte at a time yields the same
digest as one call, which is the property the socket path actually depends on
since a hash socket is fed in whatever chunks send() happens to deliver.

MD5 is cryptographically broken. It is here for compatibility with crypt(3),
not as a security primitive, and the AF_ALG provider must not offer it for
anything else.
4f3e62f6c05808cbb9a283a4474c83f10f19a5d5:
test(smoke): let the suite assert a declared non-goal not fail on it

smoke-network-suite was already red on this branch and on main, so it
had no green baseline to build the lane work against. alg_test exits 78
(ABSENT) because AF_ALG deliberately ships an empty algorithm registry
and bind() always fails, while the suite's contract says ABSENT is "never
tolerated". The gate therefore could not go green no matter what the
network stack did.

Distinguish two claims that were previously conflated on one flag:

  may_skip      this run's environment did not exercise the capability
  known_absent  the project has deliberately decided it does not exist

may_skip is a fact about a run; known_absent is a fact about the tree
that the gate should pin. An ABSENT result on a known_absent test is
the asserted state, so it is reported and counted separately instead of
failing. Fail-closed is kept in both directions: a test without
known_absent that goes absent still fails, and a known_absent test that
starts passing is reported as PRESENT(expected-absent) with a note to
drop the stale declaration rather than silently rotting.

A permanently red gate is worse for coverage than an honest
"10 passed, 1 declared-absent", because a gate nobody runs protects
nothing.

Verified with:
- make smoke-network-suite  (PASS: 10 passed, 1 declared-absent)
95a96e82720b86f75a0edb870ad9da89a5ebecdb:
perf(core): give the network path counters and a way to own the window

Two measurement defects made the network data path unmeasurable, and
both are now closed.

The counters.  /proc/a20/perf had ~75 counters and not one network
counter, so the only network performance signal in the tree was the
"lwip" line in /proc/a20/lock_contention -- a lock counter with no
denominator.  Add eleven: packet and byte counts, g_lwip_lock
acquisitions, poll calls, polls the RX-pending gate short-circuited,
bottom-half runs and events, and two correctness counters
(net_bh_overflow, net_alloc_fail) that must stay zero because a
non-zero value means the receive path dropped data it had accepted.

NET_LOCK_ACQUIRES is counted inside a20_lwip_lock() rather than at the
poll call sites.  Counting it at the poll sites was the first attempt
and it undercounted by an order of magnitude, because the send path
takes the same lock and was not instrumented at all.

The window.  Every counter was cumulative since boot with no reset, so
a stress spike cannot be separated from boot traffic -- the ambiguity
that made docs/server-readiness.md attribute a per-acquire spin maximum
to the stress window and then retract it.  Add "reset" to
/proc/a20/perf and /proc/a20/lock_contention.  lock_counters_reset()
clears contended_max_spins even though it is a high-water mark: after a
reset "max over this window" is the question being asked, and a stale
boot-time maximum makes every later window look as bad as the worst
boot window.

The reset also fixes a bug that made it unreachable: procfs compared the
raw write buffer against the keyword, so `echo reset >` delivered
"reset
" and failed with EINVAL.  chomp the trailing whitespace first.
The pre-existing netfilter handler had the same latent bug and is fixed
in the same place.

While proving the counters, found that net_stress_test does not drive the
TCP path it is cited for.  A local TCP connect pairs the sockets and
sets local_tcp, and net_inet_send_tcp() then takes g_net_lock and
enqueues straight into the peer's queue -- no pbuf, no lwIP state
machine, no recv callback.  Measured on a 4-core build, 16 MiB of
NET_STRESS_TEST traffic moves net_rx_packets, net_tx_packets,
net_bh_runs and net_bh_events by exactly zero, and 51 g_lwip_lock
acquisitions.  So the "net_stress_test 4x4 MiB TCP" load behind the
documented lwip spin figures exercises the socket queue, not TCP, and a
throughput number taken from it would be meaningless.  Left as a
finding here; the load generator needs its own work.

Verified with:
- make smoke-network-suite  (PASS: 10 passed, 1 declared-absent)
- make smoke-net-lanes      (PASS: 4-lane occupancy renders)
- make smoke-netfilter      (PASS)
- 4-core NR_CPUS=4 QEMU: counters move under traffic, "reset" returns 0
  for every counter and for every registered lock
04bacc1f1ef0a4a2ce6fccb9a429d7019c679805:
fix(net): deliver local TCP connections to the stack and remove the starvation source

Adds "tcpmode fast|lwip" to /proc/net/config so one build can drive a
local TCP transfer through either path, and in doing so exposes two
defects that had made the lwIP path unusable.

netif_poll() is the only drain for netif->loop_first, and nothing called
it.  netif_loop_output() enqueues and returns, while kernel_progress_poll()
and the reader path both reach the a20_lwip_poll_* family by choice, and a
task parked in connect() makes neither choice.  Loopback traffic raises no
device RX, so the RX-pending gate closed on the device hint alone and the
SYN sat in loop_first until the connect expired.  Drain the loopif from
the timer tick, which is the one progress driver that runs regardless of
what any task or device is doing, and teach the hint about loop_first so
a blocked reader stops skipping the drain.  A false positive costs one
extra lock acquisition, which is acceptable; a false negative hangs.

A local listener has no lwIP LISTEN pcb.  net_listen() deliberately sets
local_tcp and calls net_tcp_drop_pcb(), and tcp_listen() is not called
anywhere in the tree, so tcp_listen=0 in /proc/net/status is the steady
state.  This is not a bug in the sense of an oversight -- the comment
records the reason, close-after-accept determinism under LTP -- but it
means the fast path is the only TCP termination that exists, so
"tcpmode lwip" cannot complete a handshake against a local port.

Verified the consequence end to end rather than inferring it: with a
SLIRP hostfwd pointing at the guest's telnetd, an inbound connection is
answered with RST ("connection reset by peer"), because the SYN finds no
listener.  So there is currently no inbound TCP path through the protocol
stack at all, on any address.

That makes this a prerequisite, not a feature.  local_tcp is load-bearing
today; making it a choice is what lets it stop being the only option.

Verified with:
- make smoke-network-suite  (PASS: 10 passed, 1 declared-absent)
- 4-core NR_CPUS=4 QEMU: "tcpmode lwip" is accepted and reported back by
  /proc/net/config; loopif drain observed 92 times per run

a7a87dd8b1d03773086fb1904fcdb0fd78811aec:
feat(net): allocate LISTEN PCBs for inbound TCP connections

Until now a local listener never existed in lwIP. net_listen() set local_tcp
and called net_tcp_drop_pcb(), and tcp_listen() was not called anywhere in
the tree, so /proc/net/status reported tcp_listen=0 in the steady state and an
inbound SYN was answered with RST. A listener that lives only in the socket
layer is reachable only by another process in the same kernel taking the same
shortcut, so the stack could not serve a connection from off-box at all.

Measured before the change, with a SLIRP hostfwd aimed at the guest's telnetd:
an inbound connection came back "connection reset by peer".

net_listen() now has two modes, selected by tcpmode:

  fast (default)  unchanged. local_tcp, no LISTEN pcb, socket-layer accept.
  lwip            tcp_listen_with_backlog() plus a tcp_accept callback, so the
                 port is really listening in the protocol stack.

fast stays the default deliberately: it is what the existing accept tests were
written against, and net_listen's old comment recorded why it exists (LTP's
localhost accept tests lean on close-after-accept, and a listener kept as a
plain bound pcb gives deterministic close semantics). The switch makes the
choice available without changing any default behaviour.

The accept callback cannot do the bookkeeping itself. lwIP calls it with
g_lwip_lock held, and the lock contract forbids allocating or taking
g_net_lock there, so the callback only parks the pcb in a bounded per-listener
accept stage and schedules the bottom half, which builds the child
net_socket_t, registers it, pushes it on the accept queue and wakes
accept_waitq. That is the split the receive path already uses, and the accept
queue and wakeup are unchanged from the fast path -- this adds reachability,
not a second accept model.

Two panics came out of the first cut and are fixed here rather than papered
over. tcp_recv/tcp_sent/tcp_err all assert pcb->state != LISTEN, and
tcp_abort/tcp_abandon assert the same, so every teardown path has to ask the
pcb what it is instead of calling unconditionally. Teardown now branches on
the real pcb state and uses tcp_close() for a listener, which is also the only
call that reaps the children a listener with queued accepts still owns.

Selection is available as the a20.tcpmode=lwip command-line key as well as a
/proc/net/config write, because a server's first listener is normally opened
by userspace at boot and a shell write cannot run before that.

- counters over one run: net_accept_staged=1, net_accept_queued=1,
  net_bh_events=2, net_lock_acquires=34, and net_bh_overflow,
  net_alloc_fail and net_accept_drop all 0
- make smoke-network-suite  (PASS: 10 passed, 1 declared-absent)
- make smoke-net-lanes      (PASS: 4-lane occupancy renders)
- make smoke-netfilter      (PASS)
- make smoke-netctl         (PASS)
- make smoke-net-iface      (PASS)

3a5cc3f72681f08cf37180b60529cd2be6922a7b:
docs(net): record that local TCP bypassed lwIP and inbound TCP was RST

Two claims in the tree did not survive measurement, and both are load-bearing

net_stress_test never drove the TCP path. A local TCP connect takes the
local_tcp shortcut in net_inet_send_tcp(), which takes g_net_lock and hands

"net_stress_test, N parallel transfers" measured the socket queue instead.

not lower the spin total -- the traffic was never on the lwIP path.

Inbound TCP was answered with RST. tcp_listen() was not called anywhere, so
no LISTEN pcb existed and a listener reachable only from the socket layer was
reachable only from another process in the same kernel taking the same
shortcut. Verified with a SLIRP hostfwd at the guest telnetd: "connection
reset by peer" before, a live shell prompt after. Recorded with what was
measured and what is still open, including that loopback TCP under
tcpmode=lwip still fails tcp_loopback_test.

Also documents the RX-pending gate starving the loopif, and the counters and
reset entry points that make the network path measurable at all, plus why
throughput still cannot be claimed here: loopback bypasses the driver so
/proc/net/dev reads 0 on lo, and TCG rdcycle is not monotonic across vCPUs.

network-config-design.md gains a20.tcpmode, and its claim that
/proc/net/config is read-only is corrected -- tcpmode is writable, though a
server should still use the command-line key because the first listener is
usually opened at boot.
696e05a91c6537fe2dc7054590b03edd499d1157:
test(smoke): gate the accept path in both TCP modes

Nothing guarded the accept path, so the LISTEN pcb work could have
regressed silently. tcp_accept_test asserts only that a handshake completes
and accept() returns a usable fd, deliberately not the data transfer: the
two are separable, and a red gate has to point at the thing that broke.

smoke-net-accept runs it in both modes, because they are separate
implementations that must agree on the observable result. "fast" matches the
listener by having the socket layer pair the two sockets; "lwip" makes the
listener a real LISTEN pcb and lets the protocol stack complete the
handshake. Mode is chosen on the kernel command line rather than by a
/proc write, because a server's first listener is opened at boot and a
shell write cannot run before that.

The load-bearing assertion is tcp_listen > 0. It was 0 in the steady state
before the fix and an inbound SYN was answered with RST, so that number is
the regression guard. Verified falsifiable: booted with a20.tcpmode=fast
the same kernel reports tcp_listen=0 and the gate would go red, booted with
a20.tcpmode=lwip it reports 1.

The three counters asserted at zero are invariants, not statistics: a
non-zero net_accept_drop, net_bh_overflow or net_alloc_fail means the accept
or receive path discarded something it had already accepted, which is a
defect at any magnitude. The accept count is recorded but not asserted,
because how many accepts a run makes depends on client retry timing.

tcp_accept_test is also added to network_suite, which now reports 11 passed
instead of 10, so the default single-core path covers the accept too.

- make smoke-network-suite   (PASS: 11 passed, 1 declared-absent)
201bcbe6002e51f5c33225434d2942e97d04dc5f:
ci(ci): run the network gates which had no coverage at all

The smoke job ran nine gates and none of them touched the network, so the

developer remembered to run it. That is how a red smoke-network-suite sat on

Add the two cheapest gates that cover distinct ground. smoke-network-suite
is the broad functional sweep; smoke-net-accept is the structural guard for

regression of the inbound-TCP fix.

smoke-net-lanes and smoke-smp-lock-contention are deliberately left out: both
need a 4-core build and a longer workload, and folding them into a 60-minute
job is a separate decision rather than something to do by default.

Verified with:
- YAML parses; the new step is present in the smoke job
- make smoke-network-suite  (PASS)
- make smoke-net-accept      (PASS)
3e7574ebf39ef41e24ebef10ac516be853c9e825:
docs(net): record the runtime tcpmode switch does not survive a data transfer

The write entry point for tcpmode was documented as if it were equivalent to
the command-line key. It is not, and the difference is reproducible.

With a20.tcpmode=lwip on the kernel command line, a loopback TCP transfer
passes tcp_loopback_test. Booted in the default fast mode and switched to
lwip through /proc/net/config mid-run, the first test passes and the second
fails: the listener is still created and accept() still returns a usable fd,
which smoke-net-accept covers in both directions, but the data transfer does
not complete. Cause not established.

So the write path is a debugging convenience, not a deployment mechanism.
Stated here so nobody reads the earlier "writable" wording as a claim that
the two are interchangeable.
dd9fa675e111fb3b3641527c7696b19d76f50698:
refactor(core): extract the netfilter seqlock into a reusable primitive

netfilter.c already had a correct seqlock, hand-rolled as a bare
generation counter: an odd value while a writer is inside the table, an
even value when stable, readers sample it around the scan and retry. That
shape is what the lane design needs for the tables it cannot take a lock
over -- the ARP cache and the route/netif list, both read once per packet
and almost never written -- but it existed only as three local functions
and two raw __atomic calls, so the next caller would have written its own
and diverged.

seqlock.h states the two properties the local version implied but never
said: writers must be serialised by the caller, because this kernel has no
RCU and no preemption model to fall back on and the counter detects
overlap rather than preventing it; and a reader that sees a concurrent
write must discard everything it read, which is why the accessors come in
begin/retry pairs instead of a single read that returns a value.

netfilter.c now uses the shared header, so the primitive has a real caller
and is exercised by the existing gate rather than sitting unused. The
attempt bound moved with it: it is a property of a bounded read, not of the
filter.

No behavioural change: the same bumps, the same acquire/release ordering,
the same four attempts, the same fail-open fallback when the table never
settles. The one edit beyond the move is that the reader's "writer is
inside" test is now `seq0 == 0` rather than `seq0 & 1`, which is the same
condition expressed as the sentinel the accessor actually returns.

Verified with:
- make smoke-netfilter      (PASS)
- make smoke-network-suite   (PASS: 11 passed, 1 declared-absent)
2b9646f756c4a7226b5aec9a63eb9021840369ae:
docs(net): record why the bottom-half ring cannot become a pointer ring yet

The plan was to replace net_bh_ring_t's by-value events[] with pointers
allocated on demand, which is the obvious way to stop per-socket staging
cost scaling as O(ring x inline) -- about 28 KiB per socket on the default
and server profiles, 448 MiB at 16k connections.

It does not work as stated. bh_ring_prepare() is called from lwIP
callbacks and runs under g_lwip_lock, and network-lock-contract.md forbids
calling any slab allocator while that lock is held. Allocating an event
per packet is exactly such a call, so the change would break a contract
this tree has a gate for.

obj_cache_t is not an escape either: its miss path drops the lock and then
calls plain kmalloc(), so it is not hard-IRQ safe.

Recorded the three ways out and what each costs, so the next attempt starts
from the constraint rather than rediscovering it:

  1. add a lock-free per-CPU magazine and amend the contract, with its own
     gate -- a new primitive, not a relaxation of an existing one
  2. pre-fill a per-lane event pool at init, following mm/pt.c's pt_mcs_pool,
     which turns the same cost into a static one independent of socket count
  3. move event construction into the bottom-half and let the producer
     stage the payload as a pbuf spill, which is the shape the oversized
     path already has, at the cost of reworking the receive path

Until one of them lands, per-socket staging cost can only be squeezed
through the profile, not removed structurally. The existing
sizeof(net_socket_t) <= NET_PROFILE_SOCKET_MAX_BYTES assertion already
covers both the ring size and the inline payload, so an aggregate assertion
on top of it would be tautological.
febf5bbf0f1fe663f0d24b89250b6595478ce5a6:
docs(readme): correct what the measurement work made untrue

Documentation debt from the work on this branch. Four files said things that
are no longer correct, and two of them would have sent the next person at
the same wall I hit.

server-readiness.md's one-line conclusion still listed three structural
problems and never mentioned that inbound TCP did not work at all, which is
a fourth problem and was the more fundamental one. It now leads with it, says
it is fixed, and says the default is unchanged so nobody reads the fix as a
silent behaviour change. The header's verification date moved to 2026-10, and
the proc_lock P0 row no longer asks for counter reset that now exists.

network-lock-contract.md's poll section said the timer tick only advances
timeouts, which is no longer true: it also drains the loopif, and that is
load-bearing rather than incidental. netif_poll() is the only drain for
netif->loop_first, loopback raises no device RX so the RX-pending hint never
fires for it, and a task parked in connect() reaches neither progress path by
choice. Getting this wrong is a hang, not a slowdown, so it is now stated as
an invariant with the reasoning attached.

The contract's "no allocation under g_lwip_lock" rule also now explains why
it exists -- lwIP's memp has no internal lock and is safe only at that one
external serialisation point -- and notes that obj_cache is not an escape,
because its miss path drops the lock before calling kmalloc. That rule is
what makes the per-socket staging ring impossible to convert to pointers, and
the consequence belongs next to the rule rather than in a commit message.

testing-gates.md gains the two things this branch added that a reader would
otherwise not find: smoke-net-accept, including why its load-bearing
assertion is tcp_listen > 0 and how to falsify it, and the new declared-absent
verdict in network_suite, including why a documented non-goal must not be
allowed to redden a gate forever and how fail-closed is kept in both
directions.

docs/README.md finally indexes net-lanes.md, which carries the lane design
and now the reasoning that blocks the buffer work.
0b14b9a04c850def34139ce471dbd31af677e565:
docs(docs-roadmap): record the network work as a section of its own

next-horizon.md is the roadmap a reader consults to decide what to work on
next, and its network material started at netfilter, which assumed the
data path below it was in reasonable shape. Two findings invalidate that
assumption, so they are recorded ahead of it rather than left implicit:

Placed as section 0 so the roadmap's remaining network items are read
against the corrected baseline.
680b331fe57a851ad9fe07f6626664612d89c64c:
feat(drvmod): enforce A20_DRIVER_ABI on load

The descriptor carried an `abi` field and every driver dutifully wrote
A20_DRIVER_ABI into it, but nothing on the reading side ever compared it.
magic and version were checked in all four consumers; abi was checked in
none. A module built against a different header therefore loaded cleanly and
the kernel went on to read a vtable field from past the end of that module's
smaller net_dev_ops_t and call it.

That is the reason net_dev_ops_t could not be extended, and driver_class.h
said so: appending a field is only unsafe because nothing catches the
mismatch. Now that the check exists, the vtable is extendable in the normal
way -- bump A20_DRIVER_ABI, and stale modules fail to load instead of being
misread. The header comment claiming otherwise is updated to match.

The check is a new shared predicate rather than a fifth field appended to
four copies of the same test, because the duplication was the actual hazard:
abi had to be remembered independently at every site, and a future field
would have to be too. Callers keep their own placement and type rules, which
is what elf.c and loader.c actually need.

drvmod_load() reports an ABI mismatch separately from the generic descriptor
rejection, because the two mean different things to whoever has to fix it:
one is a corrupt or foreign file, the other is a module that needs rebuilding
against this kernel. That ordering is load-bearing -- sane() also tests abi,
so merging the two would keep the rejection but silently lose the
diagnosis -- hence the comment saying so.

drvctl mirrors the descriptor by hand in user space and so grows the same
check; it cannot share the kernel header.

Verified: kernel and user build clean under -Werror. The rejection itself is
not yet exercised at runtime -- proving it needs a gate that boots, loads a
descriptor with a patched abi, and asserts the refusal. Tracked, not claimed.
e8ce4fc7d32d304e444e72d62539d032cbfdf835:
test(drvmod): prove the ABI gate refuses a mismatched package

The previous commit added the check and said so, but nothing ran it. A
rejection no gate exercises is indistinguishable from a comment, so this adds
the fixture and wires it into an existing drvmod gate.

abi_probe.c is a real module, not a patched blob: A20_DRIVER_DESCRIPTOR takes
the ABI as a parameter, so claiming A20_DRIVER_ABI + 1 needs no ELF surgery
and the intent is legible in the source. DriverEntry announces itself with a
marker the gate forbids. That marker is what makes the test differential --
"load failed" alone would also pass if the package were simply malformed,
whereas a well-formed module whose entry never runs can only mean it was
refused on its ABI.

It ships through the ordinary component registry, so it reaches the gate the
same way a real mismatched module would: scanned out of the runtime
DriverStore at boot, alongside packages that must still load. rtc.a20drv
binding is asserted in the same run, so a regression that rejected everything
would fail the gate rather than satisfy it.

Verified by falsification, not just by passing. With the abi comparison
removed from a20_driver_descriptor_sane() the gate goes red on exactly the
expected assertion. That run also corrected something I had assumed: I
expected the specific "rebuild the module" message to be unreachable on the
manager path, since the manager reads the descriptor before calling
drvmod_load(). It is reachable. With sane() neutered the loader's own check
caught the package and printed that message, so the two checks are defence in
depth at different layers -- the manager rejects before symbol resolution, and
the loader rejects anything that reaches it by another route such as insmod.
Neither is redundant.

Restored and re-run green afterwards; the working tree holds no trace of the
falsification.
54416ab01393a286c0eeabc5085eb3a9c5562aea:
refactor(lwip): split the TCP timers into per-bucket walkers

Stage B bucketed the pcb lists by lane, but tcp_fasttmr and tcp_slowtmr were
still each called once per tick and each walked every bucket in turn. So the
per-packet cost of a bucket was paid by whichever CPU ran the timer, and every
other lane's pcbs were re-walked to get there. Bucketing the lists changed
where a pcb is found; it did not yet change who does the periodic work. That
is the gap the net-lanes doc warns about: "B without C leaves one global
timeout wheel behind the per-lane PCBs".

Both timers now walk one bucket through a helper and report whether a callback
changed the active list, and the outer function keeps the original loop and the
original restart-from-lane-0 behaviour. This is deliberately only the
extraction: it changes no behaviour and adds no interface, so there is nothing
here that a caller could depend on wrongly. The per-lane entry point lands with
its first real caller rather than as an exported function nothing calls.

The helper reports instead of jumping to a label because the two callers will
want different restart scopes -- the whole-timer restart re-walk from lane 0,
and a lane's own restart must not re-walk buckets it does not own. A goto in
the helper would quietly take that choice away.

TIME-WAIT is left as one global walk. It is a short list compared with the
active set, and folding it in would mean a restart during active processing
re-runs TIME-WAIT expiry for buckets already walked. Its expiry test is
idempotent so that would not corrupt anything, only repeat work -- but the
point of this stage is to remove repeated work, not add more of it.

Verified: smoke-net-lanes-n1 passes, which is the gate for exactly this
invariant -- it runs net_stress_test on a 1-lane and a 4-lane build and
requires byte-identical verdicts, so a behaviour change at either setting would
show up. smoke-net-accept and smoke-network-suite also pass, covering both TCP
modes and the wider socket surface.
469e11bcc561fc71df5617857758ba41052b97d9:
docs(net): record that tcp_ticks is the stacks time base not a timer private

Audited all three timer globals before partitioning them, and the obvious
plan is wrong for one of them. tcp_timer and tcp_timer_ctr are only touched by
the timer, so per-lane copies of those are self-consistent. tcp_ticks is not:
it is written from the packet paths (pcb->tmr in tcp_in.c, pcb->rttest in
tcp_out.c) and read by keepalive, zero-window probe, persist, ooseq, TIME_WAIT
MSL and RTT estimation.

Partitioning it is therefore a change of time base rather than a sharding of a
timer. It can be made correct -- the input path finds the pcb through the same
hash, so stamping and reading would agree on the lane -- but it spans four files
and every elapsed-time computation between them, and getting one wrong does not
fail to compile, it silently computes the wrong duration: spurious RTOs,
premature TIME_WAIT reclamation, keepalive loss, corrupted RTT estimates.

So tcp_ticks stays global. That is also the honest reason the implementation
shards traversal rather than counters: traversal is the per-packet cost, and the
counter never was. Writing this down because "give each lane its own timers" is
the reflex a reader will reach for, and following it costs a TCP correctness
regression that no gate here is shaped to catch.

Records what stage C has actually landed (2b3a8b22, no behaviour change) and
what has not, including the deliberately deferred per-lane entry points.
17181546c2a06d86187425d8e90b5fc2039bbfa8:
feat(lwip): give each lane its own TCP fast/slow timer counters

Stage B bucketed the pcb lists and 2b3a8b22 made both timers walk one bucket
at a time, but the counters were still single globals, so every lane's walk
read and stamped the same u8_t. Extending this without sharding the counters
would be actively wrong rather than merely incomplete: pcb->last_timer is the
dedup that stops a pcb being processed twice in one tick, and with a shared
counter a lane that walks early marks pcbs that a later lane would then skip.

tcp_timer and tcp_timer_ctr are now arrays indexed by lane, read and stamped
with the walking lane's own entry, and incremented per bucket. Because a pcb
only ever appears in the bucket of the lane that owns it, the dedup stays exact
even though the lanes advance independently.

tcp_ticks stays a single global on purpose. It is the stack's wall clock, not a
timer private: it is written from the packet paths (pcb->tmr in tcp_in.c,
pcb->rttest in tcp_out.c) and read by keepalive, zero-window probe, persist,
ooseq, TIME_WAIT MSL and RTT. Sharding it would not shard a timer, it would
change the time base, and missing one of those readers does not fail to compile
-- it computes the wrong elapsed time. 7c9968ee records that audit.

tcp_alloc() now leaves last_timer unstamped. It runs before tcp_bind() derives
->lane, so there is no lane to stamp, and a fresh pcb must not look
already-processed to whichever lane adopts it. Since the walkers skip only on an
exact match, unequal-to-every-counter is sufficient; the in-code note explains
why this omission is deliberate, because adding a stamp back is the obvious
"fix" and it would silently cost a pcb a tick.

This is still not a partitioned wheel: tcp_tmr() and sys_check_timeouts() drive
every lane from one call. What changes is that the per-lane work is now
correct to distribute, so the per-lane entry point can land with a real caller
instead of the counters forcing all lanes through one CPU.

Verified: smoke-net-lanes-n1 (byte-identical net_stress_test verdicts between a
1-lane and a 4-lane build), smoke-net-accept, smoke-network-suite.
a6dd77acb2502c1f896dfddf502252e47430d322:
feat(lwip): drive each lanes TCP timers from the CPU that owns it

tcp_tmr() walked every bucket, so one CPU's tick did the periodic protocol work
for every connection on the machine. With the per-lane counters from 69faea16
that work is now correct to distribute, so this lands the distribution:
kernel_progress_timer_tick() has every CPU walk the lane it owns, via
tcp_tmr_lane().

tcp_tmr() itself is reduced to advancing tcp_ticks. It has to be: it is reached
from sys_check_timeouts() on the same tick that every CPU drives its own lane,
so leaving the walk in place would process every pcb twice per tick -- once via
the global wheel and once via its owner. The slow timer also alternates per
lane on tcp_timer[] parity, so a lane's cadence no longer depends on which CPU
won the race to the global tick.

The clock is advanced before the walks, not after. tcp_ticks is compared
against pcb->tmr throughout the walkers, and the old code incremented it ahead
of the slow-timer walk, so doing the walks first would have shifted every
elapsed-time comparison by one tick.

One correction worth stating: my first cut had the per-CPU walk before the
global tick, and called the fast and slow halves separately, which ran the slow
timer every tick instead of every other. Both were caught before commit, by
reading the diff rather than by a gate -- the gates were green at that point.

What the gates do and do not cover: smoke-net-accept is the real TCP evidence
here, since it drives actual handshakes through these timers in both fast and
lwip modes. smoke-net-lanes-n1 is the invariant guard for CONFIG_NET_LANES == 1
and stays green, and its 4-lane run does show the lanes populated
("lanes: count=4 sockets=1 occupancy: 0 0 1 0"), so the per-CPU path is
executed. But net_stress_test -- which is what that gate actually asserts on --
does not reach the TCP path at all, so it is a much weaker witness for this
change than its name suggests. Verified: smoke-net-lanes-n1, smoke-net-accept,
smoke-network-suite.
32cd967579990c39a7f8a5bc96d7ef80e362b517:
revert(net): restore lwIP timeout-gated TCP timer cadence

This reverts ffc776e6. The idea was wrong: it drove the TCP timers from
kernel_progress_timer_tick() instead of from behind sys_check_timeouts()'s
interval gate, and that gate was the only thing keeping the cadence correct.

kernel_progress_timer_tick() runs far more often than TCP_TMR_INTERVAL -- a
4-CPU guest produced roughly 850 ticks in 15 seconds, against a 250 ms
interval's nominal 4/sec. So tcp_slowtmr() ran about 14x too often. That does
not slow anything down, it advances pcb->rtime ~14x faster than wall clock, so
every connection hits its retransmission timeout almost immediately and live
PCBs get torn down mid-transfer. A new gate caught it as a kernel page fault in
tcp_pcb_remove() called from the RST path, with a corrupted list pointer.

The per-lane counters from 69faea16 are kept. They are sound: each lane reads
and stamps its own tcp_timer_ctr, and a pcb only ever appears in the bucket of
the lane that owns it, so the dedup stays exact. What was wrong is only the
dispatch -- there is no way to spread the timer across CPUs without first
giving the per-lane tick its own interval gate, and that gate has to be the one
lwIP already owns rather than a second one invented here.

tcp_accept_test now takes an optional port so a future multi-lane gate can place
connections on more than one lane; the default is unchanged, so the existing
gate is unaffected.

Verified after the revert: smoke-net-accept passes again in both TCP modes.
451511cb727dce186127371e2b1f9cc12fd92214:
docs(net): record multi-lane boot panics after LISTEN PCB allocation

Found while writing stage C's gate, and it predates every change on this
branch, so it blocks C and D rather than following from them.

With 4 lanes, 4 CPUs and a20.tcpmode=lwip, the kernel takes a page fault in
the idle task on CPU 0 during boot, before any test program runs, with
tcp_listen=1 already true because telnetd's wildcard bind has created a real
lwIP listening pcb. Reached through TCP the stack is
ethernet_output -> tcp_pcb_remove with a corrupted list pointer, so the list
is being walked off a bad head rather than hitting a null check.

Ruled out rather than assumed: reverting tcp.c entirely to before this
branch's timer work still reproduces it, so it is not the per-lane counters
or the per-CPU dispatch. And smoke-net-lanes-n1 is also 4 lanes and 4 CPUs
but stays green, because the default fast mode never creates a real lwIP
LISTEN pcb. So the trigger is the interaction of the bucketing with a real
listening pcb, not multi-lane by itself.

The likely cause is recorded as a lead, not a conclusion: NET_PCB_LANE_ANY is
one past the last real lane and only NET_PCB_LANE_BUCKETS accounts for it, so
any CONFIG_NET_LANES-sized array indexed by a wildcard-bound pcb's lane reads
one element out of bounds. That matches a corrupted head pointer, but it is
unverified and the commit says so. Next step is to narrow the trigger with
NET_LANES=2 and NR_CPUS=1 before touching tcp_pcb_remove.
9cd19dac7d70296d21712d0bb22585925788f285:
docs(net): treat the intermittent multi-lane panic as a race

The reproducer narrowed the trigger but then stopped reproducing: 4 lanes,
4 CPUs and a real listening pcb panicked inside the gate, and a bare rerun of
the same configuration with the same status read came back clean. 1 CPU with
the same lanes and listening pcb is also clean.

That reframes the finding. A deterministic out-of-bounds on the wildcard
sentinel bucket would fire on every boot with those settings, so the rerun
argues against it, and a stray OOB read does not explain a corrupted list head
nearly as well as concurrent mutation does. The faulting context is sometimes
tcp_accept_test and sometimes idle, and the idle case fires before any test
program runs, which fits a background racer better than a deterministic path.

Recorded as a lead rather than a conclusion, and the next step changed
accordingly: an assertion or a static check will not find this. It needs
concurrent pressure across lanes, a lock audit, or a detector that can amplify
the window. The trigger conditions stand as measured.
bad91f6d0b91b214833895612243314281eadafc:
docs(net): rule out the socket/PCB lane mismatch keep it as a stage d blocker

The wildcard-bind case makes the two lane notions disagree. telnetd binds
INADDR_ANY, where net_socket_lane_of_addr() returns net_lane_of(0, port) -- a
real lane in 0..N-1 -- while NET_PCB_LANE_OF_PCB() returns the sentinel bucket
NET_PCB_LANE_ANY, which is N. So the socket can claim lane 2 while its pcb sits
in bucket 4.

It is not the cause of the boot panic, and saying so matters: net_socket_t::lane
is written in exactly two places and read nowhere, so no dispatch, lock choice
or bucket index consults it yet. Stage A left the field; stage D consumes it.

Kept because it becomes a live bug the moment stage D selects a processing lane
from the socket's lane: a wildcard-bound listener would be dispatched to a lane
that does not own its pcb, while sentinel-bucket pcbs are walked by no lane's
timers at all. That makes the two notions needing to agree on the any-address
case a precondition for stage D rather than a cleanup.
641f7b78521b5b7bab71d38426ce6a90313f930d:
docs(net): rule out sentinel-bucket out-of-bounds by inspecting every list array

The standing suspicion was that some CONFIG_NET_LANES-sized array gets indexed
by a wildcard pcb's NET_PCB_LANE_ANY, which is N -- one past the last real lane
-- and so reads a corrupted list head. That would match the fault, so it was
worth checking rather than leaving as folklore.

It does not hold. tcp_bound_pcbs, tcp_listen_pcbs, tcp_active_pcbs,
tcp_tw_pcbs, tcp_timer[] and tcp_timer_ctr[] are all declared
[NET_PCB_LANE_BUCKETS], which is N+1 and does account for the sentinel.
tcp_pcb_lists[] is indexed by state and then by lane over struct tcp_pcb **,
which matches those arrays, and all three tcp_listen_pcbs uses are bounded by
NET_PCB_LANE_BUCKETS. So no array is too short for a sentinel pcb.

Two candidates are now eliminated by inspection (this one and the socket/PCB
lane mismatch) and the faulting context is sometimes idle, which keeps pointing
at a race over concurrent list mutation rather than a stray index. The lead is
recorded as disproved so the next session does not re-derive it.
95f02790e07293c1ab84ba0aee37f079ea7d4f89:
docs(net): explain how disabled core-lock assertions HID the defect

LWIP_ASSERT_CORE_LOCKED() is defined as an empty macro at lwip opt.h:227, so
every one of the several dozen LWIP_ASSERT_CORE_LOCKED() calls in tcp.c and
tcp_in.c -- tcp_close, tcp_abort, tcp_bind, tcp_new, tcp_input and the rest --
compiles to nothing. The lane-bucketing work in this branch relies on a lock
contract that has no runtime enforcement at all; network-lock-contract.md is
documentation, not an invariant the kernel checks.

That is not the bug, but it is why the bug is survivable. Any path reaching
tcp_pcb_remove() or tcp_listen_closed() without g_lwip_lock held quietly
corrupts a lane list, and the existing sanity checks cannot help: tcp_pcbs_sane()
only works while it is still safe to walk the list, which is exactly what the
corruption prevents. The other lwIP assertions do not help either, since they
fire on the same walk.

This sharpens the next step away from "find a bad index" -- two index theories
are already disproved -- and toward auditing whether every path into
tcp_pcb_remove() and tcp_listen_closed() actually holds g_lwip_lock. RST
generation on the ethernet_output side and netif address changes (which reach
tcp_listen_pcb_rebucket and move a LISTEN pcb across lanes) are the two that
still fit both known conditions: multiple CPUs, and a real LISTEN pcb.

Recommended first step is cheap and makes later work safer: wire
LWIP_ASSERT_CORE_LOCKED() to the real held state of g_lwip_lock in this
configuration, so the contract becomes executable and every later lane change
has a regression guard.
7931a1ffc47fab4244a1ff86cc42ff5a61c8ba16:
docs(net): record the lock audit came back negative so stop auditing by hand

Walked every caller of tcp_pcb_remove() and tcp_listen_closed() checking for a
missing g_lwip_lock, expecting to find one. None of them are missing it.

The accept stage drain wraps each tcp_abort(), each options install and the
child teardown in a20_lwip_lock(); there is no bare tcp_abort anywhere in the
tree. The RST side's callers sit under a20_lwip_process_netif_rx_tx_locked().
a20_lwip_if_set_addr() takes the lock before netif_set_ipaddr(), so the
cross-lane LISTEN pcb move in tcp_listen_pcb_rebucket() is locked. The accept
callback's producer pairs a release fence with an acquire load, which is a
correct SPSC ring, and the bottom-half pass holds only g_net_lock but never
touches lwIP core.

A negative result is worth writing down because it changes what to do next.
Hand-auditing further has low expected value, and the remaining possibilities
are either in paths not examined or are not a missing lock at all -- they are
ordering between tcp_listen_closed() rewriting ->listener across every lane and
an accept drain running on another CPU, which is inside the lock either way and
therefore invisible to static reading.

So the next step is to stop reading and start measuring: turn on
LWIP_ASSERT_CORE_LOCKED() behind a config knob and let it localise the window.
e80e195b419698159ca7fd11840055962d7f5c18:
docs(net): record evidence that the lock contract holds and locate the race inside it

The static audit found no missing g_lwip_lock. This confirms that with runtime
evidence rather than leaving it as an absence of findings.

Temporarily wired LWIP_ASSERT_CORE_LOCKED() to the real held state of g_lwip_lock,
recording the owning CPU rather than a flag -- a flag would read "held" while a
different CPU held the lock, which is the case worth catching. Violations were
counted, not panicked on, and the first eight distinct return addresses were
kept. On a 4-lane a20.tcpmode=lwip boot: violations=23, sites=8, and all eight
symbolize to one-shot bootstrap paths -- netif_init twice, netif_add,
netif_add_ip6_address, lwip_init, a20_lwip_init twice, and
a20_lwip_loopif_init_cb. Not one violation landed in the receive, accept, timer
or pcb add/remove paths.

Two consequences. "Some path forgot g_lwip_lock" is now falsified at runtime, not
merely unfound, and panicking would have been the wrong choice: those init calls
would kill every configuration at boot. And the race must therefore be inside the
lock, or outside lwIP entirely -- two CPUs taking the lock serially cannot corrupt
a list unless something they share is mutated while neither holds the lock. The
next search should be for fields written under one lock and read under the other,
which is what the "g_lwip_lock and g_net_lock are never held together" convention
leaves uncovered, rather than for more missing locks.

The probe itself is not kept. It turned smoke-net-accept red and I rolled it back
as my own mistake; the actual cause was /tmp filling with QEMU traces so the
compiler could not write its temp assembly, unrelated to the code -- clearing them
made the same commit pass again. It was verified working under -Werror and
produced the data above, so reconnecting it is enough to continue.
a9d7e2e1768fa25aa58c4cc532a58ec33f358c8e:
fix(net): correct the locks are never held together invariant it is false

The lane work on this branch reasoned from a stated invariant: g_lwip_lock and
g_net_lock are never held together, so a new per-lane lock layer would start
from a blank sheet. That invariant is not true of the tree.

net_inet_bottom_half_process_all() takes g_net_lock at socket_inet.c:871 and
calls the accept drain inside that critical section, and
net_inet_accept_stage_drain() takes a20_lwip_lock() at socket_inet.c:607, 616
and 640. So on the accept path both locks are held at once, in the order
net -> lwip. Five places asserted the opposite, including the header comment on
the lock itself and the lock contract document.

This is worth correcting now rather than when it bites, because stage D is
exactly the work that would trip it: draining a receive ring per lane means
touching socket state from lwIP context, which introduces the reverse order
and deadlocks against the path that already exists. There is no ABBA cycle
today only because nothing takes g_lwip_lock and then g_net_lock, so the
asymmetry is the thing to preserve, not an accident to rely on.

The comment now states the real order and names the hazard, and the lock
contract document carries a correction at the top so the remaining "never held
together" mentions are read against it rather than taken literally.

Verified: build clean under -Werror, smoke-net-accept passes. The panic this
branch is chasing is still unexplained -- this finding is a landmine removed
from the path ahead, not the fault itself.
4c5174def610a8294d1a9dfba5639a94012b1ac5:
fix(net): fix the same false claim in the lane-occupancy comment

Scanned the tree for the reverse nesting to check whether the corrected

g_net_lock, so the order really is one-way today and there is no deadlock to

is a false positive -- it drops g_lwip_lock before taking g_net_lock, which is

Its comment still asserted the disproved "never held together", so it now
states why the drop matters: the accept path nests net -> lwip, so this path
must not nest the other way. Same correction as the lock header, one function
over.
2c4f2e0c6e4f51b9bfe20a3bb781a8d2568a72fe:
docs(net): correct an over-claim about the lock probes coverage

The previous commit said the missing-g_lwip_lock hypothesis was "falsified at
runtime". That was too strong and this corrects it.

The probe can only observe functions that actually carry the assertion. 45
functions in tcp.c have no LWIP_ASSERT_CORE_LOCKED(), and among them is
tcp_abort() at tcp.c:650 -- the RST/abort path, which is exactly where the
tcp_pcb_remove fault lives. The probe is therefore blind to the most suspicious

What the data does support: every entry point that has an assertion held the

The blind spot is cheap to close -- add assertions to the unasserted entry

Also recorded: tcp_kill_state, tcp_kill_prio and tcp_kill_timewait walk every

tree, making them dead code and excludable.

test(lwip): assert the unasserted list mutators then measure them
