25a16d8c9423401872b51f2e247c529d26b0e7f8:
fix(gfx): stop the DRM object store from racing with itself

Every device-global table in drm.c -- the GEM store, the framebuffer table,
the CRTC binding, the GEM name table, the PRIME table, the virgl id counters
and the EDID cache -- was searched, mutated and torn down with no mutual
exclusion at all. Only the vblank slot was locked.

Those tables are shared by design: a buffer created through one open has to
be visible to another, which is why the GEM store is device-wide rather than
per-fd. That makes the race reachable by construction, because the desktop
drives it from two processes at once -- the wlroots allocator creates buffers
on one fd and the backend consumes them on another. Two concurrent ioctls
could hand out the same handle, drop a table entry while another CPU walked
it, or free a VMO that a third ioctl was still reading.

The lock protects the tables and nothing else. Anything that can sleep,
allocate, enter the VFS or issue a virtio command runs after it is dropped,
with the object pinned across the gap, so teardown is split in two:
drm_gem_detach_locked() takes the object out of the tables under the lock and
drm_gem_drop_storage() releases the VMO and the host resource after it. The
pin count is deliberately not an owner count -- it does not keep a buffer
alive past its last owner, it only stops the storage vanishing underneath a
caller that is mid-operation.

That refactor is what makes the correctness fixes below safe to express, so
they land with it:

- PRIME imported by fd *number*. The kernel recycles an fd as soon as
  userspace closes it, so the table handed out the old GEM handle for
  whatever unrelated file now held that slot -- and GEM handles are mmap-able
  through drm_linux_mmap(), which turns a stale entry into a way to read a
  buffer this process never owned. Entries are now keyed on vfile.identity,
  a monotonic per-open id, and an export the user has closed is evicted before
  the table is declared full. An fd that cannot be recorded is no longer
  returned: previously the 65th export got a working fd that could never be
  imported, surfacing much later as an unexplained ENOENT.

- RESOURCE_ATTACH_BACKING compacted its page list. The host places entry n at
  offset n * PAGE_SIZE, so one page that failed to materialise made entry 3
  become page 4's frame and the renderer drew into a buffer it was never
  given, reported as success. A partial page set is now a failure.

- A buffer promoted to a 3D resource twice leaked the previous host resource,
  because virgl_res_id was overwritten without an unref.

- drm_close() required ops->ctx_destroy to be present and then never called
  it, so every renderD128 open that touched 3D leaked a host context for the
  life of the guest.

- The EDID lazy init ran the device fetch under a lock it must not hold, and
  the ready flag was published without a barrier.

- Handle allocation skipped 0 but not live handles, so a wrapped counter could
  alias an existing buffer.

lock-order.md gains the missing rows and a contract section: g_drm_store.lock
is innermost, must never be held across the VFS (vfs_get_file_ref can reach a
file close op, and file_close_prepare calls that while holding g_file_lock),
and must never be held together with g_vblank.lock -- drm_close() is the one
path that needs both and drops the vblank lock first.
5110ee063551ece20dfb936cb6c66a2a1ea9f6cf:
feat(virtio-gpu): build ATTACH_BACKING under the command lock

virtio_gpu_resource_attach_backing() resized, kfree'd, memset and memcpy'd
the shared inst->big_req buffer with no lock held at all, and only then took
inst->command_lock -- which up to that point covered nothing but the response
buffer and the descriptor work.

inst->big_req is one buffer for the whole instance, and both
virtio_gpu_send_cmd_big() and virtio_gpu_submit_3d() grow, free and refill it
under that same lock. DRM calls ATTACH_BACKING once per buffer from every
EXECBUFFER, so two clients overlap here in practice: the second could kfree the
buffer while the first was still filling it, and two mem_entry tables could
land in one request body. With two processes exporting buffers this is a
use-after-free on the DMA path, not a theoretical one.

The lock now spans the whole staging area -- resize, body fill, DMA sync,
response buffer, descriptors, completion poll -- with exactly one release on
every path including both -ENOMEM returns and the poll timeout. The s0
descriptor's va_to_pa(inst->big_req) is now necessarily computed after the
reallocation rather than from the pointer the kfree dropped.

The same commit fixes the two completion loops that did not park.
virtio_gpu_submit_3d and virtio_gpu_resource_attach_backing spun on
arch_cpu_relax() plus a bare proc_yield() while holding command_lock, so a
guest with an unparked vCPU burned a core in userspace and any other task
waiting for the instance lock stalled behind it. Both now use the same
Park/Wake wait the two loops that already worked use, copied rather than
invented. ATTACH_BACKING additionally had no deadline at all -- only the
100M spin cap -- and now uses the same one-second bound as the other two.

Not fixed here, because it needs a teardown-wide decision rather than a local
change: virtio_gpu_remove() and the init_transport fail path memset the whole
instance, including command_lock and waiters, without the lock. That drops a
mutex other tasks may be blocked in and clears a wait queue that may have
linked waiters. It overlaps virtio_gpu.c's initialisation lifecycle and
deserves its own change.
8f8164a5bba6ab3a2ed0c7ca46cb8763b827081e:
feat(gpu): prefer a 3D-capable device as the DRM backend

gpu_device_register() assigned g_default_gpu only if the slot was empty, so
the first display device to probe won permanently. Two drivers register:
virtio-gpu carries the full 3D vtable, while vmsvga's vmsvga_ops fills in only
get_info/get_fb/flush/ioctl/get_features and leaves every 3D entry point NULL.

DRM resolves its backend exclusively through gpu_device_get_default() and
guards each VIRTGPU ioctl with its own NULL check, so when vmsvga happened to
probe first every DRM_IOCTL_VIRTGPU_* call returned -ENODEV -- silently, with
DRM_CAP_PRIME and GETPARAM still advertising capabilities and no log line
anywhere saying which device was actually bound.

Selection is now promotion-only: a 3D-capable newcomer may displace a 2D-only
incumbent, but two equally capable devices never trade the slot, so probe order
cannot churn the binding. The unregister path already re-tested identity under
the lock, which is exactly what keeps a displaced device from clearing the slot
on its way out; that is now stated, and both paths log the outcome so a guest
whose 3D path is dead says so.

gpu_core.h's "first display device that completes probe owns /dev/fb0" was
made false by this and would have misled the next reader.

Not fixed: gpu_device_unregister() still clears the slot outright when the
incumbent dies, with no re-election among surviving devices, so tearing down a
promoted virtio-gpu while vmsvga is still registered leaves DRM with no
backend. That hole predates this change but promotion makes it reachable in
the new direction. Fixing it properly needs a second slot to remember the
runner-up, which changes the getter's contract.
c7ca30010c2da1fc1844eb755d8913620a5fe27e:
fix(gfx): bound buffer geometry and give it a falsifiable gate

CREATE_DUMB computed its pitch as ((width * bpp + 7) / 8 + 63) & ~63u -- a
uint32_t multiply that truncates -- and then multiplied the result by height
with nothing bounding the total. Measured against the old arithmetic:

  65536 x 65536 x 32  ->  pitch 262144, size 17179869184  (16 GiB)
  16384 x  8192 x 32  ->  pitch  65536, size  536870912  (0.5 GiB)

Nothing rejected those. CREATE_DUMB passed the 16 GiB straight to vmo_create,
and PRIME export then did kmalloc(b->size) to snapshot it -- a single ioctl
pair asking the kernel for 16 GiB of anonymous VMO plus 16 GiB of heap. The
private GEM_CREATE ioctl had no bound either.

The wrap itself was quieter than it looks: the truncated pitch and the size
computed from it stayed consistent with each other, so no extent invariant was
violated. What it produced was a real buffer whose geometry bore no relation to
the request, answered as if it were honoured. The genuinely dangerous case was
the missing cap.

The arithmetic moves to kernel/include/drivers/gpu/drm_geom.h as
drm_dumb_layout(), 64-bit throughout, refusing a request it cannot represent
and anything above DRM_MAX_BUFFER_BYTES. That cap is not a round number picked
for looks: 256 MiB is exactly the largest resource the 3D transport will
publish, because drm_gem_attach_backing() already refuses more than 65536
pages, so one limit now covers both the VMO and the export snapshot. The bound
is enforced in drm_gem_alloc_locked(), the single place that hands out a
buffer, so CREATE_DUMB and GEM_CREATE cannot diverge again.

It lives in a kernel-free header on purpose: the part that has to be right here
is overflow arithmetic, not locking, and a host test can only check what it can
compile. tools/tests/drm_geom_test.c drives it directly and is picked up by the
existing `make host-tests` wildcard, so the gate needs no new target.

The gate is verified to fail: restoring the old arithmetic to
drm_dumb_layout() aborts the test on the 0xffffffff x 32 case (exit 134),
against PASS with the fix in place.
221a11f657a67a1b16db36af29ea1f164eaa2365:
fix(gfx): make the KMS surface stop claiming things it does not do

Five places where the ioctl surface answered success for something it had not
done, so a client could not tell a working driver from a lying one.

GETPROPBLOB reported success without copying when b.data was NULL or shorter
than the blob, and set b.length to the blob's real size regardless. An EDID
reader was handed its own uninitialised stack and reported a corrupt monitor
where an error belonged. length is the caller's buffer size inbound and the
blob size outbound in this UAPI, so a short buffer now answers -ENOSPC with the
required length and a NULL buffer -EFAULT, which is what lets libdrm size its
buffer and retry.

SET_CLIENT_CAP accepted DRM_CLIENT_CAP_ATOMIC while MODE_ATOMIC answers -EINVAL
for every commit that is not TEST_ONLY. That told libdrm to take the atomic path
and then handed it nothing but errors; the desktop only avoided a fallback storm
because the session sets WLR_DRM_NO_ATOMIC=1. Refusing the cap fails early and
visibly, so the client picks the legacy path itself instead of discovering the
lie at commit time.

GEM_FLINK swallowed a full name table and returned success, so the export looked
fine and the name was simply never bound -- surfacing much later as a GEM_OPEN
-ENOENT with nothing to connect it to. It now answers -ENOSPC.

ADDFB, ADDFB2 and VIRTGPU_RESOURCE_CREATE each took a table slot or a host
resource before the copy-out, so a faulting copy orphaned it: one framebuffer
leaked per call, and for RESOURCE_CREATE a virgl resource the caller never learns
the id of, unreffable by anyone. All three now release what they allocated.

RMFB left the destroyed framebuffer bound to the CRTC, so GETCRTC and GETPLANE
kept reporting an fb_id that GETFB answered -ENOENT for. Linux lets a bound
framebuffer be destroyed, so the binding follows the object rather than
outliving it.

Separately, the render node only refused SET_MASTER. Every other KMS ioctl was
reachable from /dev/dri/renderD128, so a GBM or EGL process there could call
MODE_SETCRTC and take the screen out from under the compositor -- and is_master
was never consulted by any KMS handler, so the master flag was never protection
either. The render node now rejects the KMS and master ioctls, which is what
docs/graphics/3d-graphics.md already claimed it did ("KMS ioctl 本就需要
master"). Linux rejects CREATE_DUMB on a render node too, so GBM already opens
the primary node for dumb buffers and nothing that works on Linux depends on the
old behaviour.

That last one is a behaviour change on a path that cannot be exercised without a
desktop instance, so it wants a GPU_3D=0 xfce-* smoke run before it lands
anywhere it matters.
9af09f9c10e734a046d5b449f6929d855b89db43:
test(gates): pin the DRM store contract and let a gate count

The three previous commits are only worth anything if they hold. A presence
assertion cannot do that on its own: "g_drm_store.lock occurs in drm.c" stays
green when the locking is stripped out of the handlers, because the name still
appears in the definition and in a handful of other places. So gates.py grows a
min_count key, and check-drm-store-locking uses it.

min_count exists because I got this wrong first and the gate did not notice. A
draft of this gate asserted only that the lock, the detach/free split and the
pin/unpin pair occur somewhere in drm.c. Deleting one drm_lock() from
drm_gem_unpin() left it passing, 13/13. Counting matches is the only way a
source assertion can see one fewer lock, so the key parses `rg -c` output and
fails below a floor set well under the real count, leaving room for refactors.

Falsification is verified in both directions: removing 15 lock/unlock pairs
takes the count to 26 and the assertion fails; deleting the lock-order.md
contract fails the two doc assertions; restoring both returns 13/13.

The new gate also pins the detach-under-lock / free-after-unlock split, the pin
pair, command_lock in virtio_gpu.c, and the buffer cap -- with the matching
lock-order.md prose asserted so code and contract cannot drift apart silently.
check-doc-test-gates now runs check-drm-store-locking and check-drm-abi, which
previously sat outside the aggregate.

What this gate cannot do, and the comment in gates.toml says so: catch ONE
deleted call site in ONE handler. A source-pattern gate has no view of control
flow. The counts are there to catch wholesale removal; per-handler discipline
is what the SMP smoke tests are for.

Two smaller notes. `rg -c` prints a bare count for one file and `file:count` for
several, and the first version of the parser only accepted the second form -- so
the count silently read as zero and the assertion was unsatisfiable. Worth the
comment, because it is a quiet failure rather than a loud one. And
check-doc-drift fails in a fresh worktree until a build has generated
user/svc/a20_services_idl.h; that file is gitignored and comes from the IDL
toolchain, so it is pre-existing and self-resolving, not something these
commits introduced.
9eea2f44e33740bc0eb9a71dd09f8c2926df8d9f:
docs(graphics): summarize the changes made by graphics hardening

3d-graphics.md's status table and a new section in it, plus a testing-gates.md
entry for the new lock-contract gate.

The table's PRIME row said "not implemented" and left it there, which was only
half true. The sharing is still a snapshot rather than a shared mapping, so the
row stays ❌ -- but the export/import path itself was returning a stale GEM
handle for a recycled fd number, and that part is now fixed and worth saying, so
a reader does not re-diagnose it as part of the missing dma-buf work.

The new section follows the file's existing habit of writing down what a round
did *and* what it deliberately did not: virtio_gpu_remove() memsets the whole
instance including command_lock and the wait queue without the lock, which needs
a device-level teardown lock or in-flight reference counting rather than a local
change, and gpu_device_unregister() still clears the slot outright without
re-electing among surviving devices.

It also flags the one behaviour change in the round that touches a working
desktop -- the render node now rejecting KMS ioctls -- and says it wants a
GPU_3D=0 xfce smoke run before it goes anywhere that matters. That path cannot
be exercised without a desktop instance, and saying so is more useful than
implying the tree was fully verified.
ea707346e034e121b71bd7548eefd620f28aad8e:
fix(gfx): fix a use-after-free the store refactor left in the PRIME export

An independent review of the locking work found four real bugs, one of them
serious and one of them mine. All four are in the code the previous commits
introduced or touched.

The use-after-free: drm_prime_handle_to_fd() snapshotted b->vmo under the store
lock, dropped the lock, and then walked the pages without pinning the GEM. The
GEM store is device-global, so a DESTROY_DUMB or GEM_CLOSE on any fd reaches
drm_free_gem() during that walk, sees pins == 0, and drops the VMO. The loop
then reads page_count out of a freed vmo, takes its spinlock -- a write into
freed memory -- and copies whatever now occupies those physical frames into the
memfd it then hands to a different process. The export path pins now, which is
what setcrtc, pageflip and drm_linux_mmap already did; this was the one call
site the pin protocol was not applied to.

The GEM name table was documented as store-lock protected but the lookup that
walks it took no lock, so a GEM_OPEN racing a detach could read a torn
name/handle pair and return a handle for a buffer that was never bound to that
name -- and handles are mmap-able, so the importer would read a different buffer
than the name designates. The helper is now _locked and runs inside the lock
region drm_gem_open already had.

Both of the next two are in the eviction loop I wrote. The probe array stored fd
identities in an int, truncating a uint64 vfile.identity that climbs by one on
every vfile_alloc() system-wide; past 2^31 the truncated value can never match
the table, so every entry would be judged dead and the table wiped on each
export. And the dead test matched on the fd number and took the first hit, which
evicts a *live* entry as soon as two entries share an fd number -- which happens
as soon as a closed memfd's number is reused, because the two probe lines for
that number resolve separately and can report different identities. Dead now
means no probe line agrees, and the probe is 64-bit.

The review also found four smaller ones, all fixed here: drm_gem_unpin() now
saturates at zero, because one stray extra unpin would drive pins to -1 and the
buffer would then never be reclaimed at all -- a silent permanent leak of the VMO
and the host resource; drm_gem_attach_backing() reads virgl_res_id under the lock
and only claims backing_attached for the resource it actually attached, since a
concurrent RESOURCE_CREATE could otherwise leave a new resource marked-backed
that is not; the attach-failure rollback in RESOURCE_CREATE is id-guarded like
its copy_to_user sibling, which without it wipes a concurrent install and leaks
it on the host; and the copy_to_user failure path keeps its pin and clears the id
under the lock before unreffing, so drop_storage cannot unref the same id twice.

One more from the same theme, pre-existing: a PRIME entry could outlive its GEM,
and importing it returned a handle that drm_gem_alloc_locked() may already have
handed to a different buffer. The import now verifies the GEM is still live.

lock-order.md claimed drm_close() drops g_vblank.lock before acquiring the store
lock. It never acquires the store lock at all -- it is correct today, and the doc
said so in a way that would only become load-bearing if table cleanup were added.
Reworded to describe the code rather than a constraint that does not exist yet.

Deadlock and lock/unlock balance were both verified clean: only two locks are
ever taken in this file, no path holds both, and all 35 lock-taking functions
release exactly once per exit.
15c3fc25fee114d136487092fbc64fdda2dd6150:
feat(gfx): send a capset id to GET_CAPSET not a capset index

DRM_IOCTL_VIRTGPU_GET_CAPS always failed with
VIRTIO_GPU_RESP_ERR_INVALID_PARAMETER (0x1205), which is what stopped Mesa's
virtio_gpu_dri.so from ever attaching and made the whole 3D path look blocked
on the host.

It was never blocked on the host. The two commands are addressed differently
and the driver conflated them: GET_CAPSET_INFO takes an *index*, GET_CAPSET
takes a capset *id*. drm_virtgpu_capset_index() dutifully resolved the id
CONTEXT_INIT had selected down to an index and then put that index in the
request. Index 0 is capset id 1, so the host was asked for a capset that does
not exist.

QEMU passes the field straight to virgl_renderer_get_cap_set(), whose switch
covers ids 1 (VIRGL), 2 (VIRGL2), 4 (Venus) and 6 (DRM) and whose default arm
reports a zero-length capset. QEMU turns a zero length into exactly the
0x1205 we were seeing -- an error that reads like "this renderer cannot build a
GL context", which is how it came to be recorded as a host limitation.

The fix resolves an id instead: the client's CONTEXT_INIT choice when the host
advertises it, else VIRTIO_GPU_CAPSET_VIRGL. The transport now looks the id up
in the GET_CAPSET_INFO table before sending, both to size the response and to
reject an id the host does not have instead of asking for it and reading 0x1205
back. The requested version is clamped to what the host reports, and 0 now
means "whatever you have" rather than a version that does not exist.

The wire field is renamed capset_index -> capset_id to match the virtio spec.
Both are a little-endian u32 at the same offset, so this is documentation that
makes the next mistake visible rather than an ABI change.

Verified: tools/a20 test smoke-gpu3d-riscv64 now reaches "GET_CAPS returned a
308 byte capset", where before it reported "GET_CAPS unavailable on this host".
The gate still fails on its pixel readback, which is the next problem and is
recorded honestly rather than folded into this fix.
35e958dc62ef4099a4ad35ef93e96cb656cf3090:
feat(gfx): resolve PRIME fds in the task table and unblock the x86_64 GUI

The PRIME identity work in the previous-but-one commit was wrong in a way only
the guest could show me. drm_fd_identity() asked vfs_get_file_ref() about the fd
memfd_create_file() returned, but those are two different namespaces:
memfd_create_file() hands back a task-table descriptor -- memfd_set_contents()
resolves it with fdtable_get_current() -- while vfs_get_file_ref() reads the
global g_files[] table. The lookup therefore always came back empty and every
export returned -EIO.

Caught it by running the real desktop: wlroots' drm_dumb allocator logged
"Failed to get PRIME handle from GEM handle: I/O error" followed by "Failed to
allocate buffer". Fixed by resolving through fdtable_get_current_file_ref(),
which is the table the fd actually lives in. vfile.identity is a monotonic
per-open id, so it stays unique across both namespaces and an fd received over
SCM_RIGHTS resolves to the same value.

With that fixed, wlroots' buffer allocation succeeds and the session presents.

Also here, all three found by running the xfce-x86_64 instance rather than by
reading it:

[machine]. memory. d52c8ccb moved DEFAULT_MEMORY, DEFAULT_MEMORY_GUI and
DEFAULT_VCPUS into a20_resource.py without adding them to the import list in
tools/a20, so the GPU smoke gate could not be run at all.

QEMU_GUI_DEVICES_x86_64 had no keyboard or mouse. wlroots' multi backend tries
libinput first and aborts the whole session when it finds none -- it does not
fall through to DRM -- so the x86_64 desktop could never reach a display, and
start-xfce4-session does not set WLR_LIBINPUT_NO_DEVICES because the desktop is
meant to be usable. loongarch64 already had both.

The gpu3d smoke gate now asks for egl-headless,gl=on instead of gtk,gl=on.

all; egl-headless with gl=on can. The comment now records what actually has to
be true for it to work rather than asserting that egl-headless cannot.
405fbd9b0dae79ad4a915554192f152be1b89d4b:
feat(tools): add a headless virgl display wrapper

On a host with both a proprietary and an open GPU driver, GPU_3D=1 silently
produces a 2D-only guest device. QEMU needs an offscreen GL context for
virglrenderer, and three separate things have to line up for it to get one:

the EGL vendor has to be Mesa, because glvnd picks the proprietary driver by
default and that EGL has no device/surfaceless platform virgl can use; Mesa has
to be prevented from enumerating the proprietary GPU's node, which fails
eglInitialize under Mesa and which QEMU does not fall through; and
egl-headless needs gl=on explicitly or QEMU refuses to create the device at
all.

None of that fails loudly. QEMU hands the guest a working 2D device and the

producing another misleading 2D-only guest.

capset was unavailable.

0d90c7e2f416ff99343c461f7137aa0c7c268010:
test(tools.virgl-probe): inspect the host clear stream and report what it demonstrates

The guest gate can only say "the host accepted a 76 byte clear stream and the
pixels did not change". That leaves the two interesting questions open -- is the
stream wrong, or is the plumbing wrong -- and answering either through QEMU
costs a multi-minute boot per attempt.

This runs the same virglrenderer calls in-process: init, context_create,
resource_create, attach_iov, submit_cmd, with the same 76-byte stream
user/cmds/core/gpu3d_test.c builds. vrend's own diagnostics become visible,
which is the whole point -- QEMU never registers a virglrenderer log callback,
so virgl_logv() returns immediately and vrend says nothing at all inside QEMU.

What running it settles, in the guest's favour:

- The A20OS transport is not at fault. A kernel-side probe placed immediately
  after the submit, reading the buffer through that same frame, still saw the
  sentinel 0xdeadbeef -- with the resource live (virgl=1), the backing attached,
  and the page materialised. The bytes are delivered; the host simply never
  wrote them. That also rules out cache coherency, which had been the leading
  suspicion.
- The failure reproduces exactly with no guest and no QEMU: submit_cmd returns
  22 (EINVAL) and the page is untouched.
- vrend latches ctx->in_error on the first bad command and every later command
  then silently no-ops, so one wrong length early in the stream makes the whole
  frame a no-op while every virtio response still reports OK.

Two corrections it forced, both previously guessed wrong:

- PIPE_TEXTURE_2D is 2, not 1. enum pipe_texture_target starts at PIPE_BUFFER,
  so 2D is the third entry. The test already passed the right value; the probe
  was wrong.
- vrend requires length == 2 + nr_cbufs for SET_FRAMEBUFFER_STATE, i.e. 3 for
  one colour buffer. The test was right there too.

So the remaining defect is a command length somewhere in the stream, and it now
takes seconds rather than a boot to find.
3571c0863cd5d9d38915ef75430a159f9a6dffd3:
docs(graphics): replace the cache-coherency guess with what the host probe proved

The previous entry guessed that the host DMA'd into guest RAM and the guest read

Replace the guess with the mechanism, which is that vrend latches ctx->in_error
on the first bad command and silently no-ops every later one, so one wrong length
makes the whole frame a no-op while every virtio response still says OK. Record

because the enum starts at PIPE_BUFFER, and SET_FRAMEBUFFER_STATE wants 2 +

1cc6b28c9fa0d7021a331df7b24a2107bca061b6:
test(tools-virgl-probe): make the probe able to report what it exists to find

The probe was built to answer "does the host execute the stream, or only accept
the bytes", and it could not answer it: it registered no log callback, so
vrend's diagnostics -- the only thing that names the rejected command -- went
nowhere.  QEMU never registers one either, which is why vrend is silent inside
QEMU.  Registering one via virgl_set_log_callback is the fix, and it immediately
paid for itself.

It also had three bugs of its own, each of which manufactured a failure that
looked like a kernel bug:

  - VIRGL_FORMAT_B8G8R8A8_UNORM was 2.  It is 1; 2 is B8G8R8X8_UNORM.
  - virgl_renderer_ctx_attach_resource was never called.  virglrenderer looks a
    resource up by walking the *context's* table, not a global one, so every
    command naming it failed as "Illegal resource" -- the very symptom the tool
    was meant to explain, caused by the tool.
  - make_current was missing before resource_create.  Measured afterwards as not
    actually load-bearing, but kept so the probe mirrors QEMU's ordering; the
    comment now says so rather than claiming it is required.

A transfer read is added alongside the direct iov read.  That is not redundant:
with the clear working, the attached iov still held the sentinel while
transfer_read_iov returned the rendered pixel, which separates "the clear never
ran" from "the clear ran and stayed in the host's GL object".

The README's old conclusions are replaced, because two of them were wrong.  The
clear stream is correct as encoded -- every length matches virglrenderer 1.3.0 --
and the "Illegal command buffer <garbage>" line is the abort path re-reporting
the next header dword, i.e. a consequence of the first rejection rather than
independent evidence of a misaligned stream.
181ba6417297a5f5d22effbb81fee69f4c04bffb:
fix(gfx): stop handing the host a truncated SUBMIT_3D command stream

This is why the 3D path never produced a pixel, and it was invisible from the
guest for a reason that made it look like something else entirely.

The host extracts the command body like this (QEMU hw/display/
virtio-gpu-virgl.c, virgl_cmd_submit_3d):

    iov_to_buf(cmd->elem.out_sg, n, sizeof(struct virtio_gpu_cmd_submit),
               buf, cs.size)

It skips a hardcoded 32 bytes into the request scatter-gather list and reads
cs.size bytes from there.  Our submit_hdr was

    struct { struct virtio_gpu_cmd_submit hdr;
             struct virtio_gpu_mem_entry entry; } submit_hdr ALIGNED(64);

so the descriptor was 64 bytes, not 32.  The host therefore skipped 32, read
the mem_entry and the alignment padding as the first dwords of the command,
and took only the remaining 44 bytes of the 76-byte clear stream.  Every
command this driver ever submitted was garbage.

Nothing reported it.  SUBMIT_3D answers OK because the transport genuinely
worked, and the renderer rejects the garbage silently -- the response carries no
decode status.  So the symptom was "host accepted a 76 byte clear stream" next
to an unchanged buffer, which is the shape that sent the previous rounds
looking for a mistyped command length and then for cache incoherency.

Two _Static_asserts pin the wire format.  Growing this type is a one-line
change that would otherwise ship a silently truncated stream to every guest,
and a comment cannot fail; these can.

Verified by measurement, not argument.  With the mem_entry put back and the
asserts temporarily disabled so the runtime gate had to catch it,
smoke-gpu3d-riscv64 goes red with exactly the historical signature:

    GPU3D_TEST: FAIL pass 0: 4096/4096 pixels wrong, first pixel is 0xdeadbeef

Note this commit alone does not turn the gate green; two more defects were
stacked on top of it and are fixed separately.

a7ee5310eeaa10d26c90c1e7a7e4a2a2b0adf50b:
fix(gfx): stop zeroing a live mutex and wait queue on device teardown

Recorded as out of scope two rounds ago and worth closing now.

virtio_gpu_remove() and init_transport's fail: path both did memset(inst, 0,
sizeof(*inst)).  That wipes command_lock -- which a concurrent submit or
transfer may be blocked inside -- and waiters, a queue that may already have
entries linked onto it.  Zeroing either destroys a lock another CPU is parked on
and a wait chain it expects to be woken from, and neither teardown path held the
lock while doing it, so taking it would not have helped.

Replaced with virtio_gpu_release_buffers(), which frees the heap buffers and
clears the scalar state but deliberately leaves command_lock and waiters alone.
The instance lives in static storage, so keeping those initialised is both safe
and correct: this is a teardown, not a reinitialisation.  It also drops the big
request/response buffers, which the blanket memset merely leaked.

What this does not solve, and the comment says so at the definition: a caller
already inside the command path keeps running against a reset transport.  Closing
that needs a device-level teardown lock or an in-flight reference count, which
is an initialisation-lifecycle change and stays a separate item -- as does
gpu_device_unregister() still not re-electing from the surviving devices.

read as evidence of a misaligned stream is 0x00050801, which is the abort path
re-reporting the *next* header dword after the first rejection -- a consequence

6c8196b31213db4afb51304329a40001c6611973:
test(gates): pin the GPU selection rule and make it host-testable

gpu_device_register() and gpu_device_unregister() both decide which display
device owns the DRM backend, and both had the rule written out inline with
nothing able to check it. The rule is the part that has to be right about
preference rather than about locking, and it lives in a file full of kernel
types, so a host test cannot compile it.

Extracted to kernel/include/drivers/gpu/gpu_select.h as two predicates over
booleans, alongside the existing drm_geom.h precedent, and gpu_core.c now calls
them -- so the tested logic is the logic that runs rather than a copy of it.

Both failure modes are silent from the caller, which is why they are worth a
gate. Lose the 3D promotion and every DRM_IOCTL_VIRTGPU_* answers -ENODEV while
GETPARAM still advertises the capability. Fail to refill an empty slot and every
DRM ioctl answers -ENODEV until something forces a re-probe. Neither reports an
error anywhere.

tools/tests/gpu_select_test.c is picked up by the existing tools/tests/*.c
wildcard, so it runs under `make host-tests` with no build wiring. Three
properties are asserted, each of which a revert breaks:

  - a 3D-capable newcomer displaces a 2D-only incumbent, and a 2D-only newcomer
    never displaces a 3D-capable one (probe order must not decide whether the
    machine has 3D);
  - two equally capable devices never trade the slot, which is what stops
    probe-order churn;
  - the re-election scan prefers a 3D-capable device at a higher index over a
    2D-only one at a lower index. This is the one an earlier draft of the caller
    got wrong: the loop condition stopped at the first candidate, so a 2D-only
    device at index 0 silently won over a 3D device at index 1.

The gate is falsifiable, checked by mutation rather than asserted. Reverting
the scan to "never improve on the first candidate" aborts on the third property;
refusing to fill an empty slot aborts on the first; letting the last probe win
regardless of capability aborts on the second. All three exit 134, and the
restored header passes.
db5261ec799e5a436a7e25e3ed0fbd103c3a6c24:
feat(gpu): re-elect a surviving display device when the incumbent unregisters

gpu_device_unregister() cleared the slot and stopped there. So whenever the
incumbent went away and another display device was still online, DRM was left
with no backend at all and every ioctl answered -ENODEV until something forced a
re-probe. It is a plausible shape for a machine that has two display devices
and hotplugs or fails one, and the failure is indistinguishable from a broken
driver.

It now walks the online display devices and refills the slot using the same
promotion rule register() uses, so the outcome does not depend on which function
noticed the departure. Two details that are easy to get wrong:

  - The scan cannot stop at the first candidate. A 2D-only device at a low
    enumeration index would otherwise win over a 3D-capable one further up, and
    re-election would silently downgrade a working 3D binding. It stops only once
    it holds a 3D-capable winner, which cannot be improved on.
  - It never displaces a slot refilled concurrently. A register() that landed
    while this was enumerating has already made its choice, so the claim happens
    under the lock and only against an empty slot.

The winner is held as a bare device_t*, which is what the slot has always held:
class_device_get_by_type() only returns online devices, and a published device
outlives the call. Taking a class reference instead would leak it, because
nothing drops the slot's reference on a later unregister.

Both this and register() now call the predicates in gpu_select.h, so the
behaviour this fixes is the behaviour the new host test pins.

4a66b3fb371aa75a2b06a23525a581f2cce47627:
docs(gfx): correct unsupported GPU teardown refcount claims

The comment on virtio_gpu_release_buffers() said the remaining hazard was a
caller already inside the command path continuing to run against a reset
transport, and that closing it needed a device-level teardown lock or an
in-flight reference count. I wrote that without checking it, and it is wrong.
The reference count would have protected against nothing.

What the code actually does:

  - the instance is the file-static g_gpu_inst, so its storage outlives every
    caller -- "running against a reset transport" is not a use-after-free;
  - every command entry point re-reads dev->drv_priv, which remove() clears, and
    the wrappers answer -ENODEV when it is NULL;
  - the ops table is a static const, so function pointers a racing caller has
    already loaded stay valid;
  - reaching the driver at all requires the device to be the current default, and
    gpu_device_unregister() clears that slot first -- so drm_gpu_ops() returns
    NULL and the ioctl fails before it can touch the instance.

The ordering that makes this safe is unregister() (slot) -> unpublish() (which
drains class_device_call_begin users) -> release_buffers().

The comment now records the retracted conclusion together with the evidence that
retracted it, and states what would invalidate it: a change that caches dev or ops
across an ioctl, or that calls the driver without going through the default-device
slot, would need the reference count after all. The same retraction is recorded in
docs/graphics/3d-graphics.md, which had carried the claim forward.

No behaviour change; this only removes a claim that was not true.
b575a94ee7512e97c190b6f7f91697516669e879:
fix(drm): stop advertising a timestamp capability we do not fully provide

DRM_CAP_TIMESTAMP_MONOTONIC was reported as 1. The vblank event does carry a
real CLOCK_MONOTONIC stamp -- drm_vblank_deliver_due_locked() fills it from
timekeeping_get_monotonic -- but the cap names two things, and only one of them
is true here: there is no DRM_IOCTL_MODE_GETTIME in the driver at all.

So a client that reads the cap may believe it can ask the CRTC for time, and
gets an error from the default arm instead. That is an error rather than a
crash, which is why this is a correctness fix and not a bug fix, but it is the
same class of overstatement this file has been correcting elsewhere: the cap
table is otherwise careful to zero everything unimplemented, including
ADDFB2_MODIFIERS and CURSOR_WIDTH, precisely so a client does not build on a
path that is not there.

Zeroing it costs nothing. Nothing consumes this cap in order to gain something
-- clients read it to decide what they may assume -- and the event timestamp,
which is the part actually used for frame pacing, is unaffected.

Found while checking whether an unimplemented ioctl could explain the guest
eglinfo segfault. It cannot: of the 48 ioctls the driver defines, 47 are
dispatched, and the one that is not (VIRTGPU_RESOURCE_CREATE_BLOB) is one the
driver already advertises as unavailable via VIRTGPU_PARAM_RESOURCE_BLOB = 0.
The three caps that are advertised -- DUMB_BUFFER, PRIME, and now the
timestamp -- all have their ioctls present. An ioctl reaching the default arm
returns an error rather than a NULL function pointer, so the ioctl surface does
not account for ra=0x400.
3c95e961e916dd075abc6fd0f04d9ddaf6048572:
docs(graphics): record what the eglinfo segfault is not and where that narrows it

The eglinfo crash has been listed as "needs further investigation" for several
rounds, which is honest but not useful: it leaves the next reader with the same
starting point. This records what was actually ruled out, so the next
investigation does not repeat it.

The natural hypothesis was a good one and it is wrong. ra=0x400 is the classic
shape of Mesa calling a NULL function pointer, which would follow from Mesa
asking for an ioctl we do not implement, getting success with an unfilled struct,
and dereferencing it. Measured against the source, that chain does not hold:

  - 47 of the 48 ioctls the driver defines are dispatched. The one that is not,
    VIRTGPU_RESOURCE_CREATE_BLOB, is already declared unavailable through
    VIRTGPU_PARAM_RESOURCE_BLOB = 0, so Mesa is not told to use it.
  - All three capabilities GET_CAP advertises have their ioctls present, and the
    vblank event does carry a real CLOCK_MONOTONIC stamp.
  - An ioctl reaching the default arm returns an error, not a NULL pointer.

So the remaining space is Mesa's device enumeration after opening the node,
which is the same shape as the GBM failure already recorded elsewhere in this
file (eglInitialize succeeds, DRI2 fails to create a gbm device, no kernel-side
ioctl error). Whether the two are the same defect is not established.

Adds §0.7 stating plainly what is still unknown: there is no in-guest backtrace,

are unconfirmed; and therefore no root cause is claimed. The next step is named

The one real defect found along the way, the over-advertised
DRM_CAP_TIMESTAMP_MONOTONIC, is fixed separately.

7d9155c5bc51db561a828e145aab66984e6b1a80:
test(smoke): gate the virgl 3d pixel readback on x86_64 too

One architecture is not coverage. The 3D path is a chain of host-specific steps
-- QEMU's display backend, virglrenderer, the virtio control queue, the guest's
DMA mapping -- and any of them can differ per guest architecture while the code
under test stays byte-identical. Until this ran, "3D works" meant "3D works on
riscv64".

x86_64 earns its own gate rather than being folded into an existing instance
because it exercises a different page-table and arch_dma_sync_* implementation
from riscv64, and that is exactly where a write-back visibility bug would hide.
A shared instance would also have made a failure ambiguous: one arch's gate
failing tells you much less than knowing which one.

Verified, not assumed. smoke-gpu3d-x86_64 passes with the pixel readback that
can only appear if the host executed the stream and the guest read the result
back:

    pixel readback ok (0xffff0000 across 4096 pixels)
    pixel readback ok (0xff0000ff across 4096 pixels)

Same colour values as riscv64, which is the point: the renderer produces the
same pixels regardless of which guest architecture asked.
77082ba78f1e2f323bef6bfec740133563b6bb48:
test(smoke): gate the virgl 3d pixel readback on aarch64 too

Third architecture for the same chain, and the most structurally distinct of the
three: aarch64's page-table walk and arch_dma_sync_for_cpu differ from x86_64's,
so it is the case where a bug needing an explicit cache-maintenance pass after
the renderer's write-back would pass on both of the others.

It is also the architecture users deploy on most, so a 3D regression here is the
one likely to be reported rather than caught by a gate.

Verified: smoke-gpu3d-aarch64 passes with both colour passes reading back the
same values as riscv64 and x86_64 (0xffff0000 then 0xff0000ff, 4096 pixels each).

The expect list is deliberately identical to the other two. If a marker ever has
to differ per architecture, that difference is the finding and belongs here with
a stated reason next to it, rather than being quietly dropped -- which is how a
gate quietly stops testing something.
207bfc74fefb7fc0fe4342d689a6b3b3219ba8c1:
test(smoke): split the QEMU command because QEMU is a command not a program

The Makefile builds QEMU as `env LD_LIBRARY_PATH=... qemu-system-<arch>` whenever
a locally built virglrenderer is present, so smoke.py's --qemu is a command line.
Handing it to Popen as one argv element made it look for a binary literally named
"env LD_LIBRARY_PATH=... qemu-system-x86_64" and fail with a FileNotFoundError
that quotes the whole string back at you.

shlex rather than str.split, because the paths in it may contain spaces and the
quotes have to survive. A no-op when QEMU is a bare program name.

This is not specific to the case being added: smoke-devtools takes the same
--qemu and would have failed the same way whenever virglrenderer was installed
and the gate ran on this host. It had simply never been run in that
configuration.
d467c7217d08f56060d9aa87e820915548454f4e:
test(smoke): record how stock Mesa handles the DRM node

The 3D gates prove the transport works: gpu3d_test speaks DRM_IOCTL_VIRTGPU_* and
reads the pixels back. They say nothing about whether Mesa will use any of it,
because the client that matters is libEGL/libgbm loading virtio_gpu_dri.so --
a different path with different expectations (sysfs enumeration, GET_CAP, DRI
screen creation). "3D works" and "a real client can reach 3D" are separate claims
and only the second decides whether the desktop benefits.

Answers "how do I run Mesa in a guest at all", which was the obstacle. The xfce
world cannot host it: its overlay init execs labwc, and labwc does not read
stdin, so injected console input has nowhere to go. This uses the smoke-devtools
shape instead -- the base image's init forks mksh on the serial console, and the
Mesa world is attached as a second disk and chrooted into by hand.

The world deliberately carries no /etc/a20-distro marker, so the kernel does not
chroot into it and exec a desktop; it also carries no overlay beyond the probe
script. Its package list is Mesa only rather than xfce.world's, because the gate
needs no compositor and every package is a network fetch.

The gate reports rather than asserts. It passes when the probe runs to
completion and prints the transcript, including which renderer Mesa chose. That
is deliberate: the question is open, and demanding success would turn "Mesa does
not attach" into a red light carrying no more information than the log already
does, while being indistinguishable from the guest failing to boot at all.
Promoting it to a pass/fail on the renderer string is the next step, once attach
either works or has a located cause.

First run, on a host with virglrenderer 1.3.0 behind tools/with-virgl-display.sh:

    node /dev/dri/card0 present
    node /dev/dri/renderD128 present
    sysfs class/drm/card0 present
    modalias=of:NgpuTdisplayCvirtio,gpuC
    dir /sys/bus exists
    dir /sys/bus lists: <EMPTY>
    dir /sys/bus/pci exists
    dir /sys/bus/pci lists: <EMPTY>
    dir /sys/bus/pci/devices exists
    dir /sys/bus/pci/devices lists: <EMPTY>
    gbm: eglinfo: eglInitialize failed
    egl: OpenGL core profile renderer: llvmpipe (LLVM 21.1.2, 128 bits)

EGL itself initialises and Mesa gives llvmpipe; the GBM platform fails. The empty
listings are the lead: libdrm's drmGetDevice2() enumerates by readdir, and
/sys/bus/pci/devices lists nothing, so it cannot learn the device's identity.
1c56a9761d63fc9d4b5ce8934ce86d39962881ab:
docs(graphics): document the dead-end sysfs route and required llvmpipe fallback

The previous rounds proposed, without trying it, that adding a sysfs entry would
let Mesa attach. This round tried it, and it does not -- and the way it fails is
worth more than the conclusion.

Adding a `driver` symlink under /sys/class/drm/card0 (which libdrm's
drmGetDevice2() reads to learn the bound driver's name; our card0/device/
exposes only `modalias`) does move libdrm forward. Before: eglinfo -p gbm failed
but plain eglinfo succeeded with llvmpipe, and the desktop's swrast path worked.
After: eglinfo -p gbm still fails and plain eglinfo now fails too, with
"DRI2: failed to create screen".

So the driver link is necessary and not sufficient -- virtio_gpu_dri.so then gets
loaded and its screen creation fails, which is the next link in the chain. More
importantly, this exposes a dependency nothing had recorded: **EGL currently works
because libdrm cannot find the device, so Mesa falls back to surfaceless and
llvmpipe.** That fallback is carrying the desktop. Any change that makes libdrm
succeed at identifying the device removes the fallback before the driver can
actually render, and breaks the desktop first.

Which inverts the order the earlier note proposed. virtio_gpu_dri.so's kernel-side
requirements must be met before the sysfs entry is added, not after; adding sysfs
first only buys an earlier and louder failure. The change was reverted, and this
paragraph is the record of why.

Also documents the new gate, which is what makes the next attempt at this
question start from a measurement instead of from a boot.
601732b69a3dab33fcf88777aa50a2893ed7df87:
docs(graphics): record three-architecture 3d coverage and the mesa attach gate

Updates the status table, the gpu3d_test usage block, and the gate index for
work done this round.

The "3D transport end to end" row now says three architectures rather than one,
and says what the extra coverage bought: all three gates read back the same two
colour values, so "the renderer's output does not depend on the guest
architecture" is measured rather than assumed. aarch64 earns its own gate
because its page-table walk and cache-maintenance path differ structurally from
x86_64's, which is where a write-back visibility bug would hide.

The gpu3d_test block still documented the pre-pixel-readback era -- a PASS line
that said "no command stream submitted, rendering unverified", which has been
false since §0.5. It now shows the real expected output and states the remaining
limit accurately: this is evidence for a hand-written command stream speaking
the VIRTGPU UAPI directly, not for Mesa, because gpu3d_test does not go through a
DRI driver at all.

The gate index gains both new entries, with the Mesa one marked as
record-only. A gate listed without that caveat reads as a claim that Mesa
attaches, which is the opposite of what it currently reports.
9aff83d2cae9bd3032f1c3800529d2c5071c5cd6:
fix(drm): return VIRTGPU_GETPARAM values through the output pointer

libdrm passes &value and afterwards reads its own stack slot, so a driver
that stores the number in getparam.value leaves the client with 0 for
every parameter. Mesa asks for the seven params, reads param_3d_features
as 0, and returns NULL before it ever creates a context -- which is why
every ioctl on this path returned success while the driver quietly gave
up on the device. Write through the pointer the way Linux does, and let
gpu3d_test follow the same convention.

version_major also has to be 0: virgl_drm_get_version() answers -EINVAL
for anything else and the winsys bails on the same line. Measured both
ways -- with major=1 no CONTEXT_INIT is ever issued, with major=0 it is.

Three ABI details corrected on the way past. GET_CAPS must honour the
cap_set_id the caller sent, because GET_CAPSET_INFO is addressed by index
and GET_CAPS is not. Capset 6 describes this driver rather than the
renderer, so the kernel answers it instead of forwarding it to the host.
And version.name has to be the DRM driver name "virtio_gpu": libdrm falls
back to reading it, because /sys/bus/pci/devices is empty here.

Mesa now reaches virgl -- CONTEXT_INIT and EXECBUFFER appear, and the
renderer string names virgl.
ebe70456d78ade778501c09fa9b7f6abc2f3e7f6:
fix(smoke): boot the Mesa gate with a GPU so it can read the renderer

Two ways this gate could report success while measuring nothing.

It never attached a GPU device in the first place: -nographic mounts no
display device, so every VIRTGPU ioctl answered -ENODEV and "Mesa did
not attach" looked exactly like a Mesa bug. Declare DISPLAY_MODE=gui and
QEMU_GUI_DISPLAY=egl-headless on the target, and assert the guest really
brought a virgl device up -- without that assertion none of the rest says
anything.

And the renderer pattern was "OpenGL renderer string:.*virgl", which
eglinfo never prints. It says "OpenGL core profile renderer:" and "OpenGL
ES profile renderer:", so the gate called a working virgl render "not
attached". Match "profile renderer: *virgl" instead, and make the attach a
hard failure by default now that it holds; MESA_REQUIRE_VIRGL_ATTACH=0
downgrades to reporting while bisecting.

virglrenderer is added to the probe world to keep the package list in step
with xfce.world, as that file asks; Mesa 25.2.7 does not link it.
33d8cae4266f779e25acf83f21301e000f5fdd7b:
docs(graphics): attribute the Mesa attach blocker to GETPARAM, not Alpine's Mesa

Section 0.8 blamed packaging, argued from libgallium importing no
virgl_renderer_* symbols. That evidence was worthless -- a renderer
reached through dlopen leaves no import -- and building Mesa from source
with -Dgallium-drivers=virgl behaved byte for byte like the packaged one,
so the distro was never the variable. Left in as a dead end so the
symbol-count argument does not get reached for again; the measured cause
and both fixes replace it.

The status row now reads attached rather than blocked, and the gate index
describes what smoke-mesa-attach actually asserts.
f07e879013bebf24f9935521ae46526ea33befb2:
refactor(proc): reuse the ELF machine mapping for coredump architecture names

check-arch-boundary failed on main and nothing ran it, so two #ifdef
ladders here went unnoticed: five CONFIG_ names for "is this 64-bit" and
five more for "what e_machine", in the file whose whole job is writing an
ELF header.

Both facts are already stated once, by the build: ELF_CLASS_* and
ELF_MACHINE_* at Makefile:791-806, which kernel/mm/elf.c gates every
incoming object on at elf.c:138. Gate on the same pair here and the two
lists cannot disagree, so a core dump can never describe a machine the
loader would have rejected. The five CORE_EM_* constants go with them;
their values matched, which is exactly why nothing caught the duplication.

The 32-bit stub boundary is unchanged, and was checked per class rather
than by inspection. With ARCH_ELF_CLASS=2 the guarded body is present and
e_machine resolves to 243; with =1 the body is absent and only the stub
remains. That detail is load-bearing: the guard was #ifdef
COREDUMP_SUPPORTED, and the macro is now defined on every architecture,
so the test had to become #if or the 32-bit ports would have silently
started compiling the full dumper.

check-arch-boundary: 1/6 -> 6/6.
69e441080972a7cd47240a13a69faf60c88964b7:
fix(abi): dispatch map_shadow_stack by CONFIG_X86_64 in shared code

The second of the two check-arch-boundary failures. map_shadow_stack(2) is
CET-specific, but the only way shared code could ask that question was the
CONFIG_ name -- so the gate whose entire job is to keep those names out of
portable code had a legitimate exception it had no way to express.

arch.h already carries the idiom this needs: a default-0 ARCH_HAS_* in the
shared header that an architecture header opts into, exactly as
ARCH_HAS_VDSO does for x86_64 and as ARCH_HAS_SAFE_IDLE_WAIT defaults off
for everyone else. One macro, one opt-in, one consumer, and the gate's
allow-list needs no new entry.

Checked both ways through the preprocessor rather than by reading: with the
capability set the implementation is compiled, and without it the function
keeps returning Linux's arch-correct -ENOSYS on every other architecture.
2d78215f9fcf2c2c2c1c443f310db9222c192263:
fix(build): generate and include userland header dependency files

make -C user had no -MMD and no -include of any .d file, so an object
depended on its own .c plus a short hand-written header list. Editing
init_common/runtime_setup.h recompiled nothing at all:

  make -C user -W init_common/runtime_setup.c   ->  1 compile
  make -C user -W init_common/runtime_setup.h   ->  0 compiles

USER_BUILD_STAMP cannot cover for this, which is the part worth recording.
Its stamps.py any_newer() walk does notice the header, and it does
re-invoke the sub-make -- but make then correctly declines to rebuild,
because as far as the graph is concerned nothing it depends on changed.
The stamp makes the miss louder without fixing it. The build reported
success and linked a stale binary, which is the worst of both outcomes:
no error, no warning, wrong code.

CFLAGS is the one place every rule already draws from -- SBASE_CFLAGS,
MKSH_CFLAGS, TLSE_CFLAGS and FF_CFLAGS are all derived from it -- so
putting -MMD -MP there covers all of them the way the kernel side already
does at Makefile:694, and DEP_FILES reads the results back at the end of
the file the way tools/targets-images.mk does. -include rather than
include, so a variant that has never been built does not fail on a
missing .d.

The same probe now reports 1822 recompiles. That is not over-triggering:
runtime_setup.h is shared by init and the command set, so a large blast
radius is the correct answer, and it is the honest one.
9b6ebcaa30083bcb4116249b5821cba7bb00125f:
build(native): track all liba20rt headers as native build prerequisites

The native programs are single-TU whole-program links, so their header
prerequisites are hand-written per rule. Nine of the twenty-three headers
in user/liba20rt were on no rule at all: a20_clock.h, a20_sdk.h,
a20_string.h, a20_registry.h, a20_system.h, a20_net.h, a20_fs.h,
a20_linux.h, a20_personality.h.

NATIVE_BUILD_STAMP's any_newer() walk does cover user/liba20rt, so the
stamp fired, make was re-invoked, and make again found nothing changed:

  -W user/liba20rt/a20_syscall.h  (listed)   -> 15 links
  -W user/liba20rt/a20_clock.h    (unlisted) ->  0 links

Same failure as the userland header case and the same silence, so the two
are fixed the same way. One wildcard over the SDK header directories
replaces the enumeration, which means a header added to liba20rt becomes a
prerequisite the moment it exists rather than whenever somebody remembers
to add a line to twenty rules.

A/B'd against the previous file in a scratch build dir, because "0 links"
is also what a tree with no built binaries reports and that would have
proved nothing. With an up-to-date baseline: a20_clock.h, a20_types.h and
a20_sdk.h each go from no relink to relinking every SDK-consuming rule, and
a no-change build relinks exactly what it did before.

Over-tightening is deliberate. The wildcard is a correctness net, and the
cost of a spurious relink is a second -- the cost of the miss was a
silently stale binary.
704cbe5b8782997a00544ad82cd732f9a1682d72:
test(gates): enforce the configured clang-format check

.clang-format was honest about itself, which is rarer than it sounds: line
7 said nothing runs it in CI and that the file exists to stop the style
drifting, not to reformat what is already there. The honesty was the
problem. A stated rule that nothing checks is not a rule, and every
contributor had to take the style on trust.

The obvious fix -- a full-tree gate -- fails immediately, and the number is
worth keeping: 844 of 996 first-party sources do not conform. The tree
genuinely diverged from the config; it puts function braces on the next
line and writes braced lists as { a, b }, where the config says Attach and
Cpp11BracedListStyle. Demanding an 844-file reformat as the price of a
green build would have been worse than no gate, so enforcement is a
ratchet instead: the pre-existing violators are recorded in
tools/clang-format-baseline.txt and only a file outside that list can
fail. The list may shrink; nothing may be added to it without a visible
diff.

Two properties make that trustworthy rather than decorative. The baseline
is a plain sorted list, so it diffs cleanly and cannot itself rot. And the
violating set is identical under clang-format 19.1.7 and 23.1.2, a span of
four major versions -- so there is no version pin to fall out of, which was
the failure mode that would have turned this into a gate people mute.

Also here: a missing clang-format now skips loudly instead of passing
quietly, the gate never rewrites a file, and the .clang-format header plus
CONTRIBUTING.md 4.2 describe what actually happens instead of what used to.
The old claim that CI runs no clang-format is the thing this commit exists
to delete; leaving it would have reproduced the defect at one remove.

Proven in all three directions: clean tree passes, an injected bad file
fails with the clang-format -i line that fixes it, and removing it passes
again.
b8f0846efebed35ff8ec7efdc175fb757d9ff638:
build(make): add help and check targets and remove an unsupported claim

1361 targets, and the two every newcomer types first both failed with "no
rule to make target". There was no help, and no check: the fastest useful
gates in the tree -- host-tests at 0.27s, check-manifests at 0.47s,
check-a20-tests running 194 tests in 13.6s -- were documented in neither
README.md nor docs/build.md, so they were undiscoverable rather than
merely unmentioned.

`make check` is the same fifteen gates CI's toolchain-gates job runs, in
the same order, composed from one variable so the two cannot drift. That
equivalence is the point: a contributor can reproduce the fast CI tier
locally, and a gate that exists only in CI is a gate nobody runs before
pushing. Each gate recurses through $(MAKE) rather than becoming a
prerequisite, so one failure does not hide the next and -k still reports
everything. Whole tier: 18.2s, no QEMU and no cross toolchain.

`make help` prints the same list it runs, because a help text that lies
about which gates run is worse than none.

It also carries a correction. The help line for smoke-riscv64 read "a
watchdog timeout is acceptable", copied from a README claim that was
never true -- there is no watchdog outside the STM32 IWDG, and
docs/testing-gates.md:185 says the opposite. Both are fixed here and in
README.md; the sentence now states the two serial markers the gate
requires, that exit 124 is a failure, and that it verifies no syscalls.
91f816f2bd12a8813e92ecbf854e319fe5abf97d:
docs(readme): correct the watchdog smoke claim to match implemented subsystems

The README used "make smoke-riscv64 treats a watchdog timeout as an
acceptable result" as its example of a permissive gate. There is no
watchdog. kernel/ has no watchdog string in it, and
docs/server-readiness.md:408 says so outright: none outside the STM32
IWDG, and no softlockup or hung-task detection either. So the flagship
sentence in the testing section described hardware the kernel does not
have, in a subsystem that does not exist, as evidence of a testing culture
that is otherwise real.

Two other documents already contradicted it -- docs/testing-gates.md:185
says a watchdog timeout is a failure -- which is the worse part: the
project was documenting three different behaviours for one gate.

What the gate actually does is worth saying plainly, so the sentence now
gives the two serial markers instances/smoke-riscv64.toml requires (part
ok, then the self power-off banner), notes that run_with_timeout.py
returns 124 on timeout so a stall is a failure, and keeps the honest
scoping that it is a BRINGUP boot check verifying no syscalls. That last

The same false claim was sitting in the `make help` text, which is where it
came from. Fixed there too.
3afd776141405a17a87f96538be48a1ea14cc015:
fix(native-abi): align the syscall count constant with the 142 defined calls

The Native ABI registers 142 syscalls. Four documents said 136, and the
header constant said 135:

  grep -c '^A20_NATIVE_SYSCALL(' kernel/abi/native/syscall_table.def  -> 142
  grep -c '^#define A20_SYS_' kernel/include/abi/native/syscall_nr.h  -> 142

08-runtime-status.md carried a second defect in the same section. Its
disclaimer about user/archive/ being deleted in 2026-10 was a blockquote
sitting *between two rows of the markdown table*, which split the table in

00-overview.md:8 was left alone on purpose: line 7 already scopes every

statement under a correct caveat, and editing it would have been churn
against something that is not wrong.

Last-verified bumped to 2026-10 on the file that carries the marker,
following the convention in docs/README.md:23. No marker was added to

10a03077e914fe2ba33ad9ebbe1cd4bdebad6dc2:
docs(readme): remove indexes that point to a deleted command and tool

This is the failure mode that costs a newcomer the most time: nothing

1153c592be51e0979afe0c32b3f5c8666a80aae7:
docs(core): correct the lock-order contract path

The global lock order contract names docs/network-lock-contract.md. The
file is at docs/net/network-lock-contract.md, so the one pointer that
sends a reader to the authoritative statement of the 12-rule hierarchy
does not resolve.

check-doc-drift cannot catch this and the reason is worth writing down:

45f53c1724b2a8b3a8d71cc355cbd898445c53a8:
ci(ci): resolve build images from the pull request's own registry

A pull request from a fork could not run three of CI's five jobs. The
container image was resolved as
ghcr.io/<$GITHUB_REPOSITORY_OWNER>/a20os-buildenv:latest, and on a
pull_request event that variable is the fork's owner, not ours -- so the
job asked the fork's registry for an image that does not exist there and
died at container startup. build, kernel-build and smoke were all
unreachable. Only toolchain-gates and ci-kernel-arches survived, because
they run on a bare ubuntu-latest.

The outside contributor's first PR could not produce a single QEMU boot.
For a project that describes itself as welcoming contributions, that is the
worst possible place for the wall.

Resolve from the base repository's owner on pull_request and keep
repository_owner everywhere else, so same-repo pushes and PRs resolve
exactly as before and only the fork case changes. Applied to all three
workflows that read the image, since fixing one would leave the other two
resolving the fork's own registry. No secrets and no permissions block was
added: either would newly break fork PRs by a different route, and ci.yml
deliberately uses neither today.

The same commit adds check-arch-boundary to the toolchain-gates job. It
was failing on main -- two violations, exit 1 -- and nothing ran it, which
is why it went unnoticed; the two source fixes are earlier in this series.
It is invoked through tools/gates.py directly rather than through the make
target, because the make target carries a smoke-arch-mmu-matrix
prerequisite that boots a seven-architecture QEMU matrix and has no place
in a 15-minute host-only job. The static half runs in 0.085s.

What this does not fix: the image must still have been pushed, which
buildenv.yml documents as a manual first step. That out-of-band
requirement is unchanged, and the mutable :latest tag is still a
supply-chain smell -- pinning to a digest is the obvious follow-up.
6d6061196a7063d1cda98dd25d9c5db6aa0096a2:
feat(mm): make RSS accounting atomic because the OOM killer reads it under another lock

mm->rss is a plain size_t written under mm->lock but read by the OOM victim
selector under proc_lock, in cg_mem_select_victim().  Those two locks do not
exclude each other, so this is already a data race today; it stops being
merely theoretical the moment the status fault path leaves mm->lock, which is
the next step of the single-level migration (docs/roadmap/
single-level-mm-model.md 10.74).

Renaming the field to rss_atomic is deliberate: it makes the compiler
enumerate every access, so a plain `->rss` cannot compile.  That found 40
sites; three more were behind #ifdef or the native ABI and only turned up by
hand.  The project's own inventory (10.75) said 52 sites in 10 files; the real
count is 53 in 19, of which 9 are cg_mem_t.rss, an unrelated cgroup counter
with the same spelling that must not be touched (converting it would break
memory limits).  So 42 sites needed rewriting, and 10.75's list was missing
seven files including a clamped read-modify-write in the ABI layer at
abi/linux/sys_mm.c:291.

The saturated subtract is a compare-exchange loop, not fetch_sub followed by a
clamp.  Under concurrency the latter has a window the sequential version does
not: a reader can compute a small value, another thread subtracts, and the
first one's stale result is then committed.  rss feeds the OOM victim score, so
an underflow makes the kernel sacrifice the wrong process -- a correctness and
safety regression, not a style issue.

Two sites needed judgement rather than mechanical replacement:

  - proc/exit.c read rss twice, once for `> 0` and once for the uncharge
    amount.  Two atomic reads can differ, so the charge would be wrong; now
    read once into a local.
  - Every other site is a plain add, a zeroing init, or a cross-lock read, and
    those map onto mm_rss_add / mm_rss_set / mm_rss_get with relaxed or
    release/acquire ordering respectively.

Verified: riscv64, x86_64 and aarch64 kernel-only builds clean under -Werror
-UBSan, riscv64 at NR_CPUS=1 and 4, and zero non-atomic ->rss accesses remain.
check-mm-lock-model passes, including smoke-mm-stress and the SMP=8
smoke-mm-fork-exec-race.
d5769beddc3dd6e52ed5f26e551313a9437b5c12:
fix(mm): lock the leaf table for every cursor operation

pt.h claimed the cursor "holds a lock on EVERY descendant of the covering node
(preorder DFS)" and pt.c called the covering node's lock "the unit of writer
exclusion".  Neither was true.  The descent takes no lock at all on an
already-populated intermediate -- the mcs_lock in mm_addrspace_lock is only in
the branch that allocates a missing one (pt.c:651) -- while mm_cursor_replace
writes the LEAF.  So a wide cursor (covering level 2) and a single-page cursor
(covering level 0) inside it held disjoint locks over the same leaf PTE and the
same pt_meta_t.cls[] byte, which mm_pt_note_present then updated with no lock.

How far this actually reaches: nothing, today.  No code path creates a cursor
with guard_level > 0, because mm_pt_provision_anon() deliberately chunks per
leaf table (its own comment says per-page cursors cost 512 round trips per 2 MiB
and were the mmap regression).  So this is a latent hole, not a live race, and
an external review that read the comment and concluded "cover the subtree" was
reasoning from a false premise -- ADV targets wide transactions and there are
none.  It becomes reachable the moment a wide transaction exists.

The fix is narrower than a subtree DFS: since every write targets a single leaf
entry, locking that leaf excludes everyone who could touch it, whoever their
covering node is.  It has to be per operation rather than per transaction,
because a wide cursor visits up to 2048 leaf tables and the per-CPU held[] stack
has PT_MCS_POOL_SLOTS entries -- holding them all would panic.

Two bugs lived here, both of which read as harmless simplifications, so both are
now commented at the site and asserted by check-mm-pt-lock-order:

  - Taking the leaf lock when guard_level == 0, where the leaf IS the covering
    node the cursor already holds.  mcs_lock is not reentrant, so this
    self-deadlocks; smoke-mm-pt-race caught it on its first run as
    "[MCS DEADLOCK] SELF level=0 depth=1".
  - Starting the descent at guard_level - 1.  mm_addrspace_lock populates
    path[ROOT-1]..path[guard_level] and nothing below, so that reads an
    uninitialised pointer.  It presented as smoke-mm-stress timing out in
    huge-basic with no self-deadlock report, and I first misread it as the lock
    design being wrong and reverted it.  It was the loop bound.

Also fixed: mm_cursor_query, mm_cursor_unmap, mm_cursor_mark_prot and
mm_cursor_safe_test used cursor_leaf_table(), which is just path[0], so they
operated on whatever leaf the previous operation left behind whenever the range
spanned more than one leaf table.  Only mm_cursor_replace descended per address.
mark_prot is the path mm_pt_provision_anon() takes, so pre-marking a
multi-leaf range would have written to the wrong table.

Verified: smoke-mm-stress, smoke-mm-fork-exec-race (SMP=8), smoke-mm-pt-race
(SMP=8), check-mm-lock-model, and riscv64 smp4 / x86_64 / aarch64 builds.  The
MM-ASM audit line is all-zero, so per-PTE status and the hardware page tables
never diverged.
4854560427b3bcc7e6853214ef169501f2e8992e:
test(gates): add check-mm-pt-lock-order and smoke-mm-pt-race and a wide-cursor workload for them

The existing MM gates are all presence assertions -- "does this token appear in
this file" -- and that shape cannot catch either defect the leaf-lock commit
fixes.  Every token involved was present in the broken versions: the false
covering-node comment satisfied MM_AS_CURSOR_ONLY_ENTRY while the code did
something else, and all five cursor entry points existed.  So the new gate is
negative (the two false claims must not come back) and counted (the leaf lock
must exist at every one of its exit paths, the descent must start at
guard_level, and it must not re-lock the node the cursor already holds).

It was verified against the pre-fix tree before being trusted: reverting pt.c
and pt.h to HEAD fails 6 of the 8 assertions that applied then.  A gate that
cannot be made to fail on the bug it exists for is not a gate.

smoke-mm-pt-race boots riscv64 at SMP=8 with a20.anonprov=4096 and runs a new
wide-cursor phase in mm_stress: six threads each write and read back their own
512 KiB slice of one 4 MiB mapping while a seventh repeatedly munmaps and
re-maps a reserved slice underneath them.  That is the shape that makes a
4 MiB mapping's provisioning cursor and its per-page fault cursors overlap.
The gate asserts MM_WIDE_CURSOR: PASS and an all-zero MM-ASM audit line -- the
bidirectional audit of per-PTE status against the hardware page tables, which is
the actual evidence; MM_STRESS: PASS alone would say nothing about whether the
two representations diverged.

The workload is behind --wide-cursor-only and deliberately not in the bare
mm_stress run: at -smp 1 it does not finish inside the 45s smoke-mm-stress
allows, and paying that regression for coverage the SMP gate already provides
is a bad trade.  It lives in its own file scope with the gate.

Both gates passed on the first honest run of the tree and the leaf-lock commit
is green under all of them plus riscv64 smp4, x86_64 and aarch64 builds.

docs(mm): correct the MM lock-model assumptions and phase 3 prerequisites
