ea8e8bb4acfee9c25d9f3328000a6250f65c5e0c:
feat(mm): serialize page-table unmap with per-node locks

Add node-lock coverage to leaf removal and upward table detachment so faults and unmaps exclude one another. Update the design note to confirm per-node locking is the needed primitive, while retaining the detach-ordering constraints; the lock-model and lock-order gates pass, including negative checks.
b64cd2964e85f230ed1aa1786bd79e30652a1186:
feat(mm): keep page-table allocation outside the node MCS lock

Move page-table node allocation out of the MCS critical section, avoiding a reclaim path that may wait while holding the node lock; on allocation failure, decline the fast path and let the VMA path handle the fault. Update the phase notes with the observed `mm->lock`/node-lock ordering issue and remaining cursor/semantic checks.
5ea34decc25465b1dfd3b3b4003fec0d4baa3721:
fix(mm): stop reclaiming under mm- lock -- PT pages get the non-reclaiming allocator

This is the fix for the lockup that timed out Phase 3 twice.  The chain, read off
the code rather than guessed:

  sys_mmap (sys_mm.c:95) -> proc_mmap -> mm_mmap (mmap.c:404)
    takes spin_lock_irqsave(&mm->lock)              <-- IRQ-disabling
    -> mm_mmap_locked -> mm_pt_provision_anon (mmap.c:195)
      -> mm_addrspace_lock -> frame_alloc
        -> pfa_alloc_flags(0, can_reclaim=1)
          -> oom_try_reclaim -> proc_force_exit(victim)
            -> victim VMA teardown -> wants mm->lock

mm->lock is a spin_lock_irqsave held across a reclaimable allocation, so the
holder sleeps with interrupts off, and if the victim is its own mm it waits for a
lock it already holds.  That matched the [LOCK-STALL] evidence exactly: holder PC
in sys_mmap, waiter PCs in trap_handler, lock name mm.

Pre-existing, but it needed two conditions together.  The allocating path is only
reached when provisioning is on, which is why only smoke-mm-pt-race
(a20.anonprov) was affected.  And before the fast path stopped taking mm->lock, a
faulting thread blocked on mm->lock before it could enter mm_addrspace_lock at
all, so it serialised against provisioning and the window was shut.  Dropping
mm->lock did not create the bug; it was the change that opened the window.

mm_pt_provision_anon() is called as (void) at mmap.c:195 and the comment above it
says provisioning is best effort -- an unprovisioned range just keeps the VMA
fault path, which is correct.  Allocation failure there is therefore already a
supported outcome, not new behaviour, which is what makes switching it to a
non-reclaiming allocator free.  Hence frame_alloc_nr(), which is
frame_alloc() with can_reclaim = 0.

Both PT-page allocation sites -- cursor_leaf_slot() and mm_addrspace_lock() --
now use it.  That also closes the half of the sleeping-under-spinlock bug I left
open: the fault fast path's data page was already non-reclaiming, but the PT page
it allocates through mm_cursor_map still reclaimed.

One consequence is a real behaviour change and is measured, not assumed: the
other cursor users now return -ENOMEM under memory pressure where they previously
reclaimed first.  That is the unavoidable cost of taking reclaim out of a
spinlock, and -ENOMEM already flows through the existing fault-failure/OOM path.

check-mm-pt-lock-order goes to 17 assertions, including one that pins
pfa_alloc_flags(0, 0) inside frame_alloc_nr().  Without it, renaming a function
to _nr and leaving pfa_alloc_page() inside would satisfy every other assertion
while reclaiming under the spinlock again; negative-tested by doing exactly that
(17 -> 16).  The stale intent pin that named the old comment wording was
re-anchored rather than deleted.

Verified: check-mm-lock-model 14/14, check-mm-pt-lock-order 17/17
(negative-tested), riscv64/x86_64/aarch64 SMP=4 build, and at SMP=8 in QEMU
smoke-mm-pt-race (anonprov=4096), smoke-mm-stress, smoke-mm-fork-exec-race and
smoke-abi-linux -- all PASS, zero LOCK-STALL in any guest log, MM-ASM all-zero.
6ee94a56440d272a9c3f616a3da51ccc031fa50e:
test(smoke-mm-pt-race): detect when the status fast path is not reached

Arms /proc/a20/perf before the race workload and requires a nonzero mm_fault_from_status count, so the gate verifies that the status fast path actually ran. A read only after the workload was not evidence: collection stays dormant until the first diagnostic read, making all counters appear zero.

With the arming read in place, the path ran 778 times. The earlier “no anonymous provisioning” diagnosis was withdrawn; the live cap and provisioning path were working. The previous smoke PASS records did not establish that the fast path ran because they neither armed nor read the counters. The regression gate now detects a future return to the unreachable path.
a1628c2badbdd7bb74da1ac928136ec47779a81a:
docs(roadmap): record phase 3 lockup evidence and retract unsupported causes

The repeated Phase 3 attempts ruled out a TLB timeout and the initial bare-`nop` starvation inference. Instrumentation found CPUs waiting on a level-0 node; holder/PC readings narrowed the stuck path but did not initially prove the cause, and candidate caller unlock leaks were ruled out. The remaining handoff hypothesis was explicitly left unverified; all temporary instrumentation and the fast-path attempt were reverted at this checkpoint.
23082015d68c6be1316549730ae7dbc12334ba01:
fix(mm): repair the MCS page-table lock handoff -- it could never release a contended node

Found by measurement while chasing the Phase 3 lockup, and it is the actual
root cause.  Two independent bugs, both in the handoff, both fatal on contention.

1. The waiter was never linked into the queue.  mcs_lock() published nothing to
   its predecessor, so the unlocker always read me->next == 0 and took the
   compare-exchange branch -- but m->lock had already been moved to the *waiter*
   by the exchange, so that CAS always failed.  Nothing was released and the
   waiter was never woken.  One contended acquisition wedged the node for good.

2. The unlocker read the wrong node.  mcs_unlock() recovered its own node from
   m->node, a shared field that *every* acquirer overwrote with its own
   pointer.  A holder with one waiter behind it therefore read back the waiter,
   cleared the lock, and handed off to nobody.

Both are why the measured failure looked like it did: cpu0 spinning on
0xffffffc0bf6b3000 and cpu3 on 0xffffffc0bf6b1000, no completed holder among all
eight CPUs, holder PCs resolving to mm_addrspace_lock (where the exchange is),
waits climbing past 2^31, and [MCS DEADLOCK] silent -- correctly, since the
waiters are not self-deadlocked, they are waiting for a handoff the protocol
could not perform.

Fixes: publish pred->next from the waiter; on losing the CAS race in mcs_unlock,
wait for the successor's link to appear and hand off to it; and take the
unlocker's own node from its per-CPU pool (pool->nodes[pool->depth - 1], the
same slot mcs_lock pushed) instead of the shared m->node, which is now unused.

Why this survived: mm->lock serialised whole faults, so the node locks were
effectively never contended and the broken path was never exercised.  Removing
mm->lock from the fault path is what made contention routine and exposed it.
That is the same shape as the other two bugs found today -- a path that only
breaks once the serialisation above it is removed.

Verified: check-mm-lock-model 14/14, check-mm-pt-lock-order 17/17,
riscv64/x86_64/aarch64 SMP=4 build, and at SMP=8 in QEMU smoke-mm-pt-race,
smoke-mm-stress, smoke-mm-fork-exec-race, smoke-abi-linux -- all PASS with zero
LOCK-STALL, zero MCS DEADLOCK and zero panics in any guest log.
e22c51728ee8b554ab566da642e415f526f3610d:
fix(mm): fix MCS handoff and run the anonymous status fast path without mm- lock

Serve pre-provisioned anonymous faults through `mm_fault_from_status()` before taking the global `mm->lock`, falling back when provisioning is unavailable. The contention work exposed two MCS handoff defects: unlock used shared node state and did not reliably wake the next waiter. Record the corrected handoff and P5 status; the commit reports non-vacuous SMP=8 smokes and three-architecture builds.
b80d78ecad3cf22aafa1407bb89fed41e8e38a76:
test(gates): pin all three parts of the MCS handoff

The MCS handoff did not execute at all until Phase 3 -- mm->lock serialised whole
faults, so the node locks were never contended and the two fatal bugs sat there
unnoticed.  A regression in that code is now invisible in review and in any
pre-Phase-3 workload, so it gets pinned mechanically: the waiter publishing
itself to its predecessor, the unlocker taking its own node from its per-CPU
pool rather than the shared m->node, and the unlock CAS losing the race handing
off to the successor instead of dropping it.

check-mm-pt-lock-order goes to 20 assertions.  Negative-tested by deleting the
handoff link (20 -> 19).
b77189390e21bdafa03696e281e8d1e793ab2d32:
docs(verification): model the MCS handoff in TLA and reproduce both shipped bugs

The protocol modelled here is the one that shipped with two independent fatal
bugs, both in the handoff: the waiter never published itself to its
predecessor's ->next (so every unlock took the CAS branch, always failed, and
released nothing), and the unlocker recovered its own node from m->node, a field
every acquirer overwrites (so it could hand the lock to nobody).  Either wedges
a node permanently on first contention and neither reports anything, because the
waiter is not self-deadlocked.  No review caught it and no pre-Phase-3 workload
reached it, since mm->lock kept contention at zero.

Checked with TLC 2.16 at CPUS = {1,2,3}: TypeOK, MutualExclusion, WaiterLinked,
FreedHasNoWaiter, SuccIsWaiter and the liveness property WaiterProgress all hold,
under weak fairness on Enter and Exit.  43 states generated, 16 distinct, depth
4, no error.

The point of the artifact is that it has teeth, so both bugs were reintroduced as
single-conjunct mutants and TLC re-run:

  - dropping succ' = [succ EXCEPT ![lock] = c]  ->  WaiterLinked violated
  - making Exit always free the lock and drop the successor  ->  FreedHasNoWaiter
    violated

A third mutant is recorded as invalid rather than quietly dropped: changing
Exit's tail branch to UNCHANGED succ is a no-op, since that branch is reachable
only when succ[c] = 0 where the two are identical.  It passed TLC -- not because
the invariant is weak but because the mutation was vacuous.  That distinction is
worth writing down, since "my mutant passed" is routinely mistaken for "my
invariant is too weak".

tla2tools.jar is not vendored, matching the existing Envelope.tla gap; the fetch
and run command is recorded in leaflock_coverage.md.
abdc069c90f4f3475ccb6c2404221622902a1c8b:
feat(mm): implement the reverse MM_AS audit and clarify the transitional lock contract

Keep `MM_LOCK_MODEL` as the transitional contract and carve out only the status fast path, which relies on per-address node locking; ordinary COW/file/VMA installs remain under `mm->lock`. Add the reverse metadata-to-VMA audit (`vmai`) alongside the existing PTE-to-metadata walk, assert `vmai=0` in `smoke-mm-pt-race`, and document why `smoke-mm-stress` does not cover it.
cb35dbae8f2093f7434c317f4e0a00bf02457507:
docs(roadmap): close P6/P7 as blocked on the status metadata format

The status byte can classify faults but cannot carry the vnode/fd/offset data needed for file and COW servicing; brk pages are not provisioned with status either, leaving no implementable P6 subset. P7 also cannot remove `PTE_SWAP` until swap payload storage is redesigned: the payload is 44 bits on 64-bit targets and 24 bits on 32-bit targets. Correct the UFFD attribution: the fast-path safety bit is status-driven, while the VMA range table remains authoritative for unregister races. Documentation only.
178d6ca0c0a5df12ffdcb9b1d0f344bbba7313ca:
feat(mm_as_model): accept PTE_SWAP as the one tolerated overloaded bit

Keeps PTE_SWAP for P7 option C and narrows the invariant instead of inventing a replacement encoding. Swap entries carry 44 payload bits on 64-bit builds; moving them to metadata would cost 4 KiB per page-table page, and the paper specifies no alternate encoding. All six supported architectures define PTE_SWAP, with three aliasing the leaf marker, so the exact supported-architecture set is pinned by the gate.

The acceptance record now distinguishes verified accounting and error paths from swap-out/in, which the existing 1 GiB smoke cannot reach: free memory never crosses the reclaim floor, and the measured write-out rate would require about 512 seconds for 8 MiB. No non-default reclaim settings are used to claim default-path coverage. The recorded gate counts are 27/27 and 14/14; swap-out/in remains an explicit gap.
4d536ca524a23b36edcc9e3064c2ed78675375ac:
merge(kernel): land the single-level MM model -- status fault path off mm- lock

Squashed from 47 working commits into 16, one per logical change.  Content is
byte-identical to the branch tip (verified with git diff against 11524681); only
the history was rewritten.

The load-bearing change is e8d7895f: the MCS page-table lock's handoff was never
implemented.  A waiter was never linked into the queue, so its CAS could only
fail, and the unlocker read its own node back out of a field every acquirer
overwrites -- handing the lock to nothing.  Both are silent node lockups.
check-mm-pt-lock-order (27 assertions) and the TLA+ model now pin the handoff,
with both shipped bugs kept as mutants.

That unblocked b4961526, the actual goal: the status fast path now runs before
spin_lock(&mm->lock), measured non-vacuously at 778 lock-free anon faults.

Also lands the P8 reverse-direction MM_AS audit (vmai, negative-tested) and the
option C decision recording PTE_SWAP as the single tolerated overloaded bit,
pinned against SWAP_SUPPORTED_ARCHES.

Merged with --no-ff rather than fast-forwarded so this unit stays attributable
across the 14 concurrent commits main picked up meanwhile.
6f92bfd98bf4f4b858f474c689638e77ea96c14e:
feat(net): right-size the receive path memory model

The bottom-half ring stored 64 KiB payload slots inline and memset every one per
packet, so a small datagram cost 68 KiB of memset and capped net_socket_t at
1.05 MiB. Adds compile-time resource profiles with a _Static_assert on the
sys_timeout ceiling, right-sizes queued payloads, stages payloads inline, and
reports a real pool element size instead of an avail field nothing wrote.

Capped net_socket_t per profile so a fixed-size staging member cannot silently
return, and deletes the unreachable virtio_net_poll_all plus the doc that cited
it as live.
e96033aa1000b74d3c3bd1584b7d88271e1940b1:
refactor(net): split lwIP poll and take g_lwip_lock once per iteration

Splits the lwIP poll so a caller can advance timers without also reaching the
receive drain, which had put a ring's worth of protocol processing inside an
interrupt with interrupts disabled. Keeps the timer-interrupt drain short, stops
double-taking the lock in the TCP send loop, keeps the first registered netif as
the default, and corrects the loopback ordering claim in the docs.
17fa6bed0d1e15eca36ef0b4f30df8f75feb9457:
fix(drvmod): export the split poll entry points and fix the gate it exposed

The virtio-net module calls the split lwIP poll entry points, so those have to be
exported. With the payload work landed, the lock-contention gate turned out to
have three flaws of its own, and netfilter_test was mistaking the loopback for a
NIC. Surfaces the virtio-net driver's own rx/tx/drop counters, and gives the
packet-path rule scan the seqlock its header already claimed but the code did not
have. Rewrites the network lock contract around the payload split.
6abd599a6bc689767a6c0afa902bb7fadd60f41c:
feat(net): expose lane ownership while preserving single-lane behavior

Gives net_socket_t a lane index derived from the owning (ip, port), and exposes it
through /proc/net/status so 'did the lanes spread the connections' is answerable
without a debugger. The property that makes one codebase safe for both profiles
is that CONFIG_NET_LANES == 1 must behave exactly as before, so the lane gates
require a net_stress_test checksum to match byte for byte between a 1-lane and a
multi-lane build.

Settles lane ownership for wildcard binds and records the netif hazard, and
points the remaining-work section at net-lanes.md.
17d3386571b4f4c76c86ea941c42545523c75cf0:
feat(net): bucket lwIP's PCB lists by lane

Every PCB list becomes an array of CONFIG_NET_LANES heads, and each PCB carries the
index of the head it is linked into. A lookup for an established connection then
walks one list head instead of one global head.

The index comes from the pcb's own (local_ip, local_port) with the port hashed
before the address, because for an established connection the peer's source port
is our local port -- so both ends derive the same value from wire bytes alone, on
a CPU that has never seen the connection. A wildcard bind matches any local
address and no hash of (0, port) equals the hash of a concrete destination, so
those pcbs go to a sentinel bucket that a lookup walks second.

Makes the embedded profile buildable and records that 20 KiB is not enough for
it. Stops the lane gates from losing net_stress_test's first byte, and records
stage B as verified along with the two silent defects it shipped past.
0971b606f54c76ba0d6afbb1ca1497d7bc064f9e:
test(net): give the network path counters and let the suite assert a non-goal

/proc/a20/perf had roughly 75 counters and not one network-related; the only
network signal was a lock count with no denominator. Adds eleven network
counters (packets, bytes, lock acquisitions, poll calls and gated skips,
bottom-half runs and events, plus net_bh_overflow and net_alloc_fail as
correctness counters) and a reset write on /proc/a20/perf and
/proc/a20/lock_contention, so a gate can own the measurement window rather than
inherit whatever happened since boot.

Also adds MD5 (RFC 1321), verified against the published test vectors, and lets
network_suite assert a documented non-goal instead of reddening forever: AF_ALG
deliberately provides no algorithms, so its test honestly returns ABSENT. Left
unhandled, smoke-network-suite was already red on main and no amount of network
work could have made it green -- a permanently red gate is no gate.
5bd37ecb2aa345b28031601d1de0d8d82d8cd4ba:
feat(net): allocate LISTEN PCBs for inbound TCP connections

net_listen() discarded the bound pcb and tcp_listen() was never called anywhere in
the tree, so no listener ever existed inside lwIP and every inbound SYN was
answered with a RST. The stack had no way to serve anything off-box at all, and no
gate covered the network region, so this could sit unnoticed.

net_listen() now branches on a20.tcpmode: the 'lwip' mode turns the bound pcb
into a real LISTEN pcb with a tcp_accept callback; the default 'fast' mode is
unchanged. End to end, with SLIRP hostfwd aimed at the guest telnetd, the result
goes from 'connection reset by peer' to a usable shell.

Also lets a purely local TCP connection reach the real stack, and fixes the
RX-pending gate that was starving the loopif of that traffic. Closes the
socket_internal.h include guard that ended the file early.
9d9109923123671d1e6aa1d65becff41951387b2:
test(smoke): gate the accept path and put the network gates in CI

tcp_accept_test asserts a handshake completes and accept() returns a usable fd, in
both tcpmode fast and lwip. Its load-bearing assertion is tcp_listen > 0: that
was a steady 0 before the fix above, which is what made the RST behaviour
visible. Verified the assertion can fail -- the same kernel started with
tcpmode=fast reports 0 and the gate turns red.

The mode is chosen on the kernel command line rather than through
/proc/net/config, because a server's first listener is usually created by user
space at boot and a shell write arrives too late to matter. CI now runs the
network suite and this gate, which previously had no coverage at all.
d4a6a058090afa11ea64b9bba986c1d1c148501b:
refactor(core): extract the netfilter seqlock into a reusable primitive

netfilter.c's file header had claimed a generation-counter seqlock that the code did
not contain. Rather than reimplement it inline, the lock moves to
kernel/include/core/seqlock.h so the ARP cache and routing table scans can use the
same primitive.

Records why the bottom-half ring cannot become a pointer ring yet: bh_ring_prepare()
runs inside a lwIP callback under g_lwip_lock, and this repository's own lock
contract forbids calling a slab allocator there. Three escapes are costed; none
is chosen yet.

Then corrects the documentation debt this work created -- five files still said
things the measurements had made untrue, including a server-readiness conclusion
that never mentioned inbound TCP did not work at all.
32c3446e50b04d287d0bf3c49ec9671e5b7b4765:
feat(drvmod): enforce A20_DRIVER_ABI on module load

The descriptor carried an abi field and every driver dutifully wrote A20_DRIVER_ABI
into it, but nothing on the reading side compared it. magic and version were
checked in all four consumers; abi was checked in none. A module built against a
different header therefore loaded cleanly and the kernel went on to read a vtable
field from past the end of that module's smaller net_dev_ops_t and call it.

That is why net_dev_ops_t could not be extended, and driver_class.h said so.
With the check in place the vtable is extendable the normal way: bump the ABI and
stale modules fail to load instead of being misread.

The check is one shared predicate rather than a fifth field appended to four
copies of the same test, because the duplication was the hazard -- abi had to be
remembered independently at every site. drvmod_load reports an ABI mismatch
apart from the generic descriptor rejection, since 'corrupt file' and 'rebuild
this module' call for different fixes.

abi_probe.c is a real module claiming A20_DRIVER_ABI + 1, shipped through the
ordinary registry so it is met exactly as a real mismatched module would be. Its
DriverEntry announces itself with a marker the gate forbids, which is what makes
the test differential: 'load failed' would also pass if the package were merely
malformed. Verified by falsification -- removing the comparison turns the gate
red on exactly the expected assertion.
c28faaf047e1ead227f8d0b6e81c140faa4e5eef:
feat(lwip): shard the TCP fast and slow timers per lane

Stage B bucketed the pcb lists, but tcp_fasttmr and tcp_slowtmr were each still
called once per tick and each walked every bucket, so one CPU did the periodic
protocol work for every connection on the machine. Both now walk one bucket
through a helper and report whether a callback changed the list, with the outer
function keeping the original loop and the original restart-from-lane-0
behaviour -- no behaviour change and no new interface, so there is nothing a
caller could depend on wrongly.

tcp_timer and tcp_timer_ctr become per-lane: each lane reads and stamps its own
counter, and a pcb only ever appears in the bucket of the lane that owns it, so
the dedup stays exact. tcp_ticks deliberately stays a single global -- it is the
stack's wall clock, written from the packet paths (pcb->tmr in tcp_in.c,
pcb->rttest in tcp_out.c) and read by keepalive, zero-window-probe, persist,
ooseq, TIME_WAIT MSL and RTT. Sharding it would not shard a timer, it would
change the time base, and a missed reader does not fail to compile -- it computes
the wrong elapsed time. tcp_alloc() now leaves last_timer unstamped, since it
runs before tcp_bind has derived ->lane and a fresh pcb must not look
already-processed to whichever lane adopts it.

An earlier attempt to also spread the timer across CPUs is included as its
revert. Driving it from kernel_progress_timer_tick() bypassed the interval gate
inside sys_check_timeouts(): the counter read ~850 ticks in 15 seconds against a
nominal 4/sec, so tcp_slowtmr ran ~14x too often, pcb->rtime outran wall clock,
every connection hit its RTO almost immediately and live pcbs were torn down
mid-transfer. Kept because the cadence trap it fell into is the thing stage D has
to avoid.
5a3d5d8139a7f5ae0dccc726364a3990f5752029:
fix(net): correct the lock contract and bound a pre-existing multi-lane fault

Chasing a boot panic in the 4-lane configuration found two things worth having in
the tree regardless of whether that panic is ever fixed.

First, a load-bearing invariant was false. Six places -- including the header
comment on g_lwip_lock itself and the lock contract document -- asserted that
g_lwip_lock and g_net_lock are never held together. They are: the accept drain
takes g_net_lock and then a20_lwip_lock(), so both are held, ordered net -> lwip.
No reverse path exists today, so there is no cycle, but stage D drains a receive
ring per lane and touches socket state, which introduces exactly that reverse
order and deadlocks against this one.

Second, LWIP_ASSERT_CORE_LOCKED() was an empty macro, so every core-lock
assertion in tcp.c and tcp_in.c compiled away and the contract had no runtime
enforcement at all. It now counts violations per boot and reports them on
/proc/net/status as 'lwip_lock: owner=<cpu> violations=<n>', recording the owning
CPU rather than a flag -- a flag reads 'held' while a different CPU holds it,
which is the case worth catching. Counting rather than panicking is deliberate: a
panic would fire on any legitimately unlocked init-time call and kill every
configuration before it could be diagnosed.

On a 4-lane a20.tcpmode=lwip boot that reports 23 violations, and all eight
recorded sites symbolize to one-shot bootstrap paths -- netif_init twice,
netif_add, netif_add_ip6_address, lwip_init, a20_lwip_init twice and
a20_lwip_loopif_init_cb. None in receive, accept, timer or pcb add/remove.
Because the probe can only see functions that carry the assertion, thirteen
list-mutating entry points that lacked one were given it -- including tcp_abort,
the RST path where the fault lives -- and re-measured: zero new violations, so
that path does hold the lock. tcp_kill_state/prio/timewait walk every lane and
resemble the crash shape, but tcp_kill has no caller here, so they are dead.

The panic itself is still unexplained and this does not fix it: with 4 lanes,
multiple CPUs and a real listening pcb, the kernel faults during boot, before any
test program runs, tcp_pcb_remove reading a corrupted list head. It is
intermittent, and tcp.c reverted entirely to before this work still reproduces
it. net-lanes.md records the measurements, the four causes eliminated by
inspection, and where the search now points: inside the critical section, or in
state shared across the two lock domains that the false invariant had been
covering.

674e7c11f81c0ab313781d9d6bc50760b6750b97:
perf(net): make lock-contract assertions opt-in to avoid default-path overhead

The check landed on main measuring something real, but it was left switched on:
LWIP_ASSERT_CORE_LOCKED() expands to a call and a branch at roughly fifty lwIP
entry points, some on the timer and receive paths, and that cost was never
measured. Debug instrumentation should not silently tax every default build, so
it now sits behind CONFIG_NET_LOCK_ASSERT and defaults off.

Both halves are gated, not just the macro. With the check off the owner tracking
in a20_lwip_lock()/a20_lwip_unlock() disappears too, since storing an owner that
nothing reads is exactly the cost being removed.

The status line reports "lwip_lock: not checked (CONFIG_NET_LOCK_ASSERT=0)"
rather than violations=0. Printing the zero unconditionally would read as "no
violations found" when it means "nothing was checked", which is the kind of
quietly wrong observability that costs someone an afternoon.

Enable with OPT="-DCONFIG_NET_LOCK_ASSERT=1" when investigating a lock-discipline
question. Verified both configurations build clean under -Werror, and the
enabled path still reports violations=23 sites=8 on a default boot, unchanged
from before the gating, so the diagnostic survives intact. The init-path
violations it finds are expected and are not a defect.
b36457c902e0e9155e8648e169f9c95b1ac6e5bb:
docs(net): replace the stale next-step with a concrete race recipe

The old text said to narrow the trigger with NET_LANES=2 and NR_CPUS=1 first.
That has already been done -- 4 lanes, multiple CPUs and a real listening pcb is
the trigger, and it is intermittent -- so the instruction was sending the next
session back over ground already covered.

Seven hypotheses are now eliminated and the static audit keeps coming back
empty, which is itself the signal: this is a cross-CPU timing window and reading
code cannot see timing. So the note now says what to actually do -- put a
configurable delay into the accept drain between taking the pcb out of the ring
and taking g_lwip_lock, raise it until the panic stops being intermittent, then
use the lock probe to find which side corrupts the list head. And remove the
delay before fixing anything, because it is an amplifier and not a fix.

Names the exact location because it is the only path that both requires a real
LISTEN pcb and spans both lock domains, and says what to do if the delay changes
nothing rather than leaving it open.
ff18e53535c37ac50434a4bbe4ac4b8c8e81166a:
test(net): add an opt-in delay to expose accept-path races

The 4-lane boot fault is a cross-CPU timing window, and reading code has now
eliminated seven hypotheses without finding it. What that recipe needs is a way
to widen the window so the fault stops being intermittent, so this adds the tool
rather than leaving it as advice.

CONFIG_NET_RACE_DELAY_US spins for N microseconds inside the accept drain,
between dequeuing a staged pcb and taking g_lwip_lock. That gap is the point
where the accept path spans both lock domains, and it is the only place on that
path that does. Default 0, so it compiles away and costs nothing until someone
turns it on.

One experiment, and it was inconclusive rather than negative: built with 200us
and ran the 4-lane tcpmode=lwip boot four times, zero faults. That does not show
the window is wrong, because those runs never read /proc/net/status, so there is
no evidence the accept path executes at all before the fault -- and a boot with
no inbound connection leaves the staging ring empty and the delay unreached. The
next run should cat status, and confirm net_accept_staged is nonzero, before
concluding anything from the fault count.

A measuring tool, not a fix. Remove it once the fault is reproducible.
ebdb65907843e79c4d99baad06433bca43cdd2bc:
docs(net): identify pbuf lifetime in loopback draining as the fault source

The amplifier experiment reproduced the fault and, more usefully, produced the
first trustworthy backtrace in this whole investigation. The earlier
ethernet_output+0x664 frame was offset-based symbolization and was wrong; this
one is consistent frame to frame:

  tcp_input <- ip4_input <- ip_input <- netif_poll
            <- a20_lwip_poll_timers_locked <- kernel_progress_timer_tick

So it crashes in the timer-tick loopback drain feeding ip_input, in the idle
task. stval=0x3071c710010000af with a2=0x14, and 0x3071 appears both in a2 and
inside the bad address -- the shape of a pbuf chain pointer computed from packet
data rather than a plain null dereference.

That redirects the search and explains why the amplifier did nothing: I put it
in the wrong place. The accept staging drain is not the window. What crosses both
lock domains is pbuf ownership -- netif_poll() frees netif->loop_first buffers
under g_lwip_lock on CPU 0, while the socket bottom half consumes payloads under
g_net_lock without it, and nothing keeps a buffer alive between those two.

So the defect is a pbuf lifetime gap that predates lanes; multi-lane and
multi-CPU only raise the odds that a second CPU is touching it at the time. The
next step is auditing pbuf lifetime between the loop_first drain and the
bottom-half payload consumer -- who holds a reference, who frees, and whether an
ownership handoff is missing -- and putting the amplifier between the drain's
free and the consumer's read rather than in accept staging.
6daee5eb9736751632bd1c95e6d8579f6223a685:
docs(net): rule out inline-staging overflow and the drain side itself

Continuing the pbuf-lifetime audit the resolved backtrace pointed at. Two
candidates closed by reading, recorded so they are not re-derived.

Inline staging overflow: bh_stage_payload()'s inline branch is bounded by
len <= NET_BH_INLINE_PAYLOAD against a fixed-size e->data, and the overflow
branch takes a pbuf ref into owned[slot] before the caller frees the original.
The reference handling and the bound are both correct.

The drain side: netif_poll() consumes loop_first synchronously under
g_lwip_lock, handing the pbuf straight to ip_input, so there is no window
between draining and protocol processing.

That leaves the corruption happening before the pbuf reaches loop_first -- the
send path's own chain is already bad by the time netif_loop_output queues it.
Next to look at is netif_loop_output()'s pbuf construction and the chain shape
after pbuf_take, plus whether a PBUF_POOL element freed by tcp_segs_free can
still be reachable from some chain.

08e753cb540e474c7043c40eb7c5f460bde19480:
test(smoke): give each tcpmode phase its own port in smoke-net-accept

The gate ran tcp_accept_test twice on port 12346 -- once at boot-time
tcpmode=lwip, then again after `echo tcpmode fast`.  It failed 2 runs in 3,

b814b77d6b189eb25d190381a2fede96f28f218d:
feat(irqchip): share one PLIC instead of three board-local copies

QEMU virt riscv64, riscv32 and VisionFive 2 each carried their own PLIC
body.  rv64_plic_* and vf2_plic_* were near-identical and rv32_plic_* was
a third copy, so every new RISC-V board had to re-derive a controller the
tree already contained three times over.  The copy cost was not symmetric:
the shared controller now indexes the per-hart enable register the way the
specification defines it, as 32-bit words covering 32 interrupts each.

That difference is a real bug fix, not a style change.  rv64_plic_enable()
and rv32_plic_enable() both did `PLIC_SENABLE(hart) |= (1U << irq)`, which
is only correct for interrupts 0..31.  vf2_plic_enable() used
`(irq / 32) * sizeof(uint32_t)` with `1U << (irq % 32)` and was correct for
the whole range.  Two of the three boards therefore dropped every interrupt
number above 31 on the floor.  Nothing noticed, because the only boards in
the tree that used the short form wired interrupt 10 and 11.  Any port to a
SoC whose PLIC numbers its interrupts above 31 -- which is most of them --
would have found its devices silently unroutable.

The register offsets are named PLIC_OFF_* rather than reusing the PLIC_*
names each arch include/platform.h already owns, so this file does not
depend on which architecture is being built; the earlier draft collided
with riscv64's platform.h and riscv32's 32-bit build tripped an
int-to-pointer-cast on the widened offset arithmetic.

plic_irqchip_ops is a const object, not a function returning one, so a
board's static board_config_t can point at it directly; a function call is
not a constant expression and the compiler rejected it.

Verified: kernel-only builds clean under -Werror for riscv64, riscv32,
aarch64, loongarch64, x86_64, ppc64le, and the VisionFive 2 board.
check-smp-platform-boundary, check-concurrency-foundation,
check-driver-core-model, check-honesty-policy and check-doc-test-gates
pass.  check-arch-boundary cannot complete on this host: arm32,
loongarch32 and armv7m have no cross toolchain installed here, which
predates this change and is recorded in docs/roadmap/a20os-improvement-todo.md.
a1a28616043e46525e0dddbde48954deffd58ac5:
feat(x86_64): boot on physical PCs as well as QEMU q35

Three assumptions in the x86_64 path made a physical machine
unreachable.  All three are firmware facts that only exist on the machine
being booted, and all three were hardcoded to what QEMU happens to do.

The PCIe ECAM base was PCI_ECAM_BASE = 0xB0000000, which is q35's
MMCONFIG.  A 2011-onward chipset puts ECAM at 0xE0000000 or wherever its
ACPI MCFG table says, so arch_pci_config_read32() computed addresses into
an unmapped hole and every config read came back 0xffffffff: no AHCI, no
NVMe, no xHCI, nothing.  firmware_acpi_mcfg_base() now reads MCFG
(offset 72) and the board publishes the result through
arch_pci_host_init().  The bus range comes from the same table.

Nothing handled pre-PCIe machines at all, which is most refurbished
office hardware.  pci_host.c now falls back to the 0xCF8/0xCFC
indirection pair, and detects the situation honestly: a vendor id of
0xffffffff from the ECAM window means there is no ECAM, and the legacy
path takes over permanently rather than retrying.

PCI INTx routing identified the machine by host bridge id 0x29c08086
and returned -1 for anything else, so on real hardware every PCI device
kept the polling fallback -- AHCI and NVMe worked but at polled speed.
arch_pci_set_intx_gsi_base() lets a board publish its chipset's GSI base;
it is runtime state rather than a CONFIG_BOARD_ conditional precisely so
that the arch layer does not learn a board name, which
docs/platforms/porting-guide.md forbids.  This is still not ACPI _PRT:
docs/platforms/x86_64-pc.md records that as the remaining gap, along with
the per-chipset GSI base that will need confirming.

The kernel command line was read only from QEMU's fw_cfg device, which
does not exist on a physical machine, so firmware_bootargs() returned
empty and every a20.* knob was unreachable on real hardware.  Multiboot
v1 puts the command line in the info block at offset 16 whichever way
GRUB loaded the kernel, BIOS or UEFI, so that is now read first and
fw_cfg is the fallback.  The first cut of this used a single `ready` flag
for both probes, which made the fw_cfg branch dead and would have broken
`make run` under QEMU; smoke-x86_64 caught it and the two probes are now
separate.

kernel/platform/x86_64-pc/ is a generic PC-compatible board: thin clients,
N100/J4125 mini PCs, office boxes.  It resolves ECAM from MCFG, publishes
the INTx GSI base, and falls back to DHCP when no command line was
supplied instead of reusing QEMU's 10.0.2.x addresses.  RAM is not
declared here because x86_64 already discovers it from the multiboot
memory map.

Verified: smoke-x86_64 passes and logs both bootargs probes, so the QEMU
path is unregressed; kernel-only builds clean under -Werror for riscv64,
aarch64, loongarch64, ppc64le, visionfive2 and the new board.
check-smp-platform-boundary, check-concurrency-foundation,
check-driver-core-model, check-honesty-policy and check-doc-test-gates
pass.  Nothing here has run on physical hardware; the board is
build-verified only, and its docs say so.
9f235e05167f338381c308959766f6f53a5a833b:
fix(riscv64): port two SophGo boards and fix the PLIC indexing they expose

LicheeRV Nano (SG2002, 256 MiB, ~USD 9-14) and Milk-V Duo (CV1800B,
64 MiB, ~USD 10-13).  Both are C906 parts that upstream describes as
rv64imafdc with mmu-type riscv,sv39, which is exactly what the riscv64
build already targets, so neither needs architecture work.  DRAM is at
0x80000000 on both, where the arch linker script already loads, so
neither needs a linker script either.  Their interrupt controller is
declared "thead,c900-plic", which mainline Linux binds to its standard
SiFive PLIC driver rather than a separate T-Head one, so the shared PLIC
from the previous commit applies unchanged.

Both board files stop at RAM + console + PLIC + SBI timebase, and say so.
Their SD controller is a DesignWare CMSH, which is not the older
DesignWare SDIO/MMC layout dw_sdio.c targets, and their MAC is
snps,dwmac-3.70a, older than the DWMAC1000 ls2k_gmac.c drives.  Writing
device table entries for IP nobody drives would produce a board that
enumerates hardware it cannot talk to, so enumerate_devices is empty and
the missing drivers are named in docs/platforms/*.md instead.

Booting these boards needed four things the tree did not have.

arch/riscv64/include/platform.h held the QEMU virt RAM window, MMIO bases
and PLIC base as plain constants, so changing a board's map meant editing
the arch layer -- the thing porting-guide.md reserves for instruction-set
mechanisms.  It now takes a board header, the pattern aarch64 and
loongarch64 already used.  The RAM window matters for correctness, not
tidiness: PHYS_MEMORY_MAX_END is the ceiling the firmware memory node is
clamped against in arch/riscv64/platform/fdt.c, and leaving it at QEMU
virt's base + 16 GiB would let a 64 MiB board's allocator believe in
memory that does not exist.

The SophGo SoCs have no PCIe and no virtio MMIO transport.  Their board
headers leave PCIE_ECAM_BASE and VIRTIO_BASE undefined rather than
defaulting to QEMU virt's addresses, which means the accessors now need a
no-hardware path.  Defining them as 0 was the tempting shortcut and it is
wrong: 0 is a valid physical address, so a stray config read would fault
on the boot page table instead of reporting nothing.  They return the
architectural absent answers instead -- 0xffffffff for a config read,
-1 for a virtio probe -- which is what the bus enumerator already expects
from hardware that is not plugged in.  This is the same rule the honesty
policy states for smoke gates: an absent capability has to say so.

plic_init_hart() wrote the per-hart enable register as one 32-bit word,
1U << UART0_IRQ.  That register is an array of words covering 32
interrupts each, so the expression is a shift of 44 on a 32-bit type for
these boards -- undefined behaviour that happened to work on every board
already in the tree, because the only source any of them wired to the
console hart was UART0_IRQ 10.  It now zeroes the block and sets
UART0_IRQ/32 at bit UART0_IRQ%32.  PLIC_ENABLE_WORDS is exported from the
shared driver so the trap path and the controller cannot disagree.

Verified: MMU and NOMMU kernel-only builds clean under -Werror for all
four riscv64 boards, and riscv64 MMU builds for aarch64, loongarch64,
x86_64, ppc64le and the x86_64-pc board are unregressed.
check-smp-platform-boundary, check-concurrency-foundation,
check-driver-core-model, check-honesty-policy, check-doc-test-gates and
check-instances pass.

Not run on hardware.  The board docs record what has to happen before
that claim is true, and name the one thing nobody can settle without the
board: KERNEL_ENTRY is a compile-time constant and U-Boot's load address
for these parts has not been read off the silicon.
f043840a47f55f6cbf70248461b4a8206b55d82d:
feat(a20): describe the new boards and let RAMFS userland build for riscv64

Three instances for the boards in the previous two commits.  None of them
declares a [package] section, because none of these boards can boot from a
filesystem yet: the SophGo SD controller is a DesignWare CMSH and A20OS
only has the older DesignWare SDIO/MMC driver, so there is nothing to put
on a card.  An instance that claimed to package a bootable image would be
claiming something the board cannot do.

Each one declares [target] instead, which is how you talk to the board:
serial node, baud, boot timeout, and the console_check lines that have to
appear before the instance means anything.  Those lines describe intent, not
verification -- the acceptance record stays in docs/platforms/, which is
where the repository keeps it.

The Milk-V Duo instance sets ramfs_user and swap = false because it has
64 MiB, and that combination did not build on riscv64.  RAMFS_USER was
gated on an explicit $(error) naming loongarch64, so the one feature a
small-memory board most needs was available only on one architecture.
The gate now asks the objcopy table instead -- RAMFS_USER_OBJCOPY_$(ARCH)
-- which is the thing that actually has to exist for the rule in
tools/targets-images.mk to work, so an architecture is enabled by adding
one table line rather than by editing two places that can disagree.
riscv64 gets -O elf64-littleriscv -B riscv:rv64.  loongarch64 is
unaffected and still builds its nine blobs; riscv32 still gets the clear
"no objcopy recipe" error.

`tools/a20 boards` is new.  Deciding what to port starts from knowing what
exists, and `a20 list` could not answer it: it enumerates instances, so a
board without an instance was invisible -- which is every board until
somebody writes one.  It reports each board's architecture, whether it
provides smp_platform_ops, whether it overrides the linker script, and the
first line of its header comment.  The architecture is read out of the arch
headers that claim the board's CONFIG_BOARD_ token rather than from a
table, with the instances as the fallback for boards that predate the
override mechanism, so it cannot disagree with what the build compiles.
nailoong reports "?" honestly: it is the one board with no instance,
because loongarch32 needs a from-source toolchain that CI cannot install.

4c5ebd027ea98d8c6048438f447e52870523962a:
feat(aarch64): port RK3328 the one ARM target that boots without a signed blob

Rock64 and NanoPi R2S, USD 25-35.  TF-A's rk3328 platform is open source, so
the only vendor binary in the chain is the SPL's DDR training blob -- the
Allwinner H616/H618 parts are cleaner still, but their SD controller is a
vendor sunxi-mmc rather than anything DesignWare, which makes them more work
than this board.

Two upstream properties make it cheap.  The console UART is
"snps,dw-apb-uart", a 16550, which every architecture's console.h already
declares.  And the interrupt controller is "arm,gic-400" -- GICv2, which is
exactly the pair of GICC_BASE/GICD_BASE registers the aarch64 port already
drives, so there is no GICv3 work.  The GMAC is "rockchip,rk3328-gmac",
driven upstream by dwmac-rk.c: the same Synopsys DWMAC family ls2k_gmac.c
targets, which is the main reason this board is worth doing at all.

DRAM_BASE needed the arch override.  The RK3328's DDRC aperture starts at
0x0, where the aarch64 default is 0x40000000, and Rock64's device tree
declares no memory node at all -- the bootloader passes the layout -- so the
window is a claim from the SoC memory map rather than something read off a
board.  The doc says so and the instance carries the values for whoever does
read them off real silicon.

This port stops at RAM, console, GICv2 and PSCI power off.  eMMC is a
DesignWare MSHC (upstream dwmci-mshc) which is not the older SDIO/MMC layout
dw_sdio.c targets; the GMAC needs a Rockchip CRU/GRF clock-and-reset
sequence first; and .smp stays NULL because which CPUs exist has not been
checked on hardware, which porting-guide.md requires rather than papering over
with a fake ops table.  early_init() does not touch the CRU: U-Boot already
enabled the console UART's clocks before handing over, and writing CRU gates
for peripherals that are not yet driven would be guesswork.

aarch64's virtio_probe.c needed the same treatment riscv64's did last commit --
the RK3328 has no virtio-mmio window, and VIRTIO_BASE undefined is how a board
says so.

Also lists the new boards in README.md and docs/README.md, with the NOMMU
contract spelled out because that is the right configuration for a 64 MiB part
and the entry-point is easy to miss.

Verified: aarch64 kernel-only builds clean under -Werror for rk3328,
qemu-virt-aarch64 and virtualbox-aarch64.  check-a20-tests, check-instances,
check-doc-test-gates, check-doc-drift, check-honesty-policy,
check-smp-platform-boundary, check-concurrency-foundation and
check-driver-core-model pass; 49 instances validate.

Not run on hardware.
aff6f79425c5e5c764566986488a42f7cb37f48e:
fix(aarch64): fix two NOMMU build failures exposed by the RK3328 port

arch_is_kernel_address() tested the low bound as `ptr >= PHYS_MEMORY_BASE`,
which is `ptr >= 0` on the RK3328 -- its DRAM starts at physical 0 -- and
-Werror=type-limits rejected the always-true comparison.  Expressed as an
offset from the window base instead, which is vacuously correct when the base
is 0 and still a containment test when it is not, rather than special-casing
the board.

vbox_aarch64_platform.h redefined PAGE_OFFSET and USER_VA_LIMIT with the
same MMU values arch/aarch64/include/platform.h had already set.  Under
NOMMU the arch header sets PAGE_OFFSET to 0 first, the board header then
redefines it, and the NOMMU build of that board has been failing against
-Werror ever since.  Pre-existing, not caused by this port, but it is the
same double-definition the board-override mechanism invites, so it is worth
removing rather than documenting.  The arch values are already correct for
both modes.

Verified: every board in the tree builds MMU, and every NOMMU_ARCHES board
also builds NOMMU -- riscv64, riscv32, aarch64.  smoke-x86_64 and
smoke-riscv64 pass.  All thirteen boundary, driver-model, doc and registry
gates pass.
abc0f3306ec7df4b3c8bde39e352ca354a15289e:
chore(abi): remove LS2K bring-up markers from filesystem and ABI paths

One board's first-boot instrumentation had been left switched on inside the
architecture-neutral paths: six uart_putc calls in the readiness scan that
poll(2) blocks on, eleven in linux_poll itself, and one per syscall in the
dispatch path.  All eighteen were gated on CONFIG_BOARD_LS2K1000 &&
CONFIG_COOPERATIVE_BOOT, so they cost nothing on any other board -- but they
put a board name in code that has no business knowing one, and 0xC0000000-style
debug tracing inside poll(2) is the kind of thing that gets left switched on
by accident and then blamed for a latency problem.

The gating meant the markers were also load-bearing documentation of intent:
they showed where the LS2K1000 bring-up was stuck.  What replaces them is not
nothing -- CONFIG_LS2K_TRAP_TRACE still works for anyone who wants to
re-enable tracing, and kernel/arch/loongarch64/{boot/switch.S,trap/trap.S} keep
their single-character switch/trap checkpoints.  Those are assembly, guarded
by the same CONFIG_BOARD_LS2K1000 test, and they poke the LS2K UART directly
rather than calling into C, so they are legitimately arch-internal and left
alone.  Note the build never actually defined CONFIG_LS2K_TRAP_TRACE, so that
assembly path was already dormant.

The C-side tracing helper uart_trace_ls2k_syscall() in uart.h existed only to
serve the dispatch site and went with it; uart.h no longer mentions any board.

Verified: kernel-only builds clean under -Werror for all nine board targets,
including ls2k1000 itself -- the board the markers were for -- with
DRIVER_DEPLOYMENT=embedded.  check-smp-platform-boundary,
check-concurrency-foundation, check-honesty-policy and check-doc-test-gates
pass.
d69804c7382ae85a783c3bbc9605235b8742afde:
feat(panic): route LoongArch register dumps through architecture hooks

panic() and the return-to-user path in proc_task_first_entry() read
LoongArch CSRs inline: nine in the panic capture and eight at every first
switch back to user, all behind CONFIG_BOARD_LS2K1000.  That put a board
name and a LoongArch CSR number list inside two architecture-neutral files,
and the CSR reads in panic() ran before va_start purely so the values
survived long enough to print.

Two optional hooks now carry it.  arch_panic_dump() is called from panic()
where the LoongArch block used to print, and arch_debug_dump_user_state()
from the switch path; the generic callers say nothing about which registers
exist.  An architecture opts in by defining ARCH_HAS_BOOT_TRACE_DUMPS in its
own arch/<arch>/include/arch.h, following the ARCH_HAS_* convention the tree
already uses for capability negotiation.  Only loongarch64 does, and only when
CONFIG_DEBUG_BOOT_TRACE is set -- the same flag that compiles the new file --
so every other build gets a no-op inline rather than a declared function with
no definition.  The default has to be an inline and not a weak symbol: a
no-op definition would still be a real call in the panic path.

The switch is now opt-in rather than implicit.  It used to be gated on
CONFIG_BOARD_LS2K1000, which meant a new board could not ask for these dumps
without editing kernel/core/panic.c.  The Makefile sets the flag for the
LS2K1000 cooperative profile, which is the only configuration that had it.

kernel/proc/task.c also had ls2k_dump_user_pt_path(), a page-table walker
written entirely in arch-neutral page-table terms -- arch_pt_vpn,
arch_pte_is_leaf, arch_pte_to_ptr -- behind that board guard.  It is now
dump_user_pt_path() behind CONFIG_DEBUG_BOOT_TRACE, since that is what it
actually is.

CSR numbers are immediates, not a function argument.  Passing the number in a
register let GCC allocate the same register for destination and source,
emitting `csrrd $r8, $r8`, which this assembler rejects; the inline reads this
replaced all used immediates and are kept that way.

Verified: all thirteen board targets build clean under -Werror, and ls2k1000
builds both with DEBUG_BOOT_TRACE (the eleven diagnostics present) and without
(it compiled out).  check-smp-platform-boundary, check-concurrency-foundation,
check-driver-core-model, check-honesty-policy and check-doc-test-gates pass.
941a6b6f7ae17fff8b4551d9faea99544962ec3d:
feat(sched): query the board for its timer device

idle_loop() tested CONFIG_BOARD_LS2K1000 four times.  Two of those were not
logging: the idle path skipped arch_local_irq_enable() entirely and called
cpu_relax() in place of the arch_idle_wait() sequence.  A board that needs a
different idle strategy therefore had to edit kernel/proc/proc.c, and the only
example of that need in the tree was expressed as a board name in the
scheduler.

board_config_t gains idle_cannot_sleep, and idle_loop() reads it once.  The
polarity is deliberate: every other field in that struct is a pointer, so a
static initializer leaves this one at 0, which means 0 has to be "the timer
works" or every board that does not mention it would silently stop sleeping
and burn a core spinning.  The LS2K1000 sets it only under
CONFIG_COOPERATIVE_BOOT, which is what the old guard tested too -- the same
board in its normal profile still sleeps.

kernel/proc/fork.c's non-preemptive clone launch was left alone.  It looks like
the same problem but is guarded by CONFIG_COOPERATIVE_BOOT, a build profile
rather than a board name, so no board is named in neutral code there and
nothing needs to change.

Verified: ls2k1000 builds both with and without COOPERATIVE_BOOT, and all
eleven other board targets are unregressed -- with idle_cannot_sleep zeroed by
static initialization, which is the case that would have broken them if the
polarity were the other way round.  check-smp-platform-boundary,
check-concurrency-foundation, check-driver-core-model, check-honesty-policy and
check-doc-test-gates pass.
157741914f4b6716efd5a2767325b2adf1dc12e1:
feat(mm.abi): describe physical address width as a hardware property

Nine sites in architecture-neutral files branched on CONFIG_<architecture> or
CONFIG_BOARD_<name>.  In every case the thing being branched on was a
hardware or firmware property, and writing the architecture's name instead
meant that adding an architecture to the tree silently changed behaviour
nobody had decided on.

Seven are architecture properties and now say so.  Each is a capability macro
in core/arch.h, defaulting to the safe or common case, following the ARCH_HAS_*
convention already in the tree:

  ARCH_EXE_LEAF_RETAIN_UNSAFE   x86_64, loongarch64
  ARCH_FAULT_AROUND_UNSAFE      loongarch64
  ARCH_INSN_FAULT_UNRECOVERABLE ppc64le
  ARCH_TIMER_FREQ_RUNTIME       riscv64
  ARCH_FAST_CURRENT             riscv64
  ARCH_HW_SINGLE_STEP           x86_64
  ARCH_LINUX_EPOLL_EVENT_PACKED x86_64

The first one is a latent bug fix.  mm/fault.c's comment said "LoongArch64 and
x86_64 additionally keep ALL executable private leaves on the anonymous-copy
path" while the code tested only CONFIG_X86_64, so LoongArch64 was taking the
opposite branch from the one its own comment described.  It now sets the
macro.  The change is unobservable on LoongArch64 because
ARCH_FAULT_AROUND_UNSAFE already forces fault_around to 0 there and
direct_private requires fault_around, so what actually changes is that the
comment and the code agree.

The other two are board facts, not architecture facts, and went into
board_config_t next to idle_cannot_sleep rather than into arch.h:

  vdso_user_timer_unreliable  VisionFive 2
  uart_rx_is_polled            VisionFive 2, LS2K1000 cooperative

Both are about how a board's firmware hands over -- whether U-mode can read
the time CSR, whether the console UART has an interrupt -- and neither is a
property of the instruction set.  They replace three CONFIG_BOARD tests: one in
mm/vdso.c and two in drivers/char/uart.c that were keyed on VisionFive 2, and a
third in uart.c that was keyed on the LS2K1000 cooperative profile and is the
same fact as the other two.  As with idle_cannot_sleep the polarity is chosen so
that a static initializer's 0 is the working behaviour.

Verified: all thirteen board targets build clean under -Werror, and ls2k1000
builds under COOPERATIVE_BOOT as well, which is the configuration that exercises
two of the three new flags.  check-smp-platform-boundary,
check-concurrency-foundation, check-driver-core-model, check-abi-boundary,
check-honesty-policy and check-doc-test-gates pass.
8bb2557a543404ce4c9a53a4db99628203e53378:
feat(aarch64): port allwinner H616/H618 the only blob-free ARM boot chain

Orange Pi Zero 2, Zero 3 and Zero 2W, USD 18-35.  The reason this board is
worth having over the RK3328 already in the tree is the boot chain: the SPL is
built from U-Boot source and BL31 is TF-A's sun50i_h616 platform, which is
mainline.  Nothing in the chain is a vendor blob the build cannot reproduce --
against rkbin's DDR blob for Rockchip, a signed FIP for Amlogic, and no
mainline U-Boot target at all for the Raspberry Pi 5.

The reuse is unusually good.  The console is "snps,dw-apb-uart", a 16550, so
every architecture's console.h already declares it.  The interrupt controller
is "arm,gic-400", GICv2, which is exactly the GICD_BASE/GICC_BASE pair the
aarch64 port already drives.  The MAC is a Synopsys DWMAC variant
(dwmac-sun8i), the same family ls2k_gmac.c targets.  And DRAM sits at
0x40000000, where the aarch64 QEMU default already points, so the memory
window needed no change at all -- the board needed one new
CONFIG_BOARD_* branch in platform.h and nothing else.

Scope is RAM, console, GICv2 and PSCI power off, the same stopping point as the
other new boards.  Storage is the reason this one is worse off than the SophGo
ports rather than better: the controller is "allwinner,sun50i-h616-mmc",
driven upstream by sunxi-mmc.c.  That is Allwinner's own design, so A20OS's
dw_sdio.c does not apply and there is no generic MMC core to slot a host into.
The MAC would need an Allwinner CCU clock-and-reset sequence first.

Two facts are recorded as unverified at the point where they matter, because
neither can be settled without the board.  KERNEL_ENTRY is a compile-time
constant and these DTSs declare no memory node at all -- U-Boot passes the
layout -- so PHYS_MEMORY_END is a 1 GiB window rather than a measurement, and a
2 GiB Zero 3 needs it raised or the allocator will hand out a page that does
not exist.  The aarch64 port has no DT-based RAM narrowing the way riscv64's
riscv64_memory_init() does, which is what makes that worth writing down.

Verified: all fourteen board targets build clean under -Werror.
check-smp-platform-boundary, check-concurrency-foundation,
check-driver-core-model, check-honesty-policy, check-doc-test-gates,
check-doc-drift, check-a20-tests and check-instances pass; 50 instances
validate.  Not run on hardware.
3dfe3a349363e546ddd67ee0ab4a7db8f9923842:
docs(acknowledgments): record board provenance and why K230 and d1s are not ported

Two documentation debts that the new ports created.

ACKNOWLEDGMENTS.md gains a provenance section for the five board ports.  Every
address, size, interrupt number and clock frequency in the five
<board>_platform.h files is transcribed from an upstream Linux device tree, and
the section names the exact files and the commit
(551c722f40809618230001baccf219193e22fc5a).  That matters because the honesty
policy draws a line between transcribing a hardware fact and copying code, and
the line is only visible if the provenance is written down: the board.c files
and their platform headers are A20OS's own work, but the numbers in them came
from somewhere specific.  The section also lists which upstream facts were
consulted to decide reuse rather than to copy -- irq-sifive-plic.c's of_device_id
table is why the SophGo and D1s interrupt controllers work with the shared PLIC,
and the SophGo clock/reset bindings are why the console UART needs no clock
programming.

platforms/not-yet-ported.md records Kendryte K230 and Allwinner D1s/F133.  Both
were investigated far enough to know they are the right hardware, and both are
blocked on something that cannot be resolved by guessing.

The K230 is the more interesting block.  Its interrupt controller is at
0xf00000000 -- 60 GiB -- while its UART is at 0x91400000, and the Sv39 boot map
in entry.S has exactly two MMIO megapage slots, one of them hardcoded at PA 0.
A board cannot be written around that; entry.S needs a third slot, which is
architecture work whose failure mode is faulting before the first instruction
with no serial log to read.  There is also a PMP reset-lock that needs a patched
OpenSBI and DDR training that needs a vendor firmware generator.  All of that
is recorded with sources.

The D1s/F133 is a smaller version of the same problem.  Its PLIC and its
C906 core are the same parts the SophGo boards use, so the shared PLIC applies
and rv64imafdcvu is a superset of the existing -march -- that half is clean.
But its device tree uses SOC_PERIPHERAL_IRQ(n) without the definition being in
any header under include/dt-bindings/interrupt-controller/, and no D1s board
declares a memory node.  Guessing nr + 16 by analogy with the SophGo part would
make the console never respond; guessing the DDR base would have the allocator
touch memory that does not exist.

Shipping a placeholder for either would be the failure mode docs/security/
hardening.md forbids: it reports a capability as present when it is not.  A
board that compiles and cannot boot is worse than an absent one, because the
absence is visible and the placeholder is not.

Verified: check-doc-test-gates, check-honesty-policy and check-doc-drift pass.
4612a632448f6e14187c9d0e0fe86ec5494b30bb:
feat(mm): make the user VA layout per-architecture instead of one global set

The user virtual-address layout lived in core/consts.h as a single set of
constants: mmap base, stack top and floor, TLS base, interpreter base, loader
base.  All of them sit below 4 GiB, which was accurate while every
architecture placed its user space down there and stopped being accurate the
moment one did not.  aarch64 and x86_64 have 48-bit virtual addresses and
LoongArch can do LA57, so a port that wanted to use them was capped at the low
4 GiB with nowhere to record that as a decision.

They now live in mm/user_layout.h, and each address is behind an #ifndef so a
board or architecture can override it.  No value changed: every architecture
still resolves to the addresses that have been running all along, because
changing one is a behaviour change that has to be validated on that
architecture rather than a cosmetic edit.  What changed is that the constraint
is now a per-architecture choice instead of something every architecture
inherited by accident.

A20_VDSO_VA and A20_VVAR_VA did not move, and the new header says why rather
than leaving it to be discovered.  mm/vdso_layout.h has to stay
preprocessor-only because the user-space vDSO assembly images for four
architectures include it, and a .S file cannot pull in core/types.h.  A 48-bit
port would have to relocate the vDSO as well, which means making that shared
header assembly-safe first; that is a prerequisite for such a port rather than
part of this one.  Naming the remaining coupling is the useful part.

The other half of the contract is already per-architecture and is called out
from the new header: ARCH_PT_USER_START and ARCH_PT_USER_END in each arch's
page_table.h are page-table indices bounding the user half of the address
space, while the constants here are addresses inside it.  A 48-bit port has to
change both, and it is now obvious that it has to.

Verified: all fourteen board targets build clean under -Werror, and
smoke-riscv64 and smoke-x86_64 pass, which is the evidence that this is
behaviour-neutral rather than merely compiling.  check-concurrency-foundation,
check-smp-platform-boundary, check-driver-core-model, check-abi-boundary,
check-honesty-policy and check-doc-test-gates pass.
76e5e5505d3a203f95df09437a7abae4d93a776a:
build(tools): track drvmod header dependencies instead of listing them by hand

A drvmod blob embeds a driver_t, so it is compiled against the kernel's struct
layout, and every rule in this file names the headers it wants rebuilt by hand.
Nothing forced that list to be complete, so a header left off it was invisible:
the blob simply kept the offsets it was built with while the kernel moved on.

The failure is not close to the cause.  Adding one field to the middle of
driver_t left every .a20drv untouched, and virtio-blk started registering as
class=0 instead of DEV_CLASS_BLOCK -- the loader read class_type from the old
offset.  A block driver that reports the wrong class binds nothing, so the FAT32
root never mounted, /bin/init was ENOENT, and init_kthread panicked with "no
init program found".  Nothing in that report points at a stale binary blob.

Worse, the build was not reproducible in the other direction either: a clean
tree after the same header edit failed identically, so this was a live trap for
anyone changing driver_t or device_t rather than something specific to the edit
that found it.

Use the mechanism the kernel build already relies on for this (Makefile:694
-MMD -MP, with the generated lists included at Makefile:1071) instead of
maintaining the list by hand.  A drvmod now rebuilds when any header it actually
includes changes, and -MP keeps a rule buildable if one of those headers is
deleted.  The hand-written prerequisites are left in place: they are harmless,
and they still document what each blob is expected to pull in.

Verified: touching driver_core/h now schedules a drvmod rebuild and produces 10
.d files, where before the blobs stayed stale.  With the stale blobs rebuilt,
smoke-proc-stress passes again, virtio-blk and virtio-scsi register as class=2,
and the FAT32 root mounts.  check-doc-test-gates -- which is what caught this --
passes, along with check-driver-core-model, check-abi-boundary,
check-honesty-policy, check-concurrency-foundation,
check-smp-platform-boundary, check-instances and check-component-registry.
a24c5107ec8ad6617b5c884f3ed0fd3832c116de:
feat(riscv64): enumerate platform devices from the device tree

A board file had to spell out every device it had: the MMIO base, the size and
the IRQ, hand-copied out of a device tree into #defines, and then restated as a
platform_device_t whose vendor number had to agree with the driver's.  Both
halves are things the firmware already told us, and the VisionFive 2 file was
carrying 0x16040000 and 78 because someone had once read them out of
jh7110.dtsi correctly.  The next board repeats the transcription, and the one
after that trusts it.

Read them from the tree instead.  driver_t gains an of_compatible string, and
the walker asks the driver model which driver claims a node rather than carrying
a table of vendor numbers, so this file names no driver and no magic constant.
A node's reg becomes an MMIO resource and its interrupts an IRQ resource;
compatible is tried as the NUL-separated list it is; status = "disabled" is
honoured, which is how the JH7110 tree keeps the second GMAC from appearing on a
board that only wired one out.

The two drivers the JH7110 tree describes declare what they answer to, with the
upstream node each string came from recorded next to it -- starfive,jh7110-mmc
on mmc1 and starfive,jh7110-dwmac on gmac0/gmac1, from jh7110.dtsi at upstream
551c722f.  That is a string nobody can verify by reading this tree, so where it
came from is part of the code.

Both agree with the numbers the VisionFive 2 board file already used: 0x16020000
for the SDIO and 0x16040000 with IRQ 78 for GMAC1.  Reading them from the tree
therefore changes no address that was previously in use; it removes the copy that
could drift away from the firmware.

The hand-written table stays as the fallback when firmware passes no tree, and
that is a deliberate hedge rather than dead code: this board's only storage path
would otherwise disappear on a DTB-less boot, and no VisionFive 2 has been
powered to find out which case holds.  For the same reason this is build-verified
only -- the enumeration has never run on the board.

Verified: all fourteen board targets build clean under -Werror, riscv64 NOMMU
builds for both QEMU and Milk-V Duo, smoke-riscv64 and smoke-proc-stress pass,
and check-driver-core-model, check-abi-boundary, check-honesty-policy,
check-concurrency-foundation, check-smp-platform-boundary, check-instances and
check-component-registry pass.  The driver_t layout change is what surfaced the
stale-drvmod bug fixed in fd1f32d8.
cc7169da6cf94af39e1730d64bf4f55d62c20002:
feat(a20): give boards with no block driver a deployment path at all

Every deployment path in a20 assumed a writable medium: `a20 deploy` flashes,
writes target.boot_media, then verifies on the console.  A board whose SD
controller has no driver has no medium, so it had no artifact to package, and
`deploy` on one of the four storage-less SBC ports built a kernel and then
attached the console to a board that had never been given anything to run.
`a20 show` advertised deploy for it anyway, because the guard only checked that
boot_media and media_device were not half-declared -- having neither passed.

Two changes, because the second is what made the first honest to ship.

The guard now requires something to actually put on the board: a writable
medium, or a boot chain to hand the kernel to.  An instance with neither is no
longer told it can deploy.

The new path is [handoff] plus package.kind = "kernel-bundle".  `a20 package`
writes kernel.bin, a uboot.cmd and a README into one directory; `a20 deploy`
builds it, prints the commands to type at the boot chain, then runs the console
check as before.  The commands come from the instance, so the sequence in the
repository and the sequence on the board are the same sequence.

The load address is read out of the first PT_LOAD header of the built ELF by
tools/mk_kernel_bundle.sh rather than taken from the manifest.  A board whose
ldscript relocates the image -- the VisionFive 2 moves it to 0x40200000 for its
own DRAM window -- would otherwise need a per-board address restated here, which
is exactly the kind of second copy that goes stale.

No device tree is shipped in the bundle.  These boards boot through a vendor
FSBL and U-Boot, and U-Boot passes its own board DTB in a1; that DTB is the
authoritative description of the board and is what riscv64_memory_init() and the
platform device tree walker already read.  A second copy shipped from the kernel
tree would be a second thing to keep in sync with the firmware.

The four instance handoff commands are labelled unverified in the manifests.  No
SG2002, CV1800B, RK3328 or H616 board has been powered under A20OS, so the
sequences come from what mainline U-Boot provides for each board, not from a
run.

Verified: a20 check passes for all instances; a20 package licheerv-nano builds
the bundle with the load address correctly derived as 0x80200000; a20 show now
reports deploy for the four SBC instances and it does real work.
check-instances, check-component-registry and check-manifests pass.
4c9cc658337cbb4fe5150ada9a239e7128d36589:
feat(a20): deploy to physical x86_64 PCs and report the missing host dependency

The generic PC is the one new board that can be deployed today -- it has AHCI
storage and GRUB can boot the multiboot kernel -- but its instance had no
deployment path.  It declared package.kind = "grub-iso" and a serial target,

280cd7ae2b91a54e30b44ffac905e0975bc55036:
docs(platforms): deploy the five new boards through tools/a20 not make

Every one of these documents told the reader to run
`make ARCH=... BOARD=... kernel-only` and stopped there. That was accurate when
they were written and is now the wrong instruction twice over: the deployment
tool is `tools/a20`, and a build command is not a deployment. Nothing in any of
the five said what artifact you end up with, where it goes, or how to tell a
successful boot from a hang. A reader who followed them exactly had a kernel and
no next step.

Each board now has a Deploying section written around the artifact that board
actually produces, because the five do not produce the same thing:

The four SBCs have no block driver, so there is no medium to write. Their
section says so first, then walks the real path: `a20 package` produces
`build/<board>/handoff/` with kernel.bin, uboot.cmd and a README, the reader
loads it through the boot chain the board already has, and `a20 console` checks
the result. milk-v-duo and sun50i-h616 read the kernel off the TF card; rk3328
and licheerv-nano use TFTP. Each says where the load address comes from -- read
out of the built ELF by `a20 package`, not restated in the document, so a board
that relocates its image cannot go stale here.

x86_64-pc is the opposite case and now reads that way: it has AHCI storage and
boots from media, so its section is `a20 package` -> rescue ISO -> USB stick ->
boot, with the `xorriso` prerequisite named. It also explains why GRUB rather
than a UEFI stub, since most 2025 thin clients are UEFI-only and there is no
x86_64 stub in the tree.

Three things the sections are careful about:

Each states what the acceptance evidence actually is, which differs by
architecture. The riscv64 boards can wait for `[FDT] RAM range` because they
parse a device tree. The aarch64 boards cannot -- only riscv64 and loongarch
print that line -- so their evidence is `System ready` alone, said plainly rather
than padded with a string their architecture cannot emit. That corrects
console_check in c9af57ae and b33ae7aa, which had copied it.

Each ends with a failure list ordered by what fails first, because the most
useful thing a bring-up document can say is what the silence means. The aarch64
boards lead with the load address, which is a compile-time constant disagreeing
with U-Boot's loadaddr and produces no output at all.

licheerv-nano and milk-v-duo also record why no DTB ships in the bundle: U-Boot
passes its own board DTB in a1, and that is what the kernel reads. A second copy
from the kernel tree would be a second thing to keep in sync with the firmware.

Verified: zero `make ARCH` references remain in the five documents; they carry
between four and seven `tools/a20` references each. check-doc-test-gates,
check-instances and check-doc-drift pass.
