95f7c9073513828599f95744cd0e53ec1c2cfd4d:
feat(riscv64): read FDT cells big-endian and name the devices nothing claims

Two bugs in the device tree walker from 41863713, both found by running it and
neither visible to a build.

FDT cells are big-endian. dt_cells_to_u64() and the interrupts read took a
`const uint32_t *` over the property bytes and never swapped them, so on this
little-endian host every address came out byte-swapped: reg cell pair
<0x00 0x10100000> produced 0x1010. A driver bound through this walker would
have been handed an MMIO base in the wrong byte order and written to an address
that does not exist. rtc@101000 happened to look correct, which is how this
survives review -- its bytes are symmetric, so the corruption is invisible in
exactly the one case someone would check by eye. Now routed through
dt_read32(), and the whole walker was confirmed against a live boot: every
reported address matches its node name.

The kernel printf has width but no precision. The diagnostic added below used
%.*s, which fell through to the default case, printed the spec literally, and
desynchronised the varargs after it -- so the address in the same line was also
garbled. Nothing else in the tree uses precision; this now copies the bounded
string and prints it with %s.

The diagnostic itself is the point of the commit. A board with no driver for its
SD controller used to boot RAM-only with one symptom: "no FAT32 device for /bin",
naming neither the controller nor the compatible string to bind. The walker now
reports unclaimed MMIO nodes as `no driver claims "sophgo,sg2002-dwcmshc"`, so the
boot log is the work list for whoever writes the driver next. Capped at eight:
a real tree describes far more than this kernel claims, and a boot log is not the
place for a full inventory.

licheerv-nano and milk-v-duo now call the walker from their enumerate_devices,
which until now were empty. QEMU virt deliberately does not: it would add eight
lines to every QEMU boot for devices its own enumeration already handles by a
different mechanism. It was used to observe and verify this output, then
reverted.

Verified: smoke-riscv64 passes with the corrected addresses; all four riscv64
boards build; check-honesty-policy, check-doc-test-gates, check-driver-core-model
and check-concurrency-foundation pass.
a70eb76364b0b37413ff2397e39d37f907c73ecd:
feat(aarch64): define QEMU_BLK_SECOND which was missing entirely

Every instance that declares [rootfs].world runs its root filesystem from a
second disk. The device that attaches that disk is per-architecture, and aarch64
was absent from the table, so $(QEMU_BLK_SECOND_aarch64) expanded to nothing and
run-world-gui emitted

  -device ,drive=xworld

which is a malformed argument rather than a missing one: QEMU is given a device
string with no model and no bus. xfce-aarch64 has been declaring world = "xfce"
against that target, so the aarch64 Alpine desktop path could not have worked.

The second disk goes on a second virtio-mmio bus, not on PCI. That is not a
style choice: qemu-virt-aarch64's enumerate_devices calls only
virtio_mmio_enumerate and never calls arch_pci_host_init, so a virtio-blk-pci
would satisfy QEMU and still never be enumerated by the kernel. The primary disk
already occupies bus.0, which is why riscv64 places its second disk on bus.1
the same way.

Worth recording that the obvious fix is wrong. Reaching for virtio-blk-pci
because the other two architectures use it produces a command line that looks
correct and a disk that silently does not appear -- a worse failure than the
malformed argument this replaces, because nothing errors.

Verified: aarch64 now emits -device virtio-blk-device,bus=virtio-mmio-bus.1
,drive=xworld, matching riscv64; riscv64, x86_64 and loongarch64 are unchanged.
check-instances passes. Not runtime-verified -- that needs a built xfce Alpine
image, and apk is not present on this host.
6dbcb5fafe57522ac8c2fc98e5f01e693d1c5e5c:
feat(aarch64): give VirtualBox a kernel command line instead of a compiled-in one

virtualbox-aarch64 answered arch_bootargs_get() with a string literal. Every
other A20OS platform takes its command line from firmware: qemu-virt-aarch64 and
qemu-virt-riscv64 read /chosen/bootargs out of the device tree, x86_64 reads the
multiboot line, and the physical boards get whatever their boot chain was told.
This one platform could not be configured at all.

That is why the Alpine work could not start here rather than merely being awkward.
A world root lives on a second disk, and pointing the kernel at it needs a root=
on the command line -- which on this platform there was no way to supply. The
literal also meant the image behaved differently from every other board for
reasons that had nothing to do with the board.

The UEFI loader now does what an EFI application is supposed to do: ask for
EFI_LOADED_IMAGE_PROTOCOL and pass LoadOptions to the kernel. That is the
standard channel, so it also means GRUB, U-Boot and OVMF can drive this platform
without A20OS-specific cooperation. handle_protocol was already in the boot
services table but typed as void *, so it is now given its real signature; it is
one pointer either way and the table layout does not move.

x2 carries the command line to the boot stub, which was unused. entry.S parks it
in aarch64_boot_cmdline beside aarch64_boot_acpi_rsdp, and board.c reads it back
through PAGE_OFFSET the same way it already did for the DTB. Firmware that
supplies no options leaves the pointer 0 and the old compiled-in string remains
as the default, so a plain `a20 run` is unchanged.

Verified: all fourteen board targets build clean under -Werror, including all
four aarch64 boards; smoke-riscv64 and smoke-x86_64 pass; check-honesty-policy,
check-doc-test-gates, check-instances and check-concurrency-foundation pass.
Not runtime-verified on the EFI path -- that needs VirtualBox or OVMF, neither of
which is installed here, so the LoadOptions plumbing is build-verified only and
the literal is still the path an unconfigured VirtualBox boot takes.
036e0d2aa2b0212e6004a54d0d864e624a49aea9:
feat(x86_64): coalesce the firmware memory map and add a bootable UEFI disk image

Two things, one of them a kernel bug that only booting could find.

The bug: arch/x86_64/platform/firmware.c appended every usable entry from the
multiboot memory map verbatim, up to X86_RAM_RANGE_MAX (8). The PFA accepts at
most PFA_MAX_RANGES (4). Nothing merged anything. GRUB on a UEFI VM reports seven
entries, so pfa_init() panicked with "invalid ram range count" -- the x86_64 port
could not boot from real firmware at all. It only ever worked because QEMU's
-kernel multiboot path happens to report exactly one range, which fit.

Now the map is sorted and neighbours merged before it is handed over. Merging is
not a way around the cap, it is what the list means: two touching entries
describe one usable region. Seven entries from a real UEFI machine collapse to
one 992 MiB range. When the gaps are real and more ranges survive than the PFA
has room for, the largest is kept and the log says so rather than dropping the
rest quietly.

smoke-x86_64 still passes, so the single-range path is untouched.

The image: tools/mk_grub_disk_image.sh builds a raw GPT disk with one FAT32 ESP
holding GRUB, the kernel and the FAT32 root -- the same shape the aarch64
VirtualBox image already has, so both architectures hand an operator a disk
rather than an ISO. UEFI rather than BIOS, because most current machines are
UEFI-only with no CSM and kernel/boot/uefi/ has an aarch64 loader with no x86_64
stub.

GRUB uses an explicit /boot/grub prefix with the modules copied onto the ESP. A
grub-mkstandalone image was tried first and did boot, but never resolved a root
device: `search --file /boot/kernel.elf` returned "no such device" and multiboot
could not find a file sitting on the very ESP that had just loaded it, because the
standalone memdisk prefix does not match where its modules live.

Verified by booting it, not by building it: under OVMF, GRUB loads the multiboot
kernel off the ESP and the kernel reaches "[INIT] System ready" with a correct
992 MiB RAM map. That boot is also what found the coalescing bug.

Not finished: the kernel mounts no root from this image, so it panics with "no
init program found". PCI enumerates and virtio-blk registers, but no block device
binds. The x86_64 root path expects the specific disk arrangement the QEMU dev
flow builds, which this image does not reproduce; wiring that up, porting the
script into tools/a20, and giving aarch64 the same audited treatment are still
open.
ccef03ee9b8503b4911da0638e2d31c952ebe2fd:
fix(x86_64): read PCI ECAM from MCFG and report unsupported UEFI firmware

Chasing why a UEFI-booted x86_64 kernel mounted no root found two real problems,
one of them a bug that has been there since the port landed and the other a
limitation that was silently misreported.

The bug: qemu-virt-x86_64 called pci_enumerate() with the compiled-in
PCI_ECAM_BASE, 0xB0000000. That is the q35 layout's ECAM and is correct for
SeaBIOS, which is what QEMU's default x86 firmware is. It is wrong for OVMF, which
puts the ECAM wherever MCFG says. Reading the wrong window did not fail: it
returned all-zero vendor IDs, so enumeration "succeeded" and published 129
devices -- every one of them id=0000:0000, none matching any driver's ID table.
Nothing bound, no block device appeared, and the failure only surfaced much later
as "no init program found" with nothing in the log pointing at PCI.

x86_64-pc already read MCFG for exactly this reason. This board did not, so it
could not boot a UEFI firmware at all.

The misreport: no MCFG was logged as a neutral "falling back to <base>", which
reads like a routine path. It is not routine -- it means no RSDP was reachable,
which is normal under SeaBIOS and fatal under UEFI, and those need opposite
fixes. firmware_bios_or_uefi() answers the question the caller cannot, using the
same RSDP search acpi_find_table() uses, and the log now says which case it is
and that UEFI has no path here. Both cases verified booting:

  SeaBIOS: [PCI] no MCFG (BIOS), using the q35 default ... [INIT] Block device ->
            /bin (fat32) [INIT] System ready
  OVMF:    [PCI] no MCFG (UEFI), ... -- UEFI without an x86_64 stub cannot work

Why UEFI genuinely cannot work, established by instrumenting the multiboot tag
walk rather than assuming: GRUB 2.12 does not fill MULTIBOOT_TAG_TYPE_ACPI. The
walk reported zero ACPI tags. GRUB2 dropped that tag; the modern channel is the
RSDP published in the EFI configuration table, and kernel/boot/uefi/ holds an
aarch64 loader with no x86_64 one. So an x86_64 EFI stub is the prerequisite, and
until it exists the SeaBIOS path is the working one.

The ACPI tag and its .data slot were added on the way to that conclusion and then
removed: GRUB cannot fill them, so they would have been dead weight in the header
pretending to be a mechanism. One detour is worth recording because it was
invisible: defining the RSDP slot with a .section .data switch inside the header
block silently truncated the multiboot header, GRUB then found no header at all
and loaded the ELF as a plain kernel, and g_mb_magic read as 0x2badb0b2. The
symbol addresses all looked correct; only booting showed it.

Verified: both x86_64 boards build; smoke-x86_64 passes; check-honesty-policy,
check-doc-test-gates, check-concurrency-foundation and check-instances pass.
136043688c602accb01b366cf565b7a971e06455:
fix(uefi): fix the aarch64 VirtualBox image build broken by the LoadOptions work

4c523101 typed boot_services.handle_protocol and added the LoadedImage lookup.
That made the aarch64 VirtualBox EFI image stop compiling, and nothing caught it:
every aarch64 verification in that change was a `kernel-only` build, which never
compiles the loader at all. Found by building the image and booting it.

Two faults in one symptom:

`struct efi_guid` was referenced by handle_protocol's new prototype at line 48
but defined at line 79, so the prototype saw an incomplete tag. The compiler
treated it as a distinct type and reported the self-contradictory

  expected 'const struct efi_guid *' but argument is of type
  'const struct efi_guid *'

The type is now defined before the boot services table.

The LoadedImage GUID was initialised as one flat brace group, which landed as a
scalar initialiser for data1 and left the rest as excess elements. It now uses
the same data1/data2/data3/data4 shape as the ACPI GUIDs beside it.

What the boot then showed. Under AAVMF the ESP is found and the loader runs --
"A20OS: loading kernel" -- then reports "UEFI load failed" and returns, so the
image does not boot. The cause is VBOX_AARCH64_LOAD_ADDRESS (0x08080000) being a
VirtualBox measurement: QEMU virt puts RAM at 0x40000000 and has nothing there,
so EFI_ALLOCATE_ADDRESS fails.

Making the address optional was tried and reverted. It does clear that error --
allocation succeeds -- and the image then hangs in a firmware reboot loop,
because the kernel is not yet position independent and something in its early
path still assumes the image landed where it was linked. A boot loop is strictly
worse than a message that names the failure, so the address stays mandatory and
the reason is recorded next to the check. Relocating properly means making the
aarch64 kernel position independent, which is its own piece of work.

So this fixes the build and makes the aarch64 image's non-boot legible rather than
mysterious. It does not make that image bootable; only VirtualBox's memory map
satisfies the load address today, and nothing here has been run on VirtualBox.

Verified: the aarch64 VirtualBox EFI image builds again; all three aarch64
boards and both x86_64 boards still build; check-honesty-policy,
check-doc-test-gates and check-concurrency-foundation pass.
0dfc4a0953306070a6c155642d0d1b5a829f4bd6:
feat(a20): add a directly bootable x86_64 disk image and say where it stops

The two VirtualBox targets had different shapes: aarch64 produced a raw disk
with an EFI System Partition, x86_64 produced an ISO.  That is the sort of
difference that makes an operator read the docs to find out which is which, so
x86_64 now produces a disk too, via package.kind = "grub-disk" and a
pc-rescue-disk target over tools/mk_grub_disk_image.sh.  UEFI, because that is
what makes the form match aarch64 and what current machines boot.

It boots the kernel, and it stops there.  Measured under OVMF:

  [RAM] usable 0x900000..0x3e93f000 (992 MiB)
  [PCI] no MCFG (UEFI), using the q35 default 0x... -- UEFI without an x86_64
  stub cannot work
  [INIT] System ready
  init: no init program found

The kernel comes up with a correct RAM map -- that is the memory-map coalescing
from ca2f25a8 doing its job on a real firmware map -- and then cannot mount a
root, because UEFI keeps the RSDP in its configuration table, GRUB 2.12 does not
fill the multiboot ACPI tag, and there is no x86_64 EFI loader to receive it.  No
RSDP means no MCFG, so PCI uses a hardcoded ECAM window that holds no devices,
no block driver binds, and /bin never appears.  The log line above is the
diagnostic from 5326256a doing exactly its job.

So vbox-iso-x86_64 remains the instance that reaches userspace, because it goes
through BIOS where SeaBIOS publishes the RSDP in a region the kernel already
scans.  The new instance is the shared *form* the two architectures were asked to
have, and it starts working the moment an x86_64 EFI stub exists.  The manifest
says all of this rather than implying the two are interchangeable, because
silently preferring the older path would be worse than the inconsistency.

An x86_64 EFI stub was written for this and reverted.  It compiled to a
position-independent PE image with zero absolute relocations, but faulted on
execution with CS still 0x38 and CR0.PG still set -- a #GP inside the loader
itself, with RAX holding UEFI's 0xAF poison pattern for memory nothing had
written.  Booting a stub that crashes is worse than not having one, so it was not
committed.  The finding that stands is the one above: GRUB cannot carry the RSDP,
so an x86_64 EFI loader is a prerequisite, and that is loader work rather than
driver work.

Verified: a20 check passes for every instance; a20 package vbox-x86_64 produces
build/x86_64-pc/a20os-rescue-disk.img at 512 MiB; the image boots under OVMF as
quoted; check-instances, check-doc-test-gates, check-honesty-policy,
check-component-registry and check-manifests pass.

feat(x86_64): add a directly bootable UEFI disk path through userspace

a0b91028e97a82146bacb282b02825085b36bc49:
feat(aarch64): declare x0 and x2 clobbered by the UEFI loaders handover asm

The ExitBootServices handover block hardcodes x0 and x2 as the registers it
assembles its arguments into, but the constraint list only declared x1.  GCC
is therefore free to allocate an input operand to x0 or x2, and the block
then overwrites its own argument before using it: "mov x2, %2" clobbers x2,
so if %1 (the kernel entry) was allocated to x2, "br %1" branches to the
cmdline pointer instead of the kernel.

Declare every register the block writes.  This is the same shape as the
x86_64 loader, which lists rdi, rsi and rdx and is therefore sound.

Found by disassembly review, not observed failing: on QEMU virt the load
address 0x08080000 is not backed by RAM, so allocate_pages fails first and
this code is never reached.  It would bite wherever the allocation
succeeds -- VirtualBox, or any firmware that does map that address -- so
fix it now rather than after the relocation work unmasks it.

smoke-aarch64 passes; the loader is not covered by it.
d7e89a6ab5d2c0a0cacd681c17fc85e00444e076:
feat(aarch64): derive the UEFI loaders load address from the boards linker script

VBOX_AARCH64_LOAD_ADDRESS was hardcoded to 0x08080000, which is where the
virtualbox-aarch64 board links and also where VirtualBox ARM puts RAM.  The
qemu-virt-aarch64 board links at 0x40080000 instead, so the loader built for
it demanded an address its own kernel was never linked for -- and AAVMF, whose
RAM starts at 0x40000000, has nothing at 0x08080000.  Two constants that had
to be kept in step by hand, with no check that they were.

Read PHYS_BASE out of the active LDSCRIPT instead.  The build now produces
0x08080000 for virtualbox-aarch64 (unchanged) and 0x40080000 for
qemu-virt-aarch64, and the two can no longer drift.

This does not by itself make aarch64 boot under AAVMF: entry.S only parks the
UEFI handover registers under CONFIG_BOARD_VIRTUALBOX_AARCH64, and
qemu-virt-aarch64 discovers hardware through the device tree, which UEFI
does not supply.  That is the remaining work, and it is a board bring-up
rather than a build fix.

smoke-aarch64 passes and tools/a20 package vbox-aarch64 is unchanged.
16e89b11777495bc9feff797047c0bf21a545854:
docs(platforms): record the measured aarch64 UEFI boot and how to reproduce it

The section described this path as reaching "System ready (bringup, no

  [BUS] virtio-mmio: found 1 devices (base=0x800a000000 irq_base=16)
  [VIRTIO0] Block device ready: capacity=524288 sectors (256 MB)
  [INIT] Block device -> /bin (fat32)
  [INIT] System ready
  Welcome to A20OS!

f024646b3bc97fe8575a0c43d501df77a1d8dd1d:
perf(core): read the stall clock only after an acquire becomes contended

spin_lock_at() called timer_get_ticks() and proc_current() before the
single exchange, so all ~917 acquire sites paid a read timer and the
current-task lookup even when the lock was free.  On x86_64 that is
lfence;rdtsc plus two 64-bit divisions and a CAS loop on one global,
and a cpuid (a KVM VM-exit once NR_CPUS>1).

Both values feed the 5-second [LOCK-STALL] report, which can only fire
after this CPU has failed to take the lock, so they are now sampled on
the first contended observation instead.  next_report becomes an absolute
deadline to match, since the report interval is measured from the sample.

Measured with the kernel's own timer shape on the host, NR_CPUS=4:
55.05 ns -> 2.11 ns per uncontended acquire.
208f045e0355b3ed88d8ec9e430f632b8275f7d7:
feat(smp): acknowledge membarrier with a data barrier not an i-cache fence

smp_membarrier_ipi_ack() ran arch_fence_i() on every participating CPU.
membarrier orders data, and the ack's RELEASE store already establishes
what the barrier needs, but arch_fence_i() on aarch64 is
dsb ish; ic iallu; dsb ish; isb -- a full L1 I-cache invalidation, on a
handler that runs for every reschedule IPI those CPUs take.

The instruction-stream guarantee PRIVATE_EXPEDITED_SYNC_CORE needs is
still applied on the initiator.  Extending it to the remote CPUs means
selecting the fence per command, which lives in
kernel/abi/linux/sys_membarrier.c.
22ae8a296e7430e98f71c5443a8d7ef567524994:
fix(core): stop walking the log message twice and keep lines from splicing

klog_write() formatted into a 1 KiB stack buffer and then ran strlen()
over it to learn the length vsnprintf had already reported.  It now uses
that return value directly; strlen is gone from klog.o.

Both console writers also emitted with no lock, one polled MMIO write per
character, so two CPUs logging concurrently spliced their lines
mid-word.  vprintf() and klog_write() now share one console lock, held
across the ring append and the emission so a reader cannot see bytes
from two records interleaved.
f711804bc1e4cfe2ca867838fc00df1075067426:
test(core): gate the device progress bridge on an aggregated pending bit

kernel_progress_run_bottom_halves() runs on every scheduler and idle pass
and entered driver_progress_class(DEV_CLASS_BLOCK) each time, taking the
driver-core mutex and walking every registered device on the scheduler hot
path.  No driver publishes an idle flag, so the bridge cannot ask the driver
whether entry is worth it; it has to be told.

Producers OR KERNEL_PROGRESS_PENDING_DEVICE from the context that creates
the work, and the consumer clears the bit when it runs.  The timer re-arms
the bit on a bounded cadence so a producer that misses its notification
delays completion instead of losing it.

The network RX half is left ungated: virtio_net's poll-only transport
contract requires kernel_progress_poll() to keep draining on every pass, and
that drain already returns without taking g_lwip_lock unless a device
signalled work.
4761329ccd9640c20a37d7f651d9a317b88ac2fb:
feat(sched): sample load average without a per-tick full task walk

proc_loadavg_tick() ran from proc_sched_tick() on every CPU, so an SMP guest
walked the entire task list under proc_lock once per CPU per tick period, with
all CPUs contending for the same lock to read a number that only feeds the
1/5/15-minute EMAs.

Take the runnable count from the per-CPU runqueue tallies the PSI tracker
already uses, which is the same definition of nr_runnable and needs no lock,
and sample from CPU 0 only so the windows decay per elapsed time rather than
per CPU.  The live-task census that /proc/loadavg also prints moves to the
read path, which is where a full walk belongs.
9fc6d389164265e91669a5051d703b4f0af3422f:
feat(sched): give per-pick and per-tick counters their own cache line

At NR_CPUS=4 the object layout put sched_local_picks, sched_empty_picks,
sched_local_pick_active and sched_local_pick_parallel_peak at .sbss+0x00
through .sbss+0x1f, on one 64-byte line that every CPU bumps on every local
pick.  g_cpu_user_ticks and g_cpu_system_ticks were adjacent 32-byte arrays,
so CPU 0's user tick and CPU 1's user tick shared a line too.

Move picks and empty picks into a per-CPU struct that the diagnostic
snapshot sums.  The in-flight pick count and its high-water mark measure
concurrency across the whole system rather than per CPU, so they stay global
and only get a line of their own.  Interleave the three jiffy classes into one
per-CPU struct instead of three parallel arrays.
79cf4896f3fecf71095c9b1ec7b42c66763b5636:
perf(sched): skip the cgroup node lock when no quota needs charging

context_switch_locked() called cg_cpu_account() and then cg_cpu_check_unthrottle()
on every switch, each taking the cgroup node lock.  A node at the default
unlimited quota makes the first call return before it changes anything and the
second return because the node was never throttled, so the common case paid
two IRQ-off lock round trips plus a ticks-to-nanoseconds division to learn
nothing.

Read quota and throttled without the lock and skip both calls together.  Both
fields are written only under node->lock, and only cg_cpu_account() can set
throttled, which it does on a path an unlimited quota never reaches.
3e26d49d3b0eb2ed0469bfe9544152ebf7351f73:
perf(sched): move full runqueue membership scans behind an opt-in flag

proc_sched_assert_task_locked() takes every runqueue lock and walks every
queue so that the membership it reports cannot be torn by a concurrent picker.
CONFIG_DEBUG_SCHED_STATE turns that on for any -DDEBUG build, and the benchmark
profile is a -DDEBUG build, so the profile was measuring NR_CPUS lock round
trips at two dozen call sites per switch.

Keep the cheap per-task field assertions under CONFIG_DEBUG_SCHED_STATE and
move the scan and the three checks that need it behind
CONFIG_SCHED_MEMBERSHIP_CHECK, which defaults to off.  A bring-up run that
wants the membership invariant checked now has to name it.
f09fdfa56bb0f61369e1cc0c9986ef68ae5d6591:
fix(sched): stop paying two current-CPU sweeps for every reap pass

The zombie scan tested every task against proc_task_is_current_any_cpu()
before testing whether it was a zombie, and that test reads two slots per CPU.
The walk sees every live task while only zombies can ever be reaped, so the
sweep ran CONFIG_NR_CPUS times more often than the answer was used.

The scan also repeated until a pass reaped nothing, so any invocation that
reaped at least one task paid a second full walk to find the empty list it
knew was there.  Repeat only when a pass filled the batch: a zombie that was
left behind was rejected on parent, SIGCHLD, or thread-group liveness, and
every event that can later satisfy one of those announces itself through
proc_sched_note_zombie().
033697e770e7f95bd84b6ebba829b39b02e08f1a:
feat(fs): retire dcache entries without a write to a shared age counter

Every hit and every insert bumped g_dcache_age, a single global counter,
under nothing but the entry's bucket lock.  Two CPUs hitting two buckets
raced on that increment, and the line it lives on was written on every cache
hit from every CPU.  Nothing in the tree reads age: eviction is the
second-chance accessed bit and the LRU, so drop the counter and the field
rather than try to make an unused value correct.

vfs_dcache_invalidate_all() also took all VFS_DCACHE_BUCKET_LOCKS locks and
then scanned VFS_DCACHE_MAX entries with interrupts still disabled, which
masked interrupts across every acquisition and an interrupt that reached a
lookup would spin on a lock its own interrupted context was holding.  Empty
one bucket at a time and release before moving on.  A retired slot stays on
the LRU as an unused entry, which dcache_alloc_slot() already reclaims, so
no global LRU or free-list pass is needed.
629555bf01d800488b2de4aae1adfab1d5ff9167: merge(core): integrate lock and scheduler primitive fixes
69e113391d33afe032fc18e93c72f07017b4e2a9:
fix(loongarch32): restore SAVE1 on switch-in and skip redundant TLB flushes

__switch restored $tp but left CSR 0x31 (SAVE1) naming the outgoing task.
arch_get_task_pointer() reads SAVE1, not $tp, so every path that asks the
kernel which task is current -- including proc_current() on the syscall
path -- saw the previous task for the whole of the incoming context.
__switch_la32 must publish the incoming task in both registers, the way
loongarch64 already does.

PGDL was rewritten and invtlb op 3 issued on every switch, including the
common case where both tasks share a page table and nothing can be stale.
Compare PGDL first and invalidate only on an actual change, matching what
riscv64 already does with satp.  PRMD is restored outside that guard,
because it must be restored either way.

arch_tlb_flush_page_local() threw its address away and did a full invtlb,
which silently turned every per-page shootdown in kernel/mm/fault.c into
a whole-address-space invalidation.  INVTLB op 5 targets one VA inside the
running ASID, which is the counterpart of the sfence.vma addr, zero riscv64
uses for the same job.  The ASID has to be read out of TLBIDX[25:10].

arch_rmb() and arch_wmb() were byte-for-byte dbar 0, so neither ordered
anything.  DBAR hints 0x15 and 0x1a select ordering over completion and
cover the preceding loads and stores respectively; a core that does not
special-case a hint executes it as dbar 0, so neither can be weaker than
the barrier it replaces.

Verified: make kernel-only ARCH=loongarch32 BOARD=nailoong could not be
run here -- loongarch32-unknown-elf-gcc is not installed -- and the
assembler round-trip for invtlb 5 was checked against the loongarch64

38227505a3d951488b0032f3be1a7aa9fab0062a:
fix(loongarch64): target page TLB flushes and restore memory-barrier ordering

arch_tlb_flush_page_local() discarded its address and issued a full invtlb,
so every per-page shootdown reaching it from kernel/mm/fault.c invalidated
the whole address space.  INVTLB op 5 discards one VA inside the running
ASID, the counterpart of the sfence.vma addr, zero riscv64 uses to make the
same operation targeted.  The register-specified ASID has to occupy the
whole of rj, and the ASID lives in TLBIDX[25:10].

__switch wrote PGDL and ran invtlb op 3 unconditionally, including when the
incoming task shares a page table with the outgoing one and there is nothing
stale to discard.  Compare PGDL first and invalidate only on a real change.
PRMD stays outside that guard: it has to be restored either way.

arch_rmb() and arch_wmb() were byte-for-byte dbar 0, so neither ordered
anything.  DBAR hints 0x15 and 0x1a select ordering over completion and
cover the preceding loads and stores respectively, and a core that does not
special-case a hint executes it as dbar 0, so neither is weaker than the
barrier it replaces.
70a716b8b1035e17fb8a3b55ae81aa86cdc45790:
feat(aarch64): compare TTBR0 before invalidating and target the per-page flush

Every return to user and every kernel-trap return rewrote TTBR0 and ran
tlbi vmalle1 unconditionally, including the common case where the trap frame
carries the TTBR0 already loaded.  Read the register and invalidate only on
an actual change, which is what riscv64 already does with satp.

arch_tlb_flush_page() ignored its argument and fell through to arch_tlb_flush(),
so each of the ~18 arch_tlb_flush_page_local() sites in kernel/mm/fault.c
invalidated the whole EL1/EL0 address space on every page fault that needed
a translation dropped.  tlbi vaae1is discards one VA and shares the
invalidation across the inner-shareable domain, so a peer CPU cannot retain
a stale copy of the page being unmapped.

SET_TRAP_FLAGS ran on all four vectors and read MPIDR_EL1, masked it and
compared it against CONFIG_NR_CPUS on every exception taken, timer IRQs
included.  The clamp can only select slot 0 in a single-CPU build, so
CONFIG_NR_CPUS == 1 now drops the register read and the compare.  Measured
with objdump on both builds: each vector prologue goes from 14 instructions
to 9, and trap.o from 348 to 334.

arch_kwx_module_unprotect() flushed only locally while arch_kwx_module_protect()
flushed locally and remotely, so a peer CPU could keep executing the pages a
module unprotect had just made non-executable.  Both now share one helper,
matching what riscv64 and x86_64 already do.
045b25a1f99e4d657f267118b95b96da3cfd6e47:
fix(arm32): compare TTBR0 before invalidation and flush the instruction cache

__switch and both trap-return paths rewrote TTBR0 and ran the TLBALL
maintenance operation unconditionally, including when the frame holds the
TTBR0 already loaded.  Read it back first and invalidate only on a real
change, as riscv64 already does with satp.  The scratch registers differ per
site because each one has a different live set: the kernel return clobbers
r2, which the following ldmia reloads; the user return clobbers r3, which
the following mrs reloads, and must not touch r1/r2 because those carry the
stack pointer and the return address into the rest of the sequence.

arch_flush_icache_range() was arch_fence_i(), a dsb and an isb, which orders
memory accesses and invalidates nothing.  Module load and JIT publish
instructions through the D-cache, so the written lines have to reach the
point of coherence and every stale copy has to leave the I-cache.  Clean the
D-side lines with the c7, c10, 1 loop the DMA helpers already use, then
ICIALLU.  ICIALLU takes neither an address nor a line size, so unlike an MVA
invalidate it cannot silently miss lines when the I-line size differs from
the D-line size the clean loop is stepped by.

The switch points four banked exception-mode stacks 4096 bytes below the
incoming task_context_t, and IRQ, prefetch-abort, data-abort and FIQ all run
a vector prologue and the 88-byte trap_context_t there.  The reserve is now a
named constant with an assembly-time check against the frame size, because
the frame size lives in trap/trap.S and would otherwise be a silent contract
whose overflow lands in the context being restored.

Verified: make kernel-only ARCH=arm32 BOARD=qemu-virt-arm32 could not be run
here -- arm-linux-gnueabihf-gcc is not installed and there is no clang to
substitute -- so these assembly changes are unbuilt.  The cp15 operands were
taken from the in-tree DMA loops and from Linux's v7_coherent_user_range in
arch/arm/mm/cache-v7.S, which uses the same c7, c10, 1 clean and c7, c5, 0
invalidate.
ef7771121b49b8538980d3ed6ccc4b3651b94043:
fix(x86_64): honour the shootdown range and stop dividing twice per tick

x86_64_smp_remote_tlb_flush() took addr and size, discarded both with a
(void) cast, and every target reloaded CR3.  The kernel already computes a
page-aligned address and size for each unmap, so a remote single-page
shootdown took a full user-TLB reload instead.  Publish the range with the
request generation and let the target use invlpg when the size is one page,
which is what every COW unmap and PTE clear asks for.  Anything wider keeps
the CR3 reload, which stays correct at any size.

AP start-up counted TSC cycles between the INIT-SIPI, the SIPI and the two
start-vector SIPIs, which is only meaningful against an assumed clock
frequency and says nothing about how far the target has actually got.
lapic_send() already holds each message until the previous one has left the
ICR, so the delivery-status wait is what should order them.

timer_get_ticks() scaled the counter with two 64-bit divisions and then took
a CAS loop on a single process-wide high-water mark, so every CPU in the
system serialised on one cache line.  Precompute the reciprocal of the
reduced source-to-tick ratio and multiply; the mark moves per CPU.  The
reciprocal is assembled from a word-boundary split and a long division
because the kernel links no 128-bit divide helper, and __udivti3 is not in
the image.

Measured on an AMD Ryzen 7 7840H, 20M iterations per ratio, identical
inputs: 3.73 -> 0.54 ns per conversion at 1:1, 2.4 GHz:1 GHz and 10 GHz:1 GHz,
a 6.8-7.0x reduction, and 0.73 ns when ARCH_TIMER_FREQ exceeds the source
rate.  Dropping the remainder shortens a conversion by at most one tick and
never moves it backwards, checked exhaustively against the old arithmetic
over 901k reciprocal cases and 7.2M scale cases: the largest disagreement is
1, the count of cases off by more than 1 is 0, and the monotonicity
violations are 0.

Not fixed: the unconditional 512-byte fxsave64/fxrstor64 pair in
boot/switch.S.  riscv64 gates its FP save on sstatus.FS, which hardware
maintains per hart.  x86_64 has no counterpart: CR0.TS is cleared once at
boot by x86_64_enable_fpu_sse() and never set again, because there is no #NM
handler to emulate a deferred FP use, so it can never report "this task has
not touched FP".  The bit has to live in task_context_t, which is asserted
at exactly 640 bytes with no spare field, in an arch include this change
does not reach.
ac3ec4ad320209705a17b3a21bc0db0738df8dbc: merge(kernel): integrate architecture TLB and barrier fixes
310d16c713369e0ad28310b305e0c60987522efd:
test(mm): gate the per-page frame diagnostics behind CONFIG_DEBUG_MM_TRACE

frame_trace() runs on every frame that reaches refcount zero and every
pfa_free(), and pfa_hist_record() runs on every free-list push and remove.
Each costs an atomic, a timer read, a proc_current() walk and a ring write,
and fl_remove() additionally evaluated six membership checks whose failure
path dumps a 512-entry history. That is a tax on every page fault and every
unmap, paid by release builds that never read the output.

The history is post-mortem only, so gate the recorders and the three
redundant membership traps behind CONFIG_DEBUG_MM_TRACE, following the
existing per-subsystem trace switches in core/klog.h. The dump helpers stay
unconditional: trap.c and mm/slab.c call them from panic paths that are not
gated, so the symbols and their rings must keep existing when nothing records
into them.

The two link checks that validate the neighbours being relinked through stay
ungated. They are not diagnostics: dropping them turns a detectable list
corruption into a wild write through a bad pfn instead of a panic. The
freemap double-free bit is likewise unchanged -- it is what makes a silent
double free an attributed panic, not history.

Also read free_frames under pfa.lock in pfa_free_count(). pfa_t documents
lock as protecting every mutable field above it, and oom.c samples this on the
reclaim path, where a torn read would mis-size the batch and drive an OOM kill
loop.

No new lock is taken in a different order: this adds pfa.lock to an accessor
that previously took none, and the accessor holds it across no sleep, no
allocation and no copy.
44e20ef168336a1e98ee86dd8e143c3d43ad60d9:
feat(mm): walk madvise ranges VMA by VMA instead of page by page

Both the coverage pre-pass and the discard loop advanced one PAGE_SIZE at a
time, calling mm_find_vma() for every page of the range. mm_find_vma() is a
binary search over the VMA index, so a large MADV_DONTNEED cost
pages x log2(nvma) probes twice over: roughly half a million binary searches
for a 1GB hint where four VMAs are typically involved. Allocator arenas and
bulk-hinting runtimes submit exactly that shape.

The work loop also re-derived the VMA on every page just to test VM_VMO, so
hoist that classification out to the enclosing VMA span.

Step to vma->end in both loops, matching what mm_vma_set_lock() below already
does. Behaviour is unchanged: the loops still cover exactly [addr, end), still
reject an uncovered range with -ENOMEM, and the span they walk under mm->lock
is unchanged, so the VMA pointers the work loop now hoists stay valid for it.

Also name the 0x08000000 bit that mm_vma_set_lock() was setting as a bare
literal. It is the Native ABI vm_lock reservation marker set by a20_vm_lock,
not VM_LOCKED -- that bit is the Linux mlock/oom-unevictable flag with
different consumers in munmap.c, oom.c and mmap.c, so sharing it would change
mlock semantics. The canonical name belongs with the other VM_* flags in
mm/vm.h, which is owned by another branch, so it stays local here with a
comment recording the distinction.
db5df1183641ca0e3edb2f0442d4389304b67114:
feat(mm): pin and revalidate process_vm leaves and break COW before writing

process_vm_write_kernel() resolved a leaf with mm_query_leaf_kaddr() and
memcpy'd straight into the direct-mapped kernel pointer, then marked it dirty,
with no mm->lock and no frame reference held. The target keeps running for the
whole transfer, so the target could unmap the page and buddy-free the frame in
that window, and the memcpy would then write into a frame already handed back
to the allocator. That is a use-after-free write reachable from an ordinary
process_vm_writev against a live process, not only under stress. The read path
had the same exposure.

Resolve each leaf under the target's mm->lock and take a frame reference before
dropping it. The lock makes the PTE and the frame it names a consistent pair;
the reference is what survives the unmap that can happen the moment the lock is
released. The copy itself runs with the lock dropped -- it is page-sized, IRQs
are enabled, and holding a spinlock across it would serialise every fault and
unmap in the target behind this transfer.

A write must also break copy-on-write first. A VM_COW private leaf is shared
with the parent's page, so writing it in place silently corrupted the parent's
data instead of the target's private copy. Route through handle_cow_fault(),
which performs the same private-copy promotion as the fault path along with
its shootdown and deferred drop, and retry the address afterwards. A leaf that
is present but not writable now reports EFAULT rather than being written.

Also compute the kernel address and copy length relative to the leaf's own
base and size. A level above 0 is a huge leaf whose PTE names the block head, so
`va` can sit anywhere inside it; assuming one page and the head address would
copy from the wrong offset.

Lock ordering: this takes the target's mm->lock, which the fault path already
takes before pfa.lock, and frame_get() nests pfa.lock inside it in that same
order. No lock is held across a sleep, an allocation that can reclaim, or a
copy_to_user. The COW helper is called with no lock held because it takes
mm->lock itself.

Verified with smoke-syscall-ext, which exercises process_vm_readv: it caught
the huge-leaf assumption on the first attempt and passes now.
9ab8bf3dba2e765a7f1ff92adae0390d1167c898:
feat(mm): index swap slots with a bitmap and hold the bdev across a transfer

get_swap_page() restarted its scan at offset 1 on every call and kept no hint,
so allocating one page cost a byte load per slot in the area under
swap_locks[type] -- about 4M loads on a 16GiB device, growing linearly as the
area fills. Add a one-word-per-64-slots bitmap plus a per-area search cursor:
the scan is 64x cheaper and, because the cursor resumes where the last
allocation stopped, the common case finds a slot without re-walking the
allocated prefix at all.

The bitmap indexes swap_map, it does not replace it. Every bit transition is
paired with the swap_map store beside it under the same lock, and swap_map
remains what the I/O path validates against. Bit 0 stays clear because slot 0
is the header and was never allocatable.

swap_page_io() snapshotted bdev under the lock, dropped the lock, then called
bdev->write_sector(). swap_unregister_device() cleared si->bdev, dropped the
lock, then called bdev->release(). A reclaim transfer between those two points
drove a device the provider had already released. The lock cannot simply be
held across the I/O because a block transfer can block.

So count in-flight transfers per area instead. swap_page_io() increments the
count under the lock before dropping it and decrements on the way out;
swap_unregister_device() parks the device in a pending slot rather than
releasing it, and whichever of the two finds the count at zero claims the
release. The claim clears the slot under the lock, so the release happens
exactly once and never on a device still being driven.

Lock ordering is unchanged: swap_locks[type] is always taken before
swap_stats_lock, and no lock is held across the block I/O or either kfree.
swap.h is left untouched -- the bitmap, cursor and transfer count are
file-static in swap.c, so no exported layout changes.

Verified with smoke-swap. The bit scan and the allocator were also exercised
on the host directly, since swap_read_page() has never run in any gate:
the bit scan against 2M random words, and the allocator over page counts 1-300
checking exhaustion, no duplicate or bad slot, and correct reuse after free.
f0ad9a6c10a4922e0b3ab942b664a314edf2ebd3:
feat(mm): lock the VMAR child index and keep siblings ordered by base

vmar_create_child() walked every sibling to test for overlap and then spliced
the new node into parent->child_head, and vmar_release() walked the list a
second time to unlink and recursed into the parent while doing it. The node had
no lock field at all, so the test and the insert were not atomic: two tasks
racing on a shared parent could both observe a range as free and both insert,
breaking the one invariant the type exists to enforce.

Give vmar_t a spinlock and take it across the test and the insert. It is a leaf
lock: nothing else is acquired while holding it, and it is never held across a
sleep, an allocation, or a call into the VMA/VMO layers. That sits outside the
global order in core/lock.h because vmar.c takes no other lock at all; the one
other lock reachable nearby is slab's, and kmalloc for the new node happens
before the lock is taken rather than under it.

Order the child list by base. Only the last child starting below a candidate
and the first child starting at or above it can overlap it, so the scan stops
there instead of comparing against every sibling, and the insertion point is
well defined rather than a blind prepend. Add a tail pointer so appending a
range just past the end -- how these trees actually grow -- touches no node at
all. This turns creating N children from N scans of the whole set into N walks
to the insertion point; it is not a constant-time index, but it removes the
repeated full-set compare and, more importantly, gives the overlap test a
single, well-defined pair of candidates.

vmar_release() now takes a reference to the parent before unlinking, so a
parent whose last reference this child held cannot be freed while its lock is
held, and recurses only after the list is consistent and the lock is dropped.

The list logic has no in-tree coverage, so it was exercised on the host under
ASan/UBSan: 3000 randomized trials checking sortedness, non-overlap, the child
count and the tail pointer after every insert and every interleaved teardown,
plus explicit rejection of duplicate, straddling and partial overlaps and
acceptance of adjacent ranges.
79fc9ac35e50be9ba73456d54b07ed602d958b98:
test(user): add mm_bench probe for the frame gate and madvises VMA walk

Two hot paths were changed without numbers behind them.  This reports them
directly rather than by inference: phase A brackets a MADV_DONTNEED with the
kernel's vma_lookups / vma_lookup_steps counters so the size of the VMA walk is
visible, phase B times allocator churn, which is where the CONFIG_DEBUG_MM_TRACE
gate lands.

Phase A also settles which madvise is being measured: the Linux ABI implements
the release advice in abi/linux/sys_mm.c with its own per-page probe and never
reaches mm_madvise_dontneed, so the Native ABI vm_advise path needs a native
binary to exercise the helper this change was made in.

Not registered in tools/smoke_cases.py: that file is being edited by another
branch, and a case there would collide.
9457c70a6a10b682173e87bc00b99886a0e2ebc4:
feat(fs): keep the page-cache statistics off the descriptor array

cachestat(2) and every /proc/meminfo or /proc/a20/page_cache read walked
all g_allocated_pages descriptors with g_page_cache_lock held and local
interrupts disabled.  That array is capped at RAM/8 descriptors and 262144
entries, so a descriptor of ~170 bytes puts the walk over tens of megabytes
of memory in one spinlocked section.  A local process looping on cachestat
pins every CPU's miss, evict and statistics path for the duration, which is
a denial of service reachable without privilege.

Occupancy is now derived from counters kept at the transitions that already
run under the global lock: mapping publication and detach for valid pages,
dirty_insert_locked/dirty_remove_locked for dirty pages.  page_cache_get_stats
is O(bucket count) rather than O(cache size).

Per-file counters walk the vnode's own mapping list, so cachestat costs what
the queried file costs instead of what the whole cache costs.  The mapping
list is spliced only under g_page_cache_lock, so the walk keeps that lock;
the win is that the critical section is now bounded by one file.

The pinned count needs the refcount edges, which belong to the warm hit path,
so it is striped one counter per bucket and padded to a cache line.  Pinning
edges update it with a relaxed atomic; the bucket lock the hit path already
holds is what orders the counter.  No new lock is taken anywhere, so the
documented global -> bucket order is unchanged.
21367f2ec1fdb7f7f7e372d6fe38f14ed49b1fdd:
fix(fs): clear a new cache frame outside the allocation lock bound the evict sweep

A cache miss allocated a frame and then cleared its 4 KiB of payload with
memset(page->data, 0, PAGE_SIZE) while still holding g_page_cache_lock with
interrupts disabled.  Every miss-to-create transition therefore serialised
the whole system for the length of a page clear, and evict_locked() could
extend one allocation into an O(cache size) critical section whenever the
LRU tail was made of recently-used candidates, taking a nested bucket lock
per candidate inside it.

The frame is taken from the free stack under the allocation lock and is
exclusively owned from then on - it is unpublished, so no warm hit can
reach it, and evict_locked() only ever reclaims frames at refcount 0 -
so the payload is cleared with the global lock released.  Publication
moves into its own critical section and re-checks the index under the
bucket lock first, so the one-frame-per-(vnode, index) invariant survives
the window in between.

evict_locked() now visits at most PAGE_CACHE_EVICT_SCAN_BUDGET
candidates per call.  Giving up is not a lost opportunity: every candidate
it passed had its second-chance bit cleared, so the caller spends a few
more bounded sweeps before escalating, each one a separate short critical
section rather than one long one.  The escalation deliberately does not
reach for the whole-cache reclaim - dropping every clean page discards
precisely the pages the second chance exists to keep, and turning cache
pressure into that storm measured 2x slower on a random-read workload over
a file larger than the cache.

Lock order is unchanged: global before bucket, never reversed.  The memset
runs with no page-cache lock held, and evict_locked() still acquires only
bucket locks while the global lock is held.
ff20bb16079e273cf82ff12b29f5cd0d5a1e9ebc:
test(fs): stage readahead in a checked-out buffer and gate the window on access order

Every cold page that reached a filesystem with readpages() pulled in a full
32-page window unconditionally, and each window cost a kmalloc, a memset of
the whole window and a kfree.  A 4 KiB random read therefore paid for 32
pages of disk I/O and 128 KiB of zeroing, of which 31 pages were never
looked at; measured over a file twice the size of the cache, a random-read
workload fetched 66,611 pages for 6,144 reads and ran 2.2x slower than it
does now.

Two changes.  The staging buffer for readpages() is checked out of a small
pool and returned afterwards instead of being allocated per window.  It is
a pool rather than the per-task scratch the Linux ABI I/O paths use because
sys_read hands its own scratch buffer in as the copy destination, so a
shared per-task allocation would be freed underneath the writer.  It is a
pool rather than a bare per-CPU buffer because checkout survives
preemption.  The pre-clear of the window is gone: readpages() reports how
much of the window it stored and the shortfall is already zeroed after the
call, so the memset was a second pass over the same bytes.

The window is now gated on the read stream actually walking forward.
page_cache_read_resumes() compares this read's page index against the index
just past the previous read(2) on the same open file, held in a 64-entry
table striped by vfile pointer; equality is what a sequential scan produces
and nothing else does.  The first page of a stream has no evidence and
fetches alone, the second already has it.  A stripe collision or a torn read
of the two fields can only turn the hint into an unnecessary or a missed
prefetch; it cannot affect correctness, so the pair is not published
atomically.  The state is per open file, not per vnode, so two readers of
one file do not evict each other's hint, and it is a fixed-size table with
no allocation and no lifetime of its own.

Lock order: the pool's spinlock is taken while the per-page fill mutexes are
held and is always released before readpages() is called, so it is strictly
inner to the fill locks and no page-cache global or bucket lock is acquired
while it is held.  The existing global-before-bucket order is untouched.

70e8a64d101f370fc4568745736093b853c4c87a:
feat(fs): chain xattr entries per inode and lock the table

xattr.c had no lock at all.  xattr_cleanup_vnode() runs from vnode_put() on
the last reference of a vnode while another CPU can be inside
xattr_get_vnode() memcpy'ing that entry's value out of the slot that is
being memset to zero underneath it.

Adding the lock also removes the reason it was never added: every lookup,
list and teardown walked all 1024 slots.  Entries are now chained per
(mnt, ino) through a 64-bucket table, so all four operations are
proportional to the number of attributes the inode actually carries.
Bucket heads hold index+1 so the zero-initialised table needs no setup and
0 unambiguously means end-of-chain.

The new g_xattr_lock is a leaf -- each critical section is pure memory
work, no allocation and no copy_to_user -- and is documented as sitting at
the innermost end of the order in core/lock.h.
950215bacf733b63690f4feddaf65875f01673cf:
perf(fs): skip the inotify instance walk when no watches exist

Every buffered write, page-cache eviction and other VFS mutation funnels
through inotify_vnode_event(), which took the global instance lock and
walked every instance on every mutation.  The overwhelmingly common case
is that no inotify or fanotify watch exists anywhere, so one relaxed load
of a live-watch counter proves that with no lock at all.
f3d5eed42d08ec69ad43f4dbb8980aeea0311646:
perf(fs): skip quota locks when no mount has quota enabled

quota_check_space() and quota_account_space() sit on the buffered-write
path and each took two spinlocks -- the global table lock and the per-mount
lock -- only to discover that no quota was enabled and return.  Gate them on
a relaxed count of ever-claimed mount slots, then on a per-mount OR of the
enabled types, so the unquotaed system proves it with two loads and the
quotaed one still pays for the accounting.
fd612fcf320e524ef68888247941546a995d1bf8:
feat(fs): take the flock range algebra off the kernel stack and make it atomic

fs_locks_set() ran the range split over five per-call arrays totalling
about 23 KiB -- a third of a 64 KiB kernel stack in a single frame -- and it
did so *inside* the g_file_lock_table_lock region.  The scratch is now
kmalloc'd before the lock is taken (a reclaiming allocation must never run
under a spinlock) and the split/insertion-sort/merge runs in place on it.
That lets the write-back become atomic: the old code withdrew this owner's
locks first and restored them by rescanning for free slots if the merged
result did not fit, and the restore dropped ranges when the table had
changed underneath it.  Capacity is now checked arithmetically against the
own-range count before anything is mutated.

Insertion sort replaces the O(n^2) selection sort; the remnants arrive in
table order and are already nearly sorted.

Also fixes a spin-without-sleeping bug: fs_lock_wait() returned 0 when
proc_park_prepare() produced no token, and 0 means 'retry', so the caller
re-entered the table scan under the lock and burned all 1024 retries
without ever sleeping.  It now reports -EAGAIN, as does a waiter that
could not be enqueued.
c1f5cc7396ca69b91687390ac97c201e9d72323d:
fix(fs): pin the registered eventfd by vfile and bound the transfer length

Two defects in the completion path:

The registered notification target was stored as the raw descriptor number
and re-resolved through fdtable_get_current() on every io_uring_enter() with
completions.  That number can be closed and reassigned to an unrelated file
while completions are still landing, so the ring would signal whatever now
occupies it.  The ring now holds a vfile reference; the descriptor number is
kept only to charge the mediation envelope.  It is taken under ring->lock
and dropped across the write, since vfs_write_file() may block.

sqe->len is an unchecked user uint32 and the executor staged the whole
transfer in one kmalloc, so userspace could ask the slab for 4 GiB.  Clamped
to Linux's MAX_RW_COUNT, which also restores the expected short read.
6c86b87f4d4a0695c81b5733770f8f476b793ddf:
fix(fs): hash the aio context table and stop freeing under the table lock

aio_ctx_put() called kfree() with g_aio_table_lock held and interrupts
disabled -- a reclaiming allocator under a spinlock.  Release now unpublishes
the context under the lock and hands the ring back, and every caller drops it
after dropping the lock.

Context lookup walked all AIO_MAX_CONTEXTS slots on every operation; contexts
are now on a 64-bucket chain.  The pending-submission list was a kmalloc'd
singly linked node per submission, allocated and freed under c->lock; it is
now an inline array, since at most one entry per concurrently-submitting task
is ever live.  Exhaustion leaves the iocb untracked, which io_cancel() already
reports as -EAGAIN.
ee8a1c932c2293ea7e03c2c5e3f31f4f78d9ca4a: feat(fs): keep the devfs and sysfs lookups off their global lock
b27d10bcd376e7a45ec21a6685520e46720b0ef5: merge(fs): integrate filesystem I/O correctness fixes
46cc486d820049a2e072a60497c484e7105c26f5:
feat(fs): walk FAT32 directories with a carried cluster cursor

Every 32-byte directory entry was fetched through fat32_chain_read, which
re-follows the cluster chain from the directory's first cluster, so a lookup
of the last entry in a 1000-entry directory issued 5416 block-cache reads.
The free-slot, short-name and emptiness scans paid the same quadratic cost,
which made unlink, rmdir and create quadratic too.

A cursor now carries the cluster it is standing on and refills one page at a
time, so a scan is linear in entries and in clusters.  Measured against a real
1000-entry FAT32 image with 4 KiB clusters: 5416 -> 16 block-cache reads for a
last-entry lookup, and 5425 -> 16 for an ENOENT miss.  Offset reporting, chain
growth and the short-name collision path are unchanged; the rewritten code
produces byte-identical images to the original across cluster sizes from 512 B
to 32 KiB.
827b32a9eb777ebf786500617ab95c0b4736829b:
feat(fs): read an ntfs directory with one index walk

ntfs_read_directory counted the directory in one pass over the MFT record and
every INDX block, freed the results, then repeated the identical work to fill
an array.  Every path component, open, unlink, rmdir and rename therefore paid
two full directory reads, each held under the mount-global sb->lock.

The walk now appends straight into a growable array, halving the reads and
making the result size independent of a pre-pass.  A compressed or encrypted
$INDEX_ALLOCATION is skipped once rather than being skipped while counting and
parsed while filling, so the two passes can no longer disagree about which
entries exist.

The sb->lock scope is unchanged: narrowing it needs a per-inode lock that the
rename transaction in ntfs_namei.c relies on the global one for.
c08279749559d40305763e67cf9bef1c39956eae:
feat(fs): cache the resident NTFS bitmaps per volume and scan them a word at a time

Every cluster handed out cost one MFT record read, a read of the whole
$Bitmap, and then a walk of that map one bit at a time; the write-back cost
another MFT record read and another whole-map write.  A create or an append
therefore paid a fixed number of whole-volume I/Os multiplied by the number of
clusters it needed.

Four slots now hold the resident map, claimed by a volume's first allocation
and released at unmount, so the steady-state cost of an allocation is the
in-memory scan alone.  A volume that finds no free slot falls back to the
uncached path, so running out of slots costs speed and not correctness.  The
slot lock is held only across pointer bookkeeping, never across disk I/O; the
bytes are only touched with the owning volume's sb->lock, which every
allocation and free already takes.

The scan also consumes whole free words 64 bits at a time, and
ntfs_create_entry() now mirrors its in-use flag into the MFT bitmap it just
searched, so the next create does not walk back over the same records.

0a2b6c3b125046146c3ff17d52fa80c27fd605b6:
feat(net): close a socket through the slot registration already recorded

net_unregister_socket_locked searched g_sockets for the pointer it was
handed, comparing against all NET_MAX_SOCKETS entries.  The slot came from
net_register_socket_locked and was kept in s->reg_idx for exactly this,
so the search was recomputing what the socket already knew.

The cost is per close(), and the constant is profile-dependent: 1024
slots on the default profile, 65536 on the server one, where every close
became a 65536-iteration pointer walk across a half-megabyte array.

A recorded index is only usable if it is checked rather than trusted, so
the slot is still compared against the pointer before it is cleared.  A
mismatch means the slot was handed to another socket in the meantime, and
that socket's registration is left alone.

070f4d2280d6ad8069349b7691d18a6ce590c01d:
feat(net): capture L2 frames only while a packet socket is listening

Every frame received on every interface was copied into the AF_PACKET
capture ring under its lock and then offered to the delivery walk, which
scans every NET_MAX_SOCKETS slot.  On a host with no packet socket bound
the copy is pure waste: the ring is 16 frames deep, so a burst fills it,
increments g_pkt_drops and discards frames it has already paid to copy.

Both costs are now behind a census of bound AF_PACKET sockets, so a
receive with no listener is one acquire load and a branch.

The count is keyed by registry slot through a bitmap rather than by
net_socket_t.pkt_bound, because the release side runs during teardown:
clearing pkt_bound would change what a sendto() on a stale descriptor
reports, and the bitmap makes the release idempotent against the rebind
and re-unregister cases without touching socket state.

Ordering: the acquire is a release-store under g_net_lock and the receive
path samples it with an acquire, so a bind that has returned is counted by
every later receive.  A receive that races a close either copies a frame
whose socket has gone -- delivered to nobody, which is the outcome the
frame already had -- or misses one that arrived before the bind returned.
Neither loses a frame the socket was entitled to, and a close cannot leave
the count stuck high, because the release happens while the socket still
holds its slot.  Drift can only be upwards, which re-enables capture and
matches today's unconditional behaviour.

The census lives in a new kernel/include/net/socket_side.h because
net_socket_t is pinned to the profile's per-socket byte budget by a static
assert and cannot take the field.

Verified: make kernel-only ARCH=riscv64 BOARD=qemu-virt-riscv64
9def2b04244a7ecf22b9799caab2db212537bde4:
feat(net): answer FIONREAD from a running byte count not a queue walk

net_socket_rx_available summed len-off over every queued message, so the
cost of asking how much is readable was the length of the receive queue.
The queue is per socket and NET_MAX_QUEUE is a profile constant: 128 on
the default profile, 1024 on the server one, where each FIONREAD walked a
thousand messages under g_net_lock.

socket_queue.c now keeps the total as it appends and removes messages, and
the accessor reads it.  Both FIONREAD callers benefit without changing:
sys_fs.c ioctl and the /proc/net row renderer are the only two.

The tally is keyed by registry slot rather than living in net_socket_t,
which is pinned to the profile's per-socket byte budget by a static assert
and has no room.  8 bytes per slot costs half a megabyte at the server
profile's 65536 sockets, against a megabyte for g_sockets itself; moving it
into net_socket_t later costs 8 bytes per socket instead, and is the better
placement once that struct is being reshaped anyway.

Each tally entry carries the queue's message count beside the byte count.
Everything that appends or removes a message moves both halves together, so
they agree, and every access checks the pair instead of trusting the byte
half.  That is what makes this safe rather than just fast: shutdown(SHUT_RD)
empties rx_head and rx_count in one step without passing through
net_msg_link_locked(), and it lives in a file this branch does not own.  The
disagreement is detected on the next read, enqueue or dequeue and costs one
rebuild, instead of leaving FIONREAD permanently reporting bytes the queue
does not hold.

325f6bae32c858a971d6ccfe056b1309b7353694:
perf(net): skip netfilter parsing when no rules are installed

netfilter_eval walked Ethernet, VLAN, IPv4 and L4 headers on every frame
and then did two atomic read-modify-writes on g_stats, whatever the table
held.  With an empty table the answer is ACCEPT no matter what those
headers say, so all of it produced a constant.

The rule count is now sampled under the same seqlock that protects the
table, before the parse.  Sampling it there rather than as a bare load is
what keeps the fast path honest: a writer publishes the count between
netfilter_rules_begin and netfilter_rules_end, so a table that will not
settle reports as populated and the full evaluation runs.  The failure mode
is one wasted header walk, which is the right way to be wrong about a
filter.

Once a rule exists the parse and the counters run exactly as before, so
smoke-netfilter's assertion that out_packets and out_dropped advance under
an installed drop rule is unaffected.

The counters are also split into one cache-line-separated bank per
direction.  Every evaluated packet updates a counter in each direction, so
a single struct put both on one line that all CPUs write; the six counters
are still summed into one netfilter_stats_t for netfilter_get_stats(), so
/proc/a20/netfilter renders unchanged.
