78080a0ddada0b251aa471c574bd481315b0532a:
feat(ipc): stage sem GETALL/SETALL values instead of copying under g_sem_lock

copy_to_user/copy_from_user can fault and page-walk, and g_sem_lock is
the single lock guarding every set in the table, so semctl(GETALL/SETALL)
held it across a user access. Snapshot the values under the lock, drop it,
then copy, and resolve the set again on the SETALL path because it can be
removed and recycled while the copy is in flight.
d6484cd74471d8f61569c6accbd31b364a02d765:
feat(abi): dispatch native syscalls through a direct index not a linear scan

The lookup walked all 142 entries per native syscall and staged the hit in
one function-static entry, which two CPUs in native syscalls could overwrite
between the match and the call through it. Index the const entries by number
so the result is a pointer into storage nobody writes, and bound the index
with a per-entry static assert so a number that does not fit fails the build
rather than becoming an unreachable syscall.
a8aff2e68de5d374941fb9cfb8a9949d5da76889:
feat(abi): resolve syscall paths with length-checked copies not snprintf

Every path-taking syscall ran the path through a full vsnprintf format walk
to perform what is a memcpy, and staged absolute paths through a second
512-byte strncpy before copying them out again. Join and copy directly, and
skip the staging buffer entirely for paths that are already logical.
b4b52ff47ac46fb813fd98e01c60266cb58322ad:
feat(abi): validate copy_file_range offsets before seeking either description

A bad off_in/off_out pointer returned -EFAULT with the restore lseek still
pending, so a failed call left the caller's files repositioned. Linux keeps
both offsets untouched on -EFAULT.
4fa921d8ec570eb880781e06622b2befbf116a91:
fix(ipc): bucket shared futex waiters by physical page and remove the wake sweep

A SHARED futex word reached through two independently ASLR-randomised mm
spaces is one physical page under two virtual addresses, so virtual-address
bucketing split the peers and every wake that raced an un-parked waiter had
to sweep the other 63 buckets under 63 separate lock acquisitions to find
them. Keying the bucket on the physical page puts every sharer in one place.

The wait side cannot know whether the wake will carry FUTEX_PRIVATE_FLAG, so
it derives the bucket from the physical page and every other side follows,
including the private waker: skipping its page-table walk would put it in a
different bucket from the waiters it must find. The physical address stays
out of the match predicate for private wakes, so it still cannot match a
foreign mm by page alias.

The sweep survives only where the caller's own translation of the word
failed and its bucket is therefore a guess, which is the one case where no
single bucket is known to hold the peer.
2851d2761fc2e8dddb63ce286cf8d59b9df456f7:
feat(ipc): wake one receiver per SysV message not every blocked reader

A send publishes exactly one message, so waking the whole recv queue made N-1
readers re-run the type scan under the global message lock and immediately
re-park. Linux wakes one receiver per message for the same reason.
0981239932b331da1044fa8f35fb9288d2581de7:
fix(ipc): stop the eventfd and monitor paths from waking or locking too much

An eventfd write publishes a counter one reader can drain whole, and a read
frees exactly the room one blocked writer was waiting for, so waking every
waiter on those transitions made all but one re-check and re-park.

The monitor tick ran from the scheduler timer and called a20_event_notify --
which takes the event-hash lock -- with the registry lock still held, so the
critical section grew with the number of live monitors and sat in front of
the pick. Sample and reference the due monitors under the registry lock, then
notify once it is dropped.
efcada290ece6e607f5fda010693ea88f0bc0a6b:
feat(ipc): release faulting waiters once per supply not once per page

A bulk pager supply took the faulters lock once per page and re-walked the
waiter list each time, so 1 MiB of pages cost 256 lock/unlock pairs. The
supplied pages are contiguous, so they go out in a single pass; a one-page
supply keeps the keyed wake so faulters parked on other offsets are left
alone.

uffd unregister had the same shape one level up: re-taking the global range
lock and re-walking the range list for every page of the span, which made a
256 MiB unregister 65536 global-lock acquisitions. Hold the lock once across
the scan. uffd_io_wake released waiters per page for the same reason.
35abb73c37083208a3ea323ab406020aba71db36:
feat(ipc): make the channel crash trace opt-in and narrow g_ch_lock on poll

The trace ring is only ever read by a20_channel_trace_dump(), which no hot
path calls, yet recording ran an atomic bump on a single global, a timer
read and two proc_current() lookups on every send and every receive. Gate it
on "chtrace" in the kernel command line, matching how the syscall trace
gates on "trace=".

a20_channel_writable held the one registry lock for every channel in the
system across the peer lock and the queue read. Take a peer reference under
it -- the shape ch_try_enqueue and the park path already use -- and inspect
the queue after dropping it.
33b7825c46b50f5dba57b2721fbd6036fd9d3cae: merge(ipc): integrate IPC and ABI dispatch improvements
8a3c5c75aee75c41894643ebb3fc21e5e6a50d2b:
fix(drivers): stop the reclaiming allocator running under a spinlock

pty_alloc() held g_pty_alloc_lock across three kmalloc(PTY_BUF_SIZE), and
class_device_publish() held g_class_lock across the kcalloc/krealloc of the
whole class device array; udriver_map_mmio() held mm->lock across a kcalloc of
the VMA.  All three are single-core-critical sections.

PTY_BUF_SIZE (4096) is above SLAB_MAX_OBJ (2048), so the pty ring buffers take
the BUDDY path, and plain kmalloc/kcalloc are the reclaiming variants: kmalloc()
is kmalloc_flags(size, 1), which on a buddy failure calls oom_try_reclaim().
That path calls swap_out_victim_pages(), which takes proc_lock and mm->lock and
issues swap_write_page() disk I/O, and mm_tlb_invalidate_finish(), which waits
on remote TLB IPIs.  On exhaustion it also kerr()s and proc_force_exit()s a
victim task.  None of that is legal with interrupts disabled, and a task being
torn down while another CPU holds pty_alloc_lock is the shape of a
machine-wide hang.  The trigger is memory pressure alone -- no bug, just a busy
machine.

So memory pressure during a pty open, a class publish or an mmio map could
stall every CPU behind an irq-disabled section while the kernel wrote swap
pages and killed a process.

pty_alloc() now reserves the slot under the lock, drops it for the three
allocations, and republishes the finished pair under a second short
acquisition.  Reserving under the lock is what keeps a concurrent pty_alloc()
from taking the same index; nothing else can observe the slot in between,
because a pty_pair_t pointer only escapes once pty_alloc() returns.  The
allocations stay plain kmalloc(), so the -ENOMEM/reclaim behaviour callers
expect is unchanged -- only its position relative to the lock changed.

class_allocate_index() hands out a unique (class_type, index) pair per device
and the index cycles over 0..255, so the registry is bounded by 256 devices per
class type and 7 * 256 overall.  That is an exact bound, not an estimate: an
index is never reused while its device is published.  Backing the registry with
a fixed static array of that size therefore removes both allocations from the
locked section for good, rather than hoisting them and leaving a second
allocation site to get wrong later.  It also drops the growth path, which had
no way to serialise two racing krealloc()s on the same shared array.

udriver_map_mmio() allocates the VMA up front and fills it in once mm->lock is
held.  The fail path now drops the allocation reference with vma_put() after
releasing mm->lock, because vma_put() deliberately takes mm->vma_ref_lock
instead so a last holder can schedule the free without the lock it just
escaped.

kernel/mm/slab.c is unchanged: kmalloc_atomic() already exists and is used
here only where the caller genuinely cannot sleep.

Verified: kernel-only builds clean for riscv64/aarch64/x86_64 and riscv64
NR_CPUS=4; check-task-lifetime-boundary, check-io-progress-model,
check-driver-core-model, smoke-pty-stress, smoke-iommu-udriver-isolation,
smoke-driver-lifecycle and smoke-abi-linux all pass.
62ef15b825cfbccc233558253b6d7e269cf41b29:
feat(drivers): keep the ctrl-c task dump out of the UART top half

uart_rx_push() ran the whole Ctrl-C diagnostic from the UART IRQ handler:
uart_dump_tasks() took proc_lock with interrupts disabled and then wrote one
kdebug line per task, and uart_signal_all_user() added a second kdebug line per
signalled task.  Both bursts leave through the same UART that raised the
interrupt.

The dump is the part that cannot run there.  proc_lock is an ordinary spinlock
held by ordinary task-context code, so a UART interrupt arriving on a CPU whose
task already holds proc_lock self-deadlocks the box -- and the handler holds it
for the length of a full task-table walk.  That is a hang, not a slowdown.

The two signal walks stay in the top half.  proc_find_get() takes only pid_lock,
delivering a signal from an interrupt is what that path is for, and the
foreground process group has to learn about the key while the shell is busy
running a command and therefore nowhere near a console read: deferring the
signal would stop Ctrl-C from killing anything.

So the top half now only raises a flag and wakes the reader; uart_getc() and
uart_has_input() -- this driver's two task-context entry points -- service it.
The per-task [UART-SIG] lines are replaced by one summary line, which removes an
O(tasks) klog burst from the interrupt without losing the count.

Measured on qemu-virt-riscv64 (tools/a20 run qemu-riscv64, mksh on the serial
console), against the same test on unmodified main:

  typed "echo CONSOLE_ALIVE_1", sent 0x03, waited, checked the console again:
    main and this commit both print the echo, both shut the system down in
    response to the SIGINT, and both reach [SD] POWER_OFF with exit code 0.
    Console output is byte-identical and not garbled.

One real difference, measured rather than assumed.  With klog_level forced to
KLOG_DEBUG from uart_init() (temporary instrumentation, not in this commit),
main prints "[TTYDBG] task dump begin" plus five task lines before the signals;
this commit prints none of it.  The reason is visible in main's own output: no
foreground process group is ever established on this board (TIOCSPGRP is only
issued under job control, and mksh does not enter it here), so
uart_signal_all_user(SIGINT, spare_shells=0) SIGINTs every user task including
init, and the machine begins tearing down before the reader it just woke can
run the dump.  The dump is therefore lost exactly in the configuration where
Ctrl-C already destroys the system and a task table would tell you nothing.
Where the console is correctly configured the reader survives and services the
dump deterministically.  I could not construct that configuration on any board
available here, so the surviving case is reasoned, not measured.

uart_putc()/uart_puts() are untouched: the console serialisation lives on the
klog side and this change neither duplicates nor bypasses it.

kernel-only riscv64 build clean; smoke-riscv64 and smoke-abi-linux pass.
d6b2894be7d4708d67d4b009b3a20a19a0d4cf77:
fix(drivers): stop charging every AHCI command a fixed 800us pre-poll

ahci_wait_complete() spun udelay(20) for AHCI_HYBRID_PRE_POLL_US = 800
microseconds before it would park, unconditionally, on every command including
reads and writes that then parked on the completion IRQ a few microseconds
later.  For a 1MiB transfer that is 16 serialized submit-and-wait cycles of
which the first 800us of each is dead time.

The window is sized for a transport that never raises an interrupt.  Once
port->irq_registered is set, ahci_irq_handler() writes back the status word and
collects the parked submitter, so a command still in flight wakes the waiter
whenever it retires; the window only has to outlast a command that has already
completed by the time the first PxCI read happens.  800us becomes 50us, and the
no-ISR branch keeps polling for the whole timeout, which is where a long window
actually belongs.

The spin itself is now ahci_poll_pause().  udelay() re-reads the clock through
current_board->timer->read_ticks() -- two indirect calls per iteration -- and
carries no compiler barrier, so the MMIO reads it is meant to be spacing out
can be hoisted and the loop never yields the pipeline.  ahci_poll_pause() uses
cpu_relax() plus an explicit memory clobber and reads timer_get_ticks() directly.
udelay() itself lives in driver_hwapi.c and is shared by every driver; this
change deliberately does not touch it, but it wants the same treatment there.

Deliberately conservative: this driver only runs on real AHCI hardware (the sole
board that instantiates it is ls2k1000) and there is no emulation of it in this
tree, so nothing below was exercised against a device.  The park path already
re-checks PxCI and last_is after linking its wait queue entry, so correctness
never depended on the window's length -- only the latency of a command that
retires while nobody is polling did, and that path is the one the IRQ takes.

Verified: kernel-only builds clean for x86_64 (the only configuration in the tree
that defines CONFIG_AHCI via ARCH) and for riscv64 with STORAGE_READ_ONLY=1, both
of which compile ahci.c.
ae5231cb08aee83fec4e1f9dfe6f5b89d058d7b3:
feat(drivers): invalidate only the received bytes of a GMAC frame

ls2k_gmac_recv() invalidated GMAC_BUF_SIZE (1536) for the CPU before it knew
how long the frame was, and the descriptor carrying the length word had already
been synced a few lines earlier, so the length was available all along.  On
aarch64 that is a dsb sy plus a dc ivac for each of ~24 cache lines on every
received packet, of which two to four are ever read.  The sync is now issued
for the frame length, after the clamp to maxlen, covering exactly the bytes the
memcpy goes on to read.

The error path no longer syncs for the CPU at all: RX_DESC_ES means the buffer
is discarded unread, so the previous full-width invalidate bought nothing.

The hand-back keeps its full-width dma_sync_for_device, and this is not
redundancy.  arch_dma_sync_for_device() is dc civac on aarch64 -- clean AND
invalidate -- so it is also the invalidate that lets the DMA overwrite the lines
the CPU just read.  The driver never writes these buffers, which makes the clean
half pointless, but only on an architecture where DMA is coherent with the cache
(riscv64 and x86_64 compile both helpers to nothing).  Splitting the clean from
the invalidate needs a new driver_hwapi entry point, and driver_hwapi.c is not
this change's file, so the full-width call stays.

Verified: the only configuration in the tree that compiles this file --
ARCH=loongarch64 BOARD=ls2k1000 DRIVER_DEPLOYMENT=embedded, since the generic
profile builds it as a package -- builds clean.
79d6595039d3d2a4b2e4227986350f16aaca75da:
feat(drivers): let virtio-gpu park before it pays for the spin chunk

virtio_gpu_send_cmd() only offered its wait queue after 65536 spins, and every
one of those spins called arch_dma_sync_for_cpu() on the used ring.  On aarch64
that is a dsb sy and a dc ivac per cache line per spin, so the chunk cost
131072 dsb sy before the first sleep -- twice per page flip, plus twice more per
fb_autoflush_thread() flush at 30Hz.  With no IRQ registered the fallback
proc_yield()s instead, burning a vCPU for up to the full 1s deadline per
command.

Once a completion IRQ is registered the wait queue is the cheap way to observe
used->idx, so the poll now parks on its first iteration and lets the handler
schedule each re-check; the 65536 chunk is kept only for the no-ISR case, where
there is nothing to park on.  The bounded 20ms park chunk still caps a missed
wake and the 1s deadline still bounds the whole wait, so a device that never
completes behaves as before, just without the spin first.

The per-iteration cache maintenance itself is deliberately NOT hoisted out.  The
device writes used->idx behind the driver's back, so each observation has to be
preceded by an invalidate; a load that hits the line cached by the previous
observation would never see the completion.  arch_dma_sync_for_cpu() compiles
to nothing on the coherent ports (riscv64, x86_64) and to a real invalidate on
aarch64, so it is the observation that has to be paid for, not the loop.

Verified: kernel-only builds clean for riscv64 and, with DRIVER_DEPLOYMENT=
embedded (the only profile that compiles this file), for riscv64 and
loongarch64/ls2k1000.
9a316de34cff3f7ee985c13e1b6f1dafa16b0bcd:
fix(drivers): poll bound devices from a per-CPU mirror not the registry mutex

driver_progress_class() runs from every CPU on every scheduler pass and may
not block, so it took mutex_trylock over the whole device registry -- and a
failed trylock silently skipped every device on that pass.  Under any real
contention that turns into devices going unpolled.

Each CPU now keeps a private mirror of the bound devices that have a progress
callback, rebuilt under the lifecycle mutex only when g_progress_epoch moves.
The mutex is therefore not touched at all in the steady state, and a stale
mirror costs its CPU one pass over a stale set rather than dropping every
device.

The mirror is a caching hint, never the lifetime guard: entries are static
device_t objects that outlive every binding, and each is entered through
class_device_ref_for_device() plus class_device_call_begin().  That also fixes
a use-after-free -- reading dev->class_dev on its own races
class_device_unpublish(), which clears the field and then drops the last
reference, so a caller could be left holding freed memory.  The reference is
now taken under g_class_lock, making the load and the refcount bump a single
event relative to the clear.
d73db55d97c30f011a952a013f5bd6324fbf4c55:
feat(core): keep the lock owner behind CONFIG_DEBUG_LOCKS where it belongs

The uncontended fast path stopped reading the stall clock before the exchange,
which left 'cur' NULL unless the acquire actually spun.  The trailing
'lock->owner = cur' then published NULL on every uncontended acquire, so:

  - [LOCK-STALL] reported owner=-1 for the very holder it was trying to name,
    because that holder had taken the lock without contention and cleared it;
  - the 'owner == cur' self-deadlock test could never fire, since owner is
    NULL and cur is not.

Both are diagnostics that only matter once a lock has already spun for five
seconds, so they belong behind CONFIG_DEBUG_LOCKS rather than on every
acquire at all ~920 call sites.  spin_trylock_irqsave() already gates its own
owner write the same way; this makes spin_lock_at consistent with it.
909030f4ed820a41f4c77fba2cd2e7ca587e4ae9:
feat(virtio): cache QueueNotifyOff instead of reading it back on every kick

Every kick wrote QueueSelect, read QueueNotifyOff back out of the device,
computed the doorbell address from it, and wrote the queue index there.  The
read is the expensive half: it is an MMIO round trip on the one register a
virtio driver writes per buffer, so it is paid per received packet by
virtio-net and per submitted request by virtio-blk.

QueueNotifyOff is fixed for the lifetime of the device, so it is now read
once per queue index and cached; later kicks are a bare store to the
doorbell.  QueueSelect is still written on every kick, because the spec
defines the offset as a property of the selected queue and leaving the
selection alone keeps every later Queue* register the driver reads
unambiguous.

The cache is indexed by queue index and falls back to the read for an index
outside it, so an unusually wide device is slower rather than wrong.  All
four notify implementations get it -- the shared PCI path in drivers/bus,
which riscv64, aarch64, arm32, riscv32 and loongarch32 all use, plus the
x86_64, loongarch64 and ppc64le transports that carry their own.  Each slot
is zeroed by the same memset/designated-initializer that sets up the
transport, and transport slots are never reused, so no stale offset can
survive into a different device.

Verified: builds for riscv64, aarch64, x86_64 and loongarch64; all 15 host
gates green; smoke-riscv64, smoke-abi-linux, smoke-net-lanes,
smoke-net-tcp-lanes, smoke-netfilter and smoke-socket-stress pass.
smoke-net-accept is flaky independently of this change -- it failed 1 of 3
runs both with and without it -- so it is not evidence either way.
e090cbace1e1d806bca99e3f7fe164895ff3dfe1:
refactor(ipc): split the eventq reverse index into per-bucket locks

The 256-bucket reverse index shared one global spinlock, so every
watch registration, cancellation, object destroy, and every pushed
event (FS/IPC notify) queued behind it regardless of which object
they touched.  Each operation only ever touches one bucket, so the
global lock is now an array of per-bucket locks; the documented lock
order becomes "hash bucket -> owner eq->lock" and no operation ever
holds two different bucket locks.

Two paths needed restructuring because the bucket is only known
after a lookup:

- a20_eventq_cancel is keyed by handle: probe under eq->lock to
  learn the target object, then redo the removal under the full
  bucket -> eq order.  A concurrent cancel/destroy that wins the
  race makes the re-search come up empty (NOT_FOUND), which is the
  same answer the old code gave for an already-cancelled watch.
- a20_eventq_release steals the watch list under eq->lock and then
  detaches each node from its own bucket.  Node lifetime is now
  bucket-protected: whoever removes the node under the bucket lock
  frees the entry, and evq_hash_remove_locked reports whether that
  happened, so release cannot double-free an entry that
  a20_eventq_on_object_destroy already claimed.
5faecc5660a5e834e6384be2c418fd43e962b150:
feat(vfs): give each vnode its own buffered-write mutex instead of 64 hash buckets

Writes to page-cached files serialized on one of 64 global mutexes
picked by hashing the vnode pointer, so two unrelated files whose
pointers collided blocked each other across every core, and
vnode_t itself carried no lock at all — the size/offset/mtime
consistency of a file lived entirely in whichever bucket mutex its
pointer hashed to.

The mutex now lives in vnode_t, initialized in vnode_ref_init
(every vnode creation path routes through it), and writers take
their own file's lock.  Lifetime is safe without extra refcounting:
a writer holds the vnode alive through its open vfile, so the lock
cannot be freed under a waiter.  This removes the write-side
global serialization point on the fd I/O path; O_DIRECT, pipes and
char devices keep their previous lockless behavior.
1a75d06c908a7024791a95cbd79eb72bdda59a4f:
fix(vfs): keep mount entries stable across unmounts

mount_t lived in an inline array inside the mount namespace and
vfs_mount_remove compacted it by shifting entries down.  Every
vnode->mnt pointer (set at vnode creation and inherited by
link()/dcache), every dcache e->mnt, and the quota mount cache
pointed at array slots — after any umount below their index they
silently referred to the wrong mount.  Ext4's cross-mount rename
EXDEV check, per-mount read-only enforcement and quota accounting
all read these pointers.

Mount entries are now heap objects behind stable pointers:

- vfs_mount_alloc() kmallocs; the table is an array of pointers.
- vfs_mount_remove() detaches the pointer and parks the object on a
  per-namespace graveyard instead of freeing: open vfiles can still
  hold vnodes whose ->mnt points at it, and the old zero-the-slot
  behavior at least stayed valid memory.  Graveyard objects are
  freed when the namespace dies (mntns_put); the initial namespace
  is never freed, so its graveyard grows only with the umounts it
  actually performs.
- mntns_copy_mounts() deep-copies entry objects (the namespace
  semantics are unchanged: ns_users stays on the source entry,
  copies are detach-only VFS_MOUNT_NS_SHARED); an allocation
  failure truncates the copy instead of failing the namespace.

As a side effect the quota mount cache and mntns fork copies stop
aliasing source-namespace memory.
be63724bb6921c7a86f1f516f994b38dec629ed1:
feat(fs): shard the global vfile table lock into per-bucket locks

g_files[]/g_file_slot_refs[] were guarded by one global spinlock,
and every fd resolution in read/write/close/dup took it — a
process-wide serialization point one level below files_struct.lock,
compounding the proc_lock hotspot documented in
docs/server-readiness.md.  Per-slot state now sits under one of 128
bucket locks picked by a multiplicative hash of the gfd; the free
bitmap and allocation cursor move to their own g_file_alloc_lock.

Lock order is bucket -> alloc (only file_close_prepare's note-free
nests them); allocators reserve a slot under the alloc lock, release
it, then install under the bucket lock, so no path ever holds two
bucket locks and a reserved-but-uninstalled gfd is unreachable —
its number is published only after installation.  dup/dup3 pin the
source vfile with a reference under the source bucket and install
into the destination bucket afterwards; dup3's EBUSY path hands the
pinned reference to vfs_put_file so a concurrently-closed oldfd
still reaches the finalizer.

All 128 buckets and the alloc lock are registered in the lock
contention table (LOCK_COUNTERS_MAX 64 -> 192), so the new locks are
measurably visible rather than assumed clean.  The gfd number space
and all callers keep their semantics; the fuller per-process
vfile*-in-fd[] conversion stays open in server-readiness.md.
30625962be57c0f61cd120cc7ec47e4e7d729da5:
feat(vfs): make the last-lookup error per-task instead of a global

g_lookup_errno was a plain global written by every path resolution
and read back by the failed-open/stat callers, so two concurrent
lookups on different CPUs could overwrite each other's failure
reason and return the wrong errno (a lookup that failed with EACCES
could surface as another task's ENOENT, or as success-errno 0).

The error now lives in a per-task slot (task_t.lookup_errno, next to
the existing per-task vfs_open_errno which already followed this
pattern); tasks are kcalloc'd so the slot starts clear, and boot
paths with no current task keep a static fallback behind
vfs_lookup_errno()/vfs_set_lookup_errno().
412e861a8076855fe0e1c46165806e7ea75865ba:
feat(mm.core): add per-CPU slab object arrays and a seqlock real-time reader

Slab had one spinlock per size class, so every kmalloc/kfree of the
same class on every CPU queued behind the same lock — the hidden
hotspot behind multi-threaded server and build workloads.  Mirroring
the frame allocator's CPU page batch, each (cache, cpu) now keeps a
16-object array: a hit allocates or frees with only local IRQ
exclusion, and the cache lock is taken once per refill (8 objects)
or once per drain (8 objects) instead of once per object.  The
alloc/free state machines move unchanged into slab_alloc_obj_locked
/ slab_free_obj_locked under the cache lock, keeping every
corruption diagnostic.  A slab with objects parked in a CPU array
always has in_use > 0, so it can never reach spare/release while
pinned; stats keep counting parked objects via in_use.

timekeeping_get_realtime() took the timekeeping spinlock on every
read; it now retries on a seqlock instead (writer-writer exclusion
kept; g_realtime_set_gen becomes an atomic read), and re-reads the
anchor trio so a torn u64 on 32-bit targets can never be accepted.

Both changes verified by the multi-architecture build matrix and
smoke-mm-stress.
6afd946bde0475d47c9475437876ab6b43b3077d:
feat(mm): add a kswapd-style background reclaimer

Every reclaim path used to run synchronously inside the allocation
slow path: oom_try_reclaim() fires only after the watermark is
already violated, moves at most 8 pages, and then sits behind a 2s
cooldown, and nothing reclaims while the system is otherwise idle.
Under sustained pressure that turns the allocator into a latency
amplifier exactly when allocations are most urgent.

oom_kswapd_thread() (spawned by main.c next to init_kthread) scans
once a second and pulls the existing levers in escalating order —
slab_reclaim_spare(), page_cache_drop_clean(), then paced swap-out
via the new oom_swap_reclaim_pages() wrapper (no OOM kill, no
cooldown, refuses to run while an OOM pass is in flight).  A pass
that frees nothing backs off a full interval instead of spinning.
Pass/page counters are exported through /proc/a20/oom as
kswapd_passes / kswapd_pages_freed / kswapd_last_pass_tick.

NOMMU and MCU builds are unaffected: no swap means the swap lever
reports zero and the thread simply keeps clean-cache drops; the MCU
profile does not compile this boot path.
9a5cb88bc92d7f8c292ab3392bea8955b09211bb:
test(smoke): add SMP variants of the vfs-stress gate one of them in CI

Every smoke-* gate ran a single-core kernel behind -smp 1, so none
of them could ever observe cross-CPU lock contention or SMP
correctness regressions — the structural CI gap called out in
docs/server-readiness.md §四.  This adds two riscv64 variants of the
vfs-stress workload (fd table, dcache, mount table, vfile table,
vnode locks and slab are exactly the paths this branch touches):

- smoke-vfs-stress-smp2: NR_CPUS=2, 2 host cores — cheap enough for
  the CI smoke job, which now runs it after the single-core gate.
- smoke-vfs-stress-smp8: NR_CPUS=8, 8 host cores — the same shape as
  the existing smoke-mm-fork-exec-race; local only because the
  resource gate would wait indefinitely on a small CI runner.

Both reuse the standard -smp<N> build variant, so they exercise the
real NR_CPUS build rather than extra vCPUs on a 1-CPU kernel.  The
smoke case audit (check-smoke-cases) stays green: 78 reachable

a27e7db3e75b9056a4e4f0515e2ef2d1efa57d93:
feat(fs): mount littlefs images read-write in the VFS

The block layer could only hand out FAT, ext4, NTFS or ISO9660, which
between them cover disks but nothing that fits a microcontroller's flash:
every one of them assumes a block device with a stable erase geometry and
a writable superblock, and all of them assume the media survives being
overwritten in place.  littlefs is designed for exactly that case -- a
log-structured filesystem whose commits are atomic pair writes, so an
unclean power loss costs at most the commit in flight.

Vendored littlefs 2.9.2 under kernel/external/littlefs and adapted it at
kernel/fs/diskfs/lfs_vfs.c.  The adapter keeps an lfs_node_t per vnode
(mount pointer + path relative to the mount root + owning vnode) and an
lfs_file_priv_t per vfile holding an open lfs_file_t, so littlefs' own
file handles -- not A20OS' offset bookkeeping -- are the source of truth
for position.  Reads and writes go straight through, bypassing the page
cache, because littlefs has no readpage/writepage split to hook; the mount
type is excluded from vfs_file_uses_page_cache() accordingly.

Three details the port had to get right:

  - lfs_config lives inside lfs_mount_t, not on the caller's stack.  littlefs
    stores the pointer and reads it on every later call, so a stack config
    is a use-after-return.
  - The vendored tree compiles against kernel/external/littlefs/compat/,
    which shadows <stdlib.h>, <string.h>, <assert.h> and <inttypes.h> with
    zero kernel-header dependencies.  Without it the kernel build resolves
    <stdlib.h> to kernel/net/lwip_port/stdlib.h and the two worlds collide.
    Allocation is routed through -DLFS_MALLOC/-DLFS_FREE into lfs_kmalloc /
    lfs_kfree.
  - The kernel links -nostdlib and carries no libgcc, so the builtins
    littlefs expands to (__bswapsi2, __bswapdi2, __ctzdi2, __clzdi2) and
    the libc string helpers it calls (strcspn, strspn) are supplied as
    software implementations in the adapter.

vfile_ops grows an optional sync hook and vfs_fsync_vfile() consults it
before the generic page-cache and block-cache flush, so fsync on a littlefs
file commits that file's pairs and then flushes the device instead of
flushing the whole mount.

Formatting happens on the host: tools/mkfs_lfs.c builds an image with
/hello.txt and a 4096-byte deterministic /data/seed.bin, and
user/cmds/fs/lfs_test.c is the guest gate.  It mounts, verifies the payload
byte for byte, creates/writes/fsyncs/reads, exercises mkdir and unlink,
then unmounts, remounts and checks the guest-written file survived -- which
is what makes the commit-plus-flush path falsifiable rather than asserted.

smoke-lfs wires the whole thing into CI and the release matrix.
82a3c6d5824cf8f66e02fa9c4ac2ec095397f92a:
feat(vfs): add mount trees, object-valued process roots, and pivot_root

pivot_root(2) returned -EPERM on purpose. Its semantics need a real mount
tree -- make new_root the tree root, hang the old root under put_old, so
the caller can collect it with umount2(put_old, MNT_DETACH) -- and the
model had no way to say any of that: proc_fs_context_t held cwd and
root_path as path strings, vfs_move_mount() was a strncpy over the mount
prefix, and there was no mnt_parent link at all. Faking it would have
returned 0 while leaving the old root reachable, which is worse than
failing.

Mounts are now objects with a position. mnt_parent/mnt_mp/mnt_child say
where a mount is attached and which vnode it covers (the mount holds that
reference); mount_t::path stays as the flattened prefix the path walker
matches on. The tree answers umount's busy questions, pivot_root and
mountinfo parent ids; the prefix answers "which mount does this absolute
path resolve in". Both are set together at mount time and moved together
by move_mount, which now re-parents instead of rewriting a string.

Process roots stop being strings too. proc_fs_context_t gains root_mnt,
root_vn and cwd_vn, and the mount counts its holders: root_users is the
namespace table's own reference plus one per process rooted there, and
cwd_users is the same for the directory a process is standing in. Busy
checks are then a comparison against a constant instead of a walk over the
task list. fork copies the pointers and takes its own references;
fdtable_close_all -- the one fs hook every exit path already calls --
releases them.

That is what makes pivot_root implementable. It checks CAP_SYS_ADMIN, that
new_root is a directory and is not the current root, that new_root's mount
is not the root's own mount (a child is the normal container pattern, so it
stays legal), that put_old is a directory, and -- the condition that
actually matters -- that put_old lies under the new root and in the same
mount, so a process cannot use the pivot to keep a handle on a tree the new
root would otherwise hide. It then detaches the old root's mount, flags it
VFS_MOUNT_DETACHED so no path resolves through it any more, re-roots the
process, and moves its cwd to put_old's parent.

umount2 gains the rest of its contract: the Linux MNT_* bits are forwarded
instead of discarded, unknown bits are EINVAL, a mount that is somebody's
root or that has a submount is EBUSY, and MNT_DETACH waives all of it.
/proc/self/mountinfo reports real mount ids and real parents, and spells a
detached mount the way Linux does.

smoke-pivot-root checks the parts that would be faked: real parent ids in
mountinfo, EBUSY for a mount somebody is standing in, MNT_DETACH getting
it anyway, put_old outside the new root refused, the old root unreachable
by path after the pivot, a descriptor opened before it still reading the
old tree, and the new root writable.
a6f8bc500dd1d8aaf89e9232c24979285ab220bf:
feat(mm): invalidate the cached VMA index in vma_split

vma_split() mutates the address space's VMA list but used to take only the VMA
and leave mm->vma_index[] alone.  mprotect was its only caller, and it was the
one mutator in the tree that never called mm_vma_index_invalidate() -- the
other three (mm_insert_vma, mm_split_vma_at, vma_try_merge) all do.

The index array is a snapshot of the list's pointers, so inserting the tail
leaves every later slot one position behind.  The array is still sorted by
start, so the binary search in mm_find_vma() converges without complaint --
onto a VMA that ends before the address, or onto none at all.  Nothing reports
the mismatch; mprotect on a large address space just quietly stops working.

Give vma_split() the mm it already needs to reach the index, and mark the
mutation with MM_VMA_INDEX_INVALIDATE at the point where the link is changed.
6af574fdcb679f7c13d2e5d0c30b1a874f6f4a40:
feat(mm): retry the fault when the fault-around window loses its VMA

The anonymous fault-around window drops mm->lock to allocate its frames, and
while it is unlocked a sibling thread sharing the mm can reshape the VMA list
at that address.  When it re-acquired the lock it compared the current VMA
against the one it had captured and returned -1 on a mismatch.

That mismatch is not an error.  mm_insert_vma() coalesces adjacent anonymous
VMAs and keeps the NEW object, deferring the old one, so a mapping nobody
touched changes identity under the fault after a single unrelated mmap.
vma_can_merge() requires equal vm_flags and pte_flags, so the replacement is
equivalent: the address is still mapped, still writable.  Failing the fault
there killed the process with SIGSEGV on an address it owned -- reproducibly,
on any run with more than one CPU and a workload that mmaps and munmaps
concurrently (smoke-mtcorrupt, new in this series).

Return MM_FAULT_RETRY (-EAGAIN) instead, give the frames back, and let the
entry point start over: handle_demand_fault_access() now loops over a
handle_demand_fault_attempt() that re-resolves the VMA under the lock, which
is precisely the step the window could not take while it was unlocked.  The
bound is 8 attempts -- a window can only lose its VMA to a list mutation, so
each retry makes progress, but a pathological merger must not spin.

Fix the second, quieter half of the same window while here.  Its span was
sized from vma->end BEFORE the lock was dropped, but a concurrent munmap or a
concurrent mprotect split lowers vma->end in place without replacing the
object, so the span can reach past the mapping.  Pages installed there leave
present, zero-filled PTEs sitting in a hole: the fault reports success, no
thread ever wrote that memory, and the next mmap over the address inherits
them as if the application had faulted them in itself.  Re-clamp the span to
the VMA's current end under the lock; the frames past it are released by the
short count fault_map_window() reports.

35b8397b2e7dfbd2ef2b32052fc7b24b1f636579:
test(tests): add mtcorrupt an SMP reproducer for the shared-mm corruption

Every gate that exercises a shared mm_struct ran on -smp 1, where the
fault-around window can never lose its VMA to a sibling thread.  The defect
behind the "multi-threaded processes occasionally have their anonymous memory
scribbled on" reports in docs/distro/known-issues.md is SMP-only, so the whole
matrix was blind to it.

Two phases, both aimed at what that report describes -- a specific structure
losing a pointer field, not random garbage:

  * guarded records: 4096 bytes of data followed by a PROT_NONE guard page,
    every word filled with a unique non-zero pattern.  A zeroed word is itself
    detectable, so "the field became NULL" cannot hide behind a value that was
    never written.
  * a doubly-linked list shared by every worker, checked for the
    self-pointer identity, a magic word and acyclicity -- the exact shape both
    recorded victims died on (LuaJIT's GC list head reading back NULL, musl's
    ld.so self-pointer check with stval=0x10).

Phase 2 runs the same workers while short-lived threads are created and
reaped underneath them, so thread churn overlaps mmap/munmap, heap churn and
faults on the same address space.

Records stay mapped across both phases and are torn down only at the end.
Tearing them down in between left a window where the address was unmapped and
the pthread stack allocator handed the same range to a new thread; the test
then faulted into a PROT_NONE VMA and died in its own harness, which looked
exactly like the bug it was hunting.

Passes on one CPU by construction; before the fix, SIGSEGV on every 4-CPU run.

ebba678ab93075c7df402d06b726a9d0b51fc32a:
feat(pidfd): mediate a stolen descriptor against the receivers envelope

sys_pidfd_getfd installed the target's file into the caller's table and
handed back the number with no envelope check at all, so a FILE-only
envelope could acquire a SOCKET descriptor outright.  The comment claimed
mediation "keyed by the (foreign) fd number" made no sense cross-task, but
the number that matters is the NEW one, which is an ordinary current-task
gfd -- the same thing the SCM_RIGHTS receive path already mediates on.  The
foreign number never needed to be meaningful.

A denied fd is closed rather than left installed, so the denial cannot be
side-stepped by using the number afterwards.

This closes the pidfd-getfd scenario of smoke-envelope, which had been
failing since the envelope work landed.
eb64e06997ed78b227de5f39ef8d073187b72935:
feat(envelope): forget the fd class registry entry when a descriptor closes

env_kind_of() classifies a transferred descriptor from a one-byte-per-gfd
table written at creation time.  Nothing ever cleared it, and fd numbers
are recycled, so the byte outlived the descriptor it described and the next
occupant of that slot was classified as whatever had left it.

Concretely: the smoke-envelope receiver runs FILE-only, its socketpair
endpoint takes a low fd number, and a file arriving over SCM_RIGHTS was
installed on a recycled slot and refused as a socket -- the test saw
MSG_CTRUNC with a zero-length control buffer.  The converse direction, a
socket landing on a retired file's number and being granted FILE rights, is
a real capability over-grant rather than a test failure.

Cleared on close, on dup2 onto an occupied slot, on the exec-time CLOEXEC
sweep, and when a table is destroyed.  The fix is falsifiable: removing the
close-path call alone reproduces the original scm-receive failure.
c0f25ec92631bedaebd521da4b924170400dfa8b:
refactor(fs): split descriptor-table release out of per-task teardown

fdtable_share() gave the destination task its new descriptor table by
calling fdtable_close_all() on it.  close_all() is the hook the process
core calls when a task is genuinely going away, and it also drops the
mount, pid and user namespace references and the fs pins.  Applying it
to a live, already-initialised task therefore cleared state that
proc_task_init_common() had just established and that is still in use.

That was invisible until user namespaces arrived, at which point the
effect was total: a task that had just unshared saw its user_ns field
NULL again moments later, so its namespace read back as the initial one
and every map write was refused.

Extract fdtable_release_files() for the half that is about the table,
and keep fdtable_close_all() as the full teardown reached only from
process exit and proc_destroy_task().
99cc12e40820b979b6543aa802bfc7ae3fa4d3e4:
feat(proc): implement Linux user namespaces with ID mapping and capability semantics

CLONE_NEWUSER was refused with -EINVAL.  It is now a third real
namespace object alongside mount and pid, which is what makes the
PID ns + userns + pivot_root set complete enough to reason about.

Object model (kernel/proc/userns.c).  Each namespace holds one
reference on its parent and task_t::user_ns holds one; NULL means the
statically-pinned initial namespace.  The map is an ordered list of
(lower, parent_lower, count) extents, appended in increasing lower
order, which is what keeps lookup a plain scan.

Ids.  task_t::cred keeps GLOBAL ids and translation happens at the
syscall and procfs boundary, mirroring Linux's kuid_t/kgid_t.  A
global id with no mapping presents as USERNS_OVERFLOW_UID/GID; file
ownership checks use userns_kuid_mapped() so "unrepresentable" and
"is 65534" stay distinct.

Writing the maps.  /proc/<pid>/{uid,gid}_map and setgroups are bound
to the target's own user namespace, so a parent writes them exactly as
in Linux: CAP_SETUID/CAP_SETGID in the parent, or the one
unprivileged allowance -- a single extent of length one mapping the
writer's own id, which is `unshare -U; echo $USER >/proc/self/uid_map`.
setgroups is the one-way deny switch: "deny" is unprivileged and
irreversible, and "allow" after "deny" is EPERM even at full
capability.  The whole write is parsed before any of it is applied,
and every extent must be representable in the parent, so a namespace
can only hand out ids that mean something outside it.

Capability scoping.  userns_capable() is the single choke point for
every namespace-scoped check: walk up from the target namespace and
grant only if the walk lands exactly on the caller's own.  Walking
the other way is the bug worth naming -- it, or any "the creator
administers what it created" rule, turns `unshare -U` into host root.

Two bugs found while making the gate pass, both of which the gate now
covers: map_from_global() searched the map by `lower` (the
namespace-relative id) when the lookup key is a GLOBAL id, which is
wrong exactly when the namespace renumbers and therefore invisible for
every privileged test; and the procfs map parser did not skip
whitespace between the three fields of an extent, so the canonical
"0 0 1" was rejected.

Gate smoke-userns covers namespace identity and inheritance, the
overflow id before any map exists, translation after a map lands,
per-reason rejection of malformed and out-of-range maps, the
one-way setgroups switch, and the rootless path end to end.  It is
falsifiable both ways: granting capability to descendants of the
caller's namespace fails it with "an unprivileged second extent mapping
a foreign id was accepted", and reverting the map direction fails it
with "uid after installing its own map is 65534".

Four architectures build clean with KERNEL_WERROR=1; smoke-pidns and
smoke-mntns still pass.
d6ec611496940e785c1db7fd3b0b2c3fbcaafd28:
feat(usb): add a class-9 hub driver that publishes its downstream ports as a bus

A hub used to be a dead end: the class-9 interface matched no driver, so a
device behind one was never enumerated. The driver now binds, reads the
hub descriptor and republishes the hub's downstream ports as a second
usb_hcd_t, so a device behind a hub goes through exactly the enumeration
code a root port does and a hub behind a hub simply nests.

The hub does not own the controller: the endpoint contexts for a
downstream device live in the root controller, so every data path is
forwarded to the parent HCD carrying the token that HCD issued. Only the
bus address belongs to the hub, which is why addresses for hub-attached
devices come from a new core-wide pool rather than from the hub.

That split is what usb_hcd_ops_t::init_slot() could not express: it
returned one value for both "controller context" and "USB address".
alloc_slot() replaces it and returns a usb_slot_t, and xHCI now fills the
slot context's Hub field from the hub's address.

The descriptor request itself was the subtle part. A hub descriptor is a
class request with bmRequestType 0xA0, not a standard GET_DESCRIPTOR;
asking the obvious way stalls on every real hub, and QEMU's usb-hub is
one of them.

smoke-usb-hub-x86_64 pins this down and is falsifiable: reverting the
request code fails it with "hub descriptor read failed: -110", and
dropping the hub-status byte from the bitmap size fails it on
status_bytes. The gate cannot prove enumeration of a device *behind* the
hub -- QEMU dropped the usb-hub downstream bus in version 9 and does not
implement port reset, so nothing can be attached behind one -- so the
forbid list pins down what must not fail instead, and docs/testing-gates.md
says so rather than implying more coverage than exists.
965048c246282bd305904b5159a22a4d92bfb70c:
feat(pci): resolve MSI capabilities and deliver message-signalled interrupts

Adds kernel/drivers/bus/pci_msix.c -- a protocol-independent MSI-X layer --
and wires it into the virtio-PCI transport and the e1000e driver, so block
completions can arrive as messages instead of being polled for.

Three things had to be got right, and each was wrong in the way that still
looks right on screen:

- Where the table lives. Two fields describe it and they encode the same two
  numbers differently: Vector Control (PCI 3.7.5.3) puts the BIR in bits 3:1
  and the offset in bits 31:12 divided by sixteen, while Message Address
  Lower -- the pre-PCIe encoding the field inherits -- puts the BIR in bits
  2:0 and the byte offset unscaled in bits 31:3. Which one a device publishes
  is not a property of the device but of whether firmware ran: booting with
  -kernel means nothing wrote Vector Control, and QEMU's virtio-pci and
  e1000e both publish the location in Message Address Lower. pci_msix_
  capability() reads Vector Control first and falls back, recording which one
  answered in pci_msix_info_t::from_vector_ctrl. When neither names a table
  the enable path refuses with -EOPNOTSUPP rather than believing BIR 0
  offset 0, which for a device whose BAR0 is an I/O window would mean writing
  table entries over live registers.

- Which BAR holds it. Nothing above fixes a BAR number, and that is the
  point: virtio-pci uses BAR1, e1000e uses BAR3, and the virtio specification
  says nothing at all. pci_msix_set_table_offset() -- the override that let a
  driver assert a layout from the specification -- is gone, along with its
  export, and every table entry is read back after it is written, so a wrong
  window is caught at the write rather than diagnosed later.

- Where the message goes. The vector travels in the message data, and the
  address must be the base of the APIC's own page. Real hardware ignores the
  offset within that page, but software has no business relying on that: the
  window doubles as a register file, so an address built as 0xFEE00000 | vector
  lands inside the first kilobyte and is decoded as a register write. The
  result is a table programmed correctly, Enable set, function mask cleared,
  the device notifying on schedule, and no interrupt at all. Posting to the
  page base is the one address every implementation reads as a message.

queue_msix_vector (common config 0x1A) also had to be written with the queue
selected and given the table index rather than the interrupt line: it selects
which entry a queue posts through, so handing it a line number points the
queue past the end of the table, and an implementation is within its rights
to ignore a value it cannot use -- silently.

The platform hooks (arch_msix_message_address, arch_msix_vector_setup,
arch_irq_msix_vector_range) stay weak and keep returning a negative errno
off x86_64, which is what leaves every other board on its INTx or polling
fallback instead of programming a capability that would never be delivered.
x86_64 takes vectors 0xD0..0xF0 and programs the covering LVT before each
entry is unmasked.

Gate: smoke-msix-x86_64 boots q35 with a virtio-blk-pci and an e1000e and
asserts both capabilities resolve to their own BAR, that virtio-blk takes
vectors 208..208 and gives up its INTx line, and that the first
message-signalled completion prints "[VIRTIO-BLK] MSI-X delivery on vector
208" from the handler. That line is the whole point: reverting the message
address to the 0xFEE00000 | vector form leaves the other seven assertions
passing and fails only this one, because a correctly programmed table is
indistinguishable from a working one until a message is delivered.

Verified: smoke-msix-x86_64, smoke-usb-hub-x86_64, smoke-drvmod-x86_64 and
smoke-vfs-stress-smp8 pass; dev-build is clean with KERNEL_WERROR=1 for
riscv64, aarch64, ppc64le and loongarch64 (armv7m has no toolchain on this
host).

514c2fe7450208945e8f60de9cc91b4a57043c5b:
fix(fs-fat32): synchronize FAT copies and free unlinked chains

Four defects let a FAT32 image drift away from what fsck.fat accepts, all of
which only show up once a file is created and removed.

FAT mirroring. fat_write() updated only the first FAT. They are mirrors, and
fsck.fat answers "FATs differ but appear to be intact" the moment a cluster is
allocated, so every write now walks all num_fats copies at a sectors_per_fat
stride, reading each entry back first because the top nibble belongs to the
entry and not to the chain pointer.

FSInfo. The hints were read from the wrong sector and the wrong offsets, so
they never reached the image: the BPB names the FSInfo sector (and the code
preferred a guess one sector before the data region), and within a sector the
two signatures sit 484 bytes apart rather than adjacent, with the free count at
0x1e8 and the next-free hint at 0x1ec. Reading the structure signature where
the other FAT structures keep theirs finds nothing and silently turns off the
whole accounting path, which is how "Free cluster summary wrong" survived.
Allocation and free now move the counter the right way round, the stored count
is bounds-checked on read, and the hints are written after the FAT they describe
has been flushed -- before that they would claim a state the device does not
have. A generic sync rewrites them too, so a plain `sync` is enough.

The ".." entry. A directory directly under the root records zero, not the
root's cluster number. Both forms resolve, and fsck.fat rejects the mirror image
of the correct one with "Invalid '..' entry in the second slot".

Unlinked chains. The vnode cache holds a reference for as long as the inode is
cached, so the vnode's count never reaches zero and fat32_release_vn() -- the
thing that frees an unlinked file's clusters -- never runs. The cluster stayed
allocated with no directory entry pointing at it. Unlink and rmdir now free the
chain on the spot, and defer to the last close only while a descriptor is
genuinely open, which is tracked per vnode rather than inferred from a
refcount that cannot fall.

Verified with fsck.fat -n over a three-boot cycle on x86_64: create nested
directories and files, remove one, reboot and read the content back, then
remove the tree. Every check is clean, and the image returns to its original
237 files / 27038 clusters with nothing reclaimed and no summary warning.
46a6390c6c014d4ad06b7c4103f1d40e8fa4e245:
feat(fs): provide ordered writes through ext4's JBD2 journal

The journal was written but never consulted at mount, because the pre-sync
hook had no route back to its filesystem: bc->owner was declared and read by
both filesystem hooks and assigned by nobody. Every ext4_journal_meta_write
therefore held its metadata page forever and bcache_sync_common -- which
skips held pages on purpose -- could not flush the log before the metadata
it protects. FAT32's FSInfo writeback had been dead for the same reason.

Install the hook together with its owner so the pairing cannot be spelled
any other way, and fix the four defects the gate then exposed:

  * the commit pointer advanced one block instead of the transaction's size,
    so the commit block landed on top of the last data block and the next
    mount read its own commit block back as log data;
  * the descriptor's own checksum was computed before the per-tag data
    checksums were rewritten into it, so every committed descriptor failed
    its own verification on replay;
  * the data checksum was written into the block's last four bytes, which
    belong to the filesystem -- a block bitmap's checksum covers them -- so
    replay desynchronised the bitmap from its group descriptor. The tag now
    carries the checksum and the block is logged unmodified;
  * mount-time recovery keyed only on EXT4_FEATURE_INCOMPAT_RECOVER, which
    shares a cache page with the free counters and can be lost by a crash
    that leaves a non-empty log. ext4_journal_log_pending() reads the
    journal superblock's s_start, which is ordered before the commit block
    and therefore authoritative.

smoke-ext4-journal halts the machine at each of those four points, reboots
the same image, and checks that promised writes survived, unpromised ones
did not, replay happened exactly where it should, and e2fsck calls both the
crashed and the recovered image clean. ARCH selects the machine and the
build directory, so it runs per architecture rather than proving x86_64.
ce00c69d262fcbe9d561a60ac3f57c843a9de867:
feat(x86_64): keep the multiboot command line out of BSS

QEMU's -append string lands at 0x834000, which nm reports as inside the BSS
window (_bss_start=0x7fa000, _bss_end=0x12f4207). The BSS clear therefore
erased the command line before anything read it, so firmware_bootargs()
always came back empty on x86_64 and boot parameters -- including the ext4
journal crash points -- were silently ignored. Copy the line into .data
ahead of the clear, and fall back to the Multiboot copy when fw_cfg reports
no command line.
22a38e6fa15b2754971803710a2d1d83c43f6116:
feat(loongarch64): set the board RAM ceiling and read boot arguments

Two bring-up defects on qemu-virt-loongarch64, both invisible until a gate
tried to use the board for something other than "it booted".

The board config advertised ram_end = PHYS_MEMORY_END, a hardcoded 256 MiB,
while loongarch64_memory_init intersects that ceiling with the memory@ nodes
the firmware publishes.  On QEMU virt the DTB is generated from -m, so
`qemu-system-loongarch64 -m 1G` produced a 1 GiB memory node that the board
config then clipped to 256 MiB: the guest reported 256 MiB and the remaining
768 MiB was simply never allocated.  Raise the ceiling to 4 GiB so -m is
honoured, keeping the board's ceiling as a bound rather than a constant.

LoongArch also had no arch_bootargs_get() at all, so every -append was
silently dropped -- console= and the a20.* network keys never reached the
kernel.  Add one that extracts /chosen/bootargs from the FDT, which is the
only channel this board has: QEMU's virt firmware creates /chosen but leaves
bootargs out, and its fw_cfg is marked unmapped_translate, i.e. unreachable
without a mapping this board never builds.  The reader therefore reports when
it found nothing instead of pretending the command line was honoured, and
gates must not route anything essential through bootargs -- which is exactly
why the ext4 crash-consistency gate selects its injection point through
/proc/a20/journal rather than a20.journal_crash=, so it runs unchanged on an
architecture whose firmware drops -append.
2e1e5564467094d2ac7785e9249140f209c9f6e2:
test(ext4): add a procfs-armed journal crash-injection gate

Expose journal fault injection through procfs, make the gate exercise an observable failure path, and document its setup and filesystem limits.
6b10523ef7a8eee141772e0e7ee451a8620b8166:
fix(build): use the global stack-protector guard on PPC64LE

PPC64 ELFv2's GCC defaults to -mstack-protector-guard=tls, emitting
__stack_chk_guard as an r13-relative load (ld 9,-28688(13)).  The kernel's
guard is an ordinary .data global in kernel/core/stack_protector.c, and r13
is already claimed by arch_set_task_pointer() as the task pointer, so it
never points at a TLS base.

The result was a DSEG in the very first printf of kernel_main: the canary
load read garbage, and the subsequent program check killed the kernel before
any device was probed.  Other architectures default to the global model, so
only ppc64le needs the override.
4d1de64dc19bca6b24cc79dd83419ea224ba2aeb:
feat(ppc64le): enable FP in the user trap prologue before saving fprs

__trap_from_user rebuilds the interrupted MSR from scratch, so it inherits
whatever the user process last had in SRR1.  A process that never touched
the FPU leaves MSR[FP] clear, and the prologue's stfd pair then takes
FPU-unavailable *inside* the handler: the real-mode vector at 0xc00 branches
straight back to the same store and the machine spins forever, so the first
syscall is never delivered.

ppc64_trap_dispatch() only sets MSR_FP on CAUSE_FPU_UNAVAILABLE and MSR_VEC
on CAUSE_VPU_UNAVAILABLE, which is the right policy for a fault the user
took -- but it cannot help a fault the prologue itself takes.

Turn FP/VEC/VSX on at the top of the handler.  SRR1 still carries the
user's own MSR back out unchanged, so no process gains a capability it did
not ask for.
e01cd8e2de48b3c930dcfeed4df60bb16431e263:
fix(virtio): publish board-bound transports to the device model probe until exhausted

Two independent reasons pSeries booted with disks attached but nothing
mounted, and /bin unreachable:

1. ppc64le_enumerate_devices() called virtio_blk_init() exactly once.  The
   probe walks a sparse RTAS slot list and returns -1 at the end of it, so
   a single call bound only the first transport.  A gate run attaches a
   FAT32 disk for /bin and an ext4 disk for /extra; the second never got
   bound.  Loop until the probe reports exhaustion instead, and bound the
   network transports the same way.

2. virtio_blk_init() / virtio_net_init() initialised an instance and kept it
   entirely inside the driver.  mount_setup_block_device() and
   driver_progress_class() both resolve devices through
   device_find_by_class(), which only consults dev->drv->class_type, so a
   transport that exists solely as a driver-local struct is invisible to
   the whole storage stack.  Register each bound instance as a device.

The published records are busless on purpose: driver_matches_device() only
lets a busless driver claim a busless device through its match() callback,
and neither virtio_blk_driver nor virtio_net_driver declares one, so
device_register() cannot re-probe an instance that is already up.

Also set virtio_net_inst_t::irq_registered once request_irq succeeds, so the
IRQ teardown path knows the line is owned, and mark vt.irq = -1 before the
arch probe so a device-less slot does not inherit a stale line number.
10e16f0849fa589d273181db1a3546b51226d060:
feat(fcntl): take O_DIRECTORY/O_NOFOLLOW/O_DIRECT/O_LARGEFILE from the arch

These four bits are not asm-generic.  Linux defines them per architecture in
arch/<arch>/include/uapi/asm/fcntl.h and the layouts disagree; the header
had a single hardcoded set, so it silently misread the wire format of every
arch it did not match.

On PowerPC the generic O_DIRECTORY (00200000 == 0x10000) is in fact
O_LARGEFILE, which musl's open() passes on every call because the kernel ABI
always uses 64-bit off_t.  vfs_open() read that bit as O_DIRECTORY and
returned ENOTDIR for every open of a regular file or character device, so
'cat /hello.txt', 'cat /proc/version' and mksh's own /dev/tty all failed.
Create-path opens appeared to work because they take the !vn branch, which
never tests the bit -- which is what made this look like a filesystem bug
rather than a flag-decoding one.

arm/arm32/armv7m deviate the same way (O_DIRECTORY 040000, O_DIRECT
0200000), so give them their own values too rather than leaving the same
latent collision in place.  riscv64/riscv32/x86_64/loongarch64/loongarch32
genuinely use asm-generic and keep it.

Verified against the on-disk kernel UAPI headers
(/usr/src/linux-headers-*/arch/{powerpc,arm,arm64}/include/uapi/asm/fcntl.h).
752b28bf3bd00de3af05993433ef0463e14773c7:
feat(drvmod): export snprintf/vsnprintf and device_register to loadable drivers

A .a20drv may only reference symbols in drv_export_table; anything else
fails the load with 'unresolved symbol' and takes the whole transport down
with it, which is silent from the caller's point of view -- the device
simply never appears.

virtio-blk is built as a module on aarch64, and the device-model publication
added in a7a9eae4 needs exactly these two:

  snprintf       to build the standalone device name
  device_register to publish the already-initialised instance

Without them the aarch64 embedded build rejected virtio-blk.a20drv, both
disks stayed invisible, /bin never mounted, and init_kthread panicked with
'no init program found' -- while ppc64le, which links virtio-blk into the
kernel image, booted fine.  The arch-dependent failure is what made this
look like an aarch64 storage bug rather than a module ABI gap.

printf was already exported; only the bounded variants and the publication
entry point were missing.
3b0d06c356544477c692705dd66565fb98b97c7f:
fix(mm): reject exec faults outside the VMA permissions

A page fault on a present leaf was answered from the PTE alone: if the leaf
carried PTE_X the exec fault was reported as handled, whatever the VMA said.
That makes a leaf whose execute bit disagrees with its VMA silently
self-fulfilling. On aarch64 the disagreement is not merely bookkeeping --
arch_pte_leaf() derives the hardware UXN/PXN pair from PTE_X, so a stack page
whose leaf picked up a stray X bit really is executable at EL0, mksh jumps
into it, the retry succeeds, the PC does not move to anything meaningful, and
the same stack address faults again immediately.

That is what the post-fork hang was: ~23k prefetch aborts at a stack address
with no kernel output at all, because every round trip returned "handled"
and so no fault was ever reported. It looked like a lost wakeup and behaved
like a livelock; the machine only stopped when the harness timed out.

The VMA is the authority on what an address may be used for, not the PTE, so
cross-check it under mm->lock and refuse an exec fault on a VMA without
VM_EXEC (or write on one without VM_WRITE). The leaf may then be as wrong as
it likes and the worst outcome is the correct one: a clean SIGSEGV naming a
mapping the process was never allowed to execute.

The two demand-fault refusals in the same commit close the matching holes on
the not-present side: an instruction fault inside the stack-growth or brk
window was satisfied with a fresh read/write anon leaf, which has the same
non-advancing-PC property. A stack or heap page is never executable, so those
now fail instead.

aarch64 now reports the crash it was hiding:
  SIGSEGV: pid=5 code=32 sepc=0x3ff0c6e0 ra=0x3ff0c6e0 (a stack address)
  FATAL: pid=5 signal=11 comm=mksh pc=0x3ff0c6e0
instead of spinning until the harness kills it.
eb0e2a669cef24d60529f1050a187e0d32f92266:
docs(drivers): document cross-architecture failures behind this round's fixes

Every item fixed in this round was invisible on x86_64, which is why each one
has to be re-verified per architecture rather than once. Write down what they
actually were, so the next person does not rediscover them from a hang:

- O_DIRECTORY/O_NOFOLLOW/O_DIRECT/O_LARGEFILE are defined per architecture in
  arch/<arch>/include/uapi/asm/fcntl.h, and the three layouts (asm-generic,
  arm/arm64, powerpc) do not even share an ordering. On powerpc the
  asm-generic O_DIRECTORY value *is* O_LARGEFILE, which musl passes on every
  open() -- so the "open this directory" flag silently became "set largefile".

- ppc64le defaults to -mstack-protector-guard=tls, but the kernel's
  __stack_chk_guard is a plain .data global and r13 already belongs to
  arch_set_task_pointer(); and __trap_from_user arrives with the *user's* MSR
  in SRR1, so saving FPRs traps unless the prologue raises FP/VEC/VSX itself.

- A .a20drv may only reference drv_export_table[], and a missing symbol fails
  the whole module rather than the call. That only shows up under the loadable
  profile: virtio-blk is a module on aarch64 and built in on ppc64le.

- A board-bound transport must call device_register() itself -- device_find_by_
  class() cannot see a device the driver never published -- and board probing
  must continue until a slot reports no device.

- A fault reported as handled must actually let the PC advance. Judging an exec
  fault from the PTE alone, when the PTE carries an execute bit its VMA never
  granted, produces a silent livelock (thousands of prefetch aborts at one stack
  address, zero kernel output). The VMA is the authority; see ab700592.

The roadmap entry also records the aarch64 crash that is still open, with the
evidence that narrows it to the fork/exec/wait path.
1872f6c982b1fa8df036478ef43a00a9ee8b0cd8:
docs(roadmap): narrow the aarch64 trampoline crash and record what is already ruled out

The RWX leaf on mksh's stack is not a stray execute bit: signal_make_page_exec()
adds it on purpose so the sigreturn trampoline can run, and deliver_signal()
sets the return address straight at the trampoline. The `mov x8,#139; svc #0`
bytes are in the page, and aarch64's arch_signal_tramp_pte_flags() does carry
PTE_X, so the mapping is right. pt_unmap() explicitly does not own the leaf
frame reference and signal_make_page_exec() reuses pa unchanged, so there is no
use-after-free there either.

What is left is one narrow contradiction: the CPU refuses to fetch from the
trampoline while software says it may. List the ruled-out directions with the
evidence that killed each, so the next attempt starts from the TLB-coherence
question instead of re-walking the page-flag paths, and point at the two places
worth reading next (the PTE store / tlbi ordering, and whether
sys_rt_sigreturn_impl() un-protects the page without a later restore).
05c543f22d0692ad825acf4851869129c4c73e8c:
docs(server-readiness): describe the server image contents and its two environment blockers

its validation status. It has now been run, and the package stage passes
end-to-end: 23 Alpine packages (busybox, dropbear, chrony, ca-certificates and
their dependencies, 14.6 MiB) resolve, download and install into staging, so

5db9096de075e4cad9333bebb936822a5f841707:
feat(signal): give aarch64 a read-only trampoline page instead of an RWX stack one

The aarch64 signal-return trampoline lived in the signal frame on the user
stack, and the frame's page was mapped RWX so it could be fetched.  That
works on every architecture where a writable page may still be executed, but
aarch64 enables SCTLR_EL1.WXN (kernel/arch/aarch64/mm/kwx.c sets bit 19 once
the kernel image has been split into RO-X/RO-NX/RW-NX segments), and WXN
makes every EL0-writable stage-1 descriptor execute-never at EL0.  The page
had to stay writable to remain a usable stack, so AP could only be 01, and
the CPU then refused the fetch: ESR EC=0x20 with FSC=0x0f, a permission
fault, while the software PTE plainly carried PTE_X.

A bit-by-bit comparison against a text leaf that executes correctly in the
same process showed the only permission difference was AP (01 versus 11);
everything else -- PTE_X, UXN, PXN, nG, AF, AttrIndx -- matched.  So no flag
choice can make one page both a live stack and an executable trampoline, and
this is a design problem rather than a flag problem.  Dropping the
mm_pte_flags_make_writable_dirty() call does not help either, because PTE_D
aliases PTE_W on aarch64 and arch_signal_tramp_pte_flags() already requests
PTE_D.

Give the trampoline its own page instead, the way x86_64 has always done:

  - arch_setup_signal_trampoline() maps a dedicated read-only executable
    page per mm and records the address in the new mm->sig_tramp field.  It
    comes from mm_find_gap() rather than a constant: x86_64's fixed
    0x700000000000 sits above aarch64's USER_VA_LIMIT of 2^46 and would be
    rejected by mm_mmap().
  - the new weak hook arch_signal_tramp_addr() lets an architecture say
    where the handler returns to.  The default is the in-frame slot, so the
    other architectures are unaffected; aarch64 overrides it to the
    dedicated page.
  - signal_deliver_user() sets TRAP_CTX_RA from that hook and only upgrades
    the in-frame trampoline page when the architecture still uses it.
  - arch_signal_tramp_pte_flags() drops PTE_D on aarch64, so the dedicated
    page is RO+X -- the one combination WXN permits.  The trampoline is pure
    code written through the direct map, so it never needed write.

signal_make_page_exec() also stopped substituting the trampoline's flags for
the page's own.  Those flags are R+X without a write bit on riscv64, so a
live stack page was being made read-only and the process took a store page
fault the first time it stored through the stack again -- a crash caused by
making a page executable.  It now keeps the VMA's permissions and only adds
PTE_X.

aarch64 smoke-ext4-journal goes from FAIL to 5/5 PASS; mksh survives forking
commands such as `cat /proc/version`.  Re-verified 5/5 on x86_64, riscv64,
ppc64le and loongarch64, since signal.c and mm_struct_t are shared.
d6da3d8b30c813f8bf492e20bfcde7d9667be351:
feat(core-trap): print an executable reference leaf when a fetch is refused

A single faulting PTE only tells you what the software believes.  When the
CPU refuses an access the software thinks is permitted, the only way to tell
a wrong flag apart from a working one is to hold a leaf that demonstrably
works next to it and diff the two.  That is what localised the aarch64
sigreturn trampoline fault: the trampoline and a working text leaf differed
in AP alone (01 versus 11), which is the WXN-forced "writable, therefore
execute-never" pairing that no reading of the faulting PTE alone reveals.

dump_fault_pte() now prints [REF-EXEC] -- the pte_flags and descriptor value
of the first VM_EXEC VMA's first leaf -- but only when it is diagnostic, that
is when the faulting leaf lacks PTE_X or the covering VMA does not grant
VM_EXEC.  Ordinary faults keep their existing output.

Also drop mm_pte_flags_make_writable_dirty(), which had no callers left once
signal_make_page_exec() stopped substituting the trampoline's flags for the
stack page's own.

Re-verified smoke-ext4-journal 5/5 on x86_64, riscv64, aarch64, ppc64le and
loongarch64, plus check-doc-test-gates.
7f2e1839d30f50e087bd99a8e331107ce58f35f9: merge(kernel): bring main up to date in the kernel-core scalability branch
c3a06f372a8a4fc9022477def048f5fb78c0a858:
feat(mm): keep PTE_COW on a direct-private file leaf so its first store can copy

handle_file_fault() maps the canonical page-cache frame straight into a
MAP_PRIVATE file VMA when fault-around can alias it, and cleared PTE_W,
PTE_D and PTE_COW together to keep the leaf read-only.

Dropping PTE_COW was the part that broke.  It is the only bit that routes
a store on a read-only private leaf to mm_fault_handle_cow(), and that
handler is written for exactly this leaf -- its comment says a read-only
MAP_PRIVATE fault-around leaf "maps the canonical cache frame, so this
store must break that aliasing by cloning".  With the bit gone the leaf
matched neither the COW branch nor the PTE_W dirty-bit branch, fell
through to "unhandled", and the first store to a private file page died
as SIGSEGV on a VMA the kernel itself called writable.

Reproduced on riscv64 booting the server world: ld-musl's first .data
store faulted at stval=0x43594b20 with leaf flags=0x53 (V|R|U|A)
against vma pte_flags=0xd7 (V|R|W|U|A|D).  main reproduces it unchanged
at 0x41124b20, so this is not from the branch it was found on.

Clearing PTE_W and PTE_D is still correct and stays: the frame belongs to
the page cache, so the mapping must start read-only.  The COW handler
already refuses to make such a frame writable in place on rc==1.
2cea6808f1e24036fa11ba855e8ac1f318994564:
refactor(x86_64): remove the duplicated multiboot command-line copy

Merging main spliced this branch's Multiboot command line buffer into
main's firmware_bootargs() and left it referring to a g_fw_cfg_cmdline
that no longer exists there -- x86_64 stopped compiling outright:

  firmware.c:502: error: 'g_fw_cfg_cmdline' undeclared

The whole mechanism is redundant now.  This branch added a .data buffer
that boot/entry.S filled before the BSS clear, because QEMU's -kernel
layout puts the -append string just below the 8 MiB mark where the BSS
zeroing would erase it before any C code could read it.  main solves the
same problem without a copy: multiboot_cmdline() dereferences
mi->cmdline through the direct map, which is correct for a real loader
(GRUB keeps its command line in its own low memory, outside our BSS),
and under -kernel -append the fw_cfg file that main probes supplies the
string anyway.  So the copy was paying for a case that did not need it.

Reverting both files to main drops the branch's only contribution here
and leaves x86_64 with just the genuinely new work: LAPIC_PHYS_BASE in
platform.h and the MSI masking in trap/irqchip.c.

x86_64 both-dev kernel.elf builds clean with -Werror.
0d38bdda587028d5df1d1a2b508a0da95f2625fa:
build(tools): let a world image carry an ssh public key

A server world built by image-world had no way for anyone to authenticate.
Not a weak one -- no way at all: no authorized_keys and no shadow entry,
so dropbear started, printed its host key and then refused every login.
That left the server profile a packaging exercise with no remote access,
which is the one thing a server profile is for.

The credential has to be a public key.  A password baked into an image
lives in that image forever and travels with every copy of it, so it is
not something a build should be able to produce; a public key grants
nothing on its own, so baking one in costs the image nothing.

  make image-world PKG_WORLD=server SSH_PUBKEY=~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub

mkrootfs.py installs the keys after the overlays rather than before, so
an operator-supplied key wins over anything an overlay happens to ship,
and fixes the modes sshd's strict-mode check insists on: 0700 on /root
and .ssh, 0600 on authorized_keys, and ownership back to 0:0 under
sudo, since a key left root-owned-but-not-root-group is what a usermode
build gets by default.
d916e6980d6de031f72bebbd2d818a121c5f7124:
build(server): remove busybox-suid and declare the image requirements

busybox-suid's bbsuid needs mknod, and fakeroot fakes file ownership
without granting mknod, so the last step of the build --
`mkfs.ext4 -d` -- failed with "权限不够 while opening bbsuid" in an
unprivileged container. Dropping the package takes the server world
from "package resolution works" to "image assembles and boots", which
is the difference between a manifest and something you can run. On a
host with real root this package is not a problem and can come back.

The header was also describing the world as never having been executed
and its only known blocker as unresolved, which is no longer true, and
it said nothing about what the image needs to be reachable -- which is
the whole point of a server profile. It now records both halves of
that: a public key baked via SSH_PUBKEY (there is no password to bake,
see 6702613c) and a20.tcpmode=lwip on the kernel command line, since
the default fast mode keeps the listener out of lwIP entirely and an
inbound SYN is answered with RST before authentication is ever reached.
